Their method cancels the strong split and leaves the weak one clear. They test it on warm rubidium atoms at room heat. With the weak split alone, they can place atoms in a neat mix of two states. The trick should work for any spin size. It may help build precise atom states for sensing and for quantum work.
arxiv-2412-07910:
Erik Connerty and co-authors build a quantum version of an echo state network to forecast chaotic systems, in a research paper from 2024. Echo state networks use a large fixed reservoir to map inputs into rich patterns, which makes hard time-series tasks easier. On classical machines, that reservoir can grow huge and costly.

The quantum circuit runs on any digital quantum computer with a standard gate set. It needs no stopping or restarting, so the quantum state can evolve over long spans. The team simulated it on the chaotic Lorenz system, with and without noise in the model. Results suggest smaller reservoirs may suffice on quantum hardware. The work points toward time-series tools fit for today's noisy quantum machines.
arxiv-2412-08010:
Milan Maksimovic and Ivan Maksymov test a brain inspired neural network in a 2024 paper. Standard machine learning systems classify images well but can fail with confusing outputs or hand hard cases back to humans. Their model draws on quantum tunnelling ideas and on quantum cognition theory, which models human judgment under uncertainty.

The network classifies image data sets while mimicking human perception and decision patterns. The authors report evidence that the model can replicate human like choices. It also outperformed traditional machine learning algorithms in their tests. They present the approach as a step toward systems that express confidence and uncertainty more like people do.
arxiv-2412-08910:
W Q Chen, K J Li, and J C Xu track the solar transition region over a full activity cycle in this 2024 paper. The transition region is a thin layer between the Sun surface and its hot corona. Daily full disk images at one ultraviolet wavelength cover 2011 to 2022. Those images come from the Solar Dynamics Observatory.

Overall brightness of the layer rose and fell in step with the solar cycle. Polar brightening should therefore peak at cycle maximum. The background layer at middle and low latitudes moved against the cycle instead. Active parts of the layer seem heated mainly by active region fields. Quieter parts seem heated by the magnetic network. Surface field records match that split well, which supports the reading.
arxiv-2412-09310:
Natori and four colleagues chart exotic states in honeycomb magnets that mix two sizes of spin in twenty twenty-four. The base model, from Kitaev, pairs each spin with its neighbors by bond type and can host a liquid like state with no fixed order. Real materials may place small and large spins on the two halves of the honeycomb. The team worked out when Kitaev like forces rule in such a mix.

In the pure limit, they found four distinct spin liquid phases. Spin orbit coupling and a four pole kind of order help keep these phases stable. Their mix of theory and large scale simulation maps the full ground state. The work guides the hunt for real mixed spin materials.
arxiv-2412-11710:
Yuanzhi Wang and six co-authors tighten control in video editing in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Text-guided editing lets users change a video by editing its prompt. Large text-to-image diffusion models power most such editors. Yet objects can land in the wrong place or appear in the wrong number.

Their method, ReAtCo, attacks control without extra training. A re-attentional diffusion step refocuses cross-attention responses. Those responses link words in the edited prompt to regions in the frames. Refocusing aligns the spatial placement of target objects with the new text. Readers who edit video get a fix aimed at the most visible failures of prompt-based editing: things showing up where they should not, or in wrong counts.
arxiv-2412-11810:
Wadjih Bencheikh, Jan Finkbeiner, and Emre Neftci present a 2024 paper on training spiking and recurrent neural networks with far less memory. Such networks handle long input chains well, but training them eats memory and fast links to it. A trick called checkpointing stores only some middle states and rebuilds the rest. It saves memory yet adds compute time, so few teams use it.

The authors tailor checkpoint plans for sparse networks on a chip with many small local memory banks. Their best plan, Double Checkpointing, uses local memory well and adds little extra time. It lets them train on chains more than ten times longer, or nets four times larger, than before. The ideas may help brain-like computing grow on many kinds of hardware.
arxiv-2412-12210:
Akanksha Singh, Shaily, Singh, and Ertan Güdekli build a universe model in a modified gravity theory. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, uses an f(Q,T) theory, where gravity depends on space-time shape and matter trace. Their chosen form is simple: a square term plus a matter term. Real sky data then pin down the free values.

Hubble measures and a large supernova set do the pinning. The model universe slows early, then speeds up late, as ours does. At very high redshift it passes through a bouncing ekpyrotic phase. In that picture the Big Bang is a brane crash, not time's start. Late-time fits also ease the known Hubble tension.
arxiv-2412-12910:
Salim Amoukou and five co-authors set out a way to spot, step by step, when a shift in data starts to harm a working learning model, with no true labels at hand. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

In live use, a model's world drifts, and harm can creep in unseen. Past work could track harm over time when labels were there to count errors. The new way stands in a trained guesser of the model's error rate for the true count. Tests show the method has strong power to catch shifts, while it keeps false alarms in check. The shifts tried span field shifts, label shifts, and real drifts across place and time.
arxiv-2412-13110:
Takumi Goto, Justin Vasselli, and Taro Watanabe made grammar correction scores explainable in twenty twenty-four by crediting individual edits. Sentence-level metrics grade a corrected sentence as a whole, and reference-free ones especially hide their reasoning. That opacity blocks model debugging and useful learner feedback.

Their method assigns each edit a Shapley value, borrowed from game theory, measuring its contribution to the sentence score. The attributions stayed consistent across edit granularities and matched human judgments about seventy percent of the time. Mining the attributions exposed metric biases, such as a tendency to ignore spelling-level fixes. The work turns a single number into an audit trail for grammatical error correction.
arxiv-2412-14210:
Manuel Cebrian, Petter Holme, and Niccolo Pescetelli test a leading multimodal AI as a would-be street organizer, using a children's puzzle as the safe test bed. Their paper appeared in 2024. Asking a model to pick persuadable people out of a real crowd raises ethical alarms, so the team pointed it at crowded Where's Waldo scenes instead. Cast as an agent who must mobilize face to face, the model described scenes vividly and invented creative engagement tactics.

It could not, however, reliably find the key individuals or read the social dynamics of the crowd. The authors offer the setup as a reusable benchmark: a playful proxy that lets researchers grade AI persuasion skills as models evolve, without experimenting on real publics.
arxiv-2412-16610:
Alireza Maleki and Ahmad Sheykhi ask how quantum jitter changes black hole entropy and the expanding universe in a 2024 paper. The classic entropy formula ties a horizon's entropy to its area. Adding quantum corrections reshapes that link, and through the holographic principle the reshaped entropy rewrites the equations of cosmic expansion.

Their model alters the expansion equations in specific parameter ranges. Fitted against the Pantheon supernova data set, it can pin down the size of the quantum corrections. One sharp finding: fluctuations can swell the horizon area by up to 47 percent. Past that point the theory strains against observation. The authors frame the work as a bridge between quantum gravity ideas and measurable cosmology.
arxiv-2412-17210:
Hongsong Wang and three co-authors present a 2024 paper on spotting odd behavior in video by watching body poses. Rebuilding what it sees helps a system flag strange patterns, while predicting ahead helps it flag strange trends. Prior pose-based detectors usually picked one route. Their framework, DCMD, takes both: a diffusion model conditioned on the observed motion and on a learned summary of it.

A motion transformer inside the diffusion process reads layered features of the movement. A custom penalty sharpens the gap between normal and abnormal samples, using both time-wise and global links. At test time, a mask completion step strengthens the prediction side. On four data sets the method beat state-of-the-art rivals by clear margins and generalized well. The authors target surveillance and safety monitoring that must respect privacy by using poses, not faces.
arxiv-2412-17310:
Ashutosh Nayak and five co-authors worked on product bundles: sets of goods sold as one. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, deals with advice systems that push bundles, not lone items. Bundles can lift sales and please buyers, yet work on how to form new bundles is scarce. There is also no sound way to tell if a bundle will be popular. The team aimed at both gaps.

They built embeddings that join what a good is with the context it sits in. Those vectors feed both a popularity guess and a bundle builder. Readers who run shops get a way to mint fresh bundles with proof of taste fit. The work treats bundle craft as a task in its own right.
arxiv-2412-17910:
Vansh Nagpal, Siva Likitha Valluru, and colleagues built a meal planner that weighs health against convenience in a 2024 study. Choosing breakfast, lunch, and dinner means trading nutrition, such as salt and sugar, against cost, access, and cuisine. Groups eating together over long periods make the problem harder, since tastes and health needs differ and repeat.

Their system, BEACON, reasons over recipes described in text and images, composing full meals from starter to drink. Long-term group recommendations keep plans varied and fair across members. The work targets everyday eaters and people managing health conditions alike.
arxiv-2412-18010:
Grèbol-Tomàs and a large team of co-authors pressed and squeezed olivine crystals from a Moon meteorite to see how they differ from Earth olivine, in this 2024 arXiv paper. How planetary minerals bear stress matters for planning future missions. The sample came from NWA 12008, a lunar basalt that fell as a meteorite.

Tiny diamond-point presses showed the lunar grains are softer and springier than their Earth counterparts. High-pressure X-ray scans then tracked how the crystals compress, and one axis of the lunar olivine squeezed more than Earth's. The team also measured three common meteorites for contrast. A simple model mixing grain-scale and chemical-bond effects explains the softening. The authors offer the paired method as a new way to grade space rocks.
arxiv-2412-18610:
Zixia Wei and Yasushi Yoneta invent a new way to suddenly change a quantum system and watch it relax, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Physicists use such quenches to study how complex correlations build up over time. Most quenches start from simple, nonthermal states.

Their crosscap quench instead starts from highly structured thermal pure states. The authors ask how those states evolve toward typical ones. In conformal field theories they derive universal features of the entanglement entropy's time evolution. Holographic theories, treated through the AdS/CFT correspondence, give a tractable chaotic example. Numerical simulations of quantum spin chains confirm the picture. Both integrable and nonintegrable systems were tested against the theory.
arxiv-2412-19210:
Matías Godoy, Manuel Torres-Valdebenito, and Emilio Vilches study sweeping processes, a class of evolution problems where a moving set pushes a state along. The sets here are prox-regular, and the motion is perturbed by an operator that depends on the whole past history. The authors ask when such problems have exactly one solution that behaves well.

Their method rests on an improved form of Gronwall's lemma together with fixed-point arguments. The approach covers both state-dependent and state-independent cases in one frame. It recovers all known results for Volterra sweeping processes and adds new insight into the history-dependent kind. As a test of the theory, the authors prove that a viscoelastic model with long memory is well-posed. The paper gives analysts a compact tool kit for a family of problems that shows up in mechanics and materials with memory.
arxiv-2412-19410:
Félix del Teso and Julio Rossi present a 2024 math paper extending a classic averaging property to a nonlinear equation with a source term. For the plain Laplace equation, a function's value at a point equals its average nearby. The nonlinear cousin, the p-Laplace equation, resists that neatness once a forcing term enters.

The authors derive new asymptotic mean value formulas for exactly that forced case, where the usual rescaling trick fails. The formulas frame solutions through a game: two players tug a token, one maximizing and one minimizing, with payoff rules encoding the equation. They prove the game values exist, are unique, and converge to the solution. It is the first game reading of the forced problem.
arxiv-2412-19810:
Sam Carey wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four as the sole author. It gives a full analytic form of the Correlated Fermi Gas model for how leptons scatter off a nucleus in the quasielastic range.

Scattering of neutrinos off nuclei is key to the new round of neutrino trials, and nuclear effects are a chief source of doubt in the cross sections. Carey's form lets form factor effects and nuclear model effects be weighed apart. He sets it against the older Relativistic Fermi Gas model on both electron-carbon and neutrino-carbon data. The work speaks to those who must pin down cross sections before oscillation results can be trusted.
arxiv-2501-01310:
Peñil, Domínguez, Buson, Ajello, Adhikari, and Rico search twelve years of gamma-ray sky data for galaxies whose jets brighten or fade in a straight line. Jetted active nuclei usually flicker stochastically. A recently noticed pattern, a steady linear climb in one famous blazar, suggested a distinct long-term behavior worth hunting systematically. The sample covers over three thousand jetted sources watched by the Fermi telescope's main instrument.

Forty sources show significant long-term trends, linear or quadratic, each then characterized in detail. Such trends might betray a supermassive black hole binary slowly tightening, or physics inside the jet itself. Either origin would matter for the periodicity debates around these objects. The catalog of forty gives follow-up studies a concrete target list. A decade of patience, mined well, separates drift from noise.
arxiv-2501-01410:
Rishabh Saraswat, Rekha Verma, and Sitangshu Bhattacharya wrote a paper from 2025 on coaxing more light from a sheet one atom thick. The sheet is made of molybdenum and sulfur. It can emit light when energy pairs inside it join with the help of the sheet's own vibrations. In this material that help is weak, since the rules of symmetry block the key vibrations.

The team ran deep quantum sums and checked them against symmetry rules. In the plain sheet, the blocked modes keep the glow off at low heat. A stretch applied in two directions changes the rules. The stretch wakes a new vibration path that lets the dark pairs scatter and then shine. Strength shifts toward the paths that emit light. The team says strain could lift the glow of a whole class of such sheets.
arxiv-2501-01510:
Saurabh Sihag, Gonzalo Mateos, and Alejandro Ribeiro present a 2025 study of brain age gap in degenerative diseases, using covariance neural networks that stay explainable. Brain age gap, how much older a brain looks than its years, flags vulnerability to decline. Black-box predictors of it are hard to trust clinically. The network family used here ties its features to anatomy and to the eigenstructure of the brain's covariance pattern.

Applied to cortical thickness in Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and atypical Parkinsonian disorders, the method found distinct anatomic patterns per disease. The authors trace those patterns to how the network uses different parts of the covariance spectrum. That linkage, they argue, turns a score into an interpretable signpost for clinicians.
arxiv-2501-05010:
Min Liu and co-authors present a 2025 paper on making topological superconductors hardier by letting them leak. A one-dimensional p-wave superconductor hosts Majorana zero modes at its ends, prized for quantum computing. Disorder usually shrinks the safe region where those modes survive.

The team studied a generalized Kitaev chain with asymmetric hopping, which makes the system non-Hermitian, plus non-local disorder. Both numerics and analysis show the leakiness enlarges the region where the topological phase withstands disorder. In plain terms, opening the system stabilizes its protected edge states against stronger mess. The authors offer the result as a new angle on how openness and topology interact, with an eye to more robust quantum devices.
arxiv-2501-06810:
Kim, Jang, and Kim studied source language choice in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Speech tools for languages with little data often borrow training from richer languages. Picking the donor language, though, was usually done with little care. The team asked how sound-level similarity between languages shapes the payoff.

For phoneme recognition, training with sound-alike languages beat single-language training by a wide margin. It even topped a large self-supervised model. Within one language family, closer sound patterns helped, while distant ones hurt. Similarity across families mattered more than family ties themselves. The authors give a practical way to judge sound closeness before choosing donors.
arxiv-2501-08310:
Michał Zakrzewski and Henryk Żołądek wrote this math paper in 2025. It proves new integral formulas for hypergeometric functions. This is a broad family of special functions. The paper then follows where those formulas lead.

The authors use the stationary phase method. They apply it to WKB expansions for differential equations. They study cases with large inputs and large parameters. They also study what happens when an equation is changed by a small amount. A new proof makes clear a known result by Wasow on the Airy equation. It shows how that result differs from the Stokes phenomenon. Two key equations get close study. They link to generating functions for multiple zeta values. The paper also corrects an earlier claim about one such expansion.
arxiv-2501-08510:
Diego Salvador and colleagues mapped how the mix of star masses varies inside galaxies in a 2025 study. The initial mass function describes how many small versus large stars are born together, and it underpins all models of galaxy growth. Evidence has grown that the mix is not universal, so the team asked how it changes from place to place within single galaxies, using the SAMI survey's spatially resolved spectra.

They estimated the high-mass slope patch by patch and for whole galaxies, using population models. Local and whole-galaxy slopes tracked each other closely over most of the range, yet the local slopes spread widely inside individual galaxies. Follow-up analysis probes what local conditions drive that spread.
arxiv-2501-09410:
Lyudong Jin and six co-authors present a 2025 paper on running large language models cooperatively across edge devices. Phones and small servers differ widely in power, so pooling them could cut cost and delay. Their framework, MoE2, treats the edge models as a mixture of experts and decides which ones answer each request. The selection problem is combinatorial and tangled, harder than in classic mixture-of-experts setups.

The team found a property of the gating choices that lets training and selection be split apart, slashing complexity. A custom optimization algorithm then picks the optimal experts under energy and delay budgets. They built real edge servers on Jetson boards and high-end graphics cards to test it. Across models and resource limits, the method found better delay-energy trade-offs than the baselines. The authors target cheap, responsive AI served near the user.
arxiv-2501-10510:
Yang, Liu, and Feng gauge how a slick coat bends jets from burst suds. Burst suds at a gas-wet face can spray fine drops in the air. Those drops bear chem and live stuff to the sky in their wake. What slick coats do to that spray had stayed dim till now. A slick coat that won't mix sits on the sud face here. Jet width strays from the clean-sud tale in the runs.

The team traces crest waves at the air-oil-wet face for the cause. A thin-wave damp frame rests on coat depth and crest spread. A fresh Ohnesorge count with a scale rule fits the runs well. It holds past a wide span of coat depths and flows. The work may hone spray size guesses for sea and sky work.
arxiv-2501-10810:
Manthey and three colleagues study ant colony methods in twenty twenty-five, a math approach based on how ants search for food. Computer ants build trial answers step by step and leave a scent trail on good paths. The scent fades over time, and the fade rate can change as the search runs.

The team proves that one graph based method still finds the best answer in the end. They then test two changed forms of a second method on a shortest path task. One form can take far too long to finish. The other form solves the same task in a fair span of time. The work helps users pick safe settings for such searches.
arxiv-2501-11310:
Abdelrahman Alzarooni and co-authors survey vision-based fault finding in industry, in work from 2025. Camera checks guard quality and speed on production lines, from factories to aerospace shops. Hand checks by operators are slow and dull work. Smart vision systems now read images on their own and flag flaws as they arise.

The survey covers studies since 2019 and walks the full pipeline, from data capture and cleanup to learning and scoring. It also lists open data sets used in the field. Key blocks, such as scarce flaw samples, are paired with fixes. The authors close with paths the field may take next.
arxiv-2501-11810:
Katsumasa Nakayama and Manuel Schneider improve a physics calculation method in a 2025 paper. Their method, a form of tensor renormalization, rewrites physical quantities as networks of small tensors. It can study systems without a flaw that plagues other methods. To use it, workers first need an initial tensor network in a form suited to repeated coarsening.

They give a systematic way to turn a general tensor form into that starting form. They also show how the choice of starting network affects how the method performs. Based on that insight, they propose an improvement to the method itself. The work is method-focused and aimed at specialists in lattice physics.
arxiv-2501-12110:
Entanglement between a full system and an empty reservoir rises, peaks, and falls like a Page curve. A 2025 arXiv paper by Katha Ganguly and co-authors watches it happen two ways at once. Their fermions leak into the reservoir while a dephasing noise scrambles phases. In one setup the noise hits the system alone, and in another it hits both sides.

Two simulation styles trace the full curve in both setups. One jumps between random unitaries, the other diffuses smoothly. The peak's height and time shift with the protocol. Particle counts and currents leaking out track the curve closely, which the authors mine for general lessons.
arxiv-2501-12710:
Karaev, Blumenthal, Moshel, Diringer, and Hacohen-Gourgy wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a fresh way to set a microwave cavity mode to a chosen state. Quantum computers with long-lived memory modes must do this chore often.

Their method, Rabi Driven Reset, moves the state of the memory mode into a lossy mode that drains it away. A qubit driven in a Rabi pattern links the two modes through sideband tones. Once drained, the memory mode can be set to any coherent state sought. Computer models of the scheme predict setup times about ten times faster than the current coupling method. The gain could ease a routine but slow step in such machines.
arxiv-2501-13610:
Meijer and a team including Detterer and Yousefzadeh built a shared wait line in twenty twenty-five to hold signal delays on brain-like AI chips. Delay-tuned nets can be smaller and leaner than plain ones at the same skill. Past delay gear eats memory as nets grow, though.

Their round shared line scales with net sparseness, not just net size. That ties memory cost to how much of the net is live. It also fits joint chip-and-model tuning well. Lag, chip area, and energy per read are scored in the work.
arxiv-2501-13910:
Eleftheriou and co-authors derive formulas for counting states in a leading theory of quantum gravity, in this 2025 paper. The counts, called BPS indices, describe branes that wrap space in a curved five-dimensional world. Similar formulas were known from the dual gauge theory side, but a direct bulk derivation was missing.

The team quantize the space of giant graviton branes using a method that pins the calculation to special fixed points. They show how a known jump in the formulas, called wall-crossing, emerges from shifting the calculation. For some symmetry groups, extra terms appear from stable branes in a mirrored space.
arxiv-2501-14210:
Hammad Ayyubi and co-authors present PuzzleGPT in 2025, a system that guesses when and where a photo was taken. People solve such puzzles by spotting clues, like signs, plants, or building styles, and chaining them together. The team split that skill into parts and built a module for each.

One module spots visual clues, one reasons over them, one merges the chains, one searches the web when stuck, and one filters noise. The system needs no training on the task and explains its steps. On two test sets it beat big vision-language models, including GPT-4V, by wide margins. It even matched models trained for the job.
arxiv-2501-14510:
Faiz Muhammad Chaudhry and six co-authors train a neural network to read a camera's calibration straight from a single photo, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Classic calibration needs many shots of a known target from set angles, material that public photo sets rarely have. Their network instead learns from a large synthetic image library built in a simulator, topped up with a few real photos.

The simulator varied focal length and lens warping under the standard Brown-Conrady model, giving the network labeled examples to regress against. A ResNet backbone adapted for number prediction does the reading. The authors report accurate parameter estimates on real images despite the mostly fake training diet, a result aimed at driving, robotics, and augmented reality.
arxiv-2501-15310:
Ayo Adedeji and four colleagues test whether language models can fix speech recognition errors in medical dictation, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Automatic speech recognition often garbles critical medical terms. Undetected errors in a transcript can compromise patient care and safety.

The study compares raw and language-model-corrected transcripts of accented English. Speakers came from Nigeria, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Recognition accuracy differed significantly across the regions. The authors identify the conditions under which model corrections help most. They also note where corrections fall short. The findings matter for hospitals adopting voice tools across borders, since an accent gap in transcription could quietly become a safety gap.
arxiv-2501-15510:
Restoring a damaged photo is easier if the model first knows what kind of damage it faces. The four authors propose Degradation Classification Pre-Training: the model learns to name the degradation type of its input image. That label is nearly free, since it is already implicit in every restoration data set, making it an extremely weak but universal supervision signal. An encoder extracts features and a light decoder classifies the damage from those features alone.

After this pre-training, both convolutional networks and transformers restored better, gaining up to 2.55 decibels on a ten-degradation all-in-one task and 6.53 decibels under mixed degradations. Unlike masked image modeling, the method keeps the decoder useful: the learned classifier eases transfer between models trained on different damage types. Code and models are public.
arxiv-2501-15710:
Rasul Shafikov surveys results about Levi-flat hypersurfaces, a special kind of geometric surface, inside complex projective spaces. A long-standing puzzle asks whether such a closed, smooth surface can exist in the complex projective plane. The question matters beyond geometry, since the same object would appear in foliation theory as a special minimal set and in symplectic geometry as a limit of fillings. Writing in twenty twenty-five for nonexperts, Shafikov gathers results that are scattered, with some known only as folklore, and lays out the state of the problem.

For projective spaces of dimension above two, several authors proved no such analytic surface exists, with extensions to wider families of spaces. The survey presents three mostly self-contained proofs of that nonexistence, two due to Lins Neto and one due to Siu. The two-dimensional case remains open and is the focus of the survey framing.
arxiv-2501-16010:
Leping Qiu and four co-authors present a mixed reality tool that helps students take notes in live lectures without looking down, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Typing notes on slides or speech is slow, and eyes on a device mean ears off the talk. Key points slip past.

The team first asked students how they take notes and where they struggle. Their system, MaRginalia, pairs a stylus tablet with a headset. The slides, the speech text, and a ghost of the tablet float in view, so students can scribble and grab quotes while their eyes stay up. When fine work is needed, a look down at the real tablet still works. A study with twelve students showed the approach is workable and liked.
arxiv-2501-16810:
Pustilnik and Perepelitsyna chart the brightness changes of a rare luminous blue variable star over 36 years. Their paper appeared in 2025. The star sits in a dwarf galaxy with almost no heavy elements, about one fortieth the Sun's share. It is the only known star of its class at such low metal content, so its outbursts test theories of how massive stars shed mass.

The team combined their own monitoring with Hubble telescope photos from 2010 and 2017 to separate the star's light from its glowing gas cloud. After a giant eruption faded, the star kept swinging by more than three magnitudes over a year or so. Its full range spans about five magnitudes. The swings resemble the classic pattern of its class, but at unusually large size.
arxiv-2501-19010:
Lee and co-authors present DyPCL, a learning method tuned for speech that is hard to understand due to dysarthria. Recognition falters because severity varies by speaker and disordered speech differs from typical speech. Their method splits each utterance into sound units called phonemes. It then trains the model to keep the same unit close across speakers. A live alignment method finds where each unit falls in the audio.

Training also ramps up difficulty over time. Easy contrast cases come first, then near-twin sounds that are hard to split. This staged plan handles speaker variety better than flat training. The goal is steadier recognition for people whose speech is often misheard.
arxiv-2502-01210:
Sam Kirkham, Patrycja Strycharczuk, Rob Davies, and Danielle Welburn model how speakers shift their accents during conversation in a 2025 paper. People often drift toward the speech of the person they talk with, a process called accommodation. That short-term drift is thought to drive long-term accent change, but how live input reshapes speech planning was unclear.

Their model uses two linked fields, one for planning speech and one for memory, each changing at its own pace. Because the memory field lags, matching a partner on one turn can push speech away on the next. That rebound matches patterns in a pilot experiment. Differences in the memory effect may reflect social or language pressures that resist change. The work links moment-to-moment talk with sound change over time.
arxiv-2502-01410:
Giovanni Fantuzzi and Federico Fuentes found a new condition in twenty twenty-five. It tells when moment relaxations of polynomial optimization problems end in the exact best value. These steps turn a hard polynomial problem into a ladder of easier matrix problems. Finite convergence means the ladder reaches the true best value. Correlative sparsity keeps the ladder climbable. In it, variables meet only in small cliques.

The condition grows from a sparse form of the classical truncated moment problem. It asks for flat extensions of some moment matrices. It asks for a running intersection property among the cliques of variables. When met, an algorithm pulls out true minimizers. It gets at least as many as the largest matrix rank in the relaxation. The authors also show the intersection property is necessary. They give cases that show how it all works.
arxiv-2502-02010:
Nguyen Duc Anh and Tran Ngoc Thang proposed a gradient method for hard optimization tasks in two thousand twenty-five. The tasks include minimax problems, where one side seeks a low value while the other seeks a high one, and tasks with more than one goal. The component functions need not be convex.

Their method uses steepest descent steps whose size adapts and need not fall at each step. They prove it converges for several classes of smooth functions, from nonconvex to pseudoconvex. They then apply it to multi-goal problems and prove it reaches weakly efficient or Pareto stationary points. Numerical tests for each case matched the theory.
arxiv-2502-03510:
Yibo Liu's dissertation builds robot mapping around LiDAR fiducial markers in a 2025 thesis. LiDAR scanners guide self-driving and robotic systems, yet markers made for them lag far behind camera markers. The data are sparse and shapeless, and old marker designs assume flat images. Liu proposes a full framework to close that gap.

First, thin paper-sized markers are read from intensity images, giving the scanner's pose. Next, an enhanced detector finds markers inside full 3D maps, using both brightness and shape, which extends their range. Last, a mapping method aligns scattered, barely overlapping scans by solving an optimization over scan and marker poses. A new data set for multi-view scan matching is released. Tests across scanner models, indoors and out, showed the framework beating prior methods. Uses range from augmented reality to collecting training data.
arxiv-2502-03610:
Giulia Pozzi and six co-authors model how tiny sacs move on the surface of a nerve cell. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. These sacs, called extracellular vesicles, may carry prion protein and help spread brain disease. How they travel, and what the cell's inner frame does to that travel, was not well mapped.

Their model is built from lab data on sacs taken from star-shaped brain cells. They test sacs and cells with a drug that breaks the inner frame. In one case, motion fits a ratchet with flashes. In an other, it fits a rolling move on a wavy track. The full case mixes both. The model matches the data on the whole.
arxiv-2502-03710:
Samyobrata Mukherjee and four co-authors study waves that ride along graphene placed in a magnetic field. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, and its waves, called magnetoplasmons, sit in a band with a gap.

That band has a topological trait, summed up by a number called the Chern number. Where the field flips direction, the number changes, and protected edge waves appear. In practice the field can only flip across a soft border of some width. Such borders host a second family of edge waves, named for Volkov and Pankratov. The authors work out how the two families live side by side, and how the border's width sets the count of the second kind.
arxiv-2502-04810:
Hakon Pedersen examines a velocity concept in the theory of two fluids moving through porous rock in a 2025 study. The theory treats total flow as homogeneous in the Euler sense and builds a thermodynamics-like structure with a maximum entropy principle behind it. A co-moving velocity links the theory's intensive velocities to the physical seepage speeds of each fluid.

Pedersen shows the relations among those velocities carry a structure readable through affine and projective transformations, tools from geometry. A geometric reading can expose invariants the raw equations hide. Better theory for two-phase flow feeds reservoir engineering and groundwater modeling.
arxiv-2502-06610:
Federico Campanini, Laura Cossu, and Salvatore Tringali wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It sets up the category of atomic monoids, algebraic systems whose elements split into atoms that cannot split further.

The maps in the category are homomorphisms that keep atoms intact. The authors compute all limits and colimits in it, which shows the category is both complete and cocomplete. They then study the arithmetic of products and coproducts in this frame. Firm formulas come out for key gauges tied to factorization lengths, which count the ways an element can be built from atoms. The work gives factorization theory a category home.
arxiv-2502-07010:
Moradi, Tanneau, Zandehshahvar, and Van Hentenryck addressed renewable forecasting in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Grid operators need forecasts for whole fleets of wind and solar sites. Often each site supplies its own forecast with odds of high or low output. Those forecasts rarely say how sites move together, which fleet planning needs.

The authors join the site forecasts with a copula, a tool that links separate distributions, and Monte Carlo sampling. The result is a fleet-level forecast that stays statistically sound. Tests on synthetic data from several large United States systems checked the method. The authors say grid operators gain a better grip on swing and risk. That helps them blend renewables into the grid with more confidence.
arxiv-2502-07210:
Junyoung Park loosens a key condition in classic results on mean curvature flow in a 2025 arXiv paper. In this flow, a surface moves by its bend at each point, like a soap film settling. Many sharp tools for the flow demand that the surface be convex, which real shapes often are not.

Park proves a broad form of a known slope bound for flows that are merely mean convex, as long as the smallest bend stays above a set share of the mean. He then uses a classic peak argument to pin down old, everlasting flows of this kind. Under a like bound on sums of the smallest bends, such flows must be families of shrinking spheres. The work widens the reach of the theory.
arxiv-2502-09310:
Iasson Karafyllis and colleagues published a control theory paper in 2025 on stabilizing chemostats. A chemostat grows microbes in a tank fed with nutrients. Keeping biomass steady from any starting state is the goal. Natural death of the microbes makes that goal much harder.

Earlier simple feedback worked only when mortality was absent. With death present, nutrient-poor starts could wipe out the culture. The authors design stronger feedback laws to prevent that outcome. Their laws are written out explicitly, not left implicit. They cover both a simple two-state model and a richer age-structured one. When mortality is zero, the laws match the older simple forms. Stability is proven for all positive starting conditions.
arxiv-2502-10810:
Zhenyu Yang and co-authors built a new test set for models that watch video as it plays, in a paper from 2025. Most past tests ask one question about one clip. Real use, like a live stream, needs a model to follow events over time and answer a chain of linked questions.

Their test set, called SVBench, holds close to fifty thousand question and answer pairs drawn from more than a thousand videos. The questions come in chains, so later ones build on earlier ones across the stream. The team tested fourteen models in both chat and live modes. A closed model from OpenAI did best, while most open models struggled with long streams. The team also built a chat model that beat the other open models on the new test.
arxiv-2502-11510:
Tess O'Brien, Matthew Moores, David Warton, and Daniel Falster wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It warns that numerical integration error can split a posterior into two humps in longitudinal models, one true and one false.

Such models pair growth equations with data over time, and the equations are solved by numeric steps. The error from those steps can make a bad parameter set forecast as well as the true one. The posterior then shows two clusters, the main one near truth and a stray near the false set. The team shows the split in theory and in tests for a simple linear case. A simulation check can flag it, and a named sampling fix can dodge it.
arxiv-2502-11810:
Santos and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on two new atom-thin sheets of metal. The work builds on goldene, a sheet just one gold atom thick. The team uses math models to test twin sheets made of silver and copper atoms. They check if the sheets would hold together, how stiff they would be, and how they handle light. Both sheets prove stable in their tests, even at room heat.

The silver and copper sheets bend and stretch much like the gold sheet. All three act like metals for electric flow, yet handle light in ways more like chip materials. The authors say that mix could suit light-based electronics. The study maps fresh ground for lab work on thin metal sheets.
arxiv-2502-12210:
Papa Abdou Karim Karou Diallo and Amal Zouaq brought retrieval into a classic language task in 2025: finding the semantic frames a sentence evokes. Frame semantics describes events through structured scenes, like buying or arresting, each with its own roles. Detecting which frames a text triggers is a first step toward machine understanding. Previous systems usually needed the target word marked in advance.

Their approach, RCIF, is the first retrieval-augmented method for frame detection and works without any marked target span. It embeds frames from several representations, retrieves candidate frames for an input text, then identifies the best fits. Experiments covered zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned settings. The retrieval component significantly improved results, suggesting frames are easier to recognize by comparison than by pure generation. The method points semantic parsing toward the retrieve-then-decide pattern succeeding elsewhere.
arxiv-2502-12310:
Tesshu Fujinami, Bruce D. Lee, Nikolai Matni, and George J. Pappas study how sample-efficient domain randomization is for a classic control problem. Domain randomization trains a controller by averaging performance over a spread of model settings. The method works well in robotics practice, but its theory has lagged. The test bed here is the linear quadratic regulator, a benchmark for learning control laws.

The team proves that, with a well-chosen sampling spread, domain randomization reaches the best possible rate at which extra cost decays. It matches the benchmark method that knows the system exactly. Robust control, by contrast, can overshoot on caution, yet it does better when data is scarce because it can steady an uncertain system from rough estimates. The authors add a gradient-based algorithm for the randomization method and test it numerically. The results point to open questions about wider classes of systems.
arxiv-2502-12510:
Jiatao Li, Yanheng Li, Xinyu Hu, Mingqi Gao, and Xiaojun Wan probed language models used as peer reviewers in two thousand twenty-five. Automated review is tempting, but small changes to a paper, a review, or a rebuttal might sway the outcome. The authors set out to measure that risk.

Their framework makes targeted changes tied to aspects like contribution, soundness, and tone. They found strong reject advice swayed final meta-reviews, harsh reviews could be misread as thorough, and weak or hostile rebuttals could oddly raise acceptance. The biases held under several chain-of-thought prompts. The work gives a practical way to test review systems for such flaws.
arxiv-2502-12810:
Michael Sorochan Armstrong tackles misaligned chemistry data in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Multidimensional separations split complex samples along two axes, giving rich detail about their makeup. But peaks drift between runs in both directions, so samples cannot be compared one to one without preprocessing. Closely overlapping peaks add a second headache. Armstrong aligns the data in the frequency domain instead of the time domain.

The method uses a complex form of Procrustes analysis, a classic shape-matching tool. Aligning spectra this way can line up runs from different instruments and setups. That makes large studies of biological samples more trustworthy. The paper serves analytical chemists who run two-dimensional chromatography and related methods.
arxiv-2502-14210:
Amirreza Neshaei Moghaddam, Alex Olshevsky, and Bahman Gharesifard study how much data a controller needs to learn the best settings for a standard control problem, in a 2025 paper. The problem, known as the linear quadratic regulator, balances state error against control effort for systems with unknown behavior. Earlier learning methods needed a starting controller that was already stable, a real limit in practice.

Their new method works in rolling short horizons and is modeled on a classic policy learning rule. It drops both the stable-start demand and the costly two-point gradient guesses used before, while keeping the same order of data needs. A sharper analysis of how errors shrink through the problem's core equation improves the guarantees. The result widens where such learning control can safely be tried.
arxiv-2502-14310:
Shahar Hod wrote a compact paper in two thousand twenty-five about how a ring orbiting a black hole drags the space around it. When a ring circles close to the horizon, the hole's horizon spin rate no longer follows the simple vacuum rule. A recent result for an uncharged spinning hole found a universal shift that ignores the hole's own spin.

Hod asks whether the same universal shift holds when the hole also carries electric charge. Using analytic methods on the combined black hole and ring system, he finds that the shift in this charged case has an explicit form that does not stay spin independent. The paper thus marks a limit on how far the earlier universal pattern extends across black hole types.
arxiv-2502-14910:
Wu and six colleagues present EvoP in twenty twenty-five, a pruning framework for large language models. Large models are costly to run where computing resources are limited. Pruning removes redundant parts, but heuristic rules can cut the wrong ones. Many methods also ignore the traits of the data used for tuning.

EvoP first builds a diverse calibration data set by cluster based sampling. It then searches for the best pruning pattern with an evolutionary method. The search directly optimizes which elements, channels, or layers to remove. Across models and downstream tasks, EvoP beat existing pruning methods. It kept the best performance while also keeping the best efficiency. The authors present it as a practical path to deploy large models.
arxiv-2502-15110:
Evan Sidrow, Alexandre Bouchard-Côté, and Lloyd Elliott present a variational method for inferring evolutionary trees in a two thousand twenty-five statistics paper. Bayesian phylogenetics needs accurate, fast approximations of posterior distributions over tree shapes and timings.

Their variational family for ultrametric trees builds on coalescent times from single-linkage clustering, and it has a closed-form density. Unlike existing approaches, the method searches all of tree space, needs no Markov chain Monte Carlo subroutines, and stays differentiable end to end. Experiments on benchmark genomic datasets and on SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA reach competitive accuracy. The method uses far fewer gradient evaluations than current state-of-the-art techniques.
arxiv-2502-16610:
Francisco Caetano and co-authors present a tool that checks X-ray scans before a computer uses them to aid diagnosis. The tool, shared in 2025, is called AdverX-Ray. Scans can shift in subtle ways when they come from a new machine or new settings, and those shifts can throw off a diagnosis program. The team built the tool to catch such shifts early.

The method trains a model on small patches taken from scans made by known machines. It learns to spot the faint high-frequency flaws that fake or shifted images tend to carry. The team then tests whether a new scan matches what the model was trained on. In tests, the tool beat other detection methods and scored well using just 64 patches from one scan. It is light and fast, so it can run in real time.
arxiv-2502-17610:
Samuel Yee and a large team of astronomers report new measurements of the planet WASP-193 b in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Planets like it are called super-puffs. They weigh about as much as Neptune but span as wide as Jupiter, so they are oddly light for their size. Plain planet-forming ideas struggle to explain them. Some super-puffs also circle their stars on tilted paths.

The team used the Magellan telescope to track the star's wobble with care. They sharpened the planet's mass and size values. Their data show that this planet's orbit lines up well with its star's spin. That calm path hints that not all super-puffs were knocked around in the past. The result adds a key case to the debate on how these puffy worlds form.
arxiv-2502-17710:
Akhila Yerukola, Saadia Gabriel, Nanyun Peng, and Maarten Sap wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tests how well AI systems read hand gestures whose sense shifts by culture, where a wrong read can cause real offense.

The team built MC-SIGNS, a set of gesture and country pairs marked for offense, weight, and context, spanning many gestures and countries. Image generators showed a strong United States slant, doing worse on offense checks outside that frame. Language models flagged too much as offensive. Vision and language models fell back on United States senses for broad ideas such as wishing luck. The authors call for safety tools that know culture.
arxiv-2502-17910:
Fangyuan Yu proposes growing a language model's vocabulary during pretraining, the way children grow theirs, instead of fixing it on day one. Static vocabularies are the industry habit. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the method alternates two moves. Entropy-guided expansion adds tokens where the model needs finer grain. Optimization rounds then train with the enlarged vocabulary. Representations transfer across token sizes, so earlier learning is not wasted. A natural allocation emerges: long tokens absorb predictable stretches, while short tokens handle the hard, surprising contexts.

Experiments on small GPT-style models showed better scaling efficiency, with gains following a log-linear pattern in vocabulary size. Code is released for follow-up work. The author plans larger models and more domains. The paper reframes tokenization as a curriculum decision rather than a preprocessing afterthought.
arxiv-2502-18210:
Qian Wang, Zhenheng Tang, and Bingsheng He ask in a 2025 paper whether large language models can truly copy human behavior in social simulations. Such simulations are now used to study how people act in groups. Yet recent work shows gaps between what the models produce and how real people behave, and those gaps raise doubts about the results.

The authors look closely at where the models fall short and what would be needed to fix those flaws. They offer clear steps for making model-based studies of society more sound. Readers get a sober guide to when these tools can help and when their output should be treated with care.
arxiv-2502-18310:
Ryan Cooper and co-authors wrote this astronomy paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on gas blasting out of young galaxies. The data come from the James Webb Space Telescope, which can read the light of galaxies seen as they were billions of years ago.

From more than a thousand galaxies flagged by an oxygen glow, the team found forty with the widened spectral line that marks a fast outflow. Most are star-forming galaxies, and about two thirds are starbursts making stars at a furious rate. The typical outflow moves at over five hundred kilometers per second. Still, most flows fall short of escape speed, so the gas likely rains back. Small galaxies fling out more mass than they turn into stars. The authors link their lower count of outflows to stricter rules and the limits of their spectra.
arxiv-2502-19110:
Jiang, Liu, and Van Durme proposed this approach in twenty twenty-five for making language model answers more honest. Models can refuse to answer when unsure, which wastes useful output. Or they can hedge with words like maybe, which downstream tools find hard to use. The authors unite both ideas under one frame.

Their method treats hedged claims as answer sets, in the spirit of set prediction with guarantees. A dial controls how loose or precise the response may be. The outputs carry a formal promise about factual accuracy. Models can also be fine-tuned to rewrite claims with the dial in mind. The result is a tunable balance between being right and being specific.
arxiv-2502-19410:
Xinru Wang and eleven co-authors study how smart assistants should explain their advice on tiny watch screens in a paper from 2025. Large language models can suggest daily actions, but their wordy reasons are hard to read at a glance. The team tried two fixes: sorting each reason into clear parts, and showing reasons only when the model seems unsure.

In a user study, sorted reasons cut reading time and mental effort and sped up choices. Always-on sorted reasons also raised trust in the advice. Yet users liked them less, wanting more detail, and the timed version helped least. Lessons for watch design close the paper.
arxiv-2502-19810:
Qihao Lian and Di Wang present a static tool that bounds the resource use of Rust programs. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Rust is a systems language prized for memory safety with speed. Yet a safe program can still be slow, and its cost in time or memory is hard to call in advance.

Their tool, RaRust, is a type system that infers straight-line bounds on cost. It leans on Rust's borrow rules, the feature that makes its safety work. New prophecy potentials let it track shared and sole borrows in parts. A test build infers bounds for programs with loans, heaps, loops, and self-calls.
arxiv-2502-20010:
Alessandro De Vita and a large team of co-authors published a 2025 study of a layered magnetic material. The material belongs to a new class called altermagnets. In these materials, the pulls of tiny magnets cancel out overall, yet electrons still feel a split in their energies based on spin. That mix was once thought impossible for this kind of order. The team's text studies a compound made by inserting cobalt into a layered crystal.

Using light-based tools that map electron energies, the team charted the material's electronic structure in three dimensions. They resolved the split branches of electron states directly. Computer calculations matched the measurements. The study confirms the compound behaves as an altermagnet of a particular wave type. Layered versions of these materials are still little explored. Knowing their structure in detail is a step toward devices that use spin without stray magnetic fields.
arxiv-2502-21110:
Charles Dawson, Van Tran, Max Li, and Chuchu Fan learn models of rare failures from as little as a single recorded disaster, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Autonomous systems fail seldom, but when they do, engineers may have only seconds of data from before the event, against mountains of normal operation logs.

Generative models trained on so little either memorize noise or wash the failure out under a strong prior. Their framework, CalNF, calibrates normalizing flows with self-regularization tuned for scarce data. It reaches state-of-the-art results on data-limited failure modeling and on inverse problems. The team also runs a first-of-its-kind case study into the root causes of the two thousand twenty-two Southwest Airlines scheduling collapse. Learning from one failure is a strange statistical regime. Doing it well could change how safety-critical systems are debugged.
arxiv-2503-00010:
Zhiwei Zhu and Jiaqun Wei present a 2025 math paper on tilting subcategories. The setting is an extriangulated category, a broad frame that joins two classic algebra settings. The category is assumed to hold enough projective and injective objects. The authors define Wakamatsu-tilting and Wakamatsu-cotilting subcategories inside it. They prove the two definitions pick out the same class.

That class also matches a pair of infinity-level notions from past work. So one concept goes by several names, and all its good traits carry over. The team then glues such subcategories across a special split of categories. The reverse glue holds under stated conditions. Algebraists get a unified account that ends a naming tangle. Unified notions travel better: results proved under one name now serve readers who met the idea under another.
arxiv-2503-00110:
Gabriele Montefalcone and co-authors set new limits on a possible form of dark matter using data from the early universe, in a paper from 2025. The dark matter they study is very light and prefers to interact with electrons. It would slowly decay into light through a loop process.

Such decays would leave a trace in the cosmic microwave background, the faint glow left from the early universe. The team used the newest Planck satellite data to bound how strong the link between this dark matter and electrons can be. Their limits beat space and lab tests in some mass ranges. They report the strongest limits yet for some light mass cases. The study also treats, for the first time, how the decay energy spreads through the early cosmos in a consistent way.
arxiv-2503-02010:
Kirkpatrick and Liu find the shortest joint paths for two round-shoulder bots on a clear floor in this twenty twenty-five paper. Each bot is full and matched front-to-back, and the two must not touch en route. The grade counts the sum of the two hub paths from start to goal.

Inside, the pair gives an exact form for one such best path for all start pairs. Each bot's path is built from at most six bent parts in a chain. Parts run straight or hug the edge of the pair's joint sum shape. The sum length comes out as a neat closed form from start and goal alone. Paths can run one bot at a time or turn the pair in one smooth sweep.
arxiv-2503-03010:
Elisa Gorla and Flavio Salizzoni wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025. It develops latroids, a combinatorial structure tied to error-correcting codes, and shows they can recover a code's key weight measures in one uniform frame.

Latroids were introduced by Vertigan, who attached one to each linear block code and showed a certain polynomial of the latroid fixes the code's weight pattern. The original definition ran through a rank function. The authors give matching descriptions built from independent elements, bases, circuits, and flats, for lattices with complements. They then attach latroids to codes over rings or fields with general support rules. From the latroid, the code's generalized weights can be read back. The frame covers block codes, ring codes, and rank-based codes alike.
arxiv-2503-03910:
Sarah Moon asks, in a solo 2025 paper, how a policymaker should split funds across many programs when the gains of each are known only with noise. A planner who knew the true distribution of policy impacts would need just two quantities for each program: its posterior mean benefit and its net cost. That planner sets the locally optimal rule.

The true distribution is not known, so Moon estimates the posterior means with an empirical Bayes approach, which borrows strength across programs. She derives how fast this rule converges to the oracle planner's decision as data grow. Simpler plug-in methods, by contrast, can fail to converge at all. In an application to 127 policies, the empirical Bayes rules had positive estimated local welfare effects. The plug-in rule had negative estimated effects. The work gives a firm base for choices under uncertainty.
arxiv-2503-05310:
Anna Berryman and co-authors model how skill and place mismatches shape Brazil's green transition for workers, in work from twenty twenty-five. A greener economy needs deep structural change, but headline job gains hide local pain. The team joins a dynamic labor market simulation with farm and green factory scenarios.

Productivity shifts by sector and region are traced through the labor market, with frictions from skills and distance. Poorly managed shocks deepen inequality in the results. Farm workers fare worst, since they move less easily across jobs and places. The authors stress targeted labor policies to keep the transition just. Green growth must plan for who can actually take the new jobs.
arxiv-2503-07210:
Jacob Swindell, Madeleine Darbyshire, Marija Popovic, and Riccardo Polvara compare five ways to discretize Gaussian process maps for drone based weed mapping on farms. Exact weed maps drive precision farming, but stitched photo maps are slow to build. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Gaussian models give smooth maps of weed spread, yet real tasks need a grid form. The team tests quadtrees, wedgelets, two binary split trees, and hexagon grids on real weed fields. Scores cover look, error, and speed. Quadtrees won overall, but hexagons and one split tree suit fields with large weed patches, while quadtrees suit scattered small patches.
arxiv-2503-08810:
Daniel Abou-Ras and Matthias Maiberg revisit how fast charge carriers are lost at grain boundaries in solar cell materials in a two thousand twenty-five paper. In polycrystalline absorbers, the seams between crystal grains can trap carriers. A measure called recombination velocity captures that loss. The authors derive fresh forms of the equations for that speed and for the energy barriers met by electrons and holes.

For a fixed doping level and temperature, a measured speed turns on just two things. One is the excess charge at the boundary, and the other is a single prefactor. In data from two absorber families, both values stay in much the same range for all boundaries in one material. Yet the speeds span orders of magnitude, so the bands must bend both up and down, and by just small amounts.
arxiv-2503-09410:
Jiale Wang and three co-authors harden a classic vision algorithm in twenty twenty-five. RANSAC robustly fits models to noisy data by testing random samples. Learned versions use deep networks to guide it against outliers. Those versions are trained and tested on data from the same generator, so they generalize poorly.

The authors introduce a diffusion-based training paradigm. Noise is progressively injected into ground-truth data, simulating messy conditions. Monte Carlo sampling adds varied randomness at several stages, diversifying the training distribution. Experiments use feature matching on the ScanNet and MegaDepth data sets. The approach aims at models that survive data unlike their training set. Readers in computer vision get a training recipe for robustness where it usually fails: out of distribution.
arxiv-2503-09810:
Talya Eden, Reut Levi, Dana Ron, and Ronitt Rubinfeld count small graph motifs in sublinear time in two thousand twenty-five. Counting motifs, or small subgraphs, is a core task in graph study. Fast rough counts use queries that probe a graph bit by bit. Past best results in the plain model covered only motifs of radius one.

A richer model with edge sampling knew far more, which left a scope gap. The team narrows that gap with counts based on uniform sampling. Their main result counts any Hamiltonian motif fast in the plain model. A variant can sample such motifs near evenly. Simpler counts for stars and cliques follow too.
arxiv-2503-10710:
Eric Bridgeford and co-authors argue that brain studies should state cause assumptions plainly and check them with set tools, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A running case on sleep quality and white matter health carries the lesson. Hidden bias from mixed factors and from who gets kept in a study are framed in cause diagrams.

Hands-on cases show how to check overlap between groups and how drop rules can skew results. Multi-site data merging gets the same treatment. The frame guides both study design and data choices where random trials cannot run. Readers get concrete steps to make cause claims in brain work more honest and robust.
arxiv-2503-10810:
Robin van Bijleveld and four co-authors computed new jet functions in twenty twenty-five for quantum electrodynamics. When a heavy fermion scatters, its behavior splits into hard and soft parts — a factorization that lets physicists compute precisely. Pushing that split one order finer in the fermion's small mass needs new building blocks.

The authors define jet functions that connect to the hard part in several ways and compute them to second order in the coupling. A region-by-region test confirms the factorization formula holds with these functions in place. They handle delicate points like rapidity regulators and corrections on external lines. A pleasing pattern of relations among the jet functions also emerges. The work sharpens tools for precision tests of QED and its bigger cousin, QCD.
arxiv-2503-11310:
Igor Travěnec and Ladislav Šamaj study a one-dimensional fluid with unusual thermal behavior in a 2025 paper. Some materials shrink when heated under steady pressure, a quirk called negative thermal expansion. The authors build the simplest setting where the quirk can be solved exactly: particles in a line that repel each other over two distance scales.

When the repulsion range is short enough, each particle interacts only with its neighbors, and the thermodynamics can be written in closed form. Their equation of state links average spacing to temperature and pressure for several repulsion shapes. At low temperature they find spacing jumps at certain pressures and expansion behavior that flips with the potential's shape.
arxiv-2503-12610:
Seungwoo Lee, Mouad Ramil, and Insuk Seo derive the Eyring-Kramers law for the underdamped Langevin process, in work from twenty twenty-five. The law gives how long, on average, a noisy particle takes to hop between two wells of a double well landscape at low heat. Such hops model rare shifts in physics and chemistry.

Standard proofs lean on potential theory tools that break down for this process, since noise acts only through momentum. The authors build a fresh route that skips those tools entirely. Their result gives the low heat form of the mean hop time with full rigor. The method may extend to other processes where classic tools fail. The work sits in probability and statistical physics.
arxiv-2503-12810:
Zachary Olkin and Aaron Ames tackle, in a 2025 paper, a speed problem in controlling machines that switch between modes, like a walking robot whose feet strike and leave the ground. Planning optimal control for such hybrid systems over a rolling horizon is usually far too slow for real time. Their answer splits the job into two layers that run at different speeds.

A slow upper layer sketches a stabilizing trajectory, including which modes come in which order. A fast lower layer tracks that sketch with a standard, quickly solved controller. The lower layer wraps its plan in error tubes that tolerate drift. The team proves the re-planning speed of the fast layer ties directly to robustness, which justifies the split. Simulations on a five-link bipedal robot and a bouncing ball illustrate the theory.
arxiv-2503-13510:
Vishal Gandhi and Sagar Gandhi study how the mood of a prompt steers language model answers in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Every prompt carries a tone, warm or harsh, hopeful or bleak. Whether that tone changes the quality of the reply was little studied. The team sorted prompts by sentiment with two analysis methods. They then tested five leading models across six uses, from legal analysis to creative writing.

By rewording prompts to flip their tone, they measured shifts in coherence, factual accuracy, and bias. Negative prompts often cut accuracy and raised bias. Positive prompts tended to improve the replies. The finding matters for anyone who writes prompts for a living. Tone, it turns out, is a quality lever, not a cosmetic choice.
arxiv-2503-14210:
Maicon Hespanha and Ademir Pastor prove that some solutions of a coupled wave system must blow up in finite time. Their paper from twenty twenty-five models a light beam and its third harmonic in a Kerr-type material. The system is a cubic nonlinear Schrödinger pair. The energy-critical case, set in dimension four, is their focus.

Radial solutions are the test class. When starting energy sits below the ground state's but kinetic energy sits above, blow-up is forced. A convexity argument drives the proof. The team also proves ground states exist, as minimizers of an action score. Concentration-compactness plus variational tools do that work. A best constant for a vector Sobolev-type inequality falls out as well. The results sort which beams stay smooth and which collapse.
arxiv-2503-15010:
Fernández-Martínez and three co-authors propose a new nozzle for spraying charged liquid jets, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Such jets are used to print fine lines and to feed samples into lab instruments. With liquids that carry charge poorly, the jet often breaks up unless the flow stays above a floor rate.

Their nozzle is beveled and made of a material that does not conduct charge. That shape steadies the jet and drops the floor rate, so far thinner jets form. It also avoids chemical reactions that metal needles cause, keeping the liquid pure. Tests made jets about one micron wide and printed lines only tens of nanometers high.
arxiv-2503-16710:
Yanyan Li and five co-authors present a system that maps moving scenes in three dimensions over time, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Robots and cameras must know where they are while building a model of the world. Most systems erase moving objects and map only still surroundings, losing much of real life.

Their method sorts each pixel as still or moving, then keeps two sets of scene blobs, one fixed and one that shifts. A small network steers the moving set through learned motion fields. A new flow-checking step compares rendered motion between frames to keep the moving parts honest. Tests on real scenes show steady tracking and sharp new views of dynamic scenes.
arxiv-2503-16810:
Yuki Amari, Muneto Nitta, Chihiro Sasaki, Kenta Shigaki, Satoshi Yano, and Shigehiro Yasui model glueballs as knotted field shapes called Hopfions, in a 2025 paper. Glueballs are particles made only of the strong force's carriers. They are hard to spot in experiments. A Hopfion is a stable knot-like lump in a field. The team quantized these lumps and matched their energies to data. Lab results and large computer simulations both served as checks.

A knot with one unit of twist matches a known particle. Knots with two units read as pairs of glueballs bound together. One pair is bound tightly, one loosely. The loose pair predicts a new particle near a set mass. The team computed both binding energies. Spinning the knots predicts a family of higher-spin glueball states. Some of those states are still missing from data. Future experiments can look for them.
arxiv-2503-17410:
Josef Koumar, Timotej Smolen, Kamil Jerabek, and Tomas Cejka compare forecasting models for internet traffic in a 2025 study. Providers need good forecasts to plan capacity, improve service, and spot anomalies early. The team tests leading deep learning models on a large real data set from a national research network, covering many weeks of measurements.

Their comparison weighs accuracy against computing cost at different levels of network detail. A shared, repeatable method lets others rerun the same tests fairly. The study also maps where each model family is strong or weak. That benchmark gives later forecasting work a common starting point.
arxiv-2503-17610:
Prosper Dellah Allo and seven co-authors create light-emitting defects in silicon chips made by a mainstream foundry process, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Silicon photonics thrives on factory production, but silicon itself is a poor light source. Defect centers that glow offer one fix, yet earlier work needed custom fabrication.

Their trick is a simple end-of-line treatment applied after standard production. At the best implant energy, the glowing centers shone as brightly as in lab-made samples. Varied grating devices confirmed the light came from the device layer, not the wafer beneath. The route opens the way to building light sources, classical and quantum, straight into mass-produced photonic circuits.
arxiv-2503-17710:
Yizhou Zhou turns class slides into books made for each student, with help from a language model. A slide deck packs a course into short points. Students need the full text a book gives. Slide2Text pulls text from slides with OCR. It sorts that text into a neat frame. It then writes study stuff to fit: plain takes on hard points, drills, and source lists.

Choice tools let the book fit the needs and the grade of each class. The author casts the rig as a way to cut the grind of book work. Ease of use for all is a top gain it claims. Plans add sound and film inputs, plus deeper fits for each user. The work sits in the fast rush to use big models as course mills. Its bet: a deck and a book should be one short step apart, not a long print run.
arxiv-2503-18310:
Gernot Akemann, Sung-Soo Byun, and Yong-Woo Lee present a 2025 mathematics paper on random matrices from the elliptic Ginibre ensemble. These matrices model systems whose values, called eigenvalues, can be real or come in complex pairs. The authors ask how likely it is that almost all eigenvalues turn out real. They study the chance as the matrix grows, allowing a fixed small number of exceptions.

They derive full formulas for this probability in two regimes: one where the matrix stays strongly non-symmetric, and one where it nears symmetry as it grows. In the special case of a single allowed exception pair, they obtain the expansion to every order. The proofs use different tools in each regime, from energy methods to special polynomial techniques. The work sharpens knowledge of real eigenvalues in random matrix theory.
arxiv-2503-18710:
Miguel Albaladejo, Amador García-Lorenzo, and Juan Nieves build Coulomb effects into femtoscopy correlation functions, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Femtoscopy probes how hadrons act on each other. The authors combine strong contact potentials with Coulomb effects as one whole. Derived scattering amplitudes and wave functions then yield the functions.

Finite-range corrections to the strong interaction, tied to off-shell effects, turn out to be a must. Missing them distorts the amplitudes pulled from correlation data. The authors propose an approximate method to include these corrections. Their forms are compared with earlier theory. For proton-proton systems, results match past realistic results and recent ALICE experiment data well. The method computes the functions in full without solving the Schrödinger equation by computer. It also connects easily to amplitudes from effective field theories.
arxiv-2503-19110:
Sina Feldmann, Juliane Adrian, and Maik Boltes push crowds in controlled experiments in twenty twenty-five. How a shove travels through a standing crowd matters for safety at packed events. The phenomenon is crucial to collective dynamics yet scarcely studied. The team pushed people forward in a measured, repeatable way.

They varied push intensity, spacing between people, preparedness, and crowd formation. A pressure sensor recorded the impulse while cameras tracked head motion. Three-dimensional motion capture added detail. Propagation distance and speed depended mainly on push intensity. Preparedness showed no significant effect, a result with safety implications. Inter-person distance especially shaped propagation speed. Readers get hard data on a hazard usually discussed only after disasters.
arxiv-2503-20410:
Akylas Stratigakos and Panagiotis Andrianesis published this energy forecasting paper in 2025. Short-term forecasts, such as wind power predictions minutes to hours ahead, assume input data will be there when the model runs. In practice, sensors fail and attacks happen, leaving gaps that hurt accuracy and decisions built on it. Filling gaps with guessed values works for brief outages but degrades as gaps lengthen.

The authors build forecast models that adapt to whichever inputs are available, using robust optimization ideas from adversarial machine learning. Their models learn to partition uncertainty into a few data-driven sets, so they can adjust quickly without retraining. In wind power tests spanning fifteen minutes to four hours ahead, the models matched gap-filling for short outages and beat it for longer ones. A few partitions came close to the impractical best of retraining for every gap pattern.
arxiv-2503-21310:
Nicolò Barbieri, Kerstin Hötte, and Peter Persoon wrote this 2025 research paper on how green technology gets counted. Counts of green patents are widely used to track new ideas, judge climate policy, and spot fresh chances in clean technology. Yet those counts rest on sorting systems that change over time, so the systems shape which inventions show up at all.

The authors study patent families filed from 1980 to 2016 and compare two large patent data releases. They find that re-sorting old patents and wider coverage each raise the green patent count by roughly a tenth. Common filters, though, cut out between about two fifths and nine tenths of patents. The paper warns that headline trends in green invention partly reflect the counting tools, not just real inventive work.
arxiv-2503-21810:
Zhenyu Wu, Jiaoyan Chen, and Norman Paton use large language models in 2025 to infer the type structure hidden in data tables. A table's columns carry types, like city or price, and those types form a family tree of concepts. Finding that tree helps people search, merge, and make sense of data.

Older tools lean on word forms and table shape, and miss much of the meaning in the text. The authors offer two model-based routes.
