One turns columns into learned vectors and clusters them into a tree. The other asks a big model to name types and build the tree step by step. Tests on three real data sets showed both routes give trees that match the true ones well.
arxiv-2503-21910:
Kadaoui and a large team present a test set from twenty twenty-five for image and text models in Arabic. The set covers four Arabic dialects from Jordan, the Emirates, Egypt, and Morocco. Its tasks are writing captions for images and answering questions about them. The content is rich in local culture and daily life. The team use it to judge how well models handle dialect shifts. They test five open Arabic models and one famed paid model.

The Arabic models did poorly on both image sense and dialect text. The paid model ranked best but varied by dialect and lagged on image sense. The authors say current models leave Arabic users underserved. They call for broader training data and fairer test sets.
arxiv-2503-22510:
Simran Kaur Ghatoray and Yongmin Li build a system that extracts user experience insights from user research videos automatically. Judging a product depends on reading users' emotions, yet little work automates that reading across several channels at once. Their pipeline joins three streams: facial emotion recognition, speech-to-text transcription, and emotion detection in the resulting text.

For the face channel, they evaluate ten pre-trained models on three benchmark datasets and pick the one that generalizes best. Speech is transcribed with the Whisper model, and text emotions come from a pre-trained model with high reported accuracy. Temporal alignment and fusion merge the streams into deeper, contextual findings. Automated analysis through a data library driven by a large language model turns the merged data into answers. The authors present the work as a proof of concept for emotion-aware UX evaluation.
arxiv-2503-23010:
Mingqing Liu and four co-authors compare two wireless links in a study from 2025. One link uses terahertz waves, just below infrared light. The other uses light itself, sent from small laser chips or across open air. Both promise fast data but suffer when beams drift off target.

The team built shared models for beam drift, power use, and signal loss, for rooms and for outdoor use. They also test both links for drones, where motion makes aim hard. The results show which link fits which setting, and where each one wastes power or loses signal first.  Their aim is a fair, like-for-like view of two links often sold on claims alone.
arxiv-2503-23910:
Chakraborty and three co-authors film how drops burst in a head-on air stream in this twenty twenty-five paper. A drop that falls through fast air can tear into a spray of child drops. How it tears sets the size mix of that spray, a key fact for fuel and rain work.

Inside, shade shots and light-wave films track each burst form as air force climbs. At low force the drop blows into a bag that pops into mixed child drops. Mid force adds a stalk to the bag as it pops in the stream. High force blows two bags at once, which flips the size mix of the spray. A two-part math curve fits the size mix in all three modes.
arxiv-2504-00210:
Shivan Mittal and Bin Yan wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-five on preparing single quantum trajectories without luck. A trajectory is one run of a quantum system under unitary motion and random measurements. Individual runs carry real physics, including sharp changes in entanglement as measurement rates vary.

The trouble is post-selection: any chosen run is so unlikely that waiting for it costs exponential effort. The authors propose a deterministic method that builds a wanted trajectory in polynomial time using imaginary time evolution, a known mathematical trick. The method works for a certain class of states, and they argue no universal method can cover every trajectory. The result opens a path to experiments on this physics at scale.
arxiv-2504-01810:
Merling, Raptis, and Semikina wrote in twenty twenty-five on scissors congruence K-theory. Scissors congruence asks when a shape can be cut and rebuilt as another. Its K-theory sorts those links into a spectrum with algebra on it. Their new version is parametrized, with added structure data and topology. Oriented manifolds appear as a special case of the frame. They link the theory to cut-and-paste invariants of manifolds.

Links to cobordism categories and the K-theory of spaces are examined. On the lowest homotopy group, their theory matches a cobordism variant. In that variant, cobordisms may have free boundaries. A refined Euler map detects a classic semicharacteristic invariant. The work deepens links between geometry, topology, and algebra. It is a foundational theory contribution.
arxiv-2504-01910:
Frigerio, Paris, Lopetegui, and Walschaers wrote this physics paper in twenty twenty-five. It asks how well one can measure two things at once: a shift in a particle's position and a shift in its momentum. Quantum rules make the two hard to pin down together. States of light or matter shaped in non-Gaussian ways, which bend the usual bell curve, are the tool used here.

The authors show that any pure non-Gaussian state beats every Gaussian state for this joint task. The two shifts can, in principle, be measured with very high precision and very low conflict. Even blends of Gaussian states can help if tuned with care. The result guides the design of future quantum sensors.
arxiv-2504-02210:
Daiki Takama and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on the infrared fingerprint of solid nitrous oxide, a laughing-gas ice thought to coat distant icy worlds. Worlds past Neptune, such as Pluto, may grow this ice when sunlight or cosmic rays strike nitrogen and carbon monoxide ices. Lab data on the ice at the warmer end of its range were thin. The team froze the gas into fine grains and read their spectra with an imaging instrument.

A strong absorption band stood out, with three weaker bands beside it. Warming the grains made every band grow stronger for good, a sign the ice was settling into crystals. Under ultraviolet light, the nitrous oxide bands faded within about an hour and a half. In their place rose bands of other nitrogen oxides and ozone. The maps can guide readings of telescope spectra from far icy worlds.
arxiv-2504-03610:
Will Thacher, Yulong Pan, and Per-Olof Persson published a computer science paper in 2025 on building triangular meshes. Meshes divide shapes into small triangles for simulation and graphics. Good meshes need well-placed points and clean connections. The authors trained a mesh generator with reinforcement learning instead of fixed rules.

A graph neural network moves and adjusts the mesh points. A standard Delaunay method then connects them into triangles. Training rewards whatever quality measure the user chooses. The team tested generation, improvement, and variable-resolution tasks. Learned meshes matched the output of two popular established generators. The result points toward mesh tools that learn from goals rather than recipes.
arxiv-2504-05010:
Subash Chandra Behera and Shiv Parsad proved new forms of a classic shape rule. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with the isoperimetric inequality. In its discrete form it says: of all shapes with a set count of sides and a set area, the regular one has the least rim. The pair proves kin rules for polygons in hyperbolic geometry, where space curves out. Their forms swap the rim for the circle round or in the shape.

They treat lone shapes and sets of shapes at once. Two more forms hold for sets with a cap on area or rim. Readers in geometry get the old rule's kin on curved ground, both for round bound and tangent bound shapes.
arxiv-2504-05210:
Joshua Hatherley argues that keeping learning systems up to date creates a new kind of blindness for the people who use them. His article appeared in twenty twenty-five. Models decay as the world shifts, so teams retrain them; users then face a tool whose reasoning changed silently.

He names the problem update opacity: users cannot tell how or why an update altered the system's behavior. Standard fixes for black-box models do not reach it, since the change itself is the hidden part. He weighs three remedies: explanations that contrast before and after, live model reporting, and checks that updates stay compatible with past behavior. Each carries risks or limits. More research, he concludes, must target updating itself.
arxiv-2504-05410:
Benjamin Lipkin and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on steering the output of large language models. Users often need text that obeys a rule, such as a set format or a valid database query. The usual way checks each next word against the rule and blocks words that break it. With word lists of more than one hundred thousand, that check runs at each step and costs a great deal.

Worse, the usual way can warp the final text, since it looks only one step ahead. The team's method instead draws words and rejects some of them by a rule that adapts as it goes. That cuts the rule checks by a huge factor. It also gives fair weights that fix the warp when paired with a known sampling scheme. Tests on five tasks, from text to code queries to molecule building, beat the best past methods.
arxiv-2504-06010:
Stefanos-Iordanis Papadopoulos and co-authors attacked fake news made of real photos with wrong captions. Such miscaptioned images are hard to police because labeled examples are scarce, and earlier synthetic training sets were too crude to teach much. Their team used adversarial prompting of vision-language models to write convincing false captions, producing a realistic training set called MisCaption This.

They also built a detector, LAMAR, that learns to reconstruct what a truthful caption's internal representation should look like; captions that resist reconstruction look suspicious. Models trained on the new data transferred better to real misinformation, and LAMAR set new best scores on three benchmarks, including a fresh one the team introduced. The authors release their code for other researchers.
arxiv-2504-06710:
Vincent Kather, Burooj Ghani, and Dan Stowell compare the ears of fifteen bioacoustic models by looking at how they organize sound, not just how they classify it. Each model turns animal sounds into embedding vectors, which a classifier then labels. Accuracy scores alone cannot compare models trained on entirely different animal groups, nor judge species never seen in training.

The authors evaluate the embedding spaces directly, through clustering structure and nearest-neighbor classification. That isolates the feature extractor from its classifier head. The question is which extractors build spaces that adapt and generalize beyond their training classes. Such evidence matters for conservation work, where the target species is often rare or unrecorded in training data.
arxiv-2504-07710:
The ATLAS Collaboration wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It uses proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider to limit how often Higgs bosons are made far above their normal mass, and from that, how long a Higgs boson lives.

The team studied events where an off-shell Higgs decays into two W bosons, which then decay into charged leptons and neutrinos. The data cover years of collisions at a set energy. Events were sorted by lepton type, jet count, and neural network scores. Everything matched the Standard Model's forecast. The cap on off-shell production came out at a few times the predicted rate. Combined with on-shell results in the same channel, the Higgs total width was capped at about thirteen units of energy, a direct handle on its lifetime.
arxiv-2504-07810:
Daniel Torres, Joan Duran, Julia Navarro, and Catalina Sbert brighten dark photos with a math model and its learned twin, in a 2025 paper. Low light hides detail, flattens contrast, and buries noise. Their variational method splits the image into lighting, surface color, and noise, following the classic Retinex idea. A color fix runs first, and a nonlocal term guards fine structure while an automatic gamma step finishes the job.

The twin unfolds the same steps into a neural network whose parts learn from data. Cross-attention lets it borrow patterns from far across the image. Both versions beat most rivals on standard test sets, and the pure math model even topped most learning-based methods. The authors offer the pair as accuracy with or without training.
arxiv-2504-08610:
Lorenzo Cazon and three co-authors link particle production to air showers in twenty twenty-five. When an ultra-high-energy cosmic ray hits air, it triggers a vast shower of particles. The shower deposits the most energy at a depth called Xmax. The spread of Xmax values carries clues about the first interaction and the particles made there.

The team defines new variables built from the energy spectra of secondary particles. A linear mix of those variables predicts over half of the fluctuations in shower development depth. They then build a probabilistic mapping based on the causal link between the mix and the depth. That mapping gives model-independent predictions of Xmax moments. Its biases stay very small in their tests.
arxiv-2504-09610:
Mukhin pushes further a Q-ball mechanism he proposed for high temperature superconductivity in cuprates. The picture casts Q-balls as the agents behind odd normal state traits. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Scattering on Q-balls above the transition yields resistance that grows in a straight line with heat, he argues. The same scattering splits in plane sound branches into softened and hardened sets. Spin wave spread takes an hourglass shape near charge and spin order wave vectors. The magnetic response of a Q-ball gas above the transition matches lab data in cuprates at a broad level, the author reports.
arxiv-2504-10810:
Anmol Singhal and Navya Singhal build a license plate reader for patrol cars in a 2025 computing paper. City patrolling needs plates read from moving cars, at angles, in poor light. Most lab systems assume a clean straight-on photo. Their prototype runs on a small graphics chip inside a surveillance vehicle and watches real streets in Singapore.

The system first finds plates in the full street view, then straightens slanted ones before reading the letters. Singapore plates come in one-line and two-line forms, and a custom network handles both. The pipeline covers spotting, fixing, reading, and tracking in one package. Low power use matters because the gear must run all day on patrol.
arxiv-2504-11210:
David Trevascus and a large team weigh two baby planets caught still forming around a young star. The planets, in the PDS 70 disk, are among the few ever photographed directly. How planets are born, hot or cold, changes how bright they should shine. Mass is the missing key to telling the stories apart.

New positions from a sharp infrared instrument on a major telescope tightened the planets' orbits. From those orbits come firm upper limits on each planet's mass. A third candidate planet was tested in the fit, but its orbits proved unstable. The limits rule out the coldest birth stories for both known planets. Each must have kept a set floor of heat after forming. The work sharpens a rare direct test of planet birth theory.
arxiv-2504-12210:
Tingyang Sun, Tuan Nguyen, and Ting He cut the communication cost of group learning on thin edge networks, in a paper published in 2025. In such learning, phones and devices train a shared model by swaps with peers, with no hub. Edge networks crawl, and swap bulk eats the gain. Earlier fixes used toy communication models that miss multi-hop thin links.

Their joint design sets both the swap web and the mixing weights that steer swap need. Each piece casts as a clean solve, and their method runs fast with a proof of worth. On real maps and data, training time fell by more than four fifths at no accuracy cost. It also beat the best earlier method on computing. The authors aim at AI at the true edge.
arxiv-2504-12410:
Anuvab Banerjee and co-authors report observations from two thousand twenty-five of a blazar, a galaxy whose jet points nearly at Earth. The object is extreme in that its synchrotron glow peaks at very high energies. Polarization, the alignment of light waves, reveals how ordered the magnetic fields are where the light is made.

A space telescope measured X-ray polarization while three ground observatories tracked visible light at the same time, a first pairing for this source. X-rays were strongly polarized, above twenty percent, while visible light sat at only a few percent. That split fits a picture of energy sorting behind a shock. Yet the polarization angles in the two bands differed sharply, a rarer trait the authors weigh with a partly turbulent jet model.
arxiv-2504-14110:
Théo Jaffrelot Inizan leads a large team presenting MOFGen, a crew of cooperating AI agents that dreams up new metal-organic frameworks and checks whether chemists could actually make them. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. These spongy crystals can trap carbon dioxide or harvest water from air. But the space of possible frameworks is vast, and many designs are unmakeable.

One language-model agent proposes fresh compositions. A diffusion model then builds the crystal structures in three dimensions. Quantum agents refine and filter the candidates. Feasibility agents apply expert rules and learned models to judge makability. Trained on known frameworks, the system generated hundreds of thousands of candidates. Five AI-dreamt frameworks were then synthesized in the lab. The authors call it a step toward automated discovery of makeable materials.
arxiv-2504-15210:
Marina Sakharova, Abhinav Anand, and Mira Mezini improve code-writing AI models in their 2025 paper. These models draft software from text prompts, and their skill can be raised by training them against a reward model that grades code. The grades are only as good as the data used to teach the grader.

The team used symbolic execution, a method that runs code with abstract inputs to map its behavior, to build a richer grading data set. Graders trained on this data judged new code far better than a known baseline system. Models then tuned with those grades matched that baseline's results. The work shows that careful test data can raise the quality of AI-written code.
arxiv-2504-15510:
Haoran Li, in a solo paper from 2025, proposes a stabilized version of a classic test for group differences when there are many variables. The classic largest root test is strong at finding concentrated signals, but it breaks down when data dimensions approach the sample size because its matrices become unstable.

Li adds a ridge term, a small stabilizing addition, to the covariance estimates behind the test. He then derives the long-run distribution of the largest eigenvalue of the stabilized matrix under weak assumptions. A fast procedure estimates the centering and scaling values the test needs. Power analysis covers low-rank alternatives, where the true signal lives in a few directions. Tests on brain imaging and behavior data illustrate the method.
arxiv-2504-16310:
Leonardo Centellas-Claros and co-authors built a synthetic data set for secure code review in a 2025 paper. AI tools now help review code, learning from huge piles of real reviews. Those piles cover tests, fixes, and speed, but they hold few security flaws, the very faults that hurt most.

A model trained on such piles can wave a risky change through. The team made fake review data rich in planted flaws to fill the gap. Mixed with real data, it may teach review tools to catch holes in code. The work aims at safer automated gates for shipped software.
arxiv-2504-18610:
Arun Kumar Pati proposes a new idea, dark space-time, in a solo twenty twenty-five paper on quantum entanglement. Entanglement links two far-apart particles in a way that defies classic ideas of cause and place. Pati asks whether a hidden geometry could carry that link.

He posits a second space-time that sits alongside our own, with its own metric. In that dark sector, cause can travel faster than light, so the odd links of entanglement could flow through it unseen. States evolve by interplay between the two sectors. Pati also ties the idea to the ER equals EPR conjecture and to the black hole information paradox.
arxiv-2504-19810:
Planet-forming disks glow in infrared light scattered off their dust. Maio and a large team of co-authors present the first survey of such disks with a new instrument on the Very Large Telescope. Seven disks were imaged at four micrometers through a coronagraph that masks the star's glare. Image tricks then separated the disk light from artifacts and set limits on any planets hiding there.

All seven disks showed up, two of them at this wavelength for the first time. Gaps ringed two famous disks, and one showed flared walls with faint spiral arms. No planets were found, though the setup could have caught hot ones. The team says cooler or dust-buried planets may still lurk, and the tool proved itself for disk work.
arxiv-2504-20710:
Leonie Lorenz and co-authors present tools that turn stored biology models into runnable, viewable simulations in two thousand twenty-five. Models of cell systems help answer questions and make forecasts, but most people cannot rebuild them from raw math. That locks out many who could use them.

One tool, SBMLtoOdin, is an R package that reads models from the BioModels store and writes ready code in a known solver tongue. The second, Menelmacar, is a website that solves those models in the browser and shows them as live charts. Both are free under open licenses. The aim is models that experts and lay readers alike can run and reuse.
arxiv-2505-02010:
Ma, Cao, Jiang, Guo, and Gong present Q-Mamba, offline learning for meta black-box optimization, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Reinforcement learning can configure optimization algorithms dynamically for each new task distribution. Online learning makes that meta-training slow and costly in practice. Their framework learns the configuration policy from offline data instead of live runs.

Algorithm configuration becomes a long-sequence decision process under this framing. A decomposed Q-function eases learning in the huge configuration space. Conservative Q-learning stabilizes training on the fixed offline data set. A Mamba architecture speeds long-sequence learning further with parallel scanning. Benchmarks match or beat online baselines with far better training efficiency throughout.
arxiv-2505-02110:
Tristan Cazenave wrote a solo paper in two thousand twenty-five reporting that a long-standing puzzle benchmark has been solved. The benchmark is Eterna, a set of RNA design challenges. RNA design means finding a letter sequence that folds into a target shape, a task with uses in synthetic biology, medicine, and nanotechnology.

Cazenave's algorithm, named Montparnasse, searches by rolling out many trial solutions and keeping what works. It balances several goals at once and limits how often it repeats a line of play. Earlier methods had left some Eterna puzzles unsolved. The paper presents the algorithm and its run at the full benchmark.
arxiv-2505-02910:
You-Peng Liao, Jasper Roosmale Nepveu, and Chia-Hsien Shen prove a 2025 theorem about how the strength of forces must drift as one zooms out in an effective field theory. Such theories describe physics at low energy while leaving the high-energy detail open. A classic result in a related field fixes the direction of that drift for one key count. Their theorem does the same for the running of couplings.

The proof rests on three bedrock principles: unitarity, analyticity, and Lorentz invariance. It fixes the sign of the one-loop running when two inserted operators share the same even mass dimension. The result holds for a broad class of theories, whatever completes them at high energy. The authors show what it means for two workhorse theories used in particle and nuclear physics.
arxiv-2505-03510:
Ludovico Iannello and co-authors use living neurons as the core of a computing system, in a research paper from 2025. Their setup, called biological reservoir computing, grows a pool of cultured neurons on an electrode grid. Signals enter through some electrodes, and the rest record how the network answers.

The living network turns each input into a rich, high-dimensional pattern of firing. A simple linear classifier then reads those patterns to sort inputs, much as an echo state network does in software. The team tested the system on position codes, bars at varied angles, and a digit task. Results showed the cell network could carry out pattern recognition, a step toward bio-hybrid computing.
arxiv-2505-03610:
Fangling Jiang and six co-authors tackle a threat to face recognition: masks made in 3D that fool the system. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that past defenses lean on costly sensors or on pulse signals read from the skin, and they do not travel well to new settings.

Their method learns text prompts enriched with facts from a knowledge graph. Short written notes about real faces and mask traits guide a vision-language model to spot the fakes. A filter picks which facts matter for each image, and a causal step strips out false links. The result is a cheaper defense that holds up across varied tests.
arxiv-2505-05310:
Lott Frans, Michael Backes, Heino Falcke, and Tiziana Venturi wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on choosing a site for a new telescope in Africa. A global network of dishes already photographs giant black holes by joining their signals. Adding a dish in Africa would fill gaps in that network. Two sites in the highlands of Namibia are candidates: a mountain called Gamsberg and an existing observatory site.

Water vapor in the air is the main enemy of such work, since it blurs signals at the wavelengths used. The team estimated vapor levels at both sites using data from navigation satellites. Both sites look workable at the two lower observing bands. The highest band may work at Gamsberg in winter, when the air is driest. Median vapor at Gamsberg was clearly lower than at the other site.
arxiv-2505-05710:
Jeong and five co-authors built a foundation model for hyperspectral satellite imagery in twenty twenty-five. Hyperspectral images record hundreds of wavelength bands per pixel, giving rich material fingerprints but posing a heavy data challenge in both space and spectrum. Their model, HyperspectralMAE, learns by reconstruction: hide parts of the image and predict them.

During pre-training, half the spatial patches and half the spectral bands are masked at random, forcing the network to infer missing content in both dimensions. Learnable Fourier-based embeddings encode each band's wavelength so spectral order is respected. The loss balances pixel accuracy with spectral shape fidelity. Pre-training used two large satellite corpora, and fine-tuning on the Indian Pines land-cover benchmark set a new state-of-the-art transfer accuracy. The authors say dual masking yields robust spectral-spatial representations.
arxiv-2505-08310:
Piotrovich, Buliga, and Natsvlishvili estimate the spin of giant black holes in the most distant bright quasars known, in work from twenty twenty-five. These quasars shine from when the universe was under a billion years old. How their black holes grew so fast is a core puzzle.

For objects at redshifts six to seven and a half, the team derived spin, viewing angle, and mass together. Spins averaged above zero point nine, near the physical max. The spin spread matched patterns seen in nearer active galaxies. Strong links among the fitted values suggest growth mainly by smooth disk feeding at high rates. Such feeding spins a black hole up efficiently, the authors note.
arxiv-2505-08510:
Mario Gomez Andreu and five co-authors plan robot paths on 3D Gaussian splats in twenty twenty-five. Gaussian splatting has become a fast way to rebuild scenes in three dimensions. It stores rich spatial detail about a place. The team asks how a robot can plan a route directly on those stored Gaussians.

Their algorithm, FOCI, rests on a new way to state collisions. It uses the overlap between Gaussians as a field integral. Both the world and the robot are cast as Gaussian splats, not as crude bounding boxes. Boxes overstate how blocked a space is, while this method is orientation-aware. That lets the robot slip through very tight gaps. Tests were extensive, the authors report.
arxiv-2505-10510:
Bayesian inference often runs in two steps: fit a surrogate or impute missing data, then fit the model of interest. Done naively, the second step understates uncertainty, ignoring both data variability and the gaps in knowledge from step one. The four authors propose an efficient two-step method that carries that uncertainty through without fitting many separate models.

They pick a representative subset of draws or imputations and build a mixture distribution that approximates the target posterior, using Pareto smoothed importance sampling. Harder cases get refined with importance weighted moment matching and an iteration that widens the mixture. Examples include surrogate models of costly simulations and multiple imputation by chained equations. The method cuts computation while keeping posterior accuracy.
arxiv-2505-11510:
Rasco, Gray, and Ruland published this study in 2025. It tackles a measurement headache in nuclear physics: pulling shape numbers out of beta decay spectra. The spectrum's shape is usually fit with a plain polynomial in the electron's energy. Coefficients from such fits tangle together and shift with the polynomial's order. That makes comparing experiments, or matching theory, slippery work.

The authors propose fitting with orthogonal polynomials instead. These basis shapes stay independent of each other, so the pulled coefficients settle down. Values then hold up across fit orders, and theory-to-data matches get cleaner. Some coefficients even gain a plain physical reading. The paper also marks the statistical limits of what spectra can tell. It is a methods note aimed at precision decay experiments.
arxiv-2505-12810:
Samy Abbes and Vincent Jugé study, in a 2025 paper, the long-run behavior of concurrent systems, where many actions can occur at once in a shared state model. The catalog title is garbled, but the head gives the clean title and both authors. They model such a system as an action of a trace monoid on a finite set of states.

Starting from a spectral trait of the system, they prove that a single steady random law exists for endless paths, for any choice of weights. They also prove a strong law of large numbers for systems that cannot split into parts. That law lets them define speedup, a measure of how much true overlap the paths show on average.
arxiv-2505-13710:
Noam Avidan and Rotem Arnon open the study of computational entropy for quantum systems, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. In classical cryptography, such entropy measures how random data looks to an opponent with limited computing power, and it supports tools from random generators to leakage-resilient codes.

The quantum version of this idea had barely been explored. The authors define quantum computational unpredictability entropy by adapting a classical notion. It rests on min-entropy, which captures an opponent's best chance of guessing a value, but here the opponent must guess efficiently. They prove the new entropy behaves well in several basic ways. One key result is a chain rule that survives even when extra leaked information is unlimited before the guess. The work lays groundwork for quantum-safe cryptography built on entropy arguments.
arxiv-2505-14010:
Pu Wang and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a fast transformer system that clears haze from ultra-high-definition photos. Giant images make dehazing slow and memory-hungry. Their design adds two ideas: a self-scaling normalization borrowed from a recent language model line, and a memory cache that knows the physics of haze.

The cache keeps or drops features based on how haze forms in air, which favors the parts that matter. Training settled about five times faster while using less memory. The system restores fifty big frames per second on a top gaming card and matches leading quality scores. A heat-map tool shows which pixels drove each fix.
arxiv-2505-14410:
Jinzuomu Zhong and co-authors improve how accent likeness is judged in speech synthesis, in this 2025 paper. Making a voice speak with a target accent is only half the task; scoring whether it sounds right has lagged behind. On the human side, they refine a listening test that pits samples against a reference. Listeners get transcripts, mark where accents seem to differ, and pass strict reliability screening.

Those tweaks give stronger statistics with fewer listeners and lower cost. On the machine side, they test distance measures built from vowel shapes and sound-pattern profiles. Several such measures tracked human accent scores usefully. A common pick, word error rate, proved weak for underrepresented accents. The authors offer the paired toolkit for accent work in speech technology.
arxiv-2505-15410:
Bahar Radmehr, Ekaterina Shved, Fatma Betül Güreş, Adish Singla, and Tanja Käser wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents ClickSight, a pipeline that uses a large language model to read student clickstreams and name the learning strategies in play.

Click logs are rich but hard to read, and past tools lean on hand traits or expert marks. ClickSight takes the raw clicks and a list of candidate strategies, and writes a text account of what the student did. Four prompt plans are tried, and self-refinement is tested for lift. Expert grades in two open learning settings show fair reads, with quality shifting by prompt plan and little gain from refinement.
arxiv-2505-15710:
Tianqi Du and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on picking the safest answer from a language model by reading its inner states rather than its words. Safety checks usually grade the final text, yet the model's hidden layers carry richer signals about risk. Their framework ranks several draft answers using those hidden states.

Both the prompt and each draft are encoded from middle layers of the model. A light scorer then orders the drafts by likeness to safe patterns learned at the list level. Across several test sets, the method held up far better against trick prompts designed to jailbreak the model. The team plans to release the code on publication.
arxiv-2505-16610:
Jing Ye, Lu Xiang, Yaping Zhang, and Chengqing Zong published a 2025 paper on making AI emotional support personal. Large language models can sound caring, but their comfort is often generic. Good support depends on the person: their character, their mood, and their situation.

The authors propose a two-stage framework in which the model improves itself. First it learns basic support skills from a small set of conversations. Then it reflects on its own answers, rewrites them to fit the user better, and trains on the improved versions. Repeated rounds steadily sharpen the fit to each user’s unspoken preferences. Tests showed fewer unhelpful replies and answers that matched users more closely.
arxiv-2505-17210:
Martin Villagrana and co-authors test whether a general-purpose image segmentation model can outline kidney stones in scope images without special training, in a 2025 paper. Drawing stone borders by hand is slow and impractical across the large image sets that urology produces. The model under test, SAM, is known for segmenting almost anything it is pointed at.

The team raced SAM against three U-Net variants, the standard tools for medical outlining, on both familiar and unseen data. On familiar data SAM matched the best U-Net closely. On new data it pulled far ahead, beating every U-Net variant by margins of up to 23 percent. The authors read this as evidence that a general model can travel between hospitals and cameras better than narrow ones, a key step toward automatic stone typing.
arxiv-2505-17510:
Marcus Ma and co-authors published this language model study in 2025. Many real tasks need several labels at once, such as tagging a text with every topic it touches. How language models handle that setting is poorly understood. The team watched the models' output scores step by step as each label was produced. They found odd habits. The ranking implied by the first label often does not match the final answer.

Models tend to suppress all but one label at each step. Bigger models show sharper confidence in a single label, yet their internal ranking of labels gets better. Extra training strengthens this quirk. The authors then tackle a matching problem: aligning model scores with the spread of human judgments on subjective tasks. Their best fix is simple and free. Take each label's highest score across all steps rather than only the first, which improved both alignment and accuracy.
arxiv-2505-17710:
Rafael Corsi Ferrão, Fabio de Miranda, and Diego Pavan Soler wrote a 2025 paper on a tool that summarizes the code work of each student in class team projects. A large language model holds the pen. Real industry projects teach well: the tasks are authentic and set by outside clients. But their scope varies widely, so staff cannot give fast, detailed feedback to each student.

The tool pulls the code additions of each student from the shared repository, sorts them, and structures text runs for the model. The summaries go out each week of the sprint. The test ran two semesters, in a three-week full-time sprint with over sixty students. Staff and students both found the tool useful for grading and guidance. The summaries reported real activities for the most part, though some work was missed.
arxiv-2505-18910:
Christopher Coveney uncovers formal links between two pillars of electron theory, in a research paper from 2025. One pillar, coupled-cluster doubles theory, is a workhorse for computing how electrons correlate. The other, the electronic self-energy, frames the same physics in a different language.

Coveney derives the coupled-cluster equations by splitting the self-energy along particle, hole, and time directions. The ground-state energy formula that emerges matches the classic theory exactly. He also connects the setup to a related eigenvalue method for charged states. A tiny two-site model solved exactly confirms the links. The bridge may enrich both frameworks.
arxiv-2505-19310:
Robin Pesl, Jerin Mathew, Massimo Mecella, and Marco Aiello study how to feed software service manuals to language models that must find the right service fast. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Modern systems are stitched from many small services listed in a registry. Full manuals are too long for a model's input window.

The team tests retrieval-backed search over chopped-up manuals. They vary how the text is cut and sized, and grade how well the right endpoint is found. A new bench spans many domains to keep the test fair. A helper agent then asks only for summaries first, pulling details on demand. That two-step flow shrinks input length and lifts retrieval accuracy. Tests on both the new bench and a real-world one back the design. The work guides teams that wire services together with AI help.
arxiv-2505-19910:
Tore Gude, Marta Zagorowska, and Lars Imsland refine feedback optimization in twenty twenty-five. Online feedback optimization steers a process toward its best operating point using measurements. It needs the process's sensitivity, which is often unknown. Random perturbations are the usual way to estimate it, but they push the process off course.

Their controller generates persistently exciting inputs with minimal deviation from the descent direction. The design is a bilevel optimization program. A nonconvex rank constraint is relaxed with linear constraints and penalties. Validation uses a simulated resource allocation problem modeled on oil and gas production. Profit matched the random-perturbation controller while inputs were perturbed less. Readers in process control get gradient estimates bought with smaller disturbances to the plant.
arxiv-2505-22010:
Nasir Hussain and a team of co-authors use large language models to hunt security flaws in stripped program binaries. Their framework appeared in twenty twenty-five. Stripped files lack names and symbols, so human analysts struggle to read them, and automated flaw finding lags.

Their system, VulBinLLM, first improves decompiled code by adding flaw-focused comments without changing how the code runs. Those notes make weak spots stand out. A reasoning stage then works through the code with guided prompts and a memory agent that holds long context. The combination reached state-of-the-art results on binary flaw benchmarks. The authors argue language models can mirror the classic analyst workflow at machine scale.
arxiv-2505-22410:
Cornelius Brand, Radu Curticapean, Baitian Li, and Kevin Pratt revisited fast convolution algorithms in two thousand twenty-five. A convolution combines two vectors by a rule over a finite domain. Product domains, where each entry is a tuple, appear often in parameterized and exponential-time algorithms.

Viewing the problem through multilinear algebra streamlines older algorithms and their analysis. Using known results from fast matrix multiplication, they derive faster methods that improve the best previous time bounds. They also show that a famous open conjecture on matrix rank would imply near-linear time for these convolutions. The paper is written as a self-contained guide for an algorithms audience, with all needed algebra included.
arxiv-2505-23110:
Sugama studies Landau damping in plasmas through a quantum like equation in twenty twenty-five. Landau damping describes how plasma waves fade without collisions. The author transforms the linearized Vlasov-Poisson system into a Schrodinger equation. That form lets him apply tools from quantum mechanics to the plasma problem.

He shows a fluctuation theorem holds for a relative stochastic entropy in this process. That entropy is defined from the probability density of the particle velocity distribution. A time independent invariant emerges from energy and entropy perturbations. It takes a quadratic form and matches the squared amplitude of the Schrodinger state vector. Exact solutions built from Hamiltonian eigenvectors support the claim. Numeric checks validate the theorem for the damping process.
arxiv-2505-23710:
Zeinab Nezami, Syed Danial Ali Shah, Maryam Hafeez, Karim Djemame, and Syed Ali Raza Zaidi see sixth-generation networks as self-evolving systems, not static pipes. In their account, AI-driven intelligence lets the network adapt past mere connectivity. The paper probes what enables autonomous communication systems. The list includes reconfigurable infrastructure, adaptive middleware, and intelligent network functions. It also includes multi-agent work as a team for distributed choices.

The team looks at how these methods align with new industrial Internet of Things frames, for digital manufacturing. Their results stress gains in real-time choices, in efficiency, and in lower latency in networked control systems. The talk also treats ethical tests, research paths, and standards work. It ends with a technology stack roadmap to guide future growth.
arxiv-2505-24110:
Dhayalkar builds choice machines as unrolled feed nets with shared weights in this twenty twenty-five paper. Such machines read strings and branch on chance picks as they go. Past net takes used loop forms or dug the machine out post-drill.

Inside, states ride as bit strings and moves as sparse grid shifts in his build. Blank moves fold in as shared snap steps stacked by depth in the net. Proof shows each tongue such a machine takes fits one such net. Weight count stays fixed no count how long the string runs. Drill tests then teach fresh nets the same acts with near-full match.
arxiv-2505-24210:
Zheng Tan, Weizhen Wang, Andrea Bertozzi, and Ernest Ryu speed up image and video generation models in a 2025 paper. Diffusion and flow models make strong media, but sampling from them takes many model calls, which makes use costly. Fast sampling methods exist, yet many fail on two fronts: stiff equations and reliance on one model family's structure.

Their method, called STORK, builds on a stabilized Taylor method with an orthogonal Runge-Kutta scheme. It handles stiffness while staying independent of the semi-linear structure that limits rival methods. Across image and video tests, it consistently improved sampling quality at a given budget of calls. The authors share their code in public. Faster sampling could cut the cost of generative media tools.
arxiv-2506-00710:
Valter Hudovernik and co-authors generate fake relational databases with diffusion models in a 2025 computing paper. Real databases link many tables through foreign keys, and that web is the hard part to fake well. Earlier generators flattened the web into single tables or assumed it away. Their model, RelDiff, treats the key graph as a first-class citizen: one diffusion process fills in values across all tables at once, guided by the graph.

A block-model generator separately creates realistic link structure, so made-up rows still point at rows that exist. Tests on eleven benchmarks checked fidelity against real data. Convincing synthetic databases let companies share data's shape without sharing the data.
arxiv-2506-01010:
Hausmann and co-authors test whether a compact frame type speeds up checking of game-based logic formulas. The alternating-time mu-calculus describes what groups of agents can force over time. Its standard meaning rests on concurrent game frames. Effectivity frames carry the same facts in tighter form, at least in many cases. The team built the translation between the two frame types. They then ran a generic checker on both forms.

Benchmarks included set series plus random systems and formulas. The team also compared speed with a leading ATL checker. Gains would matter for verifying multi-agent systems. The study checks whether a theory-level edge shows up in practice.
arxiv-2506-01610:
Siarhei Finski proved a structural result in 2025 connecting two areas of complex geometry and operator theory. Toeplitz operators are a central tool for quantizing complex manifolds, turning functions into operators on spaces of holomorphic sections. Finski works on a compact complex manifold carrying a big line bundle, equipped with a Bernstein-Markov measure, a condition controlling how badly polynomials can spike. His theorem: these Toeplitz operators form an algebra, meaning composing two of them stays within the same class.

As an application, he derives a Szegő-type result describing how the operators' spectra distribute in the limit. A key ingredient is the fine asymptotic behavior of the Bergman kernel far from the diagonal, also known as the Christoffel-Darboux kernel. Algebra closure is the kind of foundational fact that later work builds on quietly. It tells geometers their quantization toolkit is internally consistent.
arxiv-2506-01910:
Krishna Acharya, Aleksandr Petrov, and Juba Ziani present a recommendation system that writes its own search queries. Their system, called GLoSS, appeared in twenty twenty-five. It aims to guess what a shopper will want next from the order of past picks.

Earlier systems matched words exactly when searching for items. GLoSS instead searches by meaning, so it can find items that share no words with the query. A small, fine-tuned language model writes the queries, which keeps the cost low on modest hardware. On three Amazon review data sets, the system beat both classic methods and rival language model systems. It did especially well for new users with little history on two of the sets.
arxiv-2506-02110:
Ritam Basu, Pratyusha Chowdhury, and colleagues connect a quantum complexity measure with random matrices and gravity in a 2025 physics study. A discrete Wigner function paints a quantum state as a real distribution over a grid phase space, and its negative patches signal states that are hard to simulate classically. The total negativity is an operational measure of that hardness.

The authors study how negativity behaves for states drawn from random matrix ensembles, the same structures that appear in models of quantum gravity and black holes. Links between simulation cost and gravitational models feed the broader effort to price quantum advantage.
arxiv-2506-03810:
Chang-Hao Fang and seven co-authors simulate how recoiling atoms in silicon share their energy in a 2025 paper. Dark matter detectors listen for tiny kicks when particles strike atomic nuclei, but only part of each kick becomes measurable charge. That fraction, the quenching factor, is hard to pin down at the lowest energies, right down to a single electron hole pair.

Their atom by atom simulations matched experiments remarkably well across a wide energy range. Below a few thousand electron volts, the crystal's binding and structure explain where older theory goes wrong. Very low energy behavior even depends on which way the crystal faces. The results sharpen how light a dark matter particle such detectors can rule out.
arxiv-2506-03910:
Shyam Prabhu and co-authors compare a classic experiment design method with machine learning for tuning a welding-based printing process. Their 2025 paper addresses materials design, where many variables make testing every combination impossible. The classic Taguchi method samples the space with a fixed grid but cannot bend with nonlinear effects.

The rival approach learns a statistical surface model and actively picks the most informative next runs. Both methods suggested settings for an arc welding printer, judged on how well they predicted bead depth, width, and height. On the held-out test cases, the learning model won on both accuracy and efficiency. The authors argue the lesson extends across materials processing, where each experiment costs time and stock.
arxiv-2506-05010:
Zhenran Xu and nine co-authors build ComfyUI-Copilot, a language-model plugin that helps users assemble workflows in the ComfyUI art platform. ComfyUI is flexible but hard on newcomers, with thin documentation, easy misconfigurations, and complex graph design. The copilot aims to lower that barrier.

A central assistant agent delegates to specialized worker agents, backed by curated knowledge bases about nodes and models. The system recommends components, constructs workflows in one click, and helps debug and deploy them. Offline evaluations and online user feedback showed accurate recommendations and faster workflow building. Case studies found benefits for beginners and experienced users alike. The package and a demo video are publicly available.
arxiv-2506-06110:
Sylvain Courte and Noah Porcelli constrain Whitehead torsion for families of Lagrangian submanifolds in two thousand twenty-five. The work is driven by the strong nearby Lagrangian conjecture. Their families are closed and exact, set in a cotangent bundle. Torsion is an algebraic gauge of how a family twists.

They prove the torsion factors through simpler maps. It thus vanishes on the two lowest homotopy groups. Its image is also divisible by the Euler characteristic. A case on a high dimensional torus shows what this means for monodromy. Twisted generating functions are the main tool, past the reach of past work.
arxiv-2506-06210:
Pavel Komarov wrote a document in two thousand twenty-five that sets out the math behind a Python package for spectral derivatives. Taking derivatives in the Fourier frequency domain is strikingly easy, a happy accident of mathematics. Using that fact on a computer, without creating artifacts, takes extra care and knowledge.

Komarov builds the needed background from the ground up. He touches on core signal processing and calculus ideas as they become necessary, then develops the spectral method step by step. The document serves as the theory guide for the package of the same name. Readers get both the formulas and the cautions that make them work in practice. It is a reference text, not a research report.
arxiv-2506-06510:
Fatibene and Orizzonte work through boundary equations for a model used in loop quantum gravity. Their lecture notes appeared in two thousand twenty-five. This is the third set in their series on the subject. The model is the Ashtekar-Barbero-Immirzi formulation of gravity. A canonical analysis is needed to extract its constraint equations. Those constraints shape any attempt at quantization.

Working in the covariant framework, they use algebraic constraints to fix key fields. The connection and its conjugate momentum then stand as an independent pair. Two parameters, tied to Immirzi and Holst terms, are left unrelated. Still, the constraints depend on only one of them. They match the standard loop quantum gravity result. A quantization scheme is stated for the next notes.
arxiv-2506-06810:
Yuan Yin, Sarah L Waters, and Ruth E Baker model how groups of cells invade the matrix that holds tissue. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. How cells and this matrix shape each other matters for tissue building, cancer care, and healing. Two forces get their focus: cues from fibre lay that guide cells, and the cells' own rework of the fibres.

Their model is a two-way hybrid that can be run on a computer with ease. Cells are lone agents, while collagen fibres form a smooth field. The model folds in random motion, fibre guidance, cell sticking, space limits, and fibre making and breaking. A wide sweep of values shows how a cell's traits change the shape of the joint invasion.
arxiv-2506-07410:
Dongzhe Zheng, writing alone, builds a new theory in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-five. It grows out of Spencer theory, a tool for studying systems with constraints. Zheng asks when the Spencer operator shrinks down to the standard one used in calculus on shapes.

The answer is a test on symmetric tensors that depends on a chosen number. When the test passes, the two theories line up in an exact way. Zheng proves the test still passes after mirror moves, which hints at a deep hidden symmetry. He then maps the special cases into a classic counting scheme for shapes. On K3 surfaces, the method picks out special classes of curves and cycles.
arxiv-2506-08110:
Picking a varied shortlist from a huge pool is a classic computing problem, and fairness adds a twist: each group in the pool must get its share of seats. Florian Adriaens and Nikolaj Tatti study the version where only a few picks per group are wanted. Their method works in stages, first pruning points that sit too close to same-group neighbors, then sorting points into clusters at random, and finally choosing one fitting pick from each cluster.

The random method beats the best known guarantee for how close the result comes to the ideal spread. Tests on large real datasets back up the math. The work suits tasks like fair shortlists, sample panels, and search results that must span groups without losing variety.
arxiv-2506-08310:
Debesh Bhattacharjee, Eduard Kontar, and Yingjie Luo present a solar physics paper from 2025 on electrons in solar flares. Flares hurl electrons to high energies, and X-rays from their braking glow reveal them. A warm-target model can pin down the low-energy cut-off of those electrons, which the common cold model cannot.

The team used X-ray data from two spacecraft to track flares over time. Around each X-ray burst, the cut-off energy traced a high-low-high path. The rate of injected electrons traced the reverse path, low-high-low. Total power followed the injection rate more than the cut-off. Extra heat from the settling electrons peaked near the X-ray peak. The results sharpen how flare energy budgets are drawn.
arxiv-2506-11110:
Jaeho Lee and Atharv Chowdhary present AssertBench, a test of whether language models hold their ground when users push back on true facts. For each evidence-backed fact drawn from a fact-checking data set, the benchmark builds two prompts. In one, the user claims the statement is correct; in the other, the user claims it is wrong. The desired behavior is that the model judges the fact the same both times.

The benchmark separates framing effects from knowledge by first checking how the model judges the same claims neutrally. It measures how much the user's stance sways the answer. The setup mirrors a common situation: users asserting things with confidence, rightly or wrongly. The authors argue that a model which flips to agree fails a basic duty of consistency. Their code is public, and they frame the tool as a probe of sycophancy in everyday model use.
arxiv-2506-11610:
Daniel Hove Paludan and co-authors study how chat tools shape early talks between clients and designers, in work from 2025. A poor grasp of the client's needs can waste a hundred hours of work, as one firm put it. The team first spoke with ten design firms about how they gather needs, then built a tool that pairs a chat agent with choice-based answers.

Fifty mock clients tested the tool in a split design. Both the chat agent and the choice format lowered one trust score, yet the input clients gave was clearer. Seven firms then weighed the tool's worth and limits. The authors draw lessons for early joint work.
arxiv-2506-11810:
Kai Dietze and co-authors show that entangled ions can run an optical clock better than separate ions, in an experimental physics paper from 2025. Optical clocks are the most precise timekeepers known, and quantum links between atoms promise still better performance. The team worked with two calcium ions.

The ions were entangled in a state that ignores first-order magnetic field shifts, which stretched their coherence time. That allowed probe times up to 550 milliseconds, near the atoms' lifetime limit. The entangled clock reached the same stability as a plain one in half the probe time, so its cycle ran faster. Its best instability set a record for a calcium ion clock. The authors compared it with a strontium lattice clock as a check.
arxiv-2506-12010:
Nathan Keenan, John Goold, and Alex Nico-Katz bring random matrix theory to quantum state checks. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, studies tomography, the rebuild of an unknown quantum state from many measures. Knowing the size and shape of rebuild errors is key for quantum machines. The authors treat the error itself as a random matrix.

They find a deep link between the error and a classic random matrix family. That link lets them swap real errors for samples from the family in many formulas. They derive mean error, spread, and a bound on how many samples a check needs. Numeric tests on common methods back the theory. A standard fix-up step leaves the bound unchanged.
arxiv-2506-14110:
Steve Hanneke and Mingyue Xu pin down how fast the workhorse learning rule can improve when no perfect rule exists, in this 2025 paper. Empirical risk minimization picks the rule with the lowest training error. Universal learning asks how quickly its excess risk shrinks for one fixed data source, not the worst case. Earlier universal results assumed a flawless rule is available, which practice rarely grants.

Dropping that assumption yields a neat trichotomy. Depending on the concept class, the rate is either exponentially fast, just faster than the classic square-root pace, or arbitrarily slow. The authors characterize exactly which classes land in each bucket. They do the same for target-based and Bayes-based variants. The result completes a map of what this basic rule can promise.
arxiv-2506-14510:
Gautam Nagaraj and a very large team report a survey's count of a class of young galaxies across cosmic time and across how crowded their homes are. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The galaxies are picked out by a bright line in their light, from hot gas lit by young stars. The count of such galaxies by brightness is a core gauge of how they form. The survey, called ODIN, maps wide fields with a set of filters tuned to that line at many past times. The team reads how the brightness count shifts with time and with the density of the place each galaxy sits in. The work ties galaxy growth to its setting.
arxiv-2506-14710:
Francis VanGessel and Mitul Pandya show in a 2025 study that deep neural networks can predict the fluid motion set off by an underwater blast far faster than standard solvers. Blasts under water create complex flows with shock fronts and mixing layers. Solvers that track them step by step are accurate but slow, and that slowness limits design work and real-time use.

Their network takes the traits of the explosive material as input and predicts how shock fronts and material borders move over time. In tests it ran thousands of times faster than the standard solver while keeping errors in the fluid measures extremely small. The method works across a broad range of ideal explosive materials. It opens a path to quick design sweeps for fields from ship building to medicine.
arxiv-2506-15810:
Gisell Lorena Osorio, Milica Banic, and Nicolas Quesada set out plans to make photon triplets with clean spectra in waveguides and ring resonators. Triplet sources show non Gaussian traits prized for quantum computing, but linked spectra can blunt their use. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The triplets arise from a third order process that splits one photon into three in photonic gear. The team studies the spectra in theory and gives ways to gauge and cut the links. One plan shapes spread in waveguides, the other shapes the pump in resonators. Both are shown on real designs, a high contrast fiber and a silicon nitride ring. Few mode triplets look within reach of current gear.
arxiv-2506-16410:
Graham Gibson and co-authors published this forecasting study in 2025. Disease forecasts guide hospital planning and public warnings, yet they often fail right at epidemic peaks, when accuracy matters most. Simple models just extend past trends, while fixed-rule models rest on rigid assumptions. The team built a hybrid method called epimodulation. It folds basic facts about how epidemics behave into existing forecast models.

Tested on simple trend models, the method raised accuracy for COVID-19 hospital admissions by about nine percent on average. Gains for flu admissions averaged near twenty percent. At the peaks themselves, accuracy improved by roughly a fifth to a quarter. The method also strengthened a major ensemble forecast used for COVID-19. The authors present it as a general add-on that makes outbreak forecasts more trustworthy at the worst moments.
arxiv-2506-16510:
Abby Mintz and co-authors study how small galaxies formed stars at cosmic noon, the busy era when the universe was a few billion years old, in a 2025 paper. Star formation in small galaxies is known to come in bursts, but the quiet gaps between bursts are hard to observe far away. The team used 43 spectra from the James Webb Space Telescope covering small galaxies seen as they were one to three billion years after the Big Bang.

Many of the spectra show strong breaks that signal a recent pause in star birth, and these breaks grow stronger as signs of current star birth fade. By matching the data against simple models of bursty histories, the authors find that these galaxies need long burst cycles. Their quiet phases last more than a hundred million years, far longer than a quick lull.
arxiv-2506-17510:
Rafael Ferreira da Silva and co-authors laid out a roadmap in a 2025 paper for linking self-driving labs into one network. AI-run labs can plan and run tests on their own, yet most sit as lone islands at one site each. A find at one lab then cannot spark a test at the next without slow human hands.

Their plan, AISLE, is a grassroots web of such labs with shared rules for data and control. It aims to shrink the path from idea to proof to impact. The authors span labs, computing, and energy science. The roadmap asks funders to back the links, not just the labs.
arxiv-2506-17910:
Mohamed Benkedadra and co-authors propose a multi-camera 3D vision pipeline for interactive spaces in a 2025 paper. Single 2D cameras miss depth, and gaming depth cameras work only at short range. Large, complex rooms defeat both. Their system fuses several stereo cameras to rebuild the whole scene in 3D.

On that rebuilt scene the system can recognize events, track people, and send notices. A feedback loop lets the system learn from the people in the room. That helps it sharpen its choices or adjust to a wholly new setting. The authors report early experiments with the pipeline. They close with a roadmap of steps needed to move it into production use.
arxiv-2506-18610:
When a star collapses into a black hole, the vacuum of space itself gives birth to particle pairs, the effect behind Hawking radiation. Exact formulas cover only the quiet late-time case; mid-process moments and messy events like merging black holes resist exact math. Pedro Duarte Baptista and co-authors build a numerical route to the problem. Their method borrows hyperboloidal slices from relativity computing, curved time surfaces reaching both the far past and far future edges of spacetime.

On those slices they evolve quantum fields through flat-space toy models, where stand-in potentials mimic gravity. They then read off the spectrum of particles arriving at the far future edge. Tests show the approach follows a scattering event start to finish in one run. The authors next aim the same frame at real gravitational settings and a stricter treatment of Hawking scattering.
arxiv-2506-18710:
Maxime Lelièvre and nine co-authors benchmark how well large language models know pedagogy, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Most benchmarks test content knowledge, not knowledge of teaching itself. Pedagogy covers method and practice, from teaching strategies to assessment and special needs support.

Their Pedagogy Benchmark draws questions from professional development exams for teachers. It covers cross-domain teaching knowledge and knowledge for special education needs and disability. They tested ninety-seven models, with accuracy from twenty-eight to eighty-nine percent. They also chart cost against accuracy and track the value frontier over time. Online leaderboards let users filter models by cost and openness. The authors argue such benchmarks guide safe use in education.
arxiv-2506-19510:
Harsh Mathur and co-authors test whether a hydrogen spectral line can read the Sun's chromospheric magnetic field, in a 2025 paper. The chromosphere is a restless layer where fields shape eruptions, yet its magnetism is hard to measure. The team synthesized the line's polarized light inside a realistic 3D solar model. Two established spectral lines served as yardsticks for comparison.

The hydrogen line's core formed about 500 kilometers higher than the calcium line's core, sampling loftier field. A simple approximation recovered the model's field maps from the synthetic signals. Even after adding realistic noise, most magnetic structures stayed visible. The authors say pairing the hydrogen line with standard ones gives a fuller altitude picture of solar magnetism.
arxiv-2506-20310:
Ion Chirica and Mário Pereira give a method to specify and verify higher order iterators in OCaml in two thousand twenty-five. Iterators are central to all languages, yet proving them right is hard. Higher order forms, where functions pass as inputs, add to that strain. Their method is generic and modular in shape.

A spec language states the joint behavior of any iteration schema. A framework then checks each client against its spec by deduction. Case studies run from classic list iterators to graph methods. The graph cases come from a wide used OCaml library. The work shows the approach holds in real code.
arxiv-2506-21210:
Christian Liedtke and Matthew Satriano give an arithmetic version of Klein's classic list of finite symmetry groups, in a paper from 2025. Klein sorted the finite subgroups of a matrix group over the complex numbers long ago. That list anchors much of modern geometry. The pair ask what the list looks like over the ring of integers of a number field.

They describe and sort the finite, flat subgroup schemes of the same matrix group over that ring. Their sorting keeps only the schemes that stay well behaved under change of base. They also prove finiteness results that cap how many such schemes can occur. Density results then cover the surface flaws tied to those schemes. The work lifts a piece of classic geometry into number theory. It opens new ground for the study of quotient flaws.
arxiv-2506-22010:
Bentert, Fomin, Golovach, and Morelle study in twenty twenty-five how to build backup-proof bases in matroids, a broad frame that captures independence in vectors, graphs, and sets. A fault-tolerant basis keeps spanning the whole set even after any fixed number of elements is removed. The goal is the smallest such set, a problem with roots in networks and robust design.

They give an efficient algorithm when both the fault count and the structure's rank are treated as fixed parameters. They also show the limits are tight. The problem is already hard in general for a single fault. For rank two or less it is easy, while for rank three or more it stays hard even with the parameter fixed.
arxiv-2506-22910:
Paul Vos proposes a new scale for reporting statistical test results, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. P-values express tail probabilities, which many users find hard to interpret. His alternative counts semi-tail units, where each unit halves the remaining tail area.

On this logarithmic scale, familiar percentiles land at memorable values. The 10th percentile sits near 3.3 units, and the 5th near 4.3. A two-sided version extends the idea symmetrically around the median. Critical values then follow simple arithmetic progressions. Evidence from independent studies combines by simple addition. Vos also defines an efficiency measure based on differences of slopes. Examples range from standardized test scores to poker hand rankings, showing one scale serving many fields.
arxiv-2506-23010:
Max Lovig, Tianhao Wang, and Zhou Fan ask when a widely used iterative method behaves the same no matter how the data is spread, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The method is approximate message passing, used to study learning dynamics in statistics.

For methods whose steps split cleanly by coordinate, such sameness was already known. Steps that mix coordinates were understood only for tidy data, such as Gaussian or rotation-friendly matrices. The authors name a condition on the method's building blocks, the Bounded Composition Property. Under it, for steps built from polynomials, the same step-by-step forecast holds for matrices with non-Gaussian entries. The work opens a study of sameness for this harder class of methods.
arxiv-2506-23310:
Sergey Foss, Masakiyo Miyazawa, and Linglong Yuan present a study from twenty twenty-five on busy spells in a network of queues. In a Jackson type network, work arrives at set rates and each station serves in its own time. A busy spell runs from when work starts to the next idle gap. The team asks how long such spells can get in rare, extreme cases.

They assume the network is stable, with service times that can be very long. For the stations with the heaviest tails, they pin down the exact growth of the chance that a busy spell tops a large mark. One key claim is a single big jump rule. A long spell comes most often from one huge service time, not from many small ones.
arxiv-2506-24010:
Yuxi Lu and co-authors cross-check two ways of dating stars in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. One method reads the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio in a star's spectrum, which shifts as a star ages. The other, gyrochronology, infers age from how fast a star spins, since spin slows over time.

Both methods are calibrated against a shared pattern: older star groups move with a wider spread of speeds. The team maps where each method can be applied, beyond the ranges covered by star clusters and vibration studies. After fixing systematic offsets, ages from the two methods agreed within uncertainty. The authors define the metal and ratio ranges where the chemical method stays reliable.
arxiv-2506-24110:
The most energetic neutrinos ever seen may interact with each other in ways the standard model forbids. Pravin Kumar Natwariya and co-authors ask what such self-interaction would do to the afterglow of the Big Bang. If fast neutrinos scatter off the sea of slow background neutrinos, they dump energy into the young universe. That extra heat would slightly warp the spectrum of the cosmic microwave background.

Two kinds of warp, named mu-type and y-type, arise at different cosmic ages. Existing limits from a past satellite, plus the planned sensitivity of a future one, cap how strong the coupling can be. For muon neutrinos near a peta-electronvolt, the cap lands near three parts in ten thousand. The authors argue future background measurements could settle whether neutrinos talk to each other.
arxiv-2507-00410:
Tristen Shields and five co-authors measure, in a 2025 preprint, the density profile of dark matter halos under a new definition. A recent proposal defines a halo dynamically: only the particles actually orbiting in the bound structure count. The authors ask how the orbiting matter is spread, halo by halo. At fixed orbiting mass, the whole profile turns out to hinge on one number, the halo radius. That radius sets how far the orbiting profile reaches. Its scatter at fixed mass is about sixteen percent.

Differences in birth time explain only a little of that spread. Late-forming halos sit slightly more compact. Counting birth time cuts the scatter to about eleven percent. The result simplifies how modelers can paint halos: mass plus radius nearly fixes the profile. That economy helps connect dark matter theory to the galaxies telescopes see.
arxiv-2507-00910:
Ken Abe and four colleagues prove that certain paired vortices must take the Sadovskii shape, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The setting is the two-dimensional incompressible Euler equations of fluid flow. A steadily translating vortex dipole is the object of study.

Their variational framework maximizes kinetic energy under fixed impulse and vorticity norm constraints. Notably, no constraint on total mass is imposed. The admissible shape is then dictated by scaling invariance alone. Every maximizer touches the symmetry axis, which is exactly the Sadovskii configuration known from physics. A sharp energy inequality and the concentration-compactness principle drive the proof. The construction explains why this vortex shape appears as the endpoint of steady dipole branches.
arxiv-2507-01310:
Sourav Chowdhury, Indrani Bose, Suparna Roychowdhury, and Indranath Chaudhuri look for shared patterns across epidemic models in a 2025 study. Their model follows people cycling between susceptible and infected states, with newcomers entering the population. Random environmental noise multiplies through the system and can push it between distinct regimes.

In one regime the steady distribution has a single peak, and in another it has two. Transitions between regimes include a critical point matching a well known class from physics. A genetics model shares the same features, suggesting a universal pattern. The authors also examine how vaccination shifts the spread or containment of disease.
arxiv-2507-01510:
Sadun Bordoni and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-five, how a clumpy ring of mass could bend the orbit of a star near the black hole at our galaxy's core. The star, called S2, loops around that black hole. Its path so far fits the path predicted for a lone black hole. That fit caps how much spread-out mass can sit inside its orbit, if the mass is smooth. The team asks what changes if the mass is made of many lumps.

They ran many simulations with clusters of equal-mass objects around the black hole. Clumps could tilt the star's orbit plane and shift its swing. Hits with lumps also made the black hole wobble a bit. Mock data show such effects might be seen.
arxiv-2507-02810: Bernhard Meirose and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on computing advances for a planned experiment hunting signs that baryon number can break. The two-stage program, set at a European neutron source, would also probe ultralight dark matter. The paper reports progress on three fronts. Machine learning methods pick out the rare events of interest. Fast approximate simulations serve detector studies. Detailed models cover the main tracking chamber and its readout electronics.
arxiv-2507-03810:
Jingeon An proves second order estimates for a phase transition in two thousand twenty five. Allen-Cahn minimizers mimic minimal surfaces as the width shrinks. Level sets converge to a minimal surface in that limit. An indicator potential turns the problem into a Bernoulli free boundary one.

The transition layers are uniformly smooth up to the free boundary. Mean curvature bounds improve and decay at an algebraic rate. A simple elliptic equation for the log gradient drives the proof. Curvature terms on the right side expose the geometry cleanly. The argument runs on general Riemannian manifolds as well.
arxiv-2507-04310:
Gyuejeong Lee, Jihwan Shin, and Daeyoung Choi present ProtoNorm, a way for many devices to train one model together without sharing raw data. Their paper appeared in 2025. In federated learning, each device trains locally and shares only small summaries. Problems arise when devices hold different kinds of data or run different models. Their method shares one average pattern per class instead of full models.

The team found these class patterns often sit too close together, which blurs decisions. Their fix has two parts. First, the patterns are spread out evenly on a sphere, borrowing an idea from physics. Second, the patterns are scaled up so gaps grow in plain space. Tests on standard data sets beat rival methods. Since only small patterns travel, the method suits phones and other weak devices.
arxiv-2507-04510:
Yikang Zhao and co-authors present DFFNet, a network that classifies land cover by fusing several kinds of satellite data. Their paper appeared in 2025. Some sensors record hundreds of colors; others use radar or laser height. Each sees the land differently, and joining them is hard. The team's design works partly in the frequency domain, where patterns repeat at different scales.

A dynamic filter block learns its own frequency filters from each input, so it adapts to varied land types. A fusion block then mixes color and space cues across the data types, shuffling channels to force interaction. On two benchmark data sets the method beat leading rivals. The authors will release the code, aiming at better maps for farming, forests, and disaster watch.
arxiv-2507-04810:
Alexandre Meneceur, Vincent Lignon, and Martin Rosalie test for chaos in economic data in a twenty twenty-five paper. They use thirty years of data on joblessness, inflation, and the exchange rate. A tool called GPoM searches the data for a set of equations that fits it.

The chosen model has three linked equations, and its path through space forms a chaotic attractor, a tangled loop the path never quite repeats.
