It lists design decisions and reader traits that shape a chart's order of communicated information, then shows how to use it when judging and redesigning graphics.
arxiv-2509-09910:
Poorna Talkad Sukumar and 2 co-authors study how people react emotionally to data pictures in this 2025 paper. The question is racial homophily, the pull toward one's own racial group. An earlier study using bar charts found no such effect in responses to mass shooting data. This team redesigned the test with anthropographics, charts built from human figures. They also used a larger sample.

In a crowdsourced study with 720 people, each viewer saw victims from one racial group highlighted, either their own group or another. Across all conditions, viewers whose own group was highlighted showed a modest but real rise in negative feeling. The authors offer this as early evidence that homophily can surface in responses to data displays, at least with human-figure charts.
arxiv-2509-10010:
Adnan Ahmad and 3 co-authors compare small open-source language models on a dialogue task in this 2025 paper. In task-oriented chatbots, one user message can carry several intents at once, and the system must catch them all. The team tested Llama2, Mistral, and Yi models, each under eight billion parameters, on the MultiWOZ 2.1 benchmark in a few-shot setup.

Mistral came out best among the generative models, leading on most of the fourteen intent classes. A supervised BERT classifier, fine-tuned in the older style, still beat every few-shot model. The paper also records inference time and memory needs, giving builders a practical guide to what small local models can and cannot yet do for dialogue understanding.
arxiv-2509-10310:
Finding every lamp post on a city map sounds simple until addresses blur and records disagree. Evan Murphy, Marco Viola, and Vladimir A. Krylov address precise geolocation of street furniture in this 2025 paper, a task councils face when monitoring public assets in dense urban areas.

Their framework paints energy maps that encode how likely each spot is to hold an asset, in a format that can absorb outside geographic data such as road maps and placement rules. A stochastic birth-and-death optimizer then searches for the most probable arrangement of objects. Trials built around real street-lighting records from central Dublin show the method can map assets accurately and at scale. The authors promise a public code release alongside the paper.
arxiv-2509-10410:
Pei Liu and five co-authors model how DNA gets knotted inside virus shells in this 2025 applied mathematics paper. Bacteriophages pack a micron-long genome into a capsid only tens of nanometers wide. That tight confinement orders the DNA like a chromonic liquid crystal and tangles it into knots, matching what experiments see.

Their model pairs a vector field, found by minimizing the Oseen-Frank energy of nematic liquid crystals under chromonic rules, with a line tracing the DNA's central axis. A snag: that energy forbids the defects knots require. So they start from the ideal field and a helical line, then add knots through random perturbations driven by splay and twist, simulated with a Langevin system. The resulting knot patterns are compared with published experiments.
arxiv-2509-10910:
Kiyoshi Igusa and Gordana Todorov tell the story of signed exceptional sequences in this 2025 paper. The concept is their own, introduced in 2017. Exceptional sequences have a long history in representation theory, with ties to combinatorics. The signed variant is newer. It was realized after the fact that the category of noncrossing partitions is a special case.

As a short history, the paper traces how the idea grew. It grew out of the authors' work on cluster combinatorics, link invariants, and algebraic K-theory. Hereditary algebras are the focus. The paper also acknowledges the sequel. Buan and Marsh introduced tau-exceptional sequences. They carried the definitions and theorems over to every finite-dimensional algebra. For readers entering the area, the paper doubles as a map. It shows who proved what, and why the signs matter.
arxiv-2509-11410:
Roberta C. R. Mota and 4 co-authors present a lens tool for exploring three-dimensional data in virtual reality in this 2025 paper. Complex scenes often mix surfaces and flow lines, and analysts need to inspect one region closely without losing the wider picture. Their 3De lens fuses two older lens ideas, a volumetric 3D lens and a surface decal lens, into one instrument that works across geometry types.

Placed inside a virtual environment, the lens supports direct hand manipulation, so exploration feels like handling the data itself. Two domain examples show the lens building custom views that combine surfaces with streamlines. The authors offer the technique as a flexible focus-and-context aid for exploratory analysis of layered 3D data.
arxiv-2509-11510:
Rishab Parthasarathy, Michael Popik, and Noah Haefner built a radio converter as an analog electronics project. This 2025 engineering paper seeks a circuit that turns AM signals into FM ones. Both signals must stay inside their proper radio bands.

The incoming AM signal is first demodulated to its audio envelope. The envelope then drives a voltage-controlled oscillator. The oscillator re-modulates it as FM, far up the dial. The leap is about eighty-six megahertz. Audio fidelity stays high through the jump. The team built, measured, and showed the working system. They note its teaching value too. The project exercised design, analysis, and building skills for radio-frequency circuits.
arxiv-2509-11610:
Michal Botur and Tomasz Kowalski generalize a classic construction of semigroup theory. This 2025 algebra paper extends the two-sided wreath product. That product combines semigroups in a layered way. The authors develop the base of a broader construction.

For groups, the new construction matches the usual wreath product. Nothing is lost in that case. The payoff comes in decomposition theory. The Krohn-Rhodes theorem breaks finite semigroups into simple pieces. Their version sharpens that theorem. The three-element flip-flop monoid in the standard statement is swapped out. A two-element semilattice takes its place. A finer building block gives a finer account of assembly.
arxiv-2509-11910:
Markus Teller and three co-authors store qubits in an array of crystal memories. This 2025 quantum optics paper treats random-access quantum memory. Any stored qubit can be fetched on demand in such a memory. Quantum repeaters and photonic processors could use one. Solid-state memories are a leading platform.

The team stored path and time-bin qubits across ten memory cells. The cells are temporally multiplexed with controllable addressing. Weak laser pulses at the single-photon level carried the qubits. Arbitrary combinations of cells held them. Read-out came on demand. Fidelities averaged in the mid-nineties for path qubits and low nineties for time-bin qubits. Classical bounds were beaten for every cell. One time-bin qubit was parked in two cells at once and read out together.
arxiv-2509-12010:
Copying an expert into a new setting fails when many reward functions explain the same demonstrations yet disagree on what to do next. Filippo Lazzati and one co-author confront that ambiguity in inverse reinforcement learning in 2025, and propose picking the average policy.

Their criterion averages, in effect, over the policies induced by a bounded subset of the rewards consistent with the expert's behavior. The surprise is practical: that average policy comes from planning with a single reward, the centroid of the subset, which the authors derive in closed form. An efficient algorithm estimates the centroid from an offline pile of demonstrations alone, and simulations illustrate how the resulting behavior relates to the expert's own.
arxiv-2509-12310:
Old Sun-like stars spin faster than theory says they should, a puzzle blamed on their magnetic braking weakening with age. Federica Chiti and three co-authors test that story in 2025 by mapping the magnetic field of tau Ceti, a nearby Sun-like star already in the weakened-braking regime.

Using polarized light gathered at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope, they build the first Zeeman Doppler image of the star. The field is strikingly simple, stable, and feeble, mostly a tilted dipole with a strength well below what standard braking models predict. The map directly confirms the weakened dipole the hypothesis requires, and sets a sensitivity benchmark.
arxiv-2509-12410:
Expansive operators stretch small differences until they become visible, a basic engine of chaos in linear dynamics. Nilson C. Bernardes and two co-authors widen that theory in 2025 from Banach spaces to arbitrary locally convex spaces, the broader setting where many natural function spaces live.

Their average expansivity notion gets full characterizations for weighted shift operators on Fréchet sequence spaces, the workhorse examples of the field. A partial answer to a recent open problem follows for uniform expansivity on Köthe sequence spaces. The paper rounds out the picture with general properties of the several expansivity flavors and concrete examples of each.
arxiv-2509-12510:
Wei Shao and 5 co-authors propose an unsupervised way to judge the quality of wearable heart signals in a 2025 paper. Photoplethysmography, an optical method used in billions of devices, tracks blood flow from the wrist. Motion, poor perfusion, and ambient light easily corrupt its waveform and endanger downstream health analytics.

Their pipeline first trains a contrastive network on hundreds of hours of raw, unlabeled data from varied devices, learning representations stable across emitters and motion. Each embedding is then converted into a small topological signature using persistent homology, a method that summarizes shape, and clustered. The densest cluster is taken as acceptable signals, yielding a binary quality index without labeled training data. The approach works for any such device, the authors argue.
arxiv-2509-13010:
Christian Kirkham, Dominic Anstey and Eloy de Lera Acedo fit drift over time in 2025 for sky radio hunts of the first stars. The faint global signal needs a rock-steady gauge. Past gauges skip time data and assume match traits of sources.

Their noise-wave gauge fits a surface over time and pitch at once. Fits fill gaps to each antenna read time. On fake REACH data with a drifting amp, drift is cut out. New terms drop source match guesses and cut clashes in fits. Fakes then match truth to a hair, with spectrum error cut by near all.
arxiv-2509-13210:
Ligang Chang, Shengkai Xu and five co-authors detect violence in public camera video in 2025 with Vi-SAFE. Small targets, clutter, and real-time needs strain watch systems. Split spatial and time steps offer a lean path.

A slimmed detector finds human zones first, using a light backbone and focus tricks plus pruning. A time segment net then sorts clips as violent or not. Training stays split by task. On the RWF-2000 set the pair beats the time net alone and prior methods on score and speed. The design suits live public safety feeds.
arxiv-2509-13310:
Liangcai Su and 21 co-authors propose continual pre-training for agent models in a 2025 paper. Language models have grown into agents: systems that use tools on their own and reason through many steps. Built that way, agents keep falling short on agent tasks.

The authors name a root cause. A solid agentic foundation model does not exist yet. So post-training must do two jobs at once. It must teach a wide range of agent behaviours, and it must line those behaviours up with expert demonstrations. Their answer is to put agentic continual pre-training first, as the opening step in training a deep research agent. On that base they built a model called AgentFounder. Across ten benchmarks it reached the best results reported, while keeping its tool use strong.
arxiv-2509-13410:
Ashwat Jain resolves in 2025 a multipartite entanglement gauge by symmetry for all distinguishable particle systems with local symmetry. The gauge is the global entanglement of Meyer and Wallach. Symmetry resolution splits a measure into charge sectors.

For Haar random state ensembles, equipartition holds in full. Leading acts plus finite-size corrections follow a power law in local degrees of freedom. Consequences for the broader symmetry-resolved paradigm are discussed. Lab checks that could test the pattern are sketched. Random ensembles thus obey a tidy split law for this multipartite gauge.
arxiv-2509-13610:
Fabian L. Seidler and three co-authors model the skies of hot rocky exoplanets in a 2025 planetary science paper. Such planets may hold thin mineral atmospheres boiled off magma oceans, and telescope spectra hint that the planet 55 Cancri e has a carbon-rich one. The team asks which spectral features reveal an atmosphere's origin and interior state.

Their coupled atmosphere-interior model computes equilibrium gases from rock-forming and volatile elements, including how gases split between magma and air. Oxygen fugacity, a measure of how oxidized the system is, turned out to control the spectral shape most. Certain features can separate accreted gas from outgassed gas, though total air mass stays hard to pin down, and current data rule out some scenarios for 55 Cancri e.
arxiv-2509-13810:
K. M. Kwan and eleven co-authors demonstrate loss-tolerant detection of squeezed light in a 2025 quantum optics paper. Squeezed states reduce noise in one property of light below the usual quantum limit, enabling sharper measurements, but at wavelengths near two micrometers photodiodes waste much of the signal, erasing the advantage.

The team place a phase-sensitive amplifier before the detector, boosting the squeezed vacuum while it is still intact. Effective detection efficiency rose from about three quarters to nearly ninety-five percent, and observed squeezing doubled to the highest level yet reported at this wavelength, in the audio frequency band. Better shot-noise clearance also widened the useful measurement band toward lower frequencies, a result aimed at future gravitational-wave detectors.
arxiv-2509-13910:
Hao Su and fifteen co-authors hunt ultra-diffuse galaxies with deep learning in a 2025 astronomy paper. These galaxies are large but incredibly faint. Their surface brightness sits below the usual detection comfort zone. Traditional searches miss them across wide sky areas. The Kilo-Degree Survey covers a large patch of sky. It is exactly where automation should pay off.

The team adapted a network built for low surface brightness systems in another survey. They retrained it in steps for KiDS data, starting from a small training sample. Confirmed ultra-diffuse galaxies are rare, so samples stay small. The network flagged roughly thirty-three hundred candidates. Visual inspection kept five hundred forty-five high-quality ones. The keepers include rediscoveries of known systems and new candidates in about fifteen local groups and clusters.
arxiv-2509-14110:
Hans Ringström, writing alone in 2025, builds a local existence theory for Einstein equations coupled to a nonlinear scalar field. The gauge choice is of constant mean curvature type, a way to slice spacetime into time steps. Initial shapes are closed and parallelisable manifolds.

Ringström proves solutions exist for a short time, are unique, and persist under a clear continuation rule. Solutions also vary stably when starting data change slightly, a property called Cauchy stability. Earlier gauge results covered only torus shaped space and missed the scalar field case. The theory is groundwork. A companion work uses it to prove past global stability results for a family of cosmological models, where control near the start matters most.
arxiv-2509-14210:
Seth Farrell, Chenghao Li and Henrik Christensen describe GLIDE in 2025, a team system for search and rescue in places no one has mapped yet. Two drones in the air work with one ground vehicle below. One drone looks for victims, while the other scouts the ground ahead.

Inside GLIDE, the searching drone marks victim spots for the ground vehicle, and the scouting drone sends updates on where the ground vehicle can safely drive. The vehicle mixes those aerial cues with its own sensors and keeps replanning its route. Tests with a golf cart as the ground vehicle, plus separate simulations, showed faster arrival and safer travel than without the split roles and guided planning.
arxiv-2509-14310:
Samuel Patrone, Nikita Blinov and Ryan Plestid revisit axion like particles in 2025, light hypothetical particles that beam dump experiments may create. Two facilities anchor the study: SHiP at CERN and BDX at Jefferson Lab. Past forecasts counted only a few production routes.

Earlier work used particles from the main beam, or high energy photons from meson decays at SHiP. Patrone and colleagues add production inside the full electromagnetic shower that spreads through the target. Including the shower raises predicted visible decays by about tenfold across a wide mass range. Updated sensitivity curves for SHiP and new forecasts for BDX follow. Both facilities could probe regions of axion parameter space that remain unexplored so far.
arxiv-2509-14510:
Sandra Q. Liu, Yuxiang Ma and Edward H. Adelson extend a soft tactile robot finger in 2025, the GelSight Baby Fin Ray. The device mixes a camera with a soft fin shaped structure that bends on contact. Camera based touch captures force, shape and texture richly.

Earlier work showed the finger digging through clutter and sorting nuts in shells. New learning tasks test finer skill: telling nut textures apart through the shell, and estimating contact force and position. Ablation studies with popular neural networks show which design choices drive performance. Soft tactile fingers that can feel texture and force could help robots handle fragile or hidden objects where vision alone fails.
arxiv-2509-14810:
Arpan Bhattacharyya, Sayed Gool, and S. Shajidul Haque study Krylov complexity in open quantum systems in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Krylov complexity measures how an operator spreads under time evolution. Open systems also exchange energy with an environment, so dissipation and decoherence, the fading of quantum coherence, shape that spread.

The authors work with Lindblad master equations for systems coupled to bosonic baths, especially the Caldeira-Leggett model. For a damped harmonic oscillator, complexity shows clear signs of energy loss. At high temperature, complexity settles to a steady value when the full equation is used. Separating the effects, the decoherence part alone keeps oscillating like a closed system. Surprisingly, complexity shows no clear marker when decoherence begins, which the authors trace to the basis used to define it.
arxiv-2509-14910:
Ediline Nguessap, Antonio Roque, and Fernando Ferreira model a ring of heat-sensitive nerve cells linked by mixed synapses, in a 2025 paper. Each cell obeys the FitzHugh-Nagumo rules, a simple two-part model of firing. An outside electric field acts on the ring, and the cells' heat response shapes how they fire.

Runs of the model range from messy, unlinked firing to clean traveling waves. Some runs show chimera states, where synced and unsynced groups live side by side. Links of the chemical kind, spread over a range, are what keep the waves and chimeras stable. Pure local electric links give only disorder. Field rate and reach act as control knobs, while cell size tunes how strongly each cell feels the field.
arxiv-2509-15110:
Dan Zhang and five co-authors train smoother reward models for language models using temporal difference learning in a 2025 machine learning paper. Reward models grade model outputs and drive both reinforcement learning and inference-time checking. Many existing reward models judge inconsistently across steps, which makes policy updates ineffective and training unstable.

Their method, TDRM, penalizes temporal differences so a process reward model's scores evolve smoothly along a solution. At inference, the smoother models lift best-of-N selection and tree search results noticeably. During reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, models guided by these reward models reach baseline quality with a small fraction of the training data. Gains appear across eight model variants from several families and sizes, suggesting temporal consistency is a broadly useful property for reward modeling.
arxiv-2509-15410:
Vishwak Srinivasan, a lone author, studies when a mix of data sources keeps nice math traits. Two traits matter here: one bounds how fast a random walk settles, the other bounds how fast doubt shrinks. Many models are built by mixing simpler parts, and users need to know if the mix keeps these traits. Past checks were split by case.

Srinivasan gives new rules that cover both traits at once, using a broad frame built on a class of entropy measures. The rules hold for many step by step random processes. That lets him track how the traits change as such a process runs. The payoff is a clean error check for estimates made by random sampling methods used in practice.
arxiv-2509-15510:
Danqing Chen leads a team that checks what large language models did to jobs in their first years. Since late 2022, these tools have spread fast, with claims of big gains and fears of lost jobs. The team ask whether pay and joblessness moved in fields more exposed to the tools. They compare fields with high and low exposure over time.

Using a method that builds a fair comparison path, they estimate the effect of exposure after ChatGPT came out. Workers in more exposed jobs saw pay rise, while jobless rates stayed flat. The team read this as an early shift through pay, not through workers moving jobs. The paper covers short term effects only.
arxiv-2509-15810:
Chen Wang leads a team that breeds new test problems for auto designed optimizers. Meta learning can train a neural policy that designs search algorithms, sparing human experts. The training set shapes how well that policy travels. Standard suites are narrow, so policies can overfit and fail on new problems.

Their method, LSRE, first trains an encoder that maps problem traits into a flat, two way space. Even sampling on a grid in that space gives hidden codes for varied problems. A genetic program then searches for formulas close to those codes. The bred problems are diverse by design. Policies trained on them should generalize better to unseen tasks.
arxiv-2509-16010:
Cloning a voice from a few clips can make speech tools feel personal, but sharing voice data raises privacy risks. Qi Wang and four co-authors propose Fed-PISA, a method that trains voice cloning across many devices without pooling raw data. Each device keeps the speaker's tone traits at home and sends only a small style part to a shared server.

A matching step, drawn from methods that pair like users, builds a custom model for each client from peers with like styles. Tests show gains in style, natural sound, and speaker likeness over standard shared training. The gains come with very low data transfer costs.
arxiv-2509-16110:
Mexican cities have grown outward for decades, even as their centers lose people. Gonzalo G. Peraza-Mues and four co-authors study sixty-nine metro areas from 1990 to 2020 with census data. They build a model of city form from size, density, and spatial layout, using a radial curve and an expansion factor to compare cities across time.

Over thirty years the urban population nearly doubled, yet centers lost about two and a half million residents. Average distance from the center grew by more than a quarter. The study gives planners a clear way to track sprawl and its costs.
arxiv-2509-16310:
Objects that mimic black holes but have a hard surface instead of a horizon ring with tones that may shift under tiny changes. Kyriakos Destounis and three co-authors test how a lump of matter placed outside such an object affects those tones. The lump stands in for the messy surroundings real objects live in.

Loosely packed objects lose their main tone under the lump, while ultra-compact ones keep theirs steady. Higher tones shift in both cases, and some outer tones can morph into main tones as the lump moves out. Matter can amplify these shifts but cannot by itself force a full modal breakdown.
arxiv-2509-16410:
Can the richness of a data set foretell when quantum learning will beat classic methods? Christophe Pere builds a frame around that claim and tests it under rules fixed in advance across twenty-seven data sets. The central forecast fails: a combined complexity score did not predict the quantum edge, which swung with the choice of classic rival instead.

Against a weak rival the signal looked real, but against the best of six classic models it vanished. A built-in quantum pattern could still be caught by a matched measure, so quantum-sensitive structure is not ruled out. The null result ties any edge to baseline, encoding, and access.
arxiv-2509-16710:
Kevin Player, working alone, revisits a classic effect in quantum theory in a 2025 paper. A fast-moving observer who speeds up at a steady rate should feel empty space as warm. That claim is the Unruh effect. Player asks how driven, linked excitations change that warm response. The work draws a likeness with squeezing, a trick from quantum optics.

He builds smooth packet models that bridge two views of the effect. One view is tied to wedge-shaped regions of space. The other is tied to tight, local sources. His packets use special functions to blend the two. The result places the classic warm response inside a wider frame where local structure also matters.
arxiv-2509-16910:
Daxiang Li and Zhichao Zhang extend a signal tool to graphs in a 2025 paper. The Hilbert transform builds analytic signals that expose envelope and phase. On graphs, the classic form is stuck in one domain, uses a fixed shift, and lacks tuning knobs. Their fractional version loosens all three limits.

They define the new transform and prove its core traits. A method for analytic signals on graphs follows. Tests cover edge detection, anomaly spotting, and speech sorting. The new tool beat the classic graph form in each test. Flexible graph signals could aid sensor networks, where data live on irregular links rather than neat grids.
arxiv-2509-17210:
Shaunak A. Mehta and Dylan P. Losey wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on making robot arms both safe and precise. Their focus is the series elastic actuator, which places a spring between motor and arm. The spring softens crashes with people, a clear safety gain. The same spring, though, makes the arm wobble and blurs fine motion.

The authors list the linear control and hardware setups for these actuators and test how each choice shapes softness, safety, and tracking. Most past work controls from the load side of the spring. They find control from the motor side works better, letting simple controllers use a wide range of gains while staying passive and safe. With a damper in the spring path, the setup tracks well. Their advice: build in low stiffness, then use strong control gains.
arxiv-2509-17310:
Gengyu Liu and Jianlu Zhang study a class of partial differential equations in a 2025 arXiv paper. The equations are contact Hamilton-Jacobi equations, set on a closed manifold, where the Hamiltonian depends on position, slope, and the unknown value itself. They ask which pairs of a solution and a constant can solve the equation in the viscosity sense.

First they prove a comparison principle, a tool that orders any two candidate solutions, by drawing on Mather measures from dynamics. Then they describe the full structure of the set of constants for which the equation can be solved at all. Worked examples test whether their approach is sharp. The Hamiltonian needs to be convex and coercive in slope, but only non-decreasing in the value, a weaker demand than many past studies used. The results firm up the theory of weak solutions.
arxiv-2509-17610:
Zhenghao Wang and Shuo Xiong propose a formal frame for studying games, built on an analogy with quantum mechanics. Their 2025 arXiv paper constructs a quantum coin toss on a quantum circuit as a first probe. The match between how a quantum system behaves and how a game behaves leads them to a state-operation paradigm.

From that paradigm grows the State Space Interpretation, or SSI. In it, a game is a state space, and a play session is a path of evolution through that space. Formal pieces such as state space and evolution path rest on linear algebra, quantum mechanics, and statistical mechanics. The authors offer SSI as a fresh lens for game design and game studies. Beyond new vocabulary, they hope it links game research to fields that already think in states and transitions.
arxiv-2509-18010:
Sara Papi and 4 co-authors ask how much of a speech model's focus scores truly explain its output. Their 2025 paper deals with speech-to-text models, where a cross-attention step links heard speech to written words. Folk have reused those scores for time stamps and word alignment, as if they showed true links.

The team checks those scores against maps of which input parts drive the output. Across tongues, tasks, and model sizes, the scores line up fair to strong with the maps. Yet they catch just about half of the input weight. Even at best, they miss a fair share of how the model reads speech.
arxiv-2509-18110:
Mrigank Dhingra and 3 co-authors shrink equation solvers by working patch by patch. Their 2025 paper deals with neural operators, nets that learn to solve a class of equations from data. A global squeeze of a huge solution field costs a lot, which caps scale.

Their frame cuts the field into small patches and squeezes each patch on its own. Two patch styles are weighed: one that pools patches into a global code, and one that keeps each patch local. Add-ons such as overlap with smoothing, and a net-based polish, lift the best style. Run time fell near fourfold, with score held high.
arxiv-2509-18410:
Principal bundles are a core shape in geometry, but each field defines them in its own way. Robin Cockett and Florian Schwarz seek one definition that covers all of them in this 2025 paper. Smooth geometry, topology, and algebraic geometry each stress a different side of the same idea. All versions share one trait: locally, the shape looks like a base space times a group.

The authors build their account in join restriction categories, a language for maps that are only partly defined. A gluing construction lets local pieces join into global objects. In that language, they define principal bundles in pure category terms. They also show the tangent bundle of a group splits as the group times its tangent space. That tangent space carries a Lie algebra structure, the classic partner of a Lie group. The work unifies results that were scattered across fields.
arxiv-2509-18510:
Matroids are abstract structures that capture how sets can be swapped while staying valid. Isabel Detherage studies a random walk on those swaps in this 2025 paper. The walk moves between bases, the maximal valid sets, by exchanging one element at a time. She measures the walk's curvature, a number that says whether nearby paths tend to merge or spread.

Detherage proves both lower and upper bounds on that curvature, using the Ollivier-Ricci notion. She gives examples of basis exchange walks with curvature that never dips below zero. She also gives examples where the curvature does go negative. The contrast shows the walk's geometry depends on the matroid's own structure. Curvature bounds matter because they hint at how fast such walks mix. The paper is a compact, proof-focused contribution to combinatorics.
arxiv-2509-19210:
Shouvik Sadhukhan and C. S. Narayanamurthy build a theory of how dense materials made of tiny dipoles respond to light, aimed at lasers wobbling through turbulence. They extend the classic Lorentz oscillator model, which pictures each dipole as a mass on a spring, by adding stronger nonlinear springs and letting dipoles interact through a shared field description. The system is written as matrices, and its collective vibration patterns, or normal modes, are found by diagonalization.

Starting from the linear response of those modes, the authors add nonlinear corrections order by order. The result is an effective description of how the material's optical response spreads nonlocally through the medium. A final step derives the structured light field that emerges. The framework links microscopic dipole motion to macroscopic beam behavior, with scintillation, the twinkling of a beam in turbulence, as the target application.
arxiv-2509-19710:
Finding the equation behind data is a shortcut to understanding, but noisy data yields many near-miss formulas. Somjit Roy and three co-authors give symbolic regression a probabilistic footing. Candidate formulas form forests of symbolic trees. A prior over tree shape favors simpler formulas, in the spirit of Occam's razor.

A summary method keeps several plausible formulas rather than crowning one winner. That spread expresses honest uncertainty about the true law. The authors also prove that the posterior concentrates near good approximations as data grows. Such guarantees are rare in this field, where heuristic search rules. Scientists in physics and biology could use the method to propose laws with confidence levels attached. Interpretable formulas remain the goal, now with error bars.
arxiv-2509-19910:
Approximations in graphical models trade accuracy for speed, and the Bethe approximation is the field's workhorse. Pascal O. Vontobel studies the ratio between the true partition sum and its Bethe estimate. Observers noticed that this ratio often sits near the square of a similar ratio for a simpler degree-two version. The squared pattern was folklore without proof.

Vontobel gives justifications for the relationship and analyzes both ratios for two families of log-supermodular models. The degree-two ratio is easier to analyze, so the link has practical value. Partition sums underlie probabilities in vision, coding, and statistical physics. Understanding the error of the standard approximation sharpens every tool built on it. The paper is a solo theoretical contribution.
arxiv-2509-20110:
Edgar Blokhuis wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on surface chemistry. It concerns surfactants, the soap-like molecules that lower the surface tension of water. For some solutions, measurements show a puzzling dip in surface tension at low concentration. Standard theory seemed to say molecules were leaving the surface, which made little sense.

The dip is now blamed on trace contamination, often by the alcohol dodecanol. Blokhuis gives the first full quantitative account of how that tiny impurity creates the dip. His analysis joins a statistical thermodynamic treatment of a mixed surface layer with a model of mixed micelle formation. From these he derives a new formula for surface tension. He then checks the formula against experiments on both ionic and non-ionic surfactant systems.
arxiv-2509-20210:
Enrique Macias-Virgos and Daniel Tanre wrote this short 2025 arXiv note in algebraic topology. They study a quasi-projective space built inside the symplectic group of quaternionic matrices. Their measure is the subspace Lusternik-Schnirelmann category, a number that gauges how hard a space is to cover with simple pieces. Earlier work had settled only the smallest case.

The authors prove the category equals two for every size of the space. Their proof uses a quaternionic logarithm, adapting an idea Singhof used in the complex case. The result extends the known second case to all cases at once. It also sits in interesting contrast with a related space whose category equals three. Short notes like this one often complete a pattern left open by several earlier papers.
arxiv-2509-20310:
Photographing planets around other stars demands extreme contrast and sharpness. Theo Bodrito and five co-authors apply deep learning to that challenge in a 2025 arXiv paper. A planet's faint light drowns in the glare and noise of its host star. Their model treats that corrupting nuisance component statistically, across whole image series and at several scales.

The statistical model is built into a learnable architecture shaped by the physics of the problem. It merges many looks at one star so the detection signal is as strong as the data allows. Tests used real data from the SPHERE instrument on the Very Large Telescope. Detection sensitivity improved significantly. Estimates of planet position and brightness also grew more accurate. The work shows how physics-aware learning can beat generic image processing at the telescope.
arxiv-2509-20910:
Information geometry puts a metric on probability distributions, and thermodynamics gives that geometry a physical flavor. Prosper Rosaire Mama Assandje and three co-authors study the Souriau-Fisher metric on the rotation groups SO(2) and SO(3) in a 2025 mathematics paper. Their tools come from Souriau's thermodynamics of Lie groups.

The authors examine how gradient systems built from these metrics behave. A key object is a 2-cocycle, which can make such a system completely integrable or disturb that property. They show how the cocycle locally modifies the Fisher metric on a coadjoint orbit. The modification is written explicitly using brackets and central extensions of the groups. The work connects statistical geometry with Hamiltonian mechanics on groups.
arxiv-2509-21010:
A drug should be judged by what it does to cells, not only by the target it binds. Haotian Guo and Hui Liu tackle that gap in a 2025 paper on making new molecules. Older tools lean on gene profiles and miss how a molecule perturbs the cell around it.

Their model, SmilesGEN, joins two autoencoders in one shared latent space. One encodes drug structures, built on a pretrained net for molecular strings. The other encodes gene expression profiles, the pattern of genes switched on in a cell. Joint training captures how a drug's push and the cell's response interact. Reinforcement learning with several goals then steers the search toward molecules with the wanted effects on cells, aiming at new drug candidates with real healing potential.
arxiv-2509-21210:
Aerial robots that can point their body any way they like need new models and new controllers. Authorship belongs to Ali Kafili Gavgani and 4 co-authors. Normal multi rotor craft cannot set their tilt apart from their position. That limits tasks that need a fixed pose in tight places. The authors study designs that add control inputs. Extra inputs let the craft aim the axes of its propellers.

They derive full dynamic models for each design and check them with multibody simulations. They build two controllers, a robust sliding mode type and a new PID based type with gravity offset. A custom allocation plan handles the complex input links. It also aims to save battery by cutting power use. Tests show the controllers coped with strong disturbances and uncertainty.
arxiv-2509-21310:
Older benchmarks no longer stretch the semantic understanding of strong language models. Its authors are Samarth Goel and 2 co-authors. Language models score well on old tests, so harder tests are needed. Semantic understanding means grasping meaning, not just matching words. The authors built SAGE to probe that skill in depth. It tests both embedding models and similarity metrics.

SAGE covers five areas, from human preference alignment to retrieval robustness. It uses adversarial cases, noisy transforms, and fine human judgment tasks. The data spans more than thirty data sets. Nine embedding models and classical metrics were tested. No single approach won across all areas. Even top models left large gaps, which shows room for growth in meaning based AI.
arxiv-2509-21710:
Knowledge graph retrieval can strengthen language model reasoning if the graph index fits the query. Xiaojun Wu and 8 co-authors present a graph retrieval framework in a 2025 paper. High quality knowledge graphs are not scalable to build by hand. Automatically extracted graphs depend on extractor quality, especially with smaller local models. Their system, Think on Graph 3.0, builds the index dynamically instead.

A multi agent mechanism evolves context and retrieval together. A heterogeneous graph index joins chunks, triplets, and communities. Dual evolution adapts both the query and the retrieved subgraph during reasoning. The targeted index enables precise evidence retrieval and reasoning. Heterogeneous graphs, mixing text chunks with structured facts, are the setting. Adaptive retrieval replaces reliance on a fixed, prebuilt graph.
arxiv-2509-22210: G. Akishev studies approximation theory in Lorentz spaces, a family of function spaces that refine the usual Lebesgue scale. The 2025 article concerns the mixed modulus of smoothness of positive order. That tool measures how smooth a function is jointly across several variables. The article also treats the best approximation of such functions by an angle, a restricted class of approximating functions. Akishev proves properties of the mixed modulus and a sharp form of the inverse theorem of approximation theory for this setting.
arxiv-2509-22410:
Testing a new chip design is slow, because cycle-accurate simulators crawl and test traces are narrow. Shayne Wadle and 3 co-authors train a deep learning model to predict cycle-level speed for designs that do not exist yet. The model learns from traits that do not depend on one chip's layout. It can then run on real, current chips to judge future ones.

A light hardware tracer and a sampling plan keep the load on users tiny. The system runs fast on a standard graphics chip with near zero slowdown. A custom on-chip helper speeds it up far more. The team shows the tool can test real apps at large scale.
arxiv-2509-22510:
Gautam Siddharth Kashyap, Mark Dras, and Usman Naseem steer language models toward three goals at once: helpful, harmless, and honest. Tuning for one goal often overwrites the others. Prior steering methods treat each goal alone, or branch the model but transform each branch on its own. Their method, AMBS, keeps the branches tied to one shared representation.

In stage one, the model computes a shared hidden state once. In stage two, that state is copied into one path per goal, and each path shifts relative to a shared reference. The paths yield goal-specific replies in a single pass, which decoding then merges. Tests across backbones showed steady gains on all three goals at good speed.
arxiv-2509-22710:
Pavan Reddy and Aditya Sanjay Gujral confine adversarial noise to a small patch of the image. Classic attacks perturb every pixel to fool a classifier. A binary mask in their study restricts the noise to chosen regions. They test three standard attacks, FGSM, PGD, and C&W, in both global and localized forms. Localized attacks cut mean pixel change a lot and scored better on standard imperceptibility measures.

The gains cost more compute and a modest drop in attack success. Iterative methods, PGD and C&W, held up far better under the mask than the single-step FGSM. The authors frame the trade-offs as guidance for both attackers and defenders designing robust systems.
arxiv-2509-23410:
Pruning a language model into tiles, each either dense or half-sparse, gives a dial between speed and quality. Younes Hourri, Mohammad Mozaffari, and Maryam Mehri Dehnavi built PATCH on that idea. Unstructured sparsity keeps accuracy but blocks GPU speedups. Fixed half sparsity runs fast but degrades quality. PATCH assigns each weight tile a learned mask choice.

Sparsity can vary by layer and land anywhere in the allowed range. Models from half a billion to thirteen billion parameters were tested. On one GPU setup, end-to-end speed rose clearly over dense runs. Accuracy also beat the top fixed-pattern pruning rival. The gap to dense accuracy narrowed throughout.
arxiv-2509-23510:
Ranking new language models by human votes is slow and costly. Ashwin Ramaswamy and 2 co-authors test a cheaper stand-in: how consistently a model judges contests between models. When a model is asked to pick winners in matchups, the steadiness of its picks forms a score of its own. That score tracks the model's human-given Elo rating with high correlation, at ninety-one percent.

The proxy needs no human data and no prior knowledge of the models. It can be computed quickly for each new release. The authors offer it as an independent check at a time when new models appear daily and some perform far above or below what their size would suggest.
arxiv-2509-24010:
Stars fleeing the galaxy faster than escape speed carry clues about what threw them. Haozhu Fu and 2 co-authors hunt distant hypervelocity candidates among RR Lyrae stars, whose period-based distances are precise. Proper motions come from Gaia's third data release, and radial velocities from SDSS and LAMOST spectra. After quality cuts on more than eight thousand stars with full data, one hundred sixty-five candidates emerged.

Light-curve checks narrowed the list to eighty-seven reliable stars, all beating escape speed on tangential motion alone. Their sky pattern splits two ways: one group aims back to the Galactic Center, another clusters near the Magellanic Clouds. Some seem ejected from dwarf galaxies instead.
arxiv-2509-24110:
Quantum computers need error correction that works amid real noise, and Floquet codes are a prized family for that job. Hideyuki Ozawa and 3 co-authors note a catch: in known Floquet codes, the error signals form tangled hypergraph patterns that slow decoding. Their fix is a hyperbolic color Floquet code.

The code runs six rounds of simple two-qubit measures on a hyperbolic tiling that uses three colors. Each fault then touches at most two detectors, so error signals form plain graph edges. A standard matching decoder can then work fast, at near-linear cost. The code keeps a finite share of logical qubits as it grows, with distance that grows as the log of its size.
arxiv-2509-24210:
Static benchmarks leak into training data, so a high score may mean recall rather than reasoning. Gaurav Srivastava and 7 co-authors built BeyondBench, a test frame that generates fresh problems by algorithm, each with a checked solution. Its suites span arithmetic and statistics, sequence patterns, and hard constraint problems, across three difficulty levels.

Each task draws from a space far larger than any fixed data set, and rewrites yield new-looking but equal problems. The team tested over a hundred models, from small open ones to large closed ones. Scores fell sharply as difficulty rose, and tool use proved decisive for the top systems. Gaps in true reasoning, the results argue, remain wide.
arxiv-2509-24410:
One text prompt should yield many views of the same scene, consistent with each other, if synthetic three-dimensional assets are the goal. Seungwook Kim and 4 co-authors built RapidMV, a text-to-multi-view model that produces dozens of views in a few seconds. Its core is a spatio-angular latent space that encodes both how a view looks and how its angle departs from the rest.

Training is split into strategic steps to make that joint space learn well. RapidMV beat existing methods on consistency and speed, with quality and text alignment that stayed competitive. Faster, steadier multi-view output shortens the path from a prompt to a usable 3D asset.
arxiv-2509-24510:
Test-time training keeps teaching a model on the very task in front of it, and it often helps a lot. Jonas Hübotter and 5 co-authors ask why, since most test data for foundation models is in-distribution, where older adaptation stories do not apply. Their answer: foundation models stay globally underparameterized, so test-time training specializes capacity on the concepts the task actually needs.

Under a linear representation picture, their model achieves far smaller in-distribution error than global training. A sparse autoencoder study on ImageNet backs the picture: related data points share just a few concepts. Scaling studies on image and language tasks confirm where specialization pays most.
arxiv-2509-25810:
Shenao Zhang and co-authors study how to train large language models in a 2025 paper on mid-training, the stage before final tuning. They argue that this stage works best when the model learns a small set of broad actions, not tiny step-by-step moves. Their theory links how well the action set is trimmed to how fast later training can improve the model.

From that theory they build a method called RA3, which finds steady patterns in reasoning and then trains on data built from them. On code-writing tests, the method raised scores on two main benchmarks and helped models learn faster. It also held up on harder test sets, which suggests the approach scales well.
arxiv-2510-00010:
Lazovsky and colleagues build a computational model of taste perception that tries to keep single-cell biophysics honest while still scaling to whole networks. It is a balance computational neuroscience models usually sacrifice one way or the other. Their hybrid design uses detailed Hodgkin-Huxley dynamics for taste receptor cells and efficient Izhikevich spiking neurons for the large network. It has modality-specific receptors for sweet, bitter, umami, salty, and sour, the five pathways in the model.

Ion currents follow Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equations, synapses include glutamate release kinetics, phosphorylation-regulated AMPA trafficking, and spike-timing-dependent plasticity. A genetic algorithm tunes the network to encode taste pleasantness and tell pure from mixed stimuli. The trained network turns unstructured inputs into reported distinct, sparse, reproducible spiking patterns that act as neural fingerprints for each taste quality. It is overall a step toward biologically faithful electronic tongues in real time.
arxiv-2510-00110:
Ylias Sadki, Abhishodh Prakash, and S. L. Sondhi wrote this 2025 theory paper on fractons, particles that barely move. A lone fracton cannot travel on its own, because the rules conserve its dipole moment. The authors build a continuum quantum mechanics for such particles from scratch. They impose symmetry and locality, then ask what single and paired fractons actually do.

A single fracton turns out to have no energy at all, only zero modes. For two fractons, the motion reduces to a classic Sturm-Liouville problem with edge effects. Past a sharp threshold in the edge behavior, the spectrum flips from discrete steps to a continuum. Wave packets then slow down and squeeze into thin layers near the edges. Three-body tests hint at the same strange attractors, suggesting these systems never fully settle.
arxiv-2510-00310:
Akash Dhasade and six colleagues published this 2025 paper on making federated inference robust against bad actors. In federated inference, a server collects predictions from many models that stay local and private. Ensembles built this way are convenient, but their defenses had never been studied. The authors formalize the robustness problem and give the first analysis of this method class.

For simple averaging, they show the combined error stays small under two friendly conditions. Either honest models must mostly agree, or one class must win by a wide margin. Beyond averaging, they recast robust aggregation as an adversarial learning problem. Their DeepSet-based method mixes adversarial training with robust test-time aggregation. It beat existing robust aggregation methods by roughly five to twenty-two accuracy points across benchmarks. The work gives federated systems a clearer security footing.
arxiv-2510-00810:
Kunz, Debess, and Simonsen study how to adapt small language models to Faroese in this 2025 arXiv paper on low-resource languages. Faroese, a North Germanic language of about seventy thousand speakers, has very little training text. Its relatives Icelandic, Danish, and Norwegian share vocabulary and grammar, so transfer from them is promising. The authors continue pretraining English models on each Scandinavian language, separately and merged, before fine-tuning on Faroese.

Since no Faroese benchmarks existed, they built two minimal-pair evaluation sets and added judgements from Faroese linguists. Transfer from related languages proved crucial, but the best source depended on the task. Icelandic improved linguistic accuracy most, while Danish helped comprehension more. The tuning method mattered too: LoRA scored better on acceptability, and full fine-tuning preserved comprehension better. The results give a practical recipe for other small languages with bigger siblings.
arxiv-2510-01110:
Briggs, McDonald, and Shan answer extremal questions about degree sequences and perfect matchings in this 2025 arXiv paper on graph theory. A degree sequence lists how many edges touch each vertex of a graph. Classic results by Lovász, Erdős, and Gallai say when such a sequence can come from a graph that contains some perfect matching. This paper asks the sharper labelled question: which specific pairings can the sequence realize?

The authors show that a sequence can realize at least one perfect matching exactly when it can realize the cross pairing that joins vertex i with vertex n plus one minus i. It can realize every perfect matching exactly when it can realize the adjacent pairing of consecutive vertices. Their main theorem characterizes that second case fully. They also settle a conjecture of Yin and co-authors about packing graphic sequences.
arxiv-2510-01210:
Konstantinidis and co-authors import medicine's rules for minimum study size into chemometrics, where prediction models often train on too little data. Small calibration sets invite overfitting, and overfit models mislead the planetary science they serve. Biomedical research solved this problem with theory-based criteria that chemometrics never adopted.

The paper restates those criteria for multivariable regression with continuous outcomes. Worked ranges show how required size shifts with the number of predictors and expected accuracy. Mars-style spectroscopic inference is exactly the high-stakes setting where the guidance bites. Broader adoption would make published prediction models more trustworthy by construction. Sample size calculation is called a pillar of evidence-based science in the paper. Continuous outcomes keep the focus on regression rather than classification. Astrobiology supplies the motivating audience beyond chemometrics itself. Reliable inference starts before the first measurement is taken or modeled.
arxiv-2510-01610:
Iosue and co-authors show how to learn a broad family of bosonic quantum states from surprisingly few measurements. Reading an unknown quantum state fully grows exponentially expensive, so learnable families matter. Their algorithm efficiently learns any Fock state after an unknown Gaussian transformation scrambles it.

Fourth moments alone pin down such states, the team proves. A hierarchy of state classes defined by finitely many moments extends the picture beyond Gaussian behavior. Invariants under Gaussian operations tell when two states could never be converted into each other. An open question from Aaronson and Grewal falls along the way. BosonSampling states are the famous special case now covered. Sample and time costs both stay efficient as systems grow. Moments act like fingerprints that survive Gaussian scrambling. Learnability results guide which experiments can certify their own states. The method needs fewer measurements for the same certainty in practice.
arxiv-2510-02310:
Davoudiasl tests a proposed ultralight particle against what stars allow. His 2025 physics paper concerns a hypothetical state called eta-w. The idea mirrors a known particle from strong force physics. Some theorists suggest the weak force hides a similar light state. Such a particle would be extremely light. Stars, though, would leak energy through it. Too much leakage would change how stars age and shine. Davoudiasl checks those stellar limits against the proposal.

Red giant stars give the sharpest test in his analysis. Avoiding excess cooling in those stars sets a strong floor. The particle coupling scale must exceed about one hundred trillion electron volts. That floor sits far above the expected weak scale value. The gap spans roughly a thousand fold or more. He also weighs the particle as dark matter or dark energy. Both roles look unlikely on current evidence.
arxiv-2510-02410:
Langer and co-authors teach language models to reason over medical signal traces. Their 2025 paper presents OpenTSLM for combined text and time series work. Clinicians juggle notes with streams like heart and brain signals. Language models read text well but stumble on raw traces. OpenTSLM feeds multivariate series beside clinical text. The model can then explain patterns in the signals themselves. Sleep staging from brain waves is one test setting. Motion sensing from accelerometers is another. Pediatric cardiology partners ground the work in real care.

The system reasons step by step over the numbers. It ties signal features to clinical meaning in words. Open release lets other hospitals test and extend it. Patient facing health tools need this kind of synthesis. Signals without narrative rarely change decisions. A model that narrates traces could support doctors directly.
arxiv-2510-02510:
Kalbouneh and co-authors measure how unevenly the nearby universe expands. Their 2025 cosmology paper avoids assuming any background geometry. They use the Cosmicflows-4 and Pantheon+ samples together. Galaxies and supernovae span a shallow redshift shell nearby. The team builds a field of expansion rate fluctuations. Its average size runs at a few percent of the mean rate. Splitting the field into angular patterns reveals its shape. A dipole pattern dominates at the lowest redshifts. That dipole amplitude sits near two point two percent there.

The dipole fades steadily as redshift grows. By the farthest shell it drops to about half. A quadrupole pattern persists at roughly half the dipole strength. Higher patterns stay smaller across the range. Such maps test whether the universe expands the same way everywhere. Local structure should leave exactly these fingerprints. Precision distance surveys gain a covariant reading tool.
arxiv-2510-02610:
Muvunza and co-authors select predictive features by estimating mutual information with neural networks. Their 2025 machine learning paper introduces a method called MINERVA. Classic filters score each feature against the target alone. That misses targets built from feature interactions. MINERVA judges feature subsets as an ensemble instead. A neural estimator approximates the shared information. Sparsity penalties inside the loss prune weak features. Two stages separate representation learning from selection itself. That split sharpens the importance estimates. The authors craft dependency structures that literature rarely captures.

Synthetic tests gave the method a clean sweep. MINERVA alone picked exactly the right feature set. A real card fraud dataset tested it next. Fraud hid in a tiny slice of three million records. The method still performed strongly there. Feature choice decides what models can learn. Interaction aware filters widen that choice wisely.
arxiv-2510-03010:
Jana and co-authors untangle light and spin effects in layered magnets. The materials are thin films of MnPS3 and NiPS3. Both are van der Waals antiferromagnets with strong direction contrast. Light can excite states where spin and light mix deeply. Sorting out which mechanism drives each glow is hard. Even the basic bandgap of these films was unsettled.

The team used high-grade ab initio theory to settle both points. Their maps show which atoms and orbitals form each band edge. The glowing states trace to a spin flip on a single metal atom. A magnetic field shifts that flip in a telling way. From the shift they read off exchange and anisotropy strengths. The values match older neutron scattering results. Optics can thus probe magnetism in flakes far too small for neutrons. That widens the toolkit for two-dimensional magnetic devices.
arxiv-2510-03110:
Lin, Chen, and Tan fill missing parts of a photo using other views as guides. Reference-driven completion borrows content from extra images. Big viewpoint gaps make that borrowing treacherous. Pure diffusion models often invent content that clashes with the scene. Their framework, GeoComplete, adds plain three-dimensional guidance. A projected point cloud conditions the diffusion process.

Two branches share the work through joint attention. One branch builds the missing region from the masked target. The other reads features from the projected cloud. A masking trick sharpens the use of references. Areas visible in references but hidden in the target are masked in training. The model learns to prize the cues that truly transfer. Benchmark tests gave a large jump in signal quality. Gains topped the best prior methods by a wide margin. Hard cases with severe viewpoint change benefited most.
arxiv-2510-03210:
Hanany shows the free group on two generators hides far more rigid simple quotients than expected. A characteristic subgroup survives every symmetry of the group. Chen, Lubotzky, and Tiep recently found certain simple quotients of this kind. Their examples were projective special linear and unitary groups. They posed two questions about how far the phenomenon extends. This paper resolves both questions affirmatively.

Infinitely many alternating groups occur as such quotients. Simple quotients of arbitrarily large Lie rank occur as well. The Yang-Baxter equation supplies the construction's engine. Generator pairs with strong invariance properties drive the argument. Every primitive element lands in a single orbit under automorphisms. The result pushes against the spirit of the Wiegold conjecture. That conjecture expects no such quotients in higher rank. Rank two behaves differently for a traceable algebraic reason. Explicit equations describe the relevant character varieties.
arxiv-2510-03510:
Dózsa and colleagues present a 2025 paper linking two classic families of methods for recovering the hidden parts of a signal. Prony methods describe signals built from eigenfunctions of an operator and extract their weights and rates. Bernoulli algorithms recover parameters of rational functions inside Hardy spaces. The authors show that any Prony problem can be recast in rational form. That single move connects the two families and lets each borrow the other's strengths.

Working in the rational setting dodges known numerical traps, such as solving huge Vandermonde systems. Experiments cover time delayed system identification and parameter recovery in kernel spaces. Even signals that are not themselves rational yielded their parameters to the rational schemes in the tests. MATLAB code for the methods is public. Engineers who identify systems from measured signals gain a sturdier toolbox, with theory that explains why the rational detour works so well.
arxiv-2510-03610:
Ezetta and Feng present a 2025 arXiv paper describing PentestMCP, a toolkit that lets AI agents run penetration testing tools. Penetration testers follow a kill chain: scanning networks, enumerating resources, fingerprinting services, scanning for flaws, exploiting them, and working after entry. The Model Context Protocol lets agents call external tools through a uniform interface instead of hard wiring each one. The authors built MCP servers wrapping common security tools for each stage of that chain. Developers can compose these servers into custom multi agent testing workflows.

Trials show agents using the toolkit completing baseline tasks that human testers traditionally perform by hand. Performance varies with the underlying model, the authors note. The code is public on GitHub along with the test results. Security teams face far more systems than they can test manually. Agent driven testing with tools could widen coverage, provided its findings stay supervised and verified by humans.
arxiv-2510-04510:
Achim Eckerle, Martin Spitznagel, and Janis Keuper wrote this 2025 paper on predicting city noise in real time. European rules require cities to map noise and plan against it on a regular cycle. Physics solvers give trusted maps, but they run far too slowly for what if studies. Planners need to test road closures, barriers, and work schedules quickly. The team trained a conditional normalizing flow model to draw sound maps from city layouts.

The model produces a standards compliant sound pressure map in about a tenth of a second on one graphics card. That speed is more than two thousand times faster than their reference solver. Tests covered three regimes: baseline spread, diffraction around edges, and reflection between surfaces. Accuracy in areas with no direct line of sight improved by up to about a quarter over prior deep models. The maps kept fine structure such as interference patterns intact.
arxiv-2510-04610:
XinXin Qi and Hao Sun wrote this 2025 paper on dark matter made of two kinds of particles. One kind froze out of the early universe, in the WIMP style. The other kind froze in, built slowly through feeble interactions, in the FIMP style. Their model adds a singlet scalar and a Majorana fermion under a symmetry. A scalar with a nonzero vacuum value gives the fermion its mass.

Either candidate can play the WIMP role, so the team scans both cases against the dark matter density. When the fermion is the WIMP and the scalar the FIMP, wide ranges of mass work. That case needs a coupling between the scalar and the fermion. When the roles swap, direct detection experiments squeeze the space hard. Two islands survive there: one near the Higgs resonance mass and one above four hundred gigaelectronvolts. Mixed production may explain why mechanism searches keep coming empty.
arxiv-2510-05010:
Sofía Perón Santana and three co-authors at the Universidad Nacional de Córdoba study quantum communication hardware in this 2025 arXiv paper, written in Spanish. Their problem is moving a quantum state from one end of a qubit chain to the other. The transfer should be fast and should lose as little information as possible.

The team shapes the transfer with constant magnetic pulses. They search for good pulse sequences with two different strategies. One uses deep reinforcement learning, where an agent learns from rewards. The other uses genetic algorithms, which breed and mutate candidate solutions. The paper compares how well each strategy performs. It also tests how each one handles real physical constraints on the hardware.
arxiv-2510-05210:
Michael Zemcov and a large international collaboration report on a rocket experiment that maps the universe's infrared glow in this 2025 arXiv paper. The extragalactic background light sums every photon emitted across cosmic history. At near-infrared wavelengths it records galaxies back to the first stars. CIBER-2 measures both its brightness and its spatial fluctuations.

The payload flies a cooled 28.5-centimeter telescope on sounding rockets. Three cameras image several square degrees through six broad bands plus linear-variable filters. The experiment flew an engineering flight in 2021 and a successful science flight in 2024. The paper reviews the design, laboratory characterization, and in-flight performance. Its noise-control methods and analysis pipeline already feed into the SPHEREx space mission.
arxiv-2510-05310:
Yining She and six co-authors show that extra context can quietly corrupt AI safety filters in this 2025 arXiv paper. Guardrail models screen the inputs and outputs of larger systems for unsafe content. Real deployments feed them retrieval-augmented context full of documents. The authors ask whether that added context changes the guardrails' own judgments.

They tested three Llama Guard models and two GPT-oss models under RAG-style contexts. Inserting even benign documents flipped about 11 percent of input judgments. Output guardrail judgments flipped in about 8 percent of cases. Dissecting the context showed each component contributed to the instability. Two mitigation attempts brought only minor improvements. The findings expose a robustness gap that current guardrail training ignores.
arxiv-2510-05410:
Junyi Fan and four co-authors align a small language model with expert nursing standards in this 2025 arXiv paper. ICU nursing notes carry vital clinical intelligence but vary wildly in style and terminology. Heart failure documentation especially needs consistency for safe handovers. The authors apply Direct Preference Optimization to the locally deployable Mistral-7B model.

Training used 8,838 heart failure notes from MIMIC-III and about 21,000 expert-verified preference pairs. BLEU scores rose by about 84 percent after optimization. Expert ratings climbed across accuracy, completeness, logical consistency, and readability. Structural clarity improved as well, though outputs still trail human documentation by wide margins. Local deployment keeps patient data private, a requirement for hospital use.
arxiv-2510-05510:
Norihama and colleagues study when reflective writing helps family caregivers most. Writing about hard experiences can ease stress, but fixed schedules often miss the right moment. The team ran a three-week field study with forty-seven caregivers. A chatbot sent daily writing cues and recorded the context of each entry.

The study tracked three kinds of distance from the stressful event. Time, place, and social closeness all shaped what caregivers wrote. Writing close to an event produced detailed, emotional accounts focused on the care recipient. Writing farther away produced calmer, self-focused accounts that supported clear rethinking. Caregivers valued the vivid detail of close writing but missed objectivity, and valued distance while risking lost detail. The team collected 958 entries and coded thousands of segments from them. The findings guide support tools that adapt timing to a caregiver's situation.
arxiv-2510-05610:
Liu and colleagues add cheap steering to autoregressive image generators. Scale-based autoregressive models now rival diffusion models at image synthesis. Yet guiding them with spatial conditions usually means expensive fine-tuning of the whole model. Their 2025 Efficient Control Model plugs in a light control module instead.

The module spreads context-aware attention layers through the frozen base model. A shared gated feed-forward network keeps the small module's capacity well used. An early-centric sampling strategy trains mostly on early control tokens, which set the scene's structure. Temperature scheduling at inference then compensates for the thinner late-stage training. A 300 million parameter model produced quality controlled images at 256 by 256 resolution. Experiments show high-fidelity, diverse control that beats existing baselines. Designers gain ControlNet-like guidance without retraining the base generator. Training and inference both run more efficiently than fine-tuned rivals.
arxiv-2510-05810:
Lim and colleagues survey tiny solar brightenings at one-second cadence. Extreme-ultraviolet brightenings pepper the quiet Sun and active regions alike. Whether they are miniature flares matters for the coronal heating problem. Their 2025 study uses Solar Orbiter's Extreme Ultraviolet Imager at unprecedented speed.

Automated detection found over eight hundred thousand brightenings across both region types. Some events live shorter than three seconds, invisible at slower cadences. About one in ten brightenings shows quasi-periodic pulsations. Pulsation periods run from five seconds to over five hundred. Period correlates moderately with event lifetime and spatial scale. Active regions produce brightenings at about triple the quiet-Sun birthrate. Non-stationary pulsations outnumber stationary ones in both environments. The statistics barely depend on the large-scale magnetic environment. A shared power-law links pulsation period and lifetime from brightenings to stellar flares.
arxiv-2510-06110:
Roy, Mukherjee, and Mohan prove a large deviation principle for a stochastic nonlinear Schrödinger equation in a 2025 probability paper. The equation has polynomial nonlinearity, gentle linear damping, and mixed random forcing. Part of the noise acts in the Itô sense and part as linear multiplicative noise in the Stratonovich sense.

Large deviation results describe how unlikely extreme behaviors become as noise shrinks. They prove the Laplace principle for the solution family using the weak convergence framework of Budhiraja and Dupuis. That step needs uniform estimates for a controlled version of the equation. Varadhan's lemma and Bryc's converse then give the Wentzell–Freidlin principle. They also settle the existence theory: the deterministic skeleton equation is locally and globally well posed via fixed point and Yosida arguments. A conservation law survives without damping and Itô noise. The work firms up rare-event analysis for noisy wave equations.
arxiv-2510-06210:
Fiori, Riebler, and Martino map geographical inequalities in Italian mortality, 2002 to 2019 in a 2025 demographic study. Italy enjoys very low mortality, yet improvements may be slowing and regional gaps widening. They analyze deaths by single year of age and sex across all one hundred seven provinces.

They extend the Lee–Carter model with spatially varying age effects and space–age–time interactions. Estimation runs in a Bayesian framework using integrated nested Laplace approximation via inlabru. Borrowing strength across provinces and years tames noise in small-area death counts. Despite national improvement, mortality geography stays uneven. Disadvantage concentrates in parts of the Centre-South and North-West, while the Centre-North and North-East fare better. These gaps widened after 2010, hitting younger adult men and older adult women hardest. Granular maps can target public health policy where excess deaths cluster.
arxiv-2510-06310:
Johnson and fourteen co-authors probe the gaseous halo of an isolated dwarf galaxy at redshift 0.57 in a 2025 astrophysics study. Models say dwarf outflows expel metal-rich gas into the circumgalactic medium, explaining why dwarfs stay metal-poor. Direct measurements of that expelled gas remain scarce.

A background quasar sightline pierces the dwarf's halo twenty-eight kiloparsecs from its center. Absorption reveals hydrogen plus carbon, oxygen, and sulfur ions, including broad, highly ionized oxygen. Photoionization modeling gives the intermediate-ion gas a mass near two hundred million solar masses. That is about four times the stellar mass, yet ten times less than the highly ionized halo gas. The halo gas carries roughly a quarter of the Sun's metal fraction. Its carbon and nitrogen ratios are unusually low, matching fresh core-collapse supernova ejecta. Supernova-enriched gas apparently escaped without mixing much with older interstellar material.
arxiv-2510-06410:
Li and Goyal test whether language models can reason together inside one shared trajectory in a 2025 artificial intelligence paper. Reasoning models verbalize their thinking, so collaborators could in principle continue each other's partial work. That requires off-trajectory reasoning: judging and extending another model's thought process.

The authors devise two tests at opposite extremes. Recoverability asks whether a model can backtrack from a misleading reasoning trace. Guidability asks whether it can build on correct steps supplied by a stronger collaborator. Fifteen open-weight models, spanning small to fairly large sizes, took both tests. Benchmark-stronger models proved surprisingly fragile under distraction. Worse, every model failed to exploit guidance on problems beyond its own ability. Solve rates stayed below nine percent in that setting, a sobering ceiling. Control studies trace these behaviors to post-training choices. A teacher's poor recoverability even transfers to distilled students trained on correct trajectories.
arxiv-2510-06510:
Horaites, Rodriguez, and Liu examine whether a solar sail would corrupt its own spacecraft's magnetometer readings in a 2025 space physics paper. Solar sails are ready for a mission carrying a science-grade magnetometer. The solar wind's magnetic field drives space weather prediction, governing reconnection at Earth's magnetopause. A huge metallic sail interacts with the surrounding plasma.

Two electromagnetic effects dominate the analysis. Eddy currents in the metallic sail significantly perturb the local field at high frequencies. Magnetic pileup distorts the spacecraft's environment under one size condition. Pileup matters when sail size rivals the plasma's electron kinetic scales. Other sizes largely escape the second effect. The results form an initial guide for mission designers. They indicate when sail-plasma interactions could degrade magnetometer performance. Future missions can plan sensor placement and frequencies around the sail's electromagnetic footprint.
arxiv-2510-06710:
Hongzhi Zang leads a large team building infrastructure for training robot-brain models. Their 2025 paper presents RLinf-VLA, a framework for vision-language-action models. These models let robots see, understand instructions, and act. Most are trained by supervised fine-tuning, which generalizes poorly when conditions shift.

Reinforcement learning could do better by letting models learn from interaction. Prior attempts were fragmented, though, with no shared platform for fair comparison. RLinf-VLA unifies several simulators, algorithms, and model designs in one system. Flexible resource allocation spreads work across machines efficiently. Training throughput improved by a factor of about two point three over the baseline framework. The team also distilled best practices for two major algorithms, PPO and GRPO. A real Franka robot test showed the payoff. Policies trained with reinforcement learning generalized to new situations better than supervised ones.
arxiv-2510-06910:
Vázquez leads a team building an anomaly detector that sips power instead of gulping it. Their paper presents Vacuum Spiker, a spiking neural network method for time series data. Spiking networks mimic brain cells and fire rarely, which saves energy. Deep learning detectors are accurate but too hungry for small devices like wearables and sensors.

Most detectors flag anomalies by spotting reconstruction or prediction errors. Vacuum Spiker instead watches the network's overall activity level. Training uses a spike-timing rule tuned to keep hidden activity low during normal data. When something abnormal arrives, activity rises, and that rise is the alarm. A new encoding scheme compresses each input into a single spike per step. Across many public time series datasets, the method matched established detectors. It did so with a design aimed squarely at low energy use. Edge devices could run such monitoring continuously without draining their batteries.
arxiv-2510-07110:
Tran and co-authors present HPQEA, a hardware system that imitates quantum circuits on a classical chip. Their 2025 paper tackles a hard trade-off in quantum emulation. Older emulators tend to be slow, narrow, or wasteful with memory. The team built its design around fast memory with very wide bandwidth. The work aims to support many kinds of quantum programs.
