The system rests on three parts. A strong computing core does the main work. A smarter method handles a key two-qubit gate. Fast memory feeds data to the core with little delay. Tests on a field-programmable board reached thirty qubits with high accuracy. The system ran faster than rival chip-based emulators. It also beat a top graphics card on speed per gate for systems up to twenty qubits. Such results help researchers test quantum programs before real quantum hardware is ready.
arxiv-2510-07210:
Pfaffmann, Klusch, and Steinmetz present HyPlan, a hybrid planner meant to keep self-driving cars collision-free. Their 2025 paper addresses driving where other road users are partly hidden. Pure learning systems react fast but can act unsafely. Pure planners reason carefully but run slowly. HyPlan blends behavior prediction, deep reinforcement learning, and an online planning method built for partial information. A pruning step trims the planner's search to keep it quick.

Tests ran on a benchmark of critical traffic scenes with pedestrians in a driving simulator. HyPlan navigated more safely than the selected rival methods. It also ran far faster than the other planning-based approaches, in both training and live use. A speed gap to pure learning methods remains, but it shrank. Careful hybrids may deliver safety without giving up real-time response, a balance central to deploying driverless cars.
arxiv-2510-07310:
Jin and co-authors probe how video generators understand interactions between people and objects. Their 2025 paper builds MATRIX-11K, a video set with captions and mask tracks for each moving instance. They then inspect a video diffusion transformer from two angles. One checks whether word tokens latch onto the right instances and relations. The other checks whether those bindings survive across frames. Both effects, they find, live in a small subset of layers that specialize in interactions.

Guided by that map, their method MATRIX nudges attention in those layers to align with the mask tracks. Two added losses reward correct grounding and steady propagation. On their new InterGenEval protocol, interaction fidelity and semantic alignment both improved. Identity drift and duplicated subjects fell. Reading a model's attention geography can point to targeted fixes for multi-subject video.
arxiv-2510-07410:
Magierski reviews how density functional theory describes superfluid systems of fermions, from atomic nuclei to neutron stars. The 2025 article grew from lectures at a summer school in Varenna, Italy. Density functional theory trades the impossible full wave function for the density alone, which is formally exact and computationally workable. Its time-dependent extension follows superfluids as they evolve, collide, and vibrate. The review lays out foundations of both versions and then surveys the approximations that practical calculations require. Applications span three very different arenas that share the same underlying mathematics.

In nuclei, the method models fission and exotic vibrations. In neutron stars, it addresses the superfluid interior that affects how pulsars glitch. In ultracold atoms, it follows turbulent quantum gases in the laboratory. Modern codes solve millions of coupled nonlinear equations in full three dimensions without imposed symmetry.
arxiv-2510-07810:
Nguyen and four coauthors wrote this 2025 computer vision paper on recognizing facial micro-expressions. These brief face movements leak emotions before a person can hide them. They matter for psychology, security, and behavior analysis, yet they are hard to capture. Most methods study optical flow only from an expression's start to its peak. That choice discards the motion of the face settling. The authors build a representation that uses both halves of the movement.

Their descriptor merges flow from the rising and falling phases and weights it by strength. On top of it sits FMANet, a network that learns the fusion and attends to telling facial regions. On three benchmarks, the method set a best result on one and stayed competitive on the others. Ablations confirmed that balanced phase weighting worked best. Using the full micro-expression, not just its onset, sharpens emotion reading.
arxiv-2510-07910:
Kwon and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on recommending drug combinations safely. Recommender systems help doctors choose medicines, but co-prescribed drugs can interact badly. Graph networks describe molecules as discrete structures, which miss how electrons actually spread and react. The authors build MMM, a framework that adds quantum-chemical detail to drug representations. It computes three-dimensional electron localization maps for each molecule.

Those maps join a bipartite graph encoder that models local substructure interactions. The two views capture global electronic behavior and local chemistry together. On the MIMIC-III hospital dataset, MMM beat graph baselines, including the SafeDrug model, on recommendation scores. Its interaction rate also improved by statistically significant margins. The authors argue that electron-level features explain part of what makes two drugs clash. Richer molecular representations could make automated prescribing both more accurate and safer in clinical decision support.
arxiv-2510-08010:
Huang, Luo, Xiao, Yang, and Zhou wrote this 2025 algorithms paper speeding up Personalized PageRank, a core measure of node importance around a chosen source. Exact computation touches the whole graph, wasteful when only a local neighborhood matters. The authors build an accelerated evolving set framework. Each stage runs a localized inexact proximal point iteration on a simplified linear system. The active set grows only where the walk actually spreads.

The framework needs only a small number of such stages, set by the damping factor. Its running time can stay independent of total graph size when the requested accuracy is moderate. That resolves an open conjecture in the local PageRank literature. Experiments on real-world graphs confirmed fast early convergence in practice. The machinery may transfer to other linear systems. Faster local rankings feed search and recommendation on graphs too large to process whole.
arxiv-2510-08210:
Balint Pato, June Vanlerberghe, and Kenneth Brown present a 2025 arXiv paper on speeding up a key calculation for quantum error-correcting codes. These codes protect fragile quantum data, and a value called the weight enumerator polynomial helps judge them. One tool, Quantum LEGO, builds the value from small tensor blocks joined step by step. The order of joining, called the contraction schedule, strongly affects the total cost.

The authors found that many blocks in these networks are mostly empty, or sparse. Standard cost tools assume full blocks, so they guess the true cost poorly. The team built a new cost rule based on the rank of check matrices for each block. This rule matched the true cost exactly in their tests. Schedules chosen with it cut real computing costs by orders of magnitude on some codes.
arxiv-2510-08310:
Herbert Fleischner, Enrico Iurlano, and Günther Raidl revisit a famous graph theory dispute in a 2025 arXiv paper. Tait once conjectured that every planar cubic graph, where each vertex has three edges, has a Hamiltonian cycle. Such a cycle visits every vertex exactly once before returning to the start. Tutte later produced a counterexample, a graph of this type with no such cycle.

The authors build an infinite family of planar cubic graphs using prism graphs and Tutte fragments. Within this family, some graphs are Hamiltonian and others are not. Tutte's counterexample appears, in a precise sense, as a minimal element of the family. The family also contains generalizations of the smallest counterexamples found by Holton and McKay. Putting the example in this family clarifies how close such graphs sit to the Hamiltonian border.
arxiv-2510-08510:
Jiayun Luo and co-authors trace where visual information flows inside large vision-language models in a 2025 arXiv paper. These models pair a vision transformer, acting as eyes, with a language model acting as brain. Image content enters as a sequence of visual tokens produced by the encoder. Prior work hunted attention sinks, dull tokens drawing heavy attention, inside the language model.

The authors shift attention to the vision encoder and find high-norm visual tokens they call ViT attention sinks. Contrary to their dull reputation in language models, these sink tokens carry high-level semantic concepts from the image. That content helps the language model understand and reason more effectively. Yet current architectures often overlook or discard these tokens during design. Qualitative and quantitative analyses measure how much information the sinks embed. The findings suggest preserving sink tokens could improve vision-language performance.
arxiv-2510-08710:
Li Zhang, Matthias Grabmair, Morgan Gray, and Kevin Ashley test language models on case-based legal reasoning in a 2025 arXiv paper. American lawyers argue by analogy to precedents and by distinguishing a current case from them. The team decomposes spotting significant distinctions into three verifiable stages. Cases are modeled with factual predicates called factors, organized into a legal knowledge hierarchy.

Models scored high on surface-level reasoning in the first stage. On hierarchical reasoning, accuracy spread widely, from 64.82 percent to 92.09 percent across the models tested in stage two of their framework. Integrated analysis in the third stage collapsed to between 11.46 percent and 33.99 percent, a steep fall from the earlier stages. Most strikingly, models spent more compute on incorrect responses than on correct ones. Thinking longer did not mean thinking smarter, the authors conclude.
arxiv-2510-08810:
Islam and co-authors build a tool that moves a software project from one code library to a similar one automatically, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Swapping libraries by hand is slow and error prone. A developer must learn both sets of commands, match up equivalents, and rewrite the code. Most existing helpers stop at suggesting the matches.

The team first tested language models on a benchmark of three hundred twenty-one real migrations and found them capable, though post-processing added gains. Their tool, PyMigTool, therefore pairs a language model with static checks of the code and dynamic checks that run it. On seven hundred seventeen real applications outside the benchmark, the tool finished about a third of migrations with complete correctness. In most of the rest, developers were left only a small share of the changes to fix.
arxiv-2510-08910:
Huang and co-authors lay groundwork for simulating a long-sought particle process on a quantum computer, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The process centers on the sphaleron, a saddle-shaped energy configuration in the electroweak theory tied to how matter came to outweigh antimatter. Its behavior unfolds in real time and resists the usual tricks of theoretical physics, so it has never been observed. A quantum simulation could follow it directly, if the setup is right.

As a proving ground the team uses a simpler cousin theory in one space dimension. They identify the matching sphaleron configuration there and tune the spacing of their computational lattice until the simulated energies match the true continuum values with controlled precision. They then design quantum algorithms that evolve the configuration forward, with quantum effects fully included. The work is a protocol step toward collider-scale questions that classical machines cannot reach.
arxiv-2510-09110:
Huang and co-authors manufacture training pictures for vision models by pasting in synthetic objects, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Detection, segmentation, and grounding, the tasks of finding, outlining, and locating described objects, all feed on huge hand-labeled datasets. Those are costly, biased toward common scenes, and hard to grow. Fully synthetic images have promised relief but usually lack variety and precise labels.

Their pipeline, SOS, cuts out high-quality synthetic object segments and composes them into fresh scenes. Structured layout rules place the objects sensibly, and generative relighting blends them into their new surroundings. Every pasted object arrives with an exact mask, box, and referring expression for free. Models trained on just one hundred thousand such images beat models trained on real datasets hundreds of times larger, on both detection and grounding tests. Mixing the synthetic images into real datasets helped further, most sharply when real data was scarce.
arxiv-2510-09210:
Zhu, Yu, and Gao propose stamping a hidden watermark into poisoned datasets so their makers can prove ownership, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Data poisoning, quietly altering training data, is usually an attack. Lately, though, some poisoning is defensive: owners corrupt their own data slightly to keep it from being scraped and used without permission. That dual use breeds confusion and disputes, because nobody can tell protective poisoning from sabotage.

The authors design two watermarking schemes with mathematical guarantees. One adds the watermark after poisoning; the other weaves it in during generation. Their analysis derives how long the watermark must be, given the data's dimension and tolerated distortion. At that length, two promises hold at once: the mark stays detectable, and the poison keeps working. Experiments across several attacks, models, and datasets confirmed the theory. Watermarking, they argue, lets benign poisoning declare itself.
arxiv-2510-09310:
Alexander Karlberg and four co-authors, among them Gavin Salam, published a 2025 arXiv release note for the HOPPET computer code. HOPPET evolves parton distribution functions, which describe how the momentum inside a proton is shared among its quarks and gluons. Physicists need these functions to predict what particle collisions will produce.

Version two of the code adds three main features. It can now evolve the functions at third order in quantum chromodynamics with a changing number of active quark types. It can also compute structure functions for light quarks at third order and handle quantum electrodynamics evolution at a matching practical accuracy. The release also adds a Python interface, a new build option, a way to save tables in the LHAPDF format, and updated speed benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-09510:
Siyue Zhang and seven co-authors, among them Arman Cohan and Chen Zhao, introduce MRMR in a 2025 arXiv paper, a benchmark for multimodal retrieval. Retrieval systems search mixed image and text collections, and the authors argue that existing tests are too easy and too narrow. MRMR holds 1,502 queries across 23 expert domains, with correct documents verified by human specialists.

The queries demand intensive reasoning, such as diagnosing microscopic slides, rather than simple matching. A new task, contradiction retrieval, asks systems to find documents with conflicting concepts. Queries and documents mix images and text in interleaved sequences, closer to real collections. Evaluating fourteen frontier models in four families, the team found a text embedding model fed with machine-written image captions scored highest. Multimodal models competed well on expert questions but lagged on the reasoning-heavy ones, leaving much room to improve.
arxiv-2510-09710:
Xiaonan Si and nine co-authors defend retrieval-augmented generation in a 2025 arXiv paper. Such systems fetch outside knowledge to ground a language model's answers, but attackers can poison the document corpus or contaminate it, corrupting the output. Harsh defences filter so hard that much good content is lost and output quality drops.

Their framework, SeCon-RAG, filters in two gentler stages. An extractor first pulls entities, hidden objectives, and relations from the query and the documents, scoring how well each fits the query and admitting good documents into a clean store. A second module then checks for clashes among the query, candidate answers, and retrieved knowledge, removing contradictions before the final answer is written. Across various models and datasets, SeCon-RAG markedly beat state-of-the-art defence methods, improving both strength and trust while preserving useful knowledge.
arxiv-2510-09810:
Victor Freire and Marco Nicotra construct safety filters for nonlinear control systems in a 2025 arXiv paper. A control barrier function certifies that a system can be steered without ever violating its constraints, on states and on inputs alike. Building such functions for nonlinear systems with arbitrary constraints has lacked a systematic method.

Their approach borrows from reference governor research, which supervises a controller by adjusting its setpoint. They define a family of backup policies, parametrised by the system's equilibrium manifold, the set of its resting states. The barrier function lives on the combined space of state and reference, and it measures the distance to any future constraint violation if the backup policy took over. A small distance means danger is near even if the present state looks safe. The authors demonstrate the construction on the classic inverted pendulum on a cart, a benchmark system that must balance while respecting limits.
arxiv-2510-09910:
Quiroz-Juarez and co-authors ask how quantum mechanics restores confinement in this 2025 arXiv paper on chaotic dynamics. Some Hamiltonian systems are unstable and chaotic classically, so particles wander freely. Yet their quantum versions can keep particles confined, held in a bounded region.

The team studies two models. One is the Contopoulos Hamiltonian, a round oscillator disturbed by a quartic coupling that mixes the two directions. The other is the purely quartic Yang-Mills Hamiltonian, a toy version of the force theory behind particle physics. By comparing classical and quantum behavior in both, the authors trace how quantum effects reinstate confinement. The pair of models lets them check that the mechanism is not tied to one setup.
arxiv-2510-10110:
Schroller and a large team couple molecular magnets with silicon qubits in this 2025 arXiv paper on hybrid quantum systems. Molecular spin qudits, units with more than two states, offer long coherence times and rich level structures, making them attractive as quantum memory. The terbium compound TbPc2 is a leading example.

Semiconductor qubits, by contrast, offer scalable readout and coupling but weaker memory. The hybrid design pairs the two: the molecule stores quantum information while industrial silicon spin qubits connect and read it. The authors examine how a single-molecule magnet qudit can be coupled to silicon devices made with industry processes. That pairing aims to combine chemical reproducibility with manufacturable hardware.
arxiv-2510-10410:
Xu analyzes code safety in Rust with execution traces in this 2025 arXiv paper on programming language security. Rust is a memory-safe language that bans undefined behavior, and its guarantees have been widely studied. Even so, unsafe code blocks remain a critical concern, since they switch the guarantees off locally.

Xu proposes a trace-based approach: record how code actually runs and analyze the traces for safety violations. Traces catch what static reading can miss, because they show the real paths and memory accesses a program takes. The work aims to audit the unsafe regions that Rust's compiler cannot check. Finding their faults matters as Rust spreads into kernels, browsers, and infrastructure.
arxiv-2510-10510:
Subhodip Panda and four co-authors fix a reliability problem in tools that estimate how much each training example shaped a model, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These influence estimates help debug models and clean data. But training involves randomness, so the same example can look critical in one run and pointless in another. That instability makes it unclear whether the right points get deleted or kept.

Their framework, f-influence, grounds estimation in hypothesis testing and accounts for training randomness directly. Their algorithm, f-INE, computes this influence in a single training run. They scale it to the instruction tuning data of Llama-3.1-8B, a large open model. There it reliably detected poisoned samples planted to steer the model's opinions, showing value for data cleanup.
arxiv-2510-10810:
Omar Islam Laskar and five co-authors help data owners share datasets without giving away privacy, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Sharing ecosystems must mask sensitive data to meet a minimum privacy threshold. Many masking settings pass that bar, but their usefulness for machine learning varies widely. Picking the best one is the challenge. Their middleware, Aegis, selects masking settings for datasets with features and class labels.

Its optimizer minimizes predictive utility deviation, measured by how masking shifts the correlations between features and labels. Aegis estimates the joint distribution from limited summaries, such as one dimensional histograms, or from none at all, using iterative proportional fitting. That suits settings where raw data cannot be accessed for privacy reasons. On real world datasets, Aegis found optimal configurations more than ten times faster than baselines. The masked data performed on par with baseline approaches on downstream learning tasks, complementing standard anonymization techniques.
arxiv-2510-10910:
Honghui Yuan and Keiji Yanai restyle the text inside scene photographs without retraining anything, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Diffusion models have advanced style transfer broadly. But flexible, localized style editing for text in real scenes stayed unsolved: earlier methods replaced content or applied only simple styles. Their framework, SceneTextStylizer, performs prompt guided style transformation on text regions while keeping the text readable and the style consistent.

A feature injection module uses diffusion inversion and self attention to transfer style features into the text region. A region control mechanism applies a distance based changing mask at each denoising step, giving precise spatial control over where the style lands. A style enhancement module based on the Fourier transform enriches the stylistic effect. In extensive experiments, the method outperformed existing state of the art approaches in both visual fidelity and text preservation.
arxiv-2510-11410:
Self-driving cars that each learn to minimize only their own travel time can destabilize a city's traffic, taking years of commuting to settle into good routes. Anastasia Psarou, Łukasz Gorczyca, Dominik Gaweł, and Rafał Kucharski show that social awareness fixes this in a 2025 arXiv paper on multi-agent reinforcement learning. Their vehicles value their own travel time but also account for the delay they impose on everyone else.

The extra signal is an intrinsic reward built from the marginal cost matrix, which quantifies how each route choice changes total travel time. Adding it aligns the agents' objectives and reduces non-stationarity, while a counterfactual formulation preserves the game's equilibria and avoids oscillations. In experiments on a toy network and on the road network of Saint-Arnoult, these agents converged to the optimal solution where selfish baselines failed, improving both system-wide and individual performance.
arxiv-2510-11610:
Single-photon emitters in hexagonal boron nitride are promising building blocks for quantum technology, but most samples are flakes or powders needing an activation step, so results resist comparison. Piotr Tatarczak and co-authors propose a cleaner platform in this 2025 arXiv materials physics paper: hBN grown by metalorganic vapor phase epitaxy, which hosts emitters readily with no activation. The film also carries bubbles blown in by electron-beam irradiation.

The bubbles add useful functions. Interference inside them enhances emission by roughly one hundred to two hundred percent, structures let emitters be relocated between systems, and bubble-wall strain can be studied directly. Unlike other bubbles, theirs stay stable at cryogenic temperatures. A mask-based method gives deterministic control over bubble shape and position. The authors present the platform as a reproducible testbed for settling what hBN emitters are and how they behave.
arxiv-2510-11710:
Louis Sharma and five co-authors compare two ways of using neural networks to simulate strongly interacting electrons. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies the Hubbard model, a stripped-down model of electrons on a square lattice. The model matters because it may explain high-temperature superconductors. Tiny energy gaps between rival states make accurate simulation hard.

The team tests two network designs, the Hidden Fermion Determinant State and a Jastrow-Backflow design built on a vision transformer. In practice the two reach similar accuracy. They also test ways of enforcing the model's symmetries. Averaging the network output over symmetries gives the lowest energies, but the cost grows fast for bigger systems. On cylinder-shaped lattices they consistently find filled stripes, meaning bands of charge. On a torus they see signs of a doped Mott insulator, with magnetic correlations and suppressed charge motion.
arxiv-2510-12110:
Ziliang Qiu and Renfen Hu grade AI creativity by asking for chains of associations. Judging creativity is plagued by tainted test data and pricey human judging. Borrowing from human creativity research, their 2025 arXiv paper proposes PACE: models build parallel association chains, word leaping to word, and the chains' traits score the model.

The metric's scores line up strongly with Chatbot Arena's creative writing rankings, with a rank match of zero point seven three nine across closed and open models. Setting machines beside humans, top models match average human associative creativity, but professional humans steadily beat every model. Word-level analysis finds both species drifting toward less concrete associations along their chains. Humans, though, show greater variety of associative patterns. PACE is cheap, hard to contaminate, and repeatable, giving the field a creativity yardstick that does not require a panel of judges for every new model release.
arxiv-2510-12210:
Song and colleagues present DiSTAR, a zero shot text to speech system, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Zero shot synthesis means the system can speak in a new voice from a short sample, without retraining. Earlier designs that mixed autoregressive models with diffusion refiners proved fragile when inputs shifted and offered few controls.

DiSTAR works entirely with discrete speech codes produced by residual vector quantization, which compresses audio into layered tokens. An autoregressive language model drafts each block of tokens, and a masked diffusion model fills in the block in parallel, guided by the draft. This avoids forced alignment and duration prediction while reducing classic autoregressive drift. In tests DiSTAR surpassed leading zero shot systems in robustness, naturalness, and speaker consistency. It also allows variable bit rate and adjustable computation by pruning code layers at test time.
arxiv-2510-12410:
Jerkstrand and a large team model the infrared light of kilonovae to read which heavy elements neutron star mergers actually make, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. A kilonova is the glow of radioactive debris from a merging neutron star pair, where rapid neutron capture builds heavy elements. Whether mergers produce the full range of these elements remains a central open question.

With advanced non equilibrium physics and new atomic data, the authors identify promising diagnostic lines from germanium, arsenic, selenium, bromine, krypton, and zirconium. Their models link features to emission volumes at early phases and to ion masses and electron densities later. Fits to the known kilonova AT2017gfo suggest its production of light r-process elements may have been well below the solar pattern, unless geometry explains the blend. They also identify which further atomic data, such as recombination rates and collision strengths, would sharpen these readings.
arxiv-2510-12610:
Sabzalipour, Shafiei, and Milošević show how to switch off the energy loss that magnetic impurities cause in films of topological insulators, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Such materials are promising for fast, low power spintronic devices, which use electron spin. In clean versions, surface electrons cannot bounce back off ordinary impurities, so current flows with no loss at all. Magnetic impurities break this shield by twisting electron spins as they pass.

The authors show how outside magnetic or electronic signals can suppress that backscattering in an ultrathin film. Under the right conditions, the result is lossless, spin polarized charge transport. Keeping spin coherence this way directly boosts the spin current that spintronic devices use. The findings suggest concrete design strategies for devices with far lower energy use, turning a known weakness of these materials into a tunable feature.
arxiv-2510-12910:
Abdollahpour and colleagues propose a smarter way to choose EEG channels in this 2025 arXiv paper. Electroencephalography records brain activity through many scalp electrodes, but not all channels carry equally useful information, and processing all of them is wasteful. Their idea ranks channels by effective connectivity, the causal influence one brain region exerts over another.

The team defined a channel importance criterion from connectivity strength and used it for unsupervised selection, meaning no labels guide the choice. They tested it on three well-known EEG datasets, computing connectivity five different ways, then extracting features with a standard spatial pattern method and classifying with a support vector machine. Accuracy improved consistently while electrode counts dropped sharply, and against leading methods their approach reached the highest accuracies while keeping only a fraction of the channels in each dataset.
arxiv-2510-13510:
Voet and Sande explore whether spline bases in isogeometric analysis can be made interpolatory again. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves explicit dynamics simulations, where mass lumping speeds every time step. Isogeometric analysis uses smooth spline functions for both geometry and solution fields. Its bases gave up interpolation, a property classical finite elements rely on for lumping.

Mass lumping replaces the full mass matrix with a simpler diagonal approximation. Good lumping needs basis functions that take clean values at chosen points. The authors test restoring that interpolation property for spline bases. The idea echoes the older spectral element method but brings fresh difficulties. They assess the surprises and challenges of the approach critically. The stakes are practical: cheaper steps for large structural dynamics problems.
arxiv-2510-13710:
Bose and co-authors measure how well the web actually performs when delivered over Starlink's satellite network. Their 2025 arXiv paper is the first study to split that performance across ground stations, DNS, and content networks. Two years of data blend hundreds of thousands of speed tests with millions of traceroutes and DNS queries. Terrestrial content delivery assumes nearby caches, an assumption satellites strain.

Three performance regimes emerge, sorted by how much ground infrastructure a region has. Where rich local ground stations exist, delays rival landline service, with the satellite hop dominating. Sparse regions suffer stacked penalties: distant stations force far-off resolvers, which misplace content lookups. Latency then balloons past two hundred milliseconds for ordinary page fetches. When Starlink moved stations closer in early 2025, median fetch times fell by sixty percent in the affected areas, the team found. Proximity, not coverage, drives web speed here.
arxiv-2510-13810:
Axelsson and Sikau imagine deliberately fragile robots that invite passersby to help them in public spaces. Their 2025 arXiv paper explores weak robots, machines with feigned fragility, cuteness, and missing abilities. Unlike delivery or cleaning robots that work alone, weak robots are built to spark collaboration. Their incompleteness is the design feature, not a flaw.

The authors queer standard notions of function and ability to explain how such robots operate socially. Cuteness can build trust, yet it can also manipulate emotions or harvest data, they warn. Two design fiction vignettes then stage future city scenes with these machines. One tells a utopian story, the other a dystopian one, about robots like struggling trash cans. Comparing the tales exposes how values steer design choices early on. The paper argues those choices shape which shared human-robot futures become likely.
arxiv-2510-13910:
Lin, Zhang, Liu, and Li benchmark the intermediate skills that agentic retrieval systems need, not just their final answers. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces RAGCap-Bench for retrieval-augmented generation with planning agents. Such systems loop through planning, searching, and reasoning on hard multi-hop questions. End-to-end scores hide which inner capability failed when answers go wrong.

The authors mined outputs from leading systems to catalogue the recurring subtasks involved. Each subtask maps to core capabilities an agent must execute reliably. A taxonomy of typical model errors then shapes targeted evaluation questions. Slow-thinking models scoring higher on RAGCap also finish with better end-to-end results. That correlation validates the benchmark as a proxy for real capability. Strengthening intermediate skills, the authors argue, is the lever for better agentic retrieval. The benchmark gives builders a diagnostic instead of a single opaque grade.
arxiv-2510-14010:
Victor Buchstaber and Mikhail Kornev connect the theory of many-valued algebraic operations with two geometric ideas, discriminants and projective duality, in this 2025 arXiv paper. An n-valued monoid is a system where combining two elements returns n results instead of one, generalizing addition. Their setting is the complex projective line, the sphere-like space of complex numbers plus infinity.

The authors apply projective duality, a transformation swapping points and lines. They follow it with a Möbius transformation, a reshaping of the sphere. Together these shift the family of these monoids down by one value count. Duality also sends each Fermat curve, a family of algebraic curves, to a curve defined by the monoid's addition polynomial. They describe the addition laws built from cubic curves, proving every such law is given by a polynomial. This differs from formal group laws on cubic curves, which need infinite series.
arxiv-2510-14310:
Mara Martinez, Veena Rao, and Mallikarjunaiah test physics-informed neural networks against the classical finite element method on an electrohydrodynamics problem, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Electrohydrodynamics couples electric fields with fluid flow and produces nonlinear differential equations that are notoriously hard to approximate accurately.

Physics-informed neural networks embed the governing equations into the training loss, so the network learns a solution rather than merely fitting data. The authors use a total loss function of a standard squared-error type and, notably, no prior knowledge of the exact solution. Their training alternates forward propagation, which adjusts gradient and curvature information, with backpropagation that refines hyperparameters. The comparative study then judges the neural approximation against finite element solutions, the long-standing workhorse for such problems. It assesses where the learning-based approach matches, beats, or trails the conventional method on this challenging nonlinear system.
arxiv-2510-14810:
Deng and co-authors revisit, in a 2025 arXiv paper, Hebbian learning, the biological rule that neurons firing together wire together. As a machine learning method, plain Hebbian updates are unstable: connection changes are unbounded, and there is no feedback path to mediate them. That has kept the approach from scaling to hard tasks, despite its biological appeal and its promise of learning without labels.

Their method, SPHeRe, adds the missing structure. Orthogonality constraints keep update sizes bounded. A small auxiliary nonlinear block projects information back toward the input, standing in for feedback, and a loss preserves structural information through that path. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, SPHeRe reached the best results reported among unsupervised synaptic plasticity methods. It also performed strongly in continual learning, where old skills must survive new data, and in transfer learning. Reconstruction tests showed the learned features are robust and general.
arxiv-2510-15110:
Shih-Yang Liu and a team at NVIDIA and partner universities ask how to make reasoning language models think more briefly without thinking worse. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that models like DeepSeek-R1 earn strong scores with very long chains of thought, wasting tokens on the way. The group revisits the simplest fix, penalizing length by cutting responses off during reinforcement learning.

Their recipe, named DLER, pairs that blunt cutoff with steadier training tricks, including batch-wise reward normalization, looser clipping limits, and dynamic sampling of training examples. The result cut output length by more than 70 percent while beating every earlier baseline on accuracy. One seven-billion-parameter version answered with several short attempts in parallel and scored 28 percent higher than DeepSeek-R1-7B, with lower delay. A difficulty-aware variant trims easy questions even harder.
arxiv-2510-15510:
Heeseong Shin and four colleagues at KAIST and NAVER borrow the eyes of image-generating models to help robots act. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models as a source of visual features for imitation learning, without retraining the big model. Frozen general-purpose features often miss what a control task needs, and simply adding text prompts barely helped in their tests.

The team blames a domain gap, since internet images differ sharply from robot camera views, and control needs dynamic, moment-specific details. Their method, ORCA, instead learns two kinds of prompts. Task prompts adapt the features to the control environment, while visual prompts capture fine details of each individual frame. Together they turn the frozen diffusion model into a task-adaptive feature source. Across several robotic control benchmarks the approach reached state-of-the-art results.
arxiv-2510-15710:
Junzhi Ning and a large team introduce UniMedVL in a 2025 paper. It is one model that both reads and creates medical images. Most medical systems do only one of these tasks. The team built training that mimics a doctor's workflow. That workflow moves from looking, to knowledge, to analysis. They also built a data set of over five million medical samples. All samples were put into a shared format.

Training used a step-by-step curriculum. Medical knowledge was layered in gradually. The model beat rival systems on five image reading tests. It matched specialist image makers across eight imaging types. Training to create images also improved the reading side. The authors say the two skills reinforce each other.
arxiv-2510-15810:
Luis Abanto-Leon and Setareh Maghsudi tackle a design problem in a 2025 paper. The setting is wireless systems that sense and communicate at once. They share the same channel. A device transmits and receives at the same time. Its own transmission leaks into its receiver. Cancelling that self-interference is never perfect.

The design must split time slots between the two tasks. It must also choose beam directions and widths. Jointly, this is a hard nonconvex problem. It mixes integer and nonlinear parts. The authors reformulate it into a linear mixed-integer form. Standard solvers can finish that form. The result is provably globally optimal allocations. Beam choices are optimal too. This holds under realistic, imperfect cancellation.
arxiv-2510-16310:
Olajumoke O Adekunle and three co-authors push automated lung cancer screening beyond a simple yes-or-no answer. Most earlier systems only separate malignant from benign nodules, while treatment planning needs the subtype; their approach classifies CT images into three classes, two malignant subtypes and one benign category.

Starting from a pretrained ResNet50 network, they add custom layers and fine-tune carefully on a dataset of fifteen thousand lung images, split into training, validation, and test portions. The finished model scores a test accuracy of 98.8 percent, a clear improvement over prior models on the same data. The authors present the result as a step toward clinically usable multi-class diagnosis support.
arxiv-2510-16410:
Changyue Shi leads six co-authors in a 2025 study on picking out objects in 3D scenes from plain speech. Their system, REALM, works on a scene format built from many soft dots that can render new views. A large model that reads both text and images does the thinking, so no long 3D training is needed.

REALM first scans wide views of the scene to find the right object. It then makes close views to draw a sharp mask around it. Tests on three data sets show strong scores for both clear and vague requests. The same tool can also remove, swap, or restyle objects in the scene.
arxiv-2510-16910:
Arkady Kitover and Mehmet Orhon revisit a classic algebra theorem in a 2025 paper. The setting is a Banach algebra, a space where elements can multiply and have size. An automorphism is a symmetry that reshuffles the algebra onto itself. The old theorem describes the spectrum, the set of special scaling values.

The Kamowitz-Scheinberg theorem says such a spectrum must contain the full unit circle. That holds whenever no power of the symmetry acts as identity. Kitover and Orhon study weighted versions of these symmetries. Their results considerably strengthen the classic statement. The work sharpens what algebraists can say about long-run behavior. Repeated symmetries, it turns out, leave a stronger spectral fingerprint than previously proved.
arxiv-2510-17210:
Chenchen Tan and six co-authors erase set facts from chat models without fake replies in this 2025 paper. Erasing facts can harm a model's skill, or leave gaps it fills with lies. Both flaws hurt trust in fact-heavy work. The team shifts model focus rather than just muting weights.

Their method damps focus on fact-bearing words in the erase set. It boosts focus on core words in the keep set at the same time. A dual loss draws a soft wall between erased and kept facts. Tests beat top rivals at keeping skill while facts stay gone. Gains reached about fifteen percent on one shared test set.
arxiv-2510-17810:
Camilo Quiceno Quintero and Sandip Varkey George measure how heart signal complexity changes with disease. Electrocardiograms record the heart's electrical activity over time. Healthy and diseased hearts produce signals with different complex patterns. The pair use nonlinear time series tools to capture those differences.

They drew data from PTB-XL, a large public electrocardiogram collection. Measures came from one lead, plus cross-channel links among three leads. Nearly all measures differed clearly between healthy and diseased groups. Adding the measures to machine learning models improved disease classification. Accuracy gains were modest but consistent across the diagnostic groups.
arxiv-2510-17910:
Sagnik Dakshit and Sushmita Sinha Roy build a way to judge not just whether a language model gets a calculus answer right, but how it reasons. Right answers alone miss shaky logic, weak concepts, and steps that only look smooth. Their method pulls out the flow of a solution and labels each operation and concept.

They also vary the prompt to test how stable the answers stay. On real university calculus exams, the models often wrote fluent steps with flawed ideas underneath. Teachers get a set of measures for spotting that gap before such tools are trusted in class.
arxiv-2510-18010:
David Eppstein, Daniel Frishberg, and William Maxwell finish a bound on the Tower of Hanoi graph by looking at how it expands. In the puzzle, disks move one at a time between pegs and never rest on a smaller disk. The graph's corners are legal setups, and its edges are single legal moves.

Earlier work by the same team pinned the graph's treewidth between two close bounds. Here they prove the upper bound is tight by giving a matching lower bound for expansion. Puzzle graphs may look playful, but the result is a firm statement about how such state spaces spread.
arxiv-2510-18110:
Minerva M Sardaneta, with five co-authors, studies gas that glows above the disks of isolated spiral galaxies. Lonely galaxies are prized because their growth is driven from inside, undisturbed for billions of years. The sample lies nearly edge-on, and hydrogen-alpha light traces the moving gas both in the disk and above it.

Rotation curves and dynamical masses are built for each galaxy and checked against radio data and scaling laws. A rotational lag shows up in the extraplanar gas. Combined with ultraviolet, optical, and infrared traits, the work shows how quiet galaxies still vent and recycle their gas.
arxiv-2510-18410:
Adeel Safder, writing alone, offers a new way to train deep networks. His method fights a common flaw. Big networks often just memorize their training data. They then fail on new data. The method is called Momentum-Adaptive Gradient Dropout. It switches parts of the network off during training. The rate of switching is not fixed. It shifts with the current gradients. It also shifts with momentum, a memory of past steps.

Safder also proves a bound on test error. The bound uses a PAC-Bayes argument. It takes the adaptive dropout into account. It came out much tighter than standard bounds. The gain was up to about twenty-nine percent. Tests ran on two well-known image sets. They were MNIST and CIFAR-10. Scores were high on both. The gap between training and test scores stayed small. He also shares full code for checking the work.
arxiv-2510-18510:
Alistair Plum, together with Anne-Marie Lutgen, Christoph Purschke, and Achim Rettinger, argues that language models need a skill they currently lack: cultural reasoning. They define it as the capacity to recognize culture-specific knowledge, values, and social norms, and to adjust answers so they fit an individual user's expectations. Without it, identity-aware systems risk repeating stereotypes, sidelining minority views, and losing user trust.

The authors review evidence that present models default to Western norms when judging moral dilemmas, reading idioms, or giving advice, and that fine-tuning on survey data only partly fixes the habit. They also note that current evaluations mostly report fixed accuracy scores, which cannot capture whether a model adapts its reasoning to context. Their position is that cultural reasoning should stand beside factual accuracy and fluent language as a core capability, and they outline first steps for measuring it.
arxiv-2510-18610:
Adeel Khan, working with Tasuki Kinjo, Hyeonjun Park, and Pavel Safronov, constructs mathematical objects called period sheaves for Hamiltonian spaces. These sheaves were predicted by an influential program linking geometry and the theory of automorphic forms, but a general construction was missing. The authors build them using perverse pullback functors, tools from their own earlier work that move sheaves between spaces in a refined way.

A central theorem, a dimensional reduction isomorphism, generalizes results from a neighboring field and shows the refined pullbacks genuinely improve on ordinary ones. The authors also connect perverse pullbacks to microstalk functors, another local probe of sheaves. With that machinery in place, their period sheaves reproduce the two previously known special constructions, the cotangent and Whittaker cases, confirming the new general theory against the examples that inspired it.
arxiv-2510-18810:
Weiqiu You and his four co-authors test an explanation method for transformers. Leave-one-out importance scores a feature by removing it. The idea is intuitive but far too slow. Layer-wise relevance propagation promises the same insight cheaply. It flows a relevance score backward through the network. Its soundness in modern transformers was largely unexamined.

Two problems surface in the study. First, recent variants use bilinear propagation rules. The authors prove those rules break implementation invariance. Equivalent networks can get distinct explanations that way. Experiments in linear attention layers confirm the proof. Second, a diagnostic variant routes relevance only through value matrices. It bypasses the softmax layer entirely. That variant aligned far better with leave-one-out scores. The gains sat in middle and late layers. Bilinear sensitivity and softmax error jointly undermine the method.
arxiv-2510-18910:
Ziquan Wei, Tingting Dan, and Guorong Wu build a base model of brain wiring from MRI scans. Brain imaging AI is held back by small sample counts. Most base models learn from unlabeled scans by self-teaching. That signal may not match the outcomes doctors care about. The authors fold in data on life context and demographics. Learning is framed as a multitask task.

Their Large Connectome Model turns brain-context links into tokens in pretraining. It then assigns pseudo-labels from those links in a fine-tuning stage. Tasks tested ranged widely, from sex prediction and behavior reading to early signs of autism, Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, and schizophrenia. Results were promising across the board. Brain-context links are presented as the missing piece for imaging base models.
arxiv-2510-19010:
C B Adams and sixty-four co-authors use VERITAS gamma-ray observations to limit axion-like particles, hypothetical particles that could mix with light in magnetic fields. A flaring radio galaxy at the center of the Perseus cluster offered a rare test, since its gamma rays cross a wide, strong cluster magnetic field on the way out.

VERITAS caught the second day of a dramatic flare from that galaxy in 2017. If axion-like particles with certain masses and coupling strengths existed, they would leave marks on the gamma-ray spectrum. Seeing no such marks lets the team rule out part of that parameter space.
arxiv-2510-19410:
Victor Morand and three co-authors introduce ToMMeR, a tiny model that detects entity mentions in text by probing the early layers of large language models. Finding which spans of text name entities is a foundation of information extraction, and also a known bottleneck, so a cheap, accurate probe is valuable.

With fewer than three hundred thousand parameters, ToMMeR reaches very high recall across thirteen benchmarks with strong estimated precision. Models of wildly different sizes converge on similar mention boundaries, suggesting mention detection emerges naturally from language modeling itself. Adding classification heads turns the probe into a competitive full named-entity recognizer.
arxiv-2510-19510:
Ishita Modak and three co-authors bring the idea of Fock-space fragmentation to disordered quantum systems, where it had not been applied. Fragmentation splits the space of possible states into disconnected pieces, blocking normal thermal behavior. It was previously tied to special constraints in clean, translation-invariant systems.

Studying the disordered XXZ model after a sudden quench, the authors define a potential-energy shell: the part of configuration space a starting state can actually reach. As disorder grows, that shell breaks into fragments, and its size fluctuates sharply between samples at weak disorder. Tracking the shell's behavior with system size gives an estimate of where strong fragmentation sets in, offering a geometric account of slow relaxation in such systems.
arxiv-2510-19610:
P. Peñil and six co-authors examine how gaps in observing schedules distort the search for periodic signals in blazars, the violently variable active galaxies. Telescopes cannot watch continuously, so light curves come with irregular sampling and holes. The team tests how those holes change apparent variability, hide real periods, and create fake ones, using both simulated and real data.

Three standard methods are compared, including the Lomb-Scargle periodogram and singular spectrum analysis. Once gaps exceed half the data, period detection degrades badly and seasonal sampling invents periods near one year. Singular spectrum analysis stayed most reliable, and signals found at high confidence were unlikely to be artifacts of noise or gaps.
arxiv-2510-20010:
Asad Hussain, Maximiliano Isi, and Aaron Zimmerman address a common problem in population studies where a quantity is limited to a fixed range. Examples include black hole spin and orbital eccentricity, both confined between zero and one. Standard methods often distort results near those edges, where scientists most want to test for clustering.

The team introduces a truncated Gaussian mixture model that handles boundaries more carefully and reduces those biases. Applied to gravitational wave catalogs, it matches published limits on the share of zero-spin binary black hole systems in GWTC-3 at much lower cost. The method is released in two open-source packages for wider use.
arxiv-2510-20310:
Mingliang Zhai and eight co-authors build ToolEQA, an agent that answers scene questions with tools and step-wise thought. The task needs a search of a 3D scene for facts, then a sound reply. Past agents search and reply in one pass, with weak thought and long, wasteful paths. Tools can add facts that steer the next search step well.

A data pipe builds tasks on its own, with thought paths and replies, to train tool use. It yields near 18,000 tasks, split for train and for tests on seen and new scenes. ToolEQA lifts win rates by near 9 to 20 points over top rivals. It also takes shorter paths to its replies.
arxiv-2510-20510: Cheng-Chiang Tsai states a local character growth for forms of a p-adic reductive group when the prime is very large. The form lives on a closed field whose trait is not that prime, and the growth holds counts tied to orbits. In place of the form character, the growth runs on counts of worn Moy-Prasad types. A mate work by Tsai shows such growths live, by a fresh and fast way.
arxiv-2510-20710:
Şahsene Altınkaya and Sibel Yalçın study a family of harmonic functions built from the error function, which itself measures the spread of a bell shaped curve. Their focus is a class defined inside the unit disk, where each function splits into a plain part and a mirrored part.

Working within that class, the pair set out basic properties and inclusion links, showing when one version of the class sits inside another as its settings change. Such results help map the safe ranges for shape and growth of these functions. Though the note is brief and formal, it adds one more piece to the long study of special function families in complex analysis.
arxiv-2510-20810:
Mingmeng Geng and Thierry Poibeau argue that research on detecting machine written text lacks a precise shared definition of its target. Without that definition, detector scores are easy to misread and their value in real use is shrinking.

Human edits to model drafts, plus the quiet influence models exert on their users writing habits, blur any clean line between machine and human text. Current benchmarks cover only a slice of what models can produce and miss many real world conditions. The authors conclude that detectors can still help under narrow stated conditions, but their outputs should count as rough references rather than firm verdicts on authorship.
arxiv-2510-20910:
Alina Cojocaru and one co-author prove an effective surjectivity result for Galois representations attached to products of elliptic curves over function fields of characteristic zero. Such results bound how large the image of the representation can be, with explicit control rather than mere existence.

The proof routes through an isogeny degree bound in this setting, assembled from curve bounds by Griffon and Pazuki and from a function field analogue of the Frey Mazur conjecture. Techniques trace back to Serre and to Masser and Wüstholz in the number field case. The curves treated are non isotrivial and pairwise non isogenous, the generic and most useful case.
arxiv-2510-21010:
Ludovic Salomon leads two co-authors on MOCVXPY, an open source Python library for convex vector optimization with several objectives at once. It extends CVXPY, the widely used language for single objective convex problems, with an algebraic style that mirrors the mathematical formulation.

Features, algorithmic background, and worked examples are presented, plus two real applications in finance and energy. Users can describe trade off problems directly and obtain solution sets rather than single compromise points. The library lowers the barrier for practitioners who need Pareto style answers inside a familiar Python workflow.
arxiv-2510-21110:
Mingxuan Li leads two co-authors on confounding robust deep reinforcement learning, a causal approach to off policy learning from biased data. Agents often must learn from past records where hidden factors skewed both actions and outcomes, and standard Q learning then chases biased rewards.

Building on the Deep Q Network, their algorithm seeks a safe policy that performs acceptably even under unobserved confounding of plausible strength. High dimensional domains are the target, where confounding cannot be ruled out in advance. Robust policies matter in health and recommendation settings, where logged data are plentiful but never randomized.
arxiv-2510-21210:
Francesco Pivi and four co-authors address a weakness of flow matching, a method that builds data by gradually turning noise into samples. In standard models, the steps along that path have no clear meaning, so users cannot tell what each step is doing or why it matters.

Their framework forces each step to match an equilibrium state of a known physical system, using the two-dimensional Ising model of magnetism as the test case. An encoder, a flow network driven by a cooling schedule, and a projector move between magnet patterns and the model's inner space. Across several lattice sizes, the method keeps physical accuracy and beats Monte Carlo generation on speed as lattices grow.
arxiv-2510-21410:
Gerhard Schindl introduces a new operation on weight functions, rulers that measure how fast a class of extremely smooth functions may grow. Such ultradifferentiable classes sort functions finer than ordinary smoothness allows, and the fastest-growing rulers break the standard regularity rules that textbooks usually demand.

He studies the new conjugate operation in depth, then uses it to move recent results, proved with a collaborator for growth measured by sequences, into the function-based setting. A companion construction, the conjugate weight matrix, ties the two viewpoints together through their linked weight functions. Older results about small Gevrey classes are extended as well. As an application, the classes can detect when certain operators on Hilbert spaces stay bounded, which matters for judging solutions of evolution equations.
arxiv-2510-21610:
Jens E. d'Hondt, Wieger R. Punter, and Odysseas Papapetrou generate synthetic data sets that keep the correlation skeleton of the original. Today's privacy-friendly data fakers have a weak point there. Most methods reproduce simple averages yet scramble the web of relationships between variables. Models trained on such fake data then learn the wrong world.

Their method, Generative Correlation Manifolds, is disarmingly direct. It breaks a target correlation matrix apart with a Cholesky factorization. It uses that factorization to stamp the same correlation structure onto fresh random data. The structure survives intact, pairwise and higher-order alike, with a mathematical proof. The authors argue this cheap, exact preservation opens safer data sharing between organizations. It also supports sturdier model training and more faithful simulations.
arxiv-2510-21910:
Mahavir Dabas leads an eleven-author team defending language models against jailbreaks, the crafted prompts that trick a model past its safety rules. Their starting claim, named the Adversarial Déjà Vu hypothesis, holds that brand-new attacks are rarely new at all: they mostly remix skills seen in older attacks.

To test the idea, the team mined thirty-two attack papers from two years, extracted the tricks those attacks use. Compressed them into a sparse dictionary of basic moves with plain-language descriptions. Fresh attacks could indeed be explained as sparse combinations of earlier moves. That finding points to a different defense strategy: instead of training against endless worst-case prompts, learn the shared vocabulary of attacks so that recombinations are recognized when they appear.
arxiv-2510-22210:
Gwihwan Go, Quan Zhang, Chijin Zhou, Zhao Wei, and Yu Jiang generate unit tests for code in any programming language, in real time, while a developer works. Language models write good tests when handed the right context about the method under test. Fetching that context is the bottleneck: fuzzy similarity search is imprecise, while proper static analysis must be rebuilt for every language.

Their framework, LSPRAG, borrows the context from the Language Server Protocol, the mature editor infrastructure that already knows where every symbol is defined and referenced in dozens of languages. Those exact definitions and call sites become the retrieval layer feeding the model, with almost no per-language engineering. Evaluations on open-source projects test whether precise, borrowed context beats bespoke pipelines at producing high-coverage tests.
arxiv-2510-22710:
Retrieval systems stumble on rare, ambiguous questions where noisy sources distort the reasoning that follows. Kaitong Cai, Jusheng Zhang, Yijia Fan, Jing Yang, and Keze Wang propose RaCoT in 2025, a plug in framework that adds contrastive thinking before retrieval rather than after it.

RaCoT automatically writes a nearby question whose answer differs, then extracts a prompt capturing the key difference. That prompt steers one retrieval pass toward details that decide between the two answers. On six benchmarks, including PopQA and TriviaQA, it beats strong baselines by small margins. Under adversarial tests its performance drops far less than rival methods, at low added cost.
arxiv-2510-23210:
Abhishek Chaudhary and Andreas Prohl present higher-order numerical schemes for stochastic partial differential equations with additive noise. Standard Euler schemes converge slowly for such equations because noise is rough in time, limiting rates to between one half and one. They study linear stochastic heat and wave equations with fixed boundary values.

For the heat equation, a modified Crank-Nicolson scheme with a proper quadrature for the noise term reaches a strong rate of three halves. A matching approach gives order two for the wave equation. Faster schemes let engineers simulate noisy heat and vibration with far fewer time steps.
arxiv-2510-23410:
Jiahao Ji leads a team of eight researchers studying online advertising bidding through a foundation model lens. Auto-bidding sets bids for advertisers automatically, but models of the bidding environment are usually tailored to one scenario and generalize poorly. The authors instead seek scenario-independent principles through a unified function.

That function estimates the effect achieved under a given bid, such as budget use, sales volume, or page views. On it they build Bid2X, a bidding foundation model meant to transfer across environments. Transferable bidding models could cut the retraining advertisers face on each new campaign.
arxiv-2510-23510:
In a 2025 paper, Shakthivelu Janardhanan and three co-authors ask how a network operator can depend less on supply firms. They call that freedom network sovereignty: when one maker fails or vanishes, a sovereign network keeps running. Heavy reliance on a single maker means low survival odds in such a failure, a trap known as vendor lock-in.

The main contribution is a new score, called Cut Set Coloring, that measures how sovereign a network design is. At its core sits an integer linear program that picks the best assignment of makers to parts. The program, named CSC-ILP, is set up to push the score as high as the design allows. The comparison shows where the new method stands against current practice.
arxiv-2510-23710:
Joshuah T. Heath and four co-authors study how two-level systems, tiny defects inside materials, can raise or lower a superconductor's critical temperature. Such defects behave like soft modes pinned at fixed spots in the material. Superconductivity is famously delicate, so whether these common flaws help or harm has practical weight for devices built from thin films.

The team shows the effect can go either way, depending on how densely the defects cover the surface and how high their average frequency sits. Using thin-film aluminium as the test case, they describe quantitatively how the defects shift both the critical temperature and the zero-temperature energy gap. The numbers match the picture of defects as a tuning knob rather than pure damage. The authors frame the result as an opening: engineering two-level systems on purpose could tailor superconducting materials to order.
arxiv-2510-23810:
Sumanta Roy and three co-authors extend a neural operator framework so it can learn physics with no training data at all, at any resolution. Operator learning maps input functions to solution functions of partial differential equations, but it usually feeds on high-fidelity datasets that engineering practice may not supply. Real data arrive on uneven grids that vary from sample to sample.

Their method projects each input function, drawn on an arbitrarily fine grid, onto pretrained basis functions to get a compact latent code. A small multilayer perceptron then maps that code plus space-time coordinates to the solution. The equations are enforced by a finite difference solver in physical space, so no labeled solutions are needed. Benchmarks with coarse and fine data test the approach on several equations. The authors present it as a way to get resolution-independent learning where data are scarce or absent.
arxiv-2510-24010:
Mirali Purohit and eight co-authors introduce Mars-Bench, the first standardized benchmark for machine learning on Mars science tasks. Foundation models have transformed fields with plentiful labeled benchmarks, but Mars research lacks shared test sets, which has slowed its own foundation models. Mars-Bench fills the gap with twenty datasets drawn from orbital and surface imagery.

The tasks span classification, segmentation, and object detection, targeting the features geologists care about: craters, cones, boulders, and frost. All datasets ship in ready-to-use form with standardized splits. The authors baseline them with models pretrained on natural images, on Earth satellite data, and with leading vision-language models. Across the analyses, Mars-specific pretraining looks advantageous over general-domain starting points. The benchmark, data, and code are public, giving the community a common yardstick. The authors hope it sparks the same cycle of progress that benchmarks enabled for Earth observation.
arxiv-2510-24310:
Guus Toussaint and Arno Knobbe extend a search method that finds short, clear formulas from data. In the past, this search served tasks where the output is a number. Their new method, EDC, serves yes or no tasks. It looks for a short analytic formula that states where the border between the two classes lies and what shape it has. That keeps the learned model easy to read and check.

On made up data and on real data, EDC found both the true form of the target rule and the values of its constants. It beat past formula search methods for class tasks. Its scores were on par with the best class tools overall. The authors suggest a grammar to guide the search and keep the found borders small and clear.
arxiv-2510-24410:
Toan Van Nguyen leads a team of four authors on a vision task. The task is multi-object tracking, which means following many things in video. Each thing must keep the same label as frames pass, even in crowds. Their method, called GenTrack2, mixes two styles of tracking in one system. One style uses chance and sampling, the other uses firm matching rules.

The sampling part spreads guesses for where each thing moves next. A swarm search pulls those guesses toward the most likely spots. The matching part pairs guesses with fresh sightings by a cost score. That score weighs place, sighting strength, and past track quality. Past speeds give trend seeds that guide both sampling and updates. Tests show the tracker beats strong rivals on video and live streams.
arxiv-2510-24710:
Wei Shen, Jiawei Zhang, Minhui Huang, and Cong Shen tackle two level math tasks where the low level has straight line limits. Such tasks show up when a top choice must sit on top of a best low choice. The top goal can be rough, and its slope needs costly second order terms.

The team recasts the task as one level with a fine and a boost term, and shows the new form tracks the old one in worth and slope. Their one loop method then uses just first order slopes. Its step count beats past two loop ways, and tests match the claim.
arxiv-2510-24810:
Rui Xing, Preslav Nakov, Timothy Baldwin, and Jey Han Lau study crowd notes that flag posts as false on big social sites. Such notes help when they are clear, but most notes are never shown; the queue is slow and what makes a note help is vague. Their set, COMMUNITYNOTES, is built to probe that help.

The set holds more than one hundred thousand posts with user notes and help marks, in more than one tongue. Their frame also grows and tunes plain word rules for why a note helps, with an auto prompt loop. Those tuned rules lifted scores on both help calls and the why calls. The work gives fact check teams a firmer base.
arxiv-2510-25710:
Priyavrat Deshpande, Amit Roy, and Rutuja Sawant present co-connected complexes. Their 2025 math paper defines a new simplicial complex family. For a graph and vertex subset, the complex is defined. A setting r at least one controls co-connectivity. When the subset is empty, Alexander duality appears. The complex becomes dual of r-independence complex there.

They uncover topological and combinatorial trait relationships. Algebraic and homological traits of dual ideals connect. The complex is vertex decomposable under connectivity settings. For several great graph classes, equivalences are established. Chordal, co-chordal, cographs, and cycles are included. Co-chordality of an associated clutter characterizes them precisely. Results extend Froberg theorem to r-connected ideals. A conjecture on linear resolution is motivated. Combinatorial topology and commutative algebra meet here.
arxiv-2510-26110:
Sandor Kisfaludi-Bak, Tze-Yang Poon, and Geert van Wordragen study shortest paths in regular hyperbolic tilings, the infinite planar graphs formed by regular polygons that only fit in hyperbolic geometry. Each vertex has the same degree and each face the same number of edges, with a numeric condition that forces negative curvature. They ask how the routes between a set of terminal points are organized.

The authors compute an isometric closure, closely tied to the geodesic convex hull of the terminals, in near linear time by reusing a classic convex hull algorithm. The hull size is linear in total path length, and its treewidth, a measure of how tree like a graph is, stays small. That bound yields fast algorithms for subset traveling salesman and Steiner tree problems.
arxiv-2510-26210:
Junlin Liu and Zhaomeng Deng lead seven co-authors in a study of how easily users can erase payment records inside super apps. Super apps bundle finance into everyday services, and security work has focused on stopping unauthorized payments before they happen. The authors argue that the audit trail after a transaction is fragile: a user can delete history from the app interface and hide activity from the account owner.

In an empirical study, six volunteers cross evaluated six super apps. All six allowed deletion of transaction records, yet five of the six did not protect deletion with strong authentication, and only one required biometric verification. The authors present this as the first concrete evidence of a near universal gap.
arxiv-2510-26410:
Lele Liu and Bo Ning prove a new bound in spectral graph theory, the study of networks through the numbers tied to their connection patterns. For a network with no large fully linked group, an older result capped the largest such number, the spectral radius, in terms of the number of links. The pair extend that cap to weighted graphs, where each link carries a weight.

Liu and Ning state the cap as a sum over links, with each link's term set by the largest fully linked group that contains it. They also name all the graphs that hit the cap exactly. From this one result flow several new forms of Turán's theorem and weighted forms of older named results. A key step is a fresh lower bound that balances an upper bound found by others.
arxiv-2510-26510:
Youssef Attia El Hili, with six co-authors, asks whether a large language model can pick the right learning model for a new data set. Choosing a model family and its settings usually takes expert feel or a costly automatic search. The team turns each data set into plain metadata, a summary a language model can read, and asks it to recommend both.

El Hili and the team test two styles of asking. One uses only the model's built-in knowledge. The other adds examples of past tasks with the models that did well on them. Across made-up and real benchmarks, the language model picked competitive models and settings without any search. The example-fed style did better, which the authors read as evidence of in-context meta-learning, learning how to learn from the prompt itself.
arxiv-2510-26710:
Nguyen Nang Thieu and Nguyen Dong Yen prove minimax theorems for functions that need not be convex. A minimax theorem swaps the order of a worst case and a best case without changing the value, and it guarantees saddle points, spots where neither side can gain by moving alone. Convexity is the usual price for such results, so dropping it widens their reach.

Thieu and Yen establish three such theorems, set on Euclidean spaces or on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. Each also guarantees that a saddle point exists. As a by-product, they fully solve an open problem about continuously differentiable functions that had been left hanging. A concrete example is worked through to show how the results apply.
arxiv-2510-26810:
Tatsuru Kikuchi builds a theory of emergency medical response zones from fluid dynamics. Response times decide survival, yet coverage analysis usually relies on distance buffers or map-based travel-time shapes with no theoretical base. Kikuchi derives continuous spatial boundaries from the Navier-Stokes equations, the laws of fluid motion, from first principles.

He finds response effectiveness decays exponentially with time, and he estimates the decay from ten thousand simulated incidents drawn from a national emergency data system. Boundaries mark where effectiveness falls below policy thresholds. The analysis finds sharp gaps. People over eighty-five waited about eight point four minutes on average, against about seven point eight for younger adults. Poor-access incidents fell heavily on the elderly. The framework is aimed at station placement and resource allocation to cut those disparities.
arxiv-2510-27010:
William Heap leads five co-authors in building a soft robot that grows into pipes to inspect them. Vine robots extend by turning soft material outward at the tip, letting them follow tight, winding paths. Older versions rely on complex exposed parts and lack proof in real industrial settings, where dirt and moisture can interfere.

The new system seals all mechanical and electrical parts inside an airtight, transparent body, shielding them while still allowing visual checks. A passive tip mount carries sensors inside the sealed body and adapts on its own. The team validates the full system by assessing and mapping a real wastewater pipe. The result is a simpler, field-tested design ready for further deployment work.
arxiv-2510-27110:
Gal Shtendel and Ayush Bhandari tackle recording signals that span several frequency bands without clipping loud parts. Standard sampling folds when signals exceed sensor range, losing the peaks. The unlimited sensing framework instead records modulo-folded samples, meaning values wrap around a fixed range, and recovers the original signal afterward by unwrapping.

Working with a low-complexity single-channel setup, the pair prove recovery guarantees showing sampling below the classic Nyquist rate is achievable in this setting. They also tighten a prior sampling theorem for bandpass signals. Hardware experiments with up to six spectral bands show up to a thirteenfold gain in dynamic range. The results enable high-range multiband capture where oversampling and clipping once blocked practical use.
arxiv-2511-00010:
Jiajun Zhang, Jianke Zhang, and Zeyu Cui introduce PlotCraft, a benchmark of one thousand challenging tasks for language models that generate data visualizations. Models write code well, but complex charts for scaled, structured data are largely unevaluated. Tasks span finance, scientific research, and sociology, organized into seven high-level visualization types and forty-eight chart types.

Single-turn generation and more interactive settings are both assessed, making it an early systematic test of its kind. AI evaluation readers get a yardstick for a daily analyst skill. Visualization is where code correctness meets design judgment, so the benchmark probes more than syntax.
arxiv-2511-00110:
YingQiao Wang, Eric Bigelow, and Boyi Li propose Chain-of-Time, a prompting method that calms physical simulation by autoregressive image generation models. Inspired by human mental simulation and in-context reasoning in language models, the method creates a series of middle images during a simulation, so each step terms on clear visual states. No extra fine-tuning is needed at inference time.

Applications cover synthetic two-dimensional graphics runs and natural three-dimensional videos, spanning varied physical motion. AI readers get an inference-time trick that also makes generated simulations easier to interpret. Showing middle frames exposes where a model's mental physics goes wrong.
arxiv-2511-00410:
Takumi Hasada and seven co-authors report a laboratory hunt for axion-like particles with masses around the electronvolt scale. Their tool is a stimulated resonant photon collider that focuses and collides three laser beams at variable angles. Changing the angles scans the collision energy smoothly across the target range, and the test needs no assumptions from cosmology or astronomy.

Running at a large-angle setup in a vacuum chamber, the team first verified the three short pulses overlapped in space and time.
