It aims to widen clinicians' view beyond the mouth.

Digestive diseases come first in the survey. Cancers linked to oral bacteria follow. Heart and vessel diseases get a full section. Alzheimer's disease and diabetes each earn one too. Rheumatoid arthritis and preterm birth close the list. For each, the authors weigh how oral microbes might contribute. They stress two-way traffic between mouth and body. Dental research, they argue, is whole-body research.
europmc-pmc8996410:
Li and co-authors review PROTACs, engineered molecules that destroy cancer proteins rather than block them. A PROTAC has two linked heads. One grips the target protein. The other recruits the cell's tagging machinery. The tag marks the protein for the proteasome shredder. The approach can remove proteins that drugs cannot inhibit. Many cancer drivers sit in that hard class. The review explains the design logic first. It then traces the method's growth since its first proof in 2001.

Target sections march through famous oncoproteins. BRD4, cell cycle kinases, and EGFR each get a chapter. BRAF, PARP1, and BCR-ABL follow. PD-L1 closes the target list. Design rules for new molecules are set out. Problems get plain treatment too. Size, delivery, and resistance all limit the class. The authors compare PROTACs with older targeted drugs. Destruction, they argue, widens the druggable map.
europmc-pmc9018410:
Andrews and co-authors measured how well COVID-19 booster shots worked in England during the Delta wave. Using a test-negative design, they compared boosted adults with people who had two doses or none. Against symptoms, a booster after either main vaccine course raised protection to around 85% to 95%. Overall effectiveness soon after boosting reached 94% to 97% across age groups.

Protection against hospital admission or death was higher still, at around 97% to 99%. Waning stayed limited through ten weeks after the booster. The authors conclude that boosters restored strong protection against both mild and severe disease.
europmc-pmc9096710:
Buetti and co-authors update expert guidance on stopping bloodstream infections tied to central lines in acute-care hospitals. Central lines are tubes placed in large veins to give drugs and fluids. Germs can enter the blood along these lines and cause grave harm. This update replaces advice last set out in 2014.

The guidance sorts steps into essential practices for all hospitals and extra approaches when infections persist. Essential steps cover staff training, hand hygiene, site choice, sterile care, and quick removal of lines no longer needed. Extra steps can be tried in units where rates stay high. Hospital teams get a short, ranked list to put into daily use.
europmc-pmc9243210:
Sun and co-authors review how metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic changes drive each other on the path to cancer. Both are well-known hallmarks of cancer and are closely linked. Many metabolites serve as raw materials or helpers for enzymes that modify chromatin. Enzyme and metabolite placement inside the cell matters too.

The review focuses on acetylation and methylation of histones and DNA. It also covers newer marks like succinylation and lactylation. These shifts can help tumors escape immunity or block immune watch. The authors update progress on therapies that target metabolism or epigenetic marks. Readers get a current view of two intertwined systems and how drugs might break their alliance in cancer.
europmc-pmc9331210:
Sarhadi and Armengol review molecular biomarkers in cancer. A biomarker is any measurable molecular sign of cancer risk, presence, or outcome. Signs can hide in genes, gene activity, or proteins. Samples may come from tumor tissue or, more gently, from blood, saliva, urine, or stool.

The review sorts biomarker types and the tools that detect them. Uses span risk checks, screening, diagnosis, outlook, and therapy choice. Precision oncology depends on them, since targeted drugs work only in patients with matching mutations. New tests read tumor DNA floating in blood or tiny vesicles called exosomes. The authors say better sensitivity and accuracy are still needed. Faster detection tech keeps widening what can be measured.
europmc-pmc9640110:
Nelson writes a 1910 journal article on Ehrlich's new cure for syphilis, made with Hata's dioxydiamidoarsenobenzol. Syphilis was then one of the great plagues of the age. It had killed and scarred people in vast numbers for centuries. A one-shot cure claim stirred the whole medical world.

Nelson reports Ehrlich's aim of sterilisatio magna, a full kill of the parasite. Animal tests came first, checked by the Wassermann method. One injection in human cases was the stated manner of use. Observers across Germany reported strong and uniform success, he writes. Praise ran high among those who tried the remedy. Effects were said to show within ten to fourteen days. The drug was reported to work at all disease stages. That spread ran from the first lesion to late tertiary signs. The piece conveys the era's hope more than hard proof.
europmc-pmc9671810:
Bowe, Xie, and Al-Aly measure the added health risks that come with SARS-CoV-2 reinfection. A first infection raises later risks in many organ systems. Whether a second infection stacks more risk on top was unclear. The study drew on the US Veterans Affairs health database.

Three cohorts were built from the national records. One held 443,588 people with a single infection. The reinfection cohort held 40,947 people with two or more. A noninfected control group held 5,334,729 people for scale. Reinfection added clear risks of death and hospital care. Aftereffects spanned lung, heart, kidney, and brain systems. Diabetes and mental health harms also rose after reinfection. The added risks showed with or without vaccination. They peaked in the acute phase yet lasted six months. Total burden grew with each added infection a person had.
europmc-pmc9728410:
Ahn and co-authors review the state of COVID-19 knowledge on spread, testing, treatment, and vaccines. The disease first surfaced in Wuhan, China in late 2019. It causes hard lung illness, pneumonia, and lung failure. Within months the virus reached pandemic scale worldwide.

The review opens with the virus itself and its likely animal source. It then walks through test kits built to find the virus fast. Repurposed drugs with early clinical promise get a survey. Vaccine efforts by firms and institutes round out the tour. By late March 2020 over 400,000 cases were confirmed. Deaths had passed 18,000 across the world by then. The authors stress that containment needs fast shared knowledge. Their summary gathers what was known at that early point. It maps the gaps that work still had to close.
europmc-pmc9977110:
Rossaint and co-authors present the sixth edition of the European guideline on major bleeding after trauma. Severe trauma is a major global public health burden. Bleeding and trauma-linked coagulopathy can cause preventable organ failure and death. Fast, correct early care is vital for these patients.

A pan-European task force from six professional societies updated the guideline. They used structured searches and an evidence-based consensus process. The advice covers the first diagnostic and treatment phases. It speaks to clinicians who manage bleeding trauma patients early. Topics span detection, resuscitation, and control of coagulopathy. The edition replaces the prior version with current evidence. Its aim is more uniform, timely care across Europe.
flaubert-temptation-st-anthony-hearn-191:
Saint Anthony sits in the Egyptian desert while wonders and horrors crowd his night in Flaubert's Temptation of Saint Anthony. Lafcadio Hearn's 1910 translation renders the work Flaubert called his life's own, rewritten across thirty years. Gods, heretics, monsters, and Death itself parade before the hermit's eyes.

Each vision tempts the saint with a different offer: power, pleasure, knowledge, rest. The book reads more like a vast stage dream than a novel, rich with the lore Flaubert loved. Odilon Redon's dark images, noted in this edition, suit a text where faith wrestles every phantom it can name.
for-better-or-worse-ship-s-company-part-:
Jacobs opens this Ship's Company tale in the King's Head, where George Wotton cadges a drink from Ben Davis. Davis has had a shock: news of the wife who left him long ago. Wotton is sent to sound out how the land lies with her.

The old lady he finds gives the story a sharp turn. In her telling, Davis went off like a cur and left his young wife to manage alone. Now she has come into a bit of money, and she guesses exactly why two gentlemen came calling. W. W. Jacobs lets the deserter's version collapse in a few lines of dialogue.
forster-howards-end-1910:
E. M. Forster published Howards End in 1910, and it became his first widely praised novel. Forster, a Cambridge graduate, wrote about the England he knew: cultured liberals, rich business families, and the clerks caught between them. A country house gives the book its title.

Two Schlegel sisters, Margaret and Helen, befriend the wealthy Wilcox family and a poor clerk named Leonard Bast. Margaret marries into the Wilcoxes, while Helen's rash choices pull Bast toward ruin. The house, Howards End, passes slowly toward the person who understands it best. Forster's famous plea, only connect, sums up the novel's hope for bridging class and feeling.
francis-little-flowers-1910:
The Little Flowers of St. Francis came down from the 1300s in Italy. T. W. Arnold gave the tales English dress in 1910. Francis of Assisi was the rich youth who wed Lady Poverty. His friars roamed the roads with songs and tales of his deeds.

Short tales tell of the wolf of Gubbio, the birds who heard his preach, and his scars of Christ. Joy, love of beasts, and scorn of gold shine in each tale. The book won hearts far past the Church that bred it. It is the most loved book of tales on the saint.
freud-three-essays-brill-1910:
Sigmund Freud published Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality in German in 1905. The English text here is A. A. Brill's translation of 1910, titled Three Contributions to the Theory of Sex. Freud argues that sexual life begins in infancy, not at puberty. Children, in his theory, pass through stages centered on the mouth, anus, and genitals.

He treats perversions as fixations or detours in that growth. The libido, or sexual drive, is the energy behind the process. The book scandalized its age and remains psychoanalysis's most daring founding text. Later editions grew with notes and changes. Its claims still provoke debate among clinicians and critics.
froude-history-england-vol-10:
Spain sends its great fleet against England in the tenth volume of Froude's History, from 1865, covering the Armada year. Drake and Howard lead the sea fight in home waters. Storms then scatter the Spanish ships along wild coasts, completing England's deliverance.

Froude treats the victory as the climax of his whole Tudor epic. Protestant England, in his telling, survives by courage, seamanship, and God's weather. The fate of a nation hangs in the balance through the summer's fighting. His account reads as patriotic pageant, done with great narrative skill, and it crowned his reputation with the reading public of his day.
frus-1861-d10:
Joseph Wright wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 June 1861. The dispatch is document 10 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861, the first year of the Civil War.

By late June both sides were in the field, and Europe watched for a quick result. Wright's reports kept his corner of that watch. The letter shows the plain, dated rhythm by which far posts fed a capital that could not see events for itself. Each dated page added one more fixed point to a map Washington drew from afar. Fixed points like this one let later readers chart the war's foreign course.
frus-1861-d110:
A letter of 24 October 1861 went from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons at the British legation.

The matched dates show the machine in motion: the Navy chief reports, the State chief answers abroad. Seward's note to Lyons carries the product of that inner talk. It is a small, clear case of how the Union turned sea power into diplomacy. Such matched dates let readers watch the inner talk become foreign policy in a day. One day from inner talk to foreign note was swift work for the age of sail and steam.
frus-1861-d210:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Mr. Wood on 22 August 1861. It was printed as Document 210 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d310:
Writing on 7 September 1861, Mr. Dryer sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 310 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d10:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 31 January 1862. It was printed as Document 10 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d110:
A letter home from Charles Francis Adams, dated 25 July 1862, landed on Seward's desk. It was printed as Document 110 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d210:
Lord Lyons replied into the file on 21 February 1862 with a note to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 210 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both men wrote on the same day, a sign of active business between them.

Same-day exchanges usually mean a matter was moving fast or a deadline pressed. Lyons wrote as Britain's eyes in Washington as well as its voice, reporting home on all Seward said and did. A note from his hand in February belongs to the routine that kept a hard relationship workable through the war's first full winter. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d310:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward opened the September Paris mail with a dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 15 September 1862, printed as Document 310 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-September found Lee's army in Maryland and the Union's foreign standing at its lowest point of the year. France had drafted a plan to propose a truce, and Britain was considering it. Seward's letter to Dayton that day went out two days before Antietam, into the most dangerous fortnight the Union faced abroad during the war. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d410:
An instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to Horace J. Perry in Madrid on 15 September 1862. It is Document 410 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Mid-September 1862 was a hinge of the war: Lee's army was in Maryland, and Lincoln waited on a victory before issuing his emancipation order. Foreign courts held back, waiting on the same news. Seward's letters in these days armed his agents with the Union's reading of events. For the Madrid legation, that meant pressing Spain to see a government that meant to win, and to keep its ports closed to Confederate use.
frus-1862-d510:
On 23 July 1862 James Shepherd Pike wrote again from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward, a week after his previous report. The dispatch is Document 510 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Weekly reports in a bad month had a hard job. They had to be truthful. Yet they must not give Washington fresh cause for worry it could not act on. Pike's July letters did that job plainly, recording Dutch steadiness while Union arms regrouped. He also tracked the war's naval fringe, where Dutch colonial ports had rules to enforce. The letter continues a correspondence notable for its regularity. In the whole of 1862, few American posts wrote home as often as Pike's. Fewer still wrote as frankly.
frus-1862-d610:
Thomas Corwin received the year's closing Mexican order from Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 21 October 1862. It is Document 610 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

October's instruction reached Mexico as the French settled in for a long war and as Washington, steadied by Antietam, took stock of its foreign position. The policy Seward repeated to Corwin had not changed in a year: friendship for Mexico's republic, refusal to accept the European enterprise, and patience. Within two years a freed Union army would stand on the Rio Grande and the patience would end. The letter is a fitting close to the volume's most principled American file.
frus-1862-d710:
On 13 September 1862, Andrew B. Dickinson wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second day in a row. Dickinson was the American minister in Nicaragua. The letter is document 710 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Two reports on two days point to a post with much to tell. From Nicaragua, an envoy tracked the transit route, the local government's acts, and the safety of Americans passing through. Dickinson's letters fed that watch. Kept in the volume, they show the pace of a small legation's work when events moved fast and mail home was slow.
frus-1863p1-d10:
On 8 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in London. A second letter to Adams bears the same date in the volume. This one is document 10 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward wrote as the year turned, with the war at a grim point and Europe still weighing its course. His letters told Adams what to say and what to hold back in talks with the British. Paired sheets like these show the secretary working a brief in parts. This letter belongs to that pair, and to the long chain that bound Washington to its London post.
frus-1863p1-d110:
On 6 March 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 110 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Early March found the legation deep in the ship question, as Southern warships took shape in British yards. Adams's mail pressed the facts on Washington and, through his talks, on the British themselves. This letter is one of a pair sent that day. It shows the post in its spring rhythm: watch, report, and press, week after week.
frus-1863p1-d210:
A dispatch dated 5 June 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 210 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For historians, this run is a prime source on Britain's choices. It shows how close London came to stepping into the war, and why it never did. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d310:
Mr. Stuart, an officer of the British legation in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 October 1862. His note is document 310 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Seward answered the legation knowing London would read every word. Even routine notes carried weight, because each answer set a precedent for the next dispute. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d410:
On 5 March 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward put the American position in writing to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. This note is document 410 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

After the Emancipation Proclamation in January 1863, Seward could frame the war as a fight against slavery. That put Britain, which had banned slavery at home, in an awkward spot when it aided the South. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d510:
The date 13 May 1863 heads a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d610:
The letter printed as document 610 was written on 13 August 1863 by Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Alone it is one note among hundreds.
frus-1910:
Argentina's centennial opens the 1910 volume in celebration. The Fourth Conference of American States meets in its file. Cable concessions granted by Argentina follow. Brazil mourns its ambassador, Joaquim Nabuco. His death fills a run of memorial papers. A naturalization convention with Brazil appears. Chile receives its president, Pedro Montt, on a visit. His death follows within the same section.

The mid-volume passage weighs a canal concession. Coasts and posts on both sides, it argues, raise its value. Later generations will esteem the privilege fully. Bulgaria extradites as an act of grace in one case. A fugitive's transit between Luxemburg and America fills many papers. The volume mixes pageantry with procedure. Centennials and extraditions share its pages.
frus-1919Parisv10:
Volume X of the Paris papers gives the Supreme Economic Council its minutes. They run from February 17, 1919 to February 7, 1920. Thirty-odd meetings fill the book. Food, coal, shipping, and credit dominate the agendas. The Council was the Allies' economic general staff. Its sessions continued long after the treaty signed. A mid-volume French paper urges coordination. Each state, it says, takes measures against its own dangers. Joint enterprises, it argues, must outlive the war itself.

The paper warns of waste without common planning. Such theory sits among supply tables and votes. The volume is peace as logistics continued. Hunger was the enemy after Germany laid down arms. The Council's minutes show the fight's paperwork.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d10: Paired with a letter to Stalin the same day, President Roosevelt's note to Prime Minister Churchill of June 18, 1943 is Document 10 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The two messages went out together as the president kept both partners in step. The record supplies date, sender, and receiver, and no topic. In the Foreign Relations series it stands early in the chain of papers that produced the Cairo and Tehran meetings.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d110: A second Churchill message to Roosevelt bears the date November 9, 1943, and it stands as Document 110 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The day's traffic also held letters from Chiang, Harriman, and Bohlen, a fair sample of the summit's whole cast. The record for this note gives the date and the names only. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the rest of that crowded day.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d210:
Foy Kohler of the State Department's Division of Near Eastern Affairs wrote a secret memorandum on 11 November 1943. It records fresh British Embassy reports on the Cairo talks between Anthony Eden and Turkish foreign minister Numan Menemencioğlu, adding two later meetings in Ankara on 7 and 8 November.

Numan, the memo shows, grew somewhat warmer in the final talk. He admitted the Moscow decisions were better than expected, yet he resented Eden's threatening tone and felt Eden spoke for Russia as much as Britain. He wanted to know exactly what Turkey must do, what Allied help she could count on, and what the political results would be. The Balkans now worried Ankara as much as the Straits once did.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d310:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 408 at Cairo on 25 November 1943, on command of British and American forces operating against Germany. It is the full American case for a single commander over the whole European war, pressed at the Sextant Conference.

Operations fall into three linked groups: the Mediterranean, northwest Europe, and the strategic air war on Germany's interior. Since events in each group shape the others, the chiefs argue, one commander must direct all three under the Combined Chiefs of Staff, and his appointment is most urgently necessary. Even named at once, he could not be organized before the end of January 1944. The paper ends with the bombing war, where it calls unified command imperative if lives and planes are to be saved.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d410:
A third draft of the Tehran communiqué is printed here with its handwritten changes shown, Roosevelt's apart from three by Hopkins. An editorial headnote presumes this was the draft discussed and put into final form at the dinner meeting of 1 December 1943.

Hopkins' hand inserted the heading Communiqué, changed Soviet Russia to the Soviet Union, and added the place and date, Tehran, Iran, 1 December 1943, at the foot. Roosevelt's changes tighten the text throughout. The leaders have shaped and confirmed our common policy. Their concord will win an enduring peace. The conferences are now friendly, a word glossed in Russian and English at the margin. A note under the signatures, in the President's papers, reads: as corrected, this becomes the final draft.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d510: Document 510 is an editorial note placed by the volume's historians. It appears in the Cairo-Tehran volume of the Foreign Relations series. Such notes fill gaps between papers with background and cross-references. They keep names, dates, and earlier decisions straight for the reader. The conferences documented here met in late 1943. Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin used them to plan the war's next phase. Read the note as part of that official record's apparatus.
frus-1944-quebec-d10:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on June 4, 1944, the day Allied troops entered Rome and two days before D-Day. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

June 4 was a hinge date: Italy's capital fell even as the invasion fleet sailed for France. Churchill, whose strategy had always prized the Mediterranean, marked the moment in his correspondence with Washington. For readers, a letter from that crowded day shows the war's two Western campaigns peaking together, and the Prime Minister keeping his hand on both through his channel to Roosevelt.
frus-1944-quebec-d110:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt this long memorandum on September 8, 1944, ahead of the Quebec Conference. Its title names the subject: lend-lease and economic relations with Britain in "Phase 2," the period after Germany's defeat but while the Pacific war went on. Britain's weakened finances frame the whole paper.

Hull urged helping Britain enter the postwar period on sound footing, with trade and finance run on Bretton Woods principles. He tied aid to full British effort against Japan and to a British reconversion program matched with America's. Done right, he argued, lend-lease could continue during the Pacific war without breeding later disputes. It set out the American position going into the Quebec talks on aid.
frus-1944-quebec-d210:
No official memorandum survives for this luncheon, and the editors again lean on Mackenzie King's notes. King lunched with Roosevelt, Churchill, and Eden, and the talk turned to timing the proposed world organization conference for October 30. That date fell just a week before the American presidential elections, which sharpened every political calculation around it.

King warned of opposition from small countries, Canada included, to any appearance that the great powers were seeking to control the world through the new organization. Churchill described the disagreement with Stalin over the council's powers, especially a Soviet veto in disputes where the Soviet Union was itself a party. Eden's diary adds that Churchill explained why Eden could not accept Roosevelt's Hyde Park invitation.
frus-1945-50-intel-d10:
Tamm sent Hoover another inside memorandum on 17 September 1945. The FBI's leadership was tracking the intelligence reorganization plans day by day that month. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Staff papers like Tamm's kept Hoover briefed on moves by the White House, the Budget Bureau, and the military services. Each report sharpened the bureau's sense of where the new central agency might cut into FBI ground. For readers, the value is in the accumulation: the volume prints the bureau's watch in near-real time. This memorandum is one tick of that clock, three days before the president dissolved the OSS and redrew the map.
frus-1945-50-intel-d110:
Souers wrote to Hoover of the FBI on 19 April 1946. The new director of central intelligence addressing the FBI's chief opened the most delicate channel in the volume. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The CIG and the FBI divided the world between them in theory. Foreign work went to the group. Home work and Latin America stayed contested, by wartime claim. Every letter between their chiefs walked that border. Readers can read Souers's approach to Hoover as diplomacy between sovereigns, which, in bureau terms, it was. The exchange that follows in the volume, letters and counter-letters through 1946, decided how America's two secret empires would share a hemisphere.
frus-1945-50-intel-d210:
Dated 14 March 1947, this memorandum runs from George M. Elsey to the President’s Special Counsel (Clifford). The State Department prints it as document 210 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d310:
On 1 June 1949, the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner) sent a memorandum to Members of His Staff. It stands as document 310 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The CIA was settling into its shape, while the Dulles Report's advice worked its way through office after office.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d410:
Fisher Howe, deputy special assistant for research and intelligence at the State Department, wrote to Sheppard on 9 January 1950. Sheppard served as a special assistant to the Secretary. The memo is document 410 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The note moves from the intelligence bureau to the Secretary's inner office in one step. Such short links mattered, since the bureau's reports did no good if they sat unread. Readers can see how State Department analysts kept a path open to the top of their own house. Sheppard's desk was a gate through which many such notes had to pass to reach the Secretary.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d10: General John Deane, who headed the American military mission in Moscow, reported to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on 17 October 1944. His message is document 10 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta. Deane dealt daily with Soviet officers, so his reports gave Washington a soldier's view of cooperation with an ally whose help the war effort still required.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d110:
Acting Secretary Stettinius sent the President a German control agreement on 25 November 1944 and asked for a quick answer. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, forwards a photostatic copy of the deal reached in the European Advisory Commission. The commission's minutes of 14 November, when the agreement was signed, came with it.

The agreement sets up the Allied control machinery for Germany during the surrender period. Stettinius stresses that it grew from close consultation with the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the War and Navy Departments. Approval from the President would let Ambassador Winant tell the commission that the United States accepts. Copies were also going to the Secretaries of War and the Navy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d210:
France asked outright for a seat at the Big Three conference, and Stettinius sent the request to the President on 18 January 1945. His covering note, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, transmits Ambassador Caffery's telegram with the French text in full. The note is dated from Paris on 16 January.

The Provisional Government says it learned from public reports of the planned meeting of the three allied powers. That meeting will fix the terms of their cooperation in the war. Paris then sets out its standing. The fighting in the West runs on French soil or hard by her frontiers. France is straining to the full extent of her present strength. The claim to be heard, the enclosure argues in effect, follows from where the war is being fought.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d310:
Supplying friendly forces in freed Europe is the subject of a United States Chiefs of Staff memorandum written at Malta on February 1, 1945. It deals with gear for Allied and liberated forces, with Greece at the front of the queue. A new Greek army was to take over guard duty inside Greece, and its needs had been spelled out in a theater message.

Most items, the memo notes, could come from British stocks in the Mediterranean or on the way there. But every issue made for this purpose would need replacement later. The paper shows supply, not strategy, filling much of the chiefs' working day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d410:
Matthews sent Stettinius a suggested reparations paper on February 9, 1945, with this covering note. The draft, meant for Molotov and Eden, rested on the Russian proposal of basic principles. Its first two sections followed the Soviet text almost word for word. Eden had suggested added words in the first paragraph.

Matthews also advised a question for Molotov: at what prices — that is, prices of what year — would the total of reparations be fixed? The attached draft itself has not been found, the editors note. A handwritten tag credits "Doc" Matthews as author. The cover note shows how technical points hid inside the grand reparations fight.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d510:
Matters on Poland have reached a dead end, Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on April 7, 1945 — and laid the blame on the Western ambassadors. In his view, Harriman and Clark Kerr, the American and British members of the Moscow Commission, had departed from the principles of the Crimea Conference. They had introduced new elements the conference never provided.

At Crimea, Stalin argued, all three leaders had treated the functioning Polish Provisional Government as the kernel of the new government of national unity. It was subject to reconstruction, not replacement. The ambassadors, he charged, now read the bargain differently. The letter, given in translation, is the alliance's Polish quarrel stated by its strongest party.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d10:
Churchill decided to risk a snub in this short telegram to Truman of May 15, 1945. Your number 39 has just arrived, he writes. I agree with what you say. I will take a chance of getting a snub from Stalin by sending him a telegram urging a friendly tripartite meeting.

The editors note the risk was real. In March, Churchill had ended a message to Stalin hoping their difficulties would be swept away if only they could meet. Stalin's reply had ignored the sentence entirely. This three-line wire thus records a deliberate gamble: the Prime Minister would ask plainly, and take the answer he got.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d110:
Edwin Pauley, the American representative on the Allied reparations commission, cabled President Truman from Moscow on June 29, 1945. The top secret telegram is document 110 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Pauley was working in Moscow with his Soviet and British counterparts on how much Germany should pay for the war.

Pauley says he is bending every effort to have a proposed reparations plan ready to lay before the three heads of government at their meeting. Soviet negotiator Maisky and Britain's Monckton expect to attend, and Pauley hopes to be there too, as Truman had discussed with him before he left the United States. He asks that the Army be told to arrange places for himself, Dr. Lubin, and four others.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d210:
Secretary Byrnes answered Justice Jackson from aboard the cruiser Augusta on July 12, 1945. The brief telegram is document 210 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Jackson had reported from London that the war crimes trial talks were slow and technical, and that he dreaded the Big Three debating the subject.

Byrnes appreciates the report and agrees with Jackson: the subject is too technical for detailed discussion by the Big Three. But if he finds discussion unavoidable, he writes, he will try to let Jackson know in time for a consultation with the President and himself. The reply kept the war crimes charter where Jackson wanted it, in the hands of the lawyers in London, while the leaders dealt with it only in broad terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d310:
Barnes took up the Soviet plan for Bulgaria's Control Commission on July 12, 1945, and set it against an older promise. He quoted Ambassador Winant's letter of October 22, 1944, to the Soviet side. That letter said the commission would work under instructions from all three allied governments.

Against that standard, Barnes measured the new Soviet talk of mere consultation. Consultation, he argued, was not joint control. The cable asks Washington to see the gap between the armistice promise and Soviet practice in Sofia. It reached the Department days before the Potsdam conference opened, capping a month of warnings from Sofia.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d410:
A sudden Soviet shift is reported in Winant's cable from London of July 10, 1945. He thanks the Department for its prompt action of July 8, which was meant to ease the French zone agreement to completion. Yet after a long discussion the night before, the European Advisory Commission still could not complete the agreement.

Gousev, the Soviet representative, now said he did not know whether his government would approve postponing the fixing of France's Berlin area. Moscow might wish the French area described within the agreement itself, and he must consult his government. Winant assumed the shift came on instructions from Moscow, since Gousev had known the proposal since June 29.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d510:
Poland's frontiers frame an extract from the briefing book paper on suggested American policy toward Poland, dated June 29, 1945. The Crimea Conference, it recalls, settled Poland's eastern frontier by adopting a slightly modified Curzon Line as the Polish-Soviet boundary. It also recognized that Poland should receive substantial additions of territory in the north and west.

The new Polish government was to be consulted on their extent, but final delimitation of the Polish-German frontiers was to await the peace conference. Meanwhile, the paper notes, the Lublin government had taken over almost at once all the territory of pre-1939 Poland, as the German population withdrew. With Soviet consent and help, it then took over German lands in the east as well.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d610:
A short extract from a British Chiefs of Staff memo of June 30, 1945, forms document 610 in the Potsdam papers. It is part of the joint debate over basic objectives, strategy, and policies for the war. The full text of the British memo is printed earlier in the volume as document 600.

The extract's weight sits in one quoted passage from the U.S. paper under review. Among the added tasks to aid the grand strategy is this one. The Allies should encourage Russian entry into the war against Japan. They should also give Russia such aid to her war-making power as is needed and practical in that link. The British note that they agree in full with the U.S. memo, subject to their earlier remarks. None of those remarks touched this passage on Russia.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1010: Admiral Ernest King, chief of naval operations, sent this short telegram from Babelsberg on July 26, 1945. It follows from Anglo-American talks at the conference on captured German small craft. King directs that an officer be chosen, in consultation with Commodore Moran, to sit on the Capcraft Commission. That body selects captured craft, including tugs. The chosen officer must be fit to pick tugs suited to American purposes. He is to report to the commander of naval forces in Europe for temporary duty on the commission.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1110:
Writing from Washington on 18 July 1945, the Acting Secretary of State addressed this message to Will Clayton. Clayton was an assistant secretary who handled the money side of foreign policy. The message went out on the second day of the Potsdam Conference.

With the president and the secretary of state in Germany, the home office still had to keep policy in step with the team abroad. Clayton was the man Washington turned to on trade, loans, and the cost of the peace. A note to him at this moment shows the capital checking with its own expert. It is one link in the chain that tied the summit to the home front.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1210: On 29 July 1945 the Acting Secretary of State in Washington wrote to the Secretary of State at Potsdam. It is a home-office message between the department's two leading men, sent in the summit's final days. Joseph Grew held the acting post while James Byrnes led the team in Germany. Word between them kept the department's two halves in step.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1310:
Stimson wrote to Harrison on 23 July 1945. The war secretary's replies kept the Interim Committee's work aligned with the summit's course. By that date the American leaders were settling how the new weapon would enter the war's endgame.

A note on this channel carried the atomic file's direction from the man who owned it. Stimson's hand guided both the committee in Washington and the brief at Potsdam. This message is his guidance at the second week's start. It belongs to the small set of papers through which the bomb's use was shaped, far from any public eye.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1410:
Caffery sent a fifth cable to Secretary Byrnes on 6 August 1945, part of the densest single-day run in the volume's French papers. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Five cables in a day from one post is close to a paper siege. Caffery knew Washington's habits and pressed his case while the Potsdam results were still fresh and open to shaping. Each cable in the run takes its own file or point, so readers should not expect repeats. Together they show an ambassador using the cable room as an instrument, and they give the French section of the volume its driving rhythm.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710:
Lieutenant Rigdon's log of the President's trip to the Berlin Conference opens on July 6, 1945. Extracts form document 710 in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The log runs day by day to August 7, 1945.

The first entry follows the party out of Washington that night. Truman left the White House by motor car at 9:40 p.m. with a small staff group. At Union Station the special train waited on Team Track No. 2. Secretary Byrnes came aboard at 10:15 p.m., while Admiral Leahy and others had boarded earlier. At 11 p.m. the train rolled for Newport News, Virginia. There the heavy cruiser Augusta waited to carry the President across the Atlantic. The next morning's entry notes the same pier had served President Roosevelt's Crimea trip that year.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-10:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the first plenary session, July 17, 1945, run parallel to the Thompson minutes. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Cohen, a U.S. adviser, took his own record as Stalin proposed Truman for the chair.

Cohen has Truman stress the urgency of preparing for the European settlements. The first concrete proposal was the draft for a Council of Foreign Ministers. Churchill suggested it be referred to the foreign secretaries. Stalin agreed to that procedure, but voiced his doubt over China in a council for the European peace. Truman then stated the U.S. policy toward Germany in his own words. The Control Council, he thought, should start to function at once under the agreement already made. His draft of principles for that council was laid before the meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-110:
Another set of Thompson minutes records Potsdam talks on July 25, 1945. The conference often ran several meetings in a day, and note-takers split the load. Thompson's sets, printed in the second Potsdam volume, form a near-daily spine for the American record. This set covers a further session from a crowded day.

Readers meet the session's flow: topics in order, speakers in turn, points left hanging. Minutes like these let later readers test claims about who agreed to what. They also catch the strain of the schedule itself. By late July the talks had run a week with the largest questions still unsettled.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d810:
Barnes reported from Bulgaria on July 23, 1945, in document 810. The representative in Sofia wrote to the Acting Secretary of State. His post stood inside a control commission where the Soviet voice ruled. The report entered the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Barnes's mid-conference report carries the pressure of his position. He reported facts his hosts would rather have hidden. Readers gain a clear sense of Bulgaria's slide from the Western orbit. The document shows reporting as a form of resistance: to write the truth home was to keep a claim alive. His letters remain a key source on the Balkans' turning.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d910: American staff drafted this short memorandum on July 22, 1945, as one response to the Soviet definition of war booty. It quotes the Soviet text in full. Under that definition, the paper says, little or nothing will remain to take as reparations from the American zone. The United States therefore accepts the definition. For the present, it will run its zone without regard to reparations as such. The editors note the paper was an alternative to the next document in the volume.
frus-1946v10:
China fills Volume X for 1946 as well, carrying the Marshall Mission to its end. The Kalgan crisis leads, with Marshall near quitting his mediator role. Third-party bids fail, and the National Assembly meets without the Communists.

Marshall's recall and his blunt parting statement close the mission. Aid papers follow, on arms holds, ship transfers, and adviser groups. Surplus property sales and loans fill the rest. Soviet stripping of Manchurian plants also appears. The record shows a mediation that failed and a civil war that hardened. Marine pullouts mark the shrinking American footprint on the ground there.
frus-1952-1954-iran-vol-10:
Volume ten of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1952 to 1954 covers Iran from 1951 to 1954. The Office of the Historian publishes the series from declassified records. The volume's center is the 1953 coup that remade Iran and shadowed its relations with the West for decades.

The documents trace the oil nationalization crisis under Premier Mohammad Mossadeq, and Britain's campaign to win Washington over. The joint operation, called TPAJAX by the CIA, overthrew Mossadeq in August 1953 and restored the Shah's power. Cables show the planning, the paid crowds, and the quick consolidation after. The volume is the official paper trail of the coup.
frus-1955-57v10:
Foreign aid and economic defense policy fill Volume X of the 1955–1957 set. Mutual security and aid policy lead, with the case for help made year by year. The defense of trade follows in the longest block.

Controls on sales to the Soviet Union and the People's Republic fill hundreds of papers. Stockpiles of key goods and commodity deals close the volume. Allies pressed for looser lists while Washington held firm. The record shows aid and embargo as two sides of one plan, each argued in the same files by the same officers.
frus-1961-1963-cuba-vol-10:
This tenth volume of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1961 to 1963 covers Cuba from January 1961 to September 1962. The Office of the Historian publishes the series from declassified files. The Kennedy years in Cuba policy begin here, at their most violent.

The documents cover the Bay of Pigs invasion of April 1961 and its bitter aftermath. Covert operations against Castro, run under Operation Mongoose, fill many pages. The embargo hardens, exile raids multiply, and intelligence watches Soviet shipping ever closer. The volume stops just before the missile crisis, which its sequel takes up. It is the fullest official record of the secret war on Castro.
frus-1964-68v10:
National security policy is the subject of Volume X in the 1964-1968 Foreign Relations series. The volume prints 227 documents in a single run. They span force plans, budgets, and the broad choices that shaped U.S. defense in these years. Topics include nuclear forces, troop levels, and the draft. The papers also weigh how much risk the country should accept in each region.

The records come from the White House, the Pentagon, and the State Department. They include memos to the President and notes of high-level talks. One strand deals with a proposed exchange with the Soviets on control of nuclear weapons. The volume suits readers who want the top-level defense debate of the Johnson years.
frus-1969-76ve10:
Documents on the American republics, 1969 to 1972, make up Volume E-10 of the 1969-1976 series. A regional section opens the volume. Country sections follow for Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, Panama, Peru, Venezuela, and others. A short section covers the Soccer War between El Salvador and Honduras. Peru's section is among the longest. It deals with the military regime there and seized U.S. property.

A cable on Ecuador shows aid loans used as leverage, released one by one to test good faith. Panama's section covers the canal talks of those years. The volume shows a hemisphere policy driven by aid, property fights, and one small war.
frus-1977-80v29-d110: A brief letter from President Carter to General Torrijos of Panama, dated Washington, October 11, 1977, forms document 110 in Volume XXIX of the 1977-1980 series. Carter notes that questions have arisen over how the new Panama Canal Treaties are being read in each country. He proposes a private meeting to clear up the points at issue. Torrijos would be passing through the United States on his way home from Europe. Carter closes with warm regards and his signature.
frus-1981-88v10:
Eastern Europe fills Volume X of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1981-1988. A regional section opens the volume. Romania then takes the largest share, with documents 63 through 185. Sections follow for Yugoslavia, East Germany, Hungary, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, and Albania. The Romania papers deal with trade status, emigration, and Ceausescu's separate course. The Yugoslavia papers track its debts and ethnic strains after Tito.

One cable reports a Belgrade visit by Fatah's deputy military chief, Abu Jihad, in talks with Yugoslav ministers. The records show Washington courting the East's mavericks while pressing the rest. The volume ends just before the bloc's collapse.
gao-gaoreports-b-293073-10:
Creative Information Technology, Inc., protested an Army award in GAO decision B-293073.10, dated March 16, 2005. The Army had bought information management and technology support for its Information Management Support Center. Awards went to Daston Corporation and Focused Management, Inc. GAO sustained the protest. The digest states the flaw in one contrast of numbers: the Army's own estimate set the work at seven full-time staff, worth about $13 million. The protester first proposed 37 staff, priced near $110 million.

In talks, the Army told the firm only that its price looked overstated. That, GAO held, was not the meaningful discussion the rules require. This copy is redacted for public release.
gao-gaoreports-b-296510:
Evergreen Fire and Security protested an Army award for alarm systems work in GAO decision B-296510, dated August 22, 2005. The winner was Shane Gelling Company. The site was Fort Hood, Texas. The work was care and fix work for intrusion detection systems. The buy was set aside for small firms.

GAO denied the protest. Proof of staff skill was not due before award. Whether staff would meet the terms was a job-run point, not a GAO point. Past work marks of very good for the winner fit its record. The one bad note was not its fault. The firm's own low mark was sound. Its bid missed skill in some named systems.
gao-gaoreports-b-297136-10:
TPL protested an Army award for bomb disposal work on old shells in GAO decision B-297136.10, dated June 29, 2006. The winner was General Dynamics-Ordnance and Tactical Systems. The firm hit past work marks, tech marks, the trade-off, and bias. It also claimed a clash. Staff who wrote a past work note also scored the bids.

GAO denied the protest. That dual role is not a clash on its own. Past work and tech marks fit the tests and were sound. A pick lead may set aside staff marks when the record backs a new view. The trade-off named tech gaps and found the higher rated bid worth its cost. No bias was shown.
gao-gaoreports-b-297210:
WorldWide Language Resources protested an Air Force order for language help in GAO decision B-297210, dated November 28, 2005. The winner was SOS International. The work needed 22 linguists on call day and night. They would back the Air Force probe office in Central and Southwest Asia. Tongue and dialect skill were key.

GAO denied the protest. The firm's linguists did not meet the call terms. That find was sound. Round-the-clock probe work needs staff who meet each term on skill. A quote with staff who miss the terms is not fit. The order thus stood on the staff facts.
gao-gaoreports-b-298110:
Bristol Group protested a lease term in a twin case in GAO decision B-298110, dated June 2, 2006. The buyer was the General Services Administration. The tenant was the Veterans Affairs office. Space sought was 88,000 square feet in Washington. The term set a walk range of 2,500 feet to food and shops. The firm called the term too strict.

GAO denied the protest. The walk rule had a sound aim. Staff must be able to walk to food and tasks in a lunch break. That need is real for a work block. A term that tracks a true staff need is not too strict. Claims of hidden tests were not shown. The term thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-308010:
An aircraft buy tied to a joint pact is judged in this GAO decision, B-308010, dated April 20, 2007. The Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service works with the Wyoming Woolgrowers Association. The group bought a plane for work on animal predation. The Service paid cash to help the buy in 2000. The pact for joint use was not yet in writing.

GAO held the spend did not break the bona fide needs rule. The Service had power to make the joint pact. But GAO did not praise the acts. Pay went out before the pact was signed in writing. GAO told the Service to guard public funds from loss in such deals.
gao-gaoreports-b-310210:
Strategic e-Business Solutions, Inc. lost its protest. That ruling is B-310210, dated November 8, 2007. Medicare's agency sought training goods for its phone staff. The call asked bidders to show a sub deal for a key skill area. The firm's bid was cast out at a first pass-or-fail screen. It fought the cast-out and the talks that came before it.

GAO denied the protest. The claimed sub deal named no work type and no price terms. No proof showed the sub's offer had been taken up. Talks did lead the firm to the weak point. No fresh round of talks was owed once the fix still fell short.
gao-gaoreports-b-311310:
Rhonda Podojil saw her protest thrown out (GAO decision B-311310, dated May 9, 2008). She spoke for the in-house team in an Army A-76 race. The race dealt with food care at 10 base hospitals. The work went to Sodexho Management, Inc. She said talks had led her team to staff past the need. That shift drove up the team's cost in the race.

GAO dismissed the protest as too late. It came more than 10 days past the date she knew its base. A plea for more time needs a fast ask for a debrief. That ask came late as well. Late claims die at the gate, fair or not.
gao-gaoreports-b-316010:
Words in a side note to a spending law are ruled binding in this GAO opinion, B-316010, dated February 25, 2008. The Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2008 held seven such clauses. Each clause points to a House note in the Congressional Record. The note splits funds into set shares for set uses. Two Senate leaders asked if those shares bind the shops that spend the funds.

GAO held that they do. Each clause takes the note into the law by its point. Shops must pledge and spend the funds as the note directs. A point-in clause can give a side note the force of law. Draft care in such clauses shapes how funds may flow.
gao-gaoreports-b-316510:
A bar on sharing gun trace facts is ruled lasting law in this GAO opinion, B-316510, dated July 15, 2008. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives keeps the Firearms Trace System. A clause in the 2008 funds law bars use of funds to share the files. Set law and court hands may get the facts. A House member asked if that clause is a one-year rule.

GAO held that it is not. The clause is permanent law, like a twin clause from 2006. Its words reach past the year of the funds law. The bar binds the bureau in years to come as well. Yearly laws can hold rules that outlast the year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1010:
International Finance: Treasury Has Reduced the Number of Attaches Overseas, GAO-05-1010 of September 23, 2005, traces a long shrink in one U.S. post abroad. Treasury financial attaches watch world money trends from U.S. embassies in key states. Their reports help shape U.S. policy on the world economy. The corps fell from about 30 posts in 1981 to 7 at the start of fiscal year 2005.

GAO sets out what attaches do day to day. It then shows how Treasury picks where to place the few who remain. Treasury called the account fair and sound. State gave small fixes, which GAO folded in.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-210:
Managing Diabetes, GAO-05-210 of February 25, 2005, checks whether health plans cover the care that keeps this disease in check. Diabetes hits millions of Americans. Steady care with set services and tools can blunt its harm. Those tools cost cash, so cover shapes who gets them. Hard facts on cover were scarce.

GAO read the laws of all 50 states and the District of Columbia on diabetes cover. It asked 13 large firm plans and 3 federal staff plans what they pay for, across 10 services and nine tools. It then used national data to see what care patients in fact got.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-410:
National Park Service, GAO-05-410 of May 6, 2005, asks if park fees the law lets lie are left on the ground. Parks grant passes for set uses: fairs, meets, film shoots, and photo work. A pro football launch on the National Mall in 2003 raised the ask. Was the use in line with park rule and law? Were all fees owed in fact charged?

GAO lists the guides that rule such passes. It tests how they were used in fiscal year 2003. It tests how far the film and photo place fees, owed by law, were in fact claimed. Cash could rise by charge of fees now let pass.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-710:
New rights for identity theft victims need publicity, GAO-05-710 finds on June 30, 2005. A 2003 law lets victims demand the records of deals made in their name. The trade commission, postal inspectors, police chiefs, and credit unions have spread the word. Most other agencies tout theft help generally but skip this specific right. A required federal campaign due by December 2005 will cover it, the commission says.

Victims' advocates expect faster cleanups and stronger cases for police. Little use so far makes the right hard to judge. Some worry businesses will hand records over slowly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-10:
Workplace bias agency restructuring is checked in GAO-06-10, a report dated October 28, 2005. In May 2001, the budget office told agencies to plan flatter structures. Plans were due with fiscal year 2003 budgets. GAO asked whether the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission built such a plan. It also tracked what the agency is doing to run leaner and better.

The title states the balance GAO found. The agency has taken actions to restructure. Its efforts would gain from a more systematic look at its advisory panel's recommendations. The report gives Congress the plan's history and the steps since. Readers can judge how far the reorganization has come and what the panel urged that remains undone.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1010:
Help for families of fallen troops is graded in GAO-06-1010, a report dated September 22, 2006. Almost 6,000 troops died from October 2001 through September 2005. Three bodies aid their survivors: Defense, Veterans Affairs, and Social Security. Aid spans funeral plans, benefit claims, and moves. A 2006 law told GAO to assess the help. GAO focused on the Defense Department's oversight and cost picture.

Section headings state the gaps. The department has no oversight framework for this work. It lacks key standards for the services' programs. Help differs among and even within the services. No standard procedures govern coordination with the pay agency. Survivors get no single integrated statement of benefits. Cost visibility is limited. Veterans and Social Security bodies mainly supply long-term benefits, the headings add.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-110:
Weapon system program managers, and the support they get, are examined in GAO-06-110, dated November 30, 2005. The Department of Defense relies on a small cadre of officials to build and deliver weapons. GAO drew lessons from top commercial product firms to test defense practice. It asked how strong companies position their program managers. It then asked how DOD positions its own, and why the two differ. GAO also surveyed program managers for this study.

Commercial firms give program managers a sound business case and real authority from the start. DOD managers often inherit programs with shaky funding and weak foundations. They face pressure from funding contests that no leader has tamed. GAO urged DOD to give managers an executable business case before launch. It also urged clear accountability for results, backed by firm strategic leadership. DOD agreed with the recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-210:
Why remittance totals never quite agree is the puzzle in GAO-06-210, a report issued on March 28, 2006. Money sent home by the foreign born has grown fast, and leaders want better figures. In 2004 the Group of Eight called for improved data on these flows. Each estimator uses its own method, so the totals spread wide. GAO studied the method behind the official U.S. estimate, from the Bureau of Economic Analysis. It compared methods used by other nations and world bodies, and tracked joint work to improve the data.

GAO made no recommendations this time. It noted that method alone drives much of the spread between estimates. Better figures would help the Treasury size aid choices with care. Firms could also judge foreign investments on firmer ground. GAO suggested that policy makers explore ways to sharpen U.S. remittance statistics. Treasury agreed with the observations, and Commerce agreed as well.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-310:
Unfinished rules for defining what new tax systems must do occupy GAO-06-310, issued March 20, 2006. The tax agency's modernization drive has suffered delays and cost growth for years. Weak handling of requirements is one cause. The agency set up a Requirements Management Office to write clear policies for the work. GAO judged whether those policies are adequate. It also tested whether big projects follow sound requirements practice in the meantime.

The office's work is not done, GAO found. Draft policies from January 2006 cover some ground but leave gaps. Projects lack a firm guide while they build live systems. GAO urged the agency to finish the policies on schedule. It also urged stopgap rules for projects that cannot wait. The commissioner agreed and listed steps already taken. Requirements sound dull; overruns are born there. This report locates the dull point where billions in later costs are decided.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-710:
Phone help from Medicare drug plans is tested in GAO-06-710, a GAO report dated June 30, 2006. Under Medicare Part D, private plan sponsors answer questions from seniors about drug coverage. Their call centers are a main source of facts on costs, covered drugs, and pharmacy networks. GAO placed calls to sponsor call centers with set questions and scenarios. GAO judged speed, accuracy, and completeness of the replies.

GAO found that call center staff generally gave prompt, courteous, and helpful service. Callers did not wait long for answers. But the centers did not consistently give accurate and complete information. Some answers on drug costs and coverage rules were wrong or partial. GAO's test shows the gap between friendly service and reliable facts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-810:
Debt reduction at the Tennessee Valley Authority is examined in GAO-06-810. The report is dated August 31, 2006. The authority sells power across the Tennessee Valley and faces rising competition in the electricity industry. To meet market prices, it needs lower fixed costs and more flexibility. Its 2004 strategic plan set a goal of cutting statutory debt by $3 to $5 billion. GAO reviewed the plan and the wider set of financing duties behind it.

GAO found that the authority later widened its debt effort. It folded in debt-like deals, such as lease-leasebacks and energy prepayment arrangements. Together these form its total financing obligations. The 2007 budget carried the expanded target forward. GAO weighed whether the cuts can proceed while demand for power keeps growing. The report tests a public utility's balancing act.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1010:
A license bid for a nuclear waste site is previewed in GAO report GAO-07-1010, dated August 2, 2007. The Department of Energy aims to store highly radioactive waste at Yucca Mountain, about 100 miles from Las Vegas, Nevada. In July 2006 it set a bid date of June 30, 2008.

The bid must be full, sound, clear, and linked to source data, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission says. Past flaws in quality checks had slowed the project. GAO traced how the bid schedule was set, and who was asked. It weighed the regulator's view of readiness. It checked headway on past GAO points. Quality checks are better, GAO found, but bid quality stays unclear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1110:
Advance payment of a tax credit sees low use, GAO reports in GAO-07-1110, dated August 10, 2007. The Advance Earned Income Tax Credit lets workers take part of the credit in each paycheck. The rest comes at tax time. Small sums and high rule breaches mark the option.

GAO counted how many people took the advance form in tax years 2002 through 2004, beside the main credit. It asked what steps were taken to lift use, and what lift is likely. It sized rule breaches tied to the advance form. It tested how tax agency steps meet those breaches. The work rests on wage forms, tax returns, and agency talks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-310:
Every two years, GAO names the federal programs most prone to waste and failure. The 2007 update is GAO-07-310, dated January 31, 2007. The list has run since 1990. This edition reports status for areas named in 2005. It also adds and removes areas for the 110th Congress. Fixes could save billions and improve public service.

Three areas joined the list this year, GAO announced. They are transport funding, protection of critical technology, and food safety oversight. Two areas came off the list. Postal reform and a housing insurance program had improved enough. The defense department still dominates the roster. It owns eight areas outright and shares seven governmentwide ones. For each area, GAO states what remains to be done. It urges steady follow-through by agencies and Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-110:
Terrorist watch list screening is examined in GAO report GAO-08-110, issued October 11, 2007. The Federal Bureau of Investigation's Terrorist Screening Center keeps one merged list of known or suspected terrorists. It sends list records to agencies that screen travelers and others. GAO probed how names get on the list and how screening works.

List choices rest on a standard of reasonableness, which leaves room for judgment. GAO reviewed what happens when screeners meet listed people. It found weak spots where some agencies cannot take in all list records. GAO urged stronger oversight, fewer gaps, and wider use of the list. Five actions were set out in a restricted version.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-610:
People who rushed to help after the World Trade Center attack breathed dust that harmed their health. Health programs were set up to screen, watch, and treat them. GAO-08-610, dated May 30, 2008, draws lessons from those programs so future disaster health programs start stronger. About $369.2 million had gone to the health programs.

GAO drew five lessons. Crews should sign up all responders at the scene. Health checks should be built so doctors can study long-term effects. Mind and body checks should come together, and care should reach all responders alike. GAO asked the health department to write one plan that uses these lessons.
garland-other-main-travelled-1910:
Other Main-Travelled Roads came from Harper as a sunset edition, with rights dates of 1892, 1899, and 1910. Garland opens with verses on prairie folks, starting with the pioneers. They rise, he writes, to mastery of wind and snow, and go like soldiers into strife.

Nearly twenty years after his first farm tales, Garland returns to the same ground here. The farms look familiar, and the struggles have not vanished. Time has passed, though, and the tone grows riper and more thoughtful. With the first volume, the book forms a full portrait of rural life in the Middle West at the century's turn.
goldman-anarchism-other-essays-1910:
Emma Goldman published Anarchism and Other Essays in 1910 in New York. Goldman, a Russian-born lecturer and publisher of Mother Earth magazine, was then the best known anarchist in America. The essays gather her talks on the subjects that filled her halls.

Goldman defined anarchism as freedom from government and from the dead weight of church and property. Other essays treat patriotism as a threat to peace, marriage as an economic bargain, and the traffic in women as a product of poverty. She wrote in a direct, urgent voice for working readers. The book stands as the American anarchist manifesto of its era and the clearest short statement of her thought.
hagenbeck-beasts-and-men-1910:
Carl Hagenbeck, the great animal dealer of Hamburg, told his life in Beasts and Men in 1910. His men traded beasts from every wild corner of the earth. In its pages sits the first Western print of a giant dinosaur said to live in the Congo.

Hagenbeck reports what his agents heard of a huge beast in the swamps and rivers of the far interior. He sets the tale down with care, as a dealer's note on stock not yet caught. The story grew into the hunt for Mokele-mbembe, the Congo's famed living dinosaur. Expeditions still sail on the strength of Hagenbeck's few pages.
harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-volum:
Book Ten of Harold is titled The Sacrifice on the Altar. It opens with the good Bishop Alred, now raised to the See of York, summoned from his cathedral by the King. Edward has undergone a severe illness during Harold's absence. That illness was preceded and followed by mystical presentiments of the evil days to fall on England after his death. He has sent for the best and holiest prelate in his realm, to advise and counsel with him.

The bishop returns late to his London lodging, in a Benedictine abbey near Aldgate, much disturbed by what the King told him. Then his door is abruptly thrown open. The part turns on prophecy, confession, and the claims that will be made over a dying king's words. Lytton darkens the air: the altar of the title waits for its sacrifice.
hegel-phenomenology-baillie-1910:
G. W. F. Hegel published The Phenomenology of Spirit in 1807, the founding text of his philosophy. The English text here is J. B. Baillie's translation of 1910. Hegel traces how consciousness grows, stage by stage, toward full self-knowledge. Sense, perception, understanding, and self-awareness each fail in instructive ways.

The famous master and slave passage shows selves forming through struggle and work. Later parts move through culture, religion, and history toward absolute knowing. Hegel's dialectic, in which ideas grow through conflict, shaped Marx and many others. The book is dense and demanding. It remains a summit of German idealism and modern thought.
hicks-stoic-and-epicurean-1910:
R. D. Hicks wrote Stoic and Epicurean in 1910 as a clear English guide to the two great schools that led Greek thought after Aristotle. Both schools taught in Athens, drew loyal bands of pupils, and shaped Roman life for centuries. Hicks treats each school on its own terms and in plain terms.

He walks through their views on nature, logic, and knowledge, then gives most space to their rival ways of life. The Stoics taught calm in the face of fate. The school of Epicurus taught quiet pleasure and freedom from fear. Hicks wrote for the general reader, and his survey long served as the first book students were handed on these schools.
his-other-self-night-watches-part-10:
W W Jacobs wrote this short tale for his Night Watches set. A night-watchman on a wharf tells the stories, in broad dockside speech. He begins with twin brothers, Sam and Bill, who share one face. The watchman mixes them up and praises the wrong man to his face.

He then tells how a likeness once trapped him too. A smooth stranger who shared his looks drew him into a dockside plot. An actor, dark corners, and men off a ship fill the night scenes. Jacobs wrings dry comedy from error, pride, and faces that will not stay matched to their owners.
history-of-egypt-from-330-b-c-to-the-pre:
S Rappoport wrote this tenth volume of a history of Egypt from 330 before Christ. Rappoport was an orientalist trained at Basel and Paris. The publisher notes he drew largely on earlier authorities. Results from Flinders Petrie and other diggers are set forth and pictured.

This volume treats Egypt under the Ptolemies, the Greek kings. Alexandria's mobs, ministers, and Macedonian troops fill the scenes. Crowds test the palace and the mercenaries' quarters in one tense passage. Greek rule, native hatred, and court intrigue drive the tale. Readers get the long twilight of pharaonic Egypt under foreign crowns, told in rich detail.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle's tenth volume holds Book Ten of the Friedrich history, At Reinsberg, 1736 to 1740. The Crown Prince, married and granted the Ruppin district's revenues, hinted that Reinsberg, an old country seat, might please him if repaired. His father instantly bought it for him, and Friedrich built there his brief paradise.

At Rheinsberg the prince reads, makes music, and writes his Anti-Machiavel. He corresponds with Voltaire while Europe slides toward war. Carlyle notes a Russian war with the Turk, and twenty thousand inhabitants for one sad item of news. The volume ends at the old king's death in 1740. Carlyle lingers lovingly over Reinsberg, knowing the shepherd's pipe is about to become a sword.
holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-2-of-6-slice-:
