Raphael Holinshed's chronicle turns to Henry the First in this slice. Henry, youngest son of the Conqueror, was surnamed Beauclerk for his learning. He began on the first of August 1100, the sidenote records. York and London crowned him while Anselm was exiled.

Normandy pulls the king across the sea again and again. Fulk of Anjou, envying Henry's estate, takes Constances by corrupting its people in 1111. Priories, burials, and border towns fill the annals between campaigns. Holinshed names his sources in the margin, from Matthew Paris to Gervase. The slice covers the reign's first decades, order kept by a clerkly king.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-10:
Hedda Gabler burns a manuscript, manipulates her circle, and courts ruin out of boredom and pride. The Master Builder follows Halvard Solness, an aging architect who climbs his own tower toward doom. Archer's tenth volume, from 1908, pairs Ibsen's two most fascinating self-destroyers.

Hedda remains the role great actresses measure themselves against, brilliant and trapped at once. Solness fears the young, clings to his fame, and hears a younger woman knocking at the door. Ibsen's psychology cuts deepest in these late plays. Fear of decline and hunger for freedom drive both plots. The volume shows a master in his sixties outwriting everyone younger.
james-moral-equivalent-war-1910:
The Moral Equivalent of War began as an address and was published in 1910; it is James's most famous short piece. A pacifist who honored soldiers, he asked how a society could keep the virtues war breeds, discipline, loyalty, and sacrifice, without the killing.

His answer is a conscription of youth into peaceful service: an army enlisted against nature, sent to mines, roads, and fisheries to earn civic honor by labor. The proposal influenced later service programs like the Civilian Conservation Corps. James admits the scheme's difficulty and presses it anyway. The essay remains the classic statement of his moral imagination.
jargon-file-2-9-10:
Eric Raymond edited version 2.9.10 of the Jargon File, the hacker's dictionary. Programmers at early labs built the file over years of shared use. It records the slang, jokes, and lore of their culture.

Entries define terms from real work and pure play alike. Foo, bar, and countless coinages get their due. Short essays explain hacker manners, humor, and pride in craft. The file is part glossary and part folk record. It reads like geek poetry in places. Anyone curious how early coders talked, joked, and saw themselves will find no better primary source.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-10:
Brébeuf's long study of the Huron people crowns Volume 10, from 1897. Thwaites devotes the book to the Huron mission in the year 1636. No writer of the age left a fuller account of Iroquoian life in print.

Towns, councils, feasts, dreams, and beliefs unfold in Brébeuf's calm prose. He explains kinship, healing rites, and the great feast of the dead. His respect for Huron thought sets the text apart from its time. Scholars still call it study of a culture before that field had a name. It was written in a bark mission house, by firelight.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-abraham-b: Aaron Abraham ben Baruch Simeon ha-Levi, a cabalist born in the first quarter of the sixteenth century, is treated in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He published a small cabalistic work, Iggeret ha-Te'amim, or Letter on the Accents, about the middle of the century. Each accent and its name are explained as holding references to the Ten Sefirot and to Israel. A Prague cabalist wrote a large commentary on it in 1612, praising Aaron as a great master. The entry judges the work, more coolly, as cabalistic trifles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ab-ninth-day-of:
The Ninth Day of Ab is a day of fasting and mourning set by tradition. It marks the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple by the Chaldeans in 586 B.C. and by the Romans in 70. The fast falls near the start of August. The sources differ on the exact day, naming the seventh day and the tenth day of the fifth month.

Three linked fasts stand with it: the Tenth of Tebet, the Seventeenth of Tammuz, and the Third of Tishri. Over time the mourning rules for the day grew stricter, with wider bans on meat and wine. The liturgy for its evening service recited the Book of Lamentations, and later ages added fresh hymns of grief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abduction-geneb:
Abduction, in Talmudic law, is the stealing of a human being. The entry bases the ban on the eighth of the Ten Commandments, read as a ban on stealing a person. Stealing goods is banned apart, in Leviticus. Two further verses, in Exodus and Deuteronomy, set death as the price for stealing a man and selling him, or holding him.

The law then works through four heads: the doer, the victim, the crime, and the penalty. Any grown, sound person can be guilty, priest and slave alike. The victim must be free-born or made free, so no case lies for a slave. The crime needs a true taking from the home, holding on the taker's own ground, enslavement, and a sale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abin-or-abun-31: Abin, also read Abun, was a noted cabalist of Le Mans, dated to about the year 1040. He came of the line of R. Simon of Le Mans. He was the grandfather of R. Simon the Great. That grandson was a man of the age of R. Gershom ben Judah of Metz, the great teacher of his time. The entry rests on two later works, by Michael and by Zunz. Gross, in his book on the Jews of France, also reads the name as Abun, it notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-yom: Abraham ben Yom-Tob of Tudela was a commentator who flourished in Spain about 1300. He wrote a commentary on Baba Batra, a Talmudic treatise. The work still rests in manuscript in the Bodleian Library at Oxford, England. The entry gives that one book and that one shelf mark, and nothing about his life, teachers, or death. His name survives through the Oxford manuscript alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-malak-o:
Russian rabbi Abraham Malak was the only son of Dob Baer of Mezhirich, first leader of the South Russian Hasidim. He followed the Ba'al Shem-Tob's way and married into the family of Meshullam Phoebus of Kremenetz. He died young at Fastov, about 1780.

Shy and unpractical, he did not follow his father as sect head. He lived like a hermit at Hannipol, then preached at Fastov in the same withdrawn style. That pious seclusion earned him the name Malak, Angel. His Pentateuch commentary came out long after his death, in 1851. In it he protests against Hasidism's decline and the crude cult of the pious leaders.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-abraham-j:
Abraham Jacob Koppel Adler was a German rabbi and teacher born in 1813. He died at Worms in 1856. His father Isaac was a fellow rabbi in Worms. His brother was Rabbi Samuel Adler. Abraham studied at Bonn and Giessen. He taught at Frankfort and in Hungary. In 1842 he was chosen rabbi of Worms. He left the post that same year. With his wife he opened a school for girls.

At the rabbis' meet at Frankfort in 1845 he stood out as a scholar and a bold reformer. His tract on that meet made a stir. In 1848 he backed the fight for free rule with heat. He did no act that could be charged, yet police seized him and held him for months. A jury cleared him in the end. Temple Emanu-El in New York sought him in 1854. Ill health forced him to decline.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adolescentoli-d: Adolescentoli, or Degli Fanciulli, was a noble family of legend. Lore says Titus moved four or five such houses from Jerusalem to Rome. The years run 70 to 81. Sound trace of this house starts in the fourteenth century. In the fifteenth century its seat was Bologna. Moses ben Judah Nagari was a famed man of the house. Like names show in Spain and south France in the same years. Those houses were rich and learned. The entry holds it likely that they link to the Italian house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ai-or-ha-ai-pro:
Ai, or Ha-'Ai, probably meaning "The Ruin," was a royal Canaanite town. It lay east of Beth-el, in the north of Benjamin's territory. It had its own king. Joshua destroyed it after one failed attack. Scripture calls it a ruin unto this day.

Yet Ai must have been rebuilt by the time of Isaiah, who names it Aiath. Men of Beth-el and Ai appear after the Exile in Ezra and Nehemiah. Abraham had once camped on a mountain between Ai and Beth-el. The entry gives two rival sites for the town. Van de Velde placed it at Tell el-Hajar. Robinson placed it at Khirbet Hayan, just to the south.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aleksyeyev-alek:
Aleksander Aleksyeyev, also called Wolf Nachlass, was an author and a convert to the Greek Catholic Church. He was born in 1820 at Nazarinetz, in Podolsk, Russia, of poor Jewish parents. At the age of ten the press-gang seized him for military service. He was sent far away to Volsk, in Saratov.

Aleksyeyev held to his fathers' faith for a long time. About 1845 he changed sides wholly. He joined the Orthodox Church and brought over more than five hundred Jewish cantonists. In 1848 he was made a non-commissioned officer and thanked by the emperor. About 1855 he lost the use of his legs and settled in Novgorod. There he wrote many missionary and descriptive books, from 1859 to 1886. He was the first Jew in Russia to describe Jewish life there, and he refuted the blood charge. His stance toward Judaism itself stayed hostile.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-algazi-abraham-: Abraham ben Solomon Algazi is a shadowy figure in the entry. He is said to have lived at Smyrna in 1659. The entry calls him the son of an author. That author wrote a book of sermons on part of the Torah. The book came out at Smyrna in 1659. Beyond that link, the entry states plainly that very little is known about his writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alpron-jacob-13: Jacob Alpron was an Italian translator of religious books. He died on Dec. 22, 1622. He turned a Hebrew work into Italian. The work was a book of precepts for women. It was meant for the Jewish women of Italy. The book won wide favor with readers. New printings came out at Padua and Venice. The years were 1625, 1652, and 1710. The entry adds that Alpron is a worn form of Heilprin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ammihud-1410: Ammihud is a name borne by five men in the Bible. The first was father of Elishama, chief of Ephraim. That was in the second year from the exodus. The second was father of Shemuel of Simeon. Shemuel helped split the land among the tribes. The third was father of Pedahel of Naphtali. The fourth was father of Talmai, king of Geshur. David wed into that house by Talmai's line. The fifth was a son of Omri in Jerusalem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-andronicus-son-:
Andronicus, son of Meshullam, lived in the second century before the common era. Josephus, as cited here, makes him the Jewish spokesman in a religious dispute with the Samaritans. The hearing took place before King Ptolemy VI Philometor, about 150 B.C.

Andronicus argued from Scripture that the line of Jewish high priests ran unbroken. He also stressed the respect that even pagan kings of Asia paid to the Temple at Jerusalem. That, he said, disproved the Samaritan claim for Mount Gerizim. The entry reports that the losing side's champions were executed, then warns that this detail casts doubt on the whole tale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aranyi-miksa-17: Miksa Aranyi was a Hungarian writer born at Trencsen on May 13, 1858. He graduated from the university in Budapest. The secretary of state for education then sent him to Paris to finish his studies. He returned to Budapest in 1884 and edited the Gazette de Hongrie until 1887. He turned several works on economics from Hungarian into French. Up to the year 1901 he sat as a deputy in the Hungarian Diet. His family's German name was Aufrecht, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arons-leo-1810:
Leo Arons, a German physicist, taught as privat-docent at the University of Berlin while taking an open part in the Socialist movement. In April 1899 the minister of education, Bosse, suspended him from his post for that activity. Arons had money of his own, and in 1895 he spent large sums to advance his party. At the Hamburg Socialist convention of 1897 he carried a motion ending Socialist abstention from Prussian Diet elections.

His science ran in two channels, theory and experiment, with a focus on electricity. The entry lists a long run of papers in the Annalen der Physik und Chemie from 1885 onward. Subjects include interference bands in the spectrum, the electric arc, polarization at platinum mirrors, and a mercury arc lamp shown to the Berlin Physical Society.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashan-1910: Ashan was a town counted in the domain of Judah in Joshua chapter 15. In practice it lay in Simeon's hands, as Joshua chapter 19 and First Chronicles chapter 4 show. Priests also lived there, by First Chronicles chapter 6. A matching passage in Joshua chapter 21 gives Ain instead, which may be a copying slip for Ashan. Bor-ashan in First Samuel chapter 30 is perhaps the same place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asia-minor-2010:
Asia Minor, the western tip of Asia, was known to the Jews fairly early. Most of the sons of Japhet in the lists of Genesis chapter 10 belong to that region. Von Gutschmid placed a Jewish spread there in the middle of the fourth century B.C. The entry judges that Jewish settlement most likely began no earlier than the Seleucid kings, though Josephus tells of ties with Pergamus reaching back to Abraham.

Settlement came with royal backing. Toward the end of the third century, Antiochus the Great, who reigned from 223 to 187 B.C., planted 2,000 Jewish families from Mesopotamia in the thinly peopled districts of Phrygia. They formed military colonies at places such as Apamea, Laodicea, and Hierapolis. Rome, taking the region before Antiochus died, kept the same kind policy toward the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auerbach-baruch:
Baruch Auerbach was an educator and philanthropist. He was born in Inowrazlaw, in the province of Posen, Prussia, on Aug. 14, 1793. He died at Berlin on Jan. 22, 1864. He was the son of a poor rabbi, raised on Talmud study. In 1829 he became principal of a school for Jewish boys in Berlin.

In 1833 Auerbach took four orphans into his own house, since no provision existed for them. From that small start grew the Jewish Orphan Asylum of Berlin. By 1853 it housed 50 boys and 26 girls in its own building. Nearly 300 children passed through his care in his lifetime. He raised 600,000 thalers for the work, about $450,000. His own words sum up his aim: an asylum must give orphans not just bread and shelter, but parental love and practical training too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azevedo-david-c: David Cohen d'Azevedo was ḥakam of Amsterdam in the eighteenth century. He died in 1792. He gave himself to rabbinical study, and in 1782 he was chosen ḥakam in Amsterdam. One printed sermon of his is recorded here. Its title, in Portuguese, means Triumphs of Virtue. He preached it for the birthday of William the Fifth, Prince of Orange. It was published at Amsterdam in 1788.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bachrach-judah-: Judah b. Joshua Heskiel Bachrach was a rabbi and Talmud scholar born in Lithuania about 1775. He died at Seiny on April 25, 1846. The entry says he gave all his pay as rabbi at Seiny to the poor. He lived instead on the yield of a small fund friends had placed for him. His notes on the Talmud were printed in the Rom edition issued at Wilna, under a title formed from his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ballin-ada-sara: Ada Sara Ballin was an English author and journalist born in London. She studied at University College, London, and won scholarships in Hebrew and German. Her field became public health. She lectured for the National Health Society for years, with a focus on the health of children. She ran a monthly journal, "Baby, the Mother's Magazine," and then "Womanhood." The entry lists her books from a Hebrew grammar of 1881, written with her brother, to works on dress, feeding small children, and early education in 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-basel-congress-:
Basel Congress was the name for the Zionist conventions held at Basel, the first on Aug. 29, 30, and 31, 1897. Dr. Theodore Herzl called that meeting, held in the Stadt Casino. Jews came from many countries to discuss relief for Jews facing anti-Semitic pressure.

About one hundred and fifty delegates attended the first Congress. Later meetings drew about two hundred and fifty, then 300 at the fifth. The entry explains the shekel system for electing delegates and notes the founding of the Jewish Colonial Trust. It also records that women gained voting rights at the second Congress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beard-2510:
Beard, in Bible lands, marked manhood itself, and men swore by it while touching it. Stone images show western Semites in full, round beards kept with care. The entry tests claims about shaved lips and finds them wrong.

Cutting another man's beard was a deep disgrace, while mourners clipped or plucked their own. Law barred cutting the corners of the beard. Later sections follow razors, barbers, and rules in Talmud and codes. Polish Jews, the entry ends, still swear by the beard, often in jest. Anointing the beard with oil is read into a well known verse of the Psalms, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beck-karl-2710:
Karl Beck was an Austrian poet born on May 1, 1817, at Baja, Hungary. Raised as a Protestant though of Jewish parentage, he gave up medical study for ill health, then left trade for philosophy at Leipsic. There he found his calling as a poet.

His first poems of 1838 won wide praise, and a critic foretold the fame of a Byron for him. A later epic on a Hungarian horse herder is called his masterpiece here. Beck pled in verse for mercy after the Hungarian revolt of 1848. He died on April 10, 1879, near Vienna. His play Saul, though rich in fine and spirited lines, failed on stage for want of dramatic action.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belilhos-jacob-: Jacob Belilhos was a rabbi at Venice about the year 1680 and a relative of Daniel Belilhos of Amsterdam. The entry is very brief. It names one work by him, a book meant for the training of youth. That book answered and refuted Samuel Aboab. It was never published, the entry states, and no dates or other facts of Jacob Belilhos's life are given in this short notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bendery-2910: Bendery was a district town in the government of Bessarabia. In 1898 it counted a Jewish population of 12,000 out of 33,000 inhabitants in total. Commerce was the main work of its Jews, and only 1,061 of them followed handicrafts. Ten Jewish families farmed about sixty-eight acres inside the city and grew grapes. The entry names the Jewish Hospital, spending 6,400 rubles a year, and the Talmud Torah as leading charities. It also counts children getting religious teaching in Jewish and public schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bentwich-herber: Herbert Bentwich, an English lawyer and communal worker, was born in London in 1856. He trained at University College and the University of London, taking a law degree. He helped found the Hampstead Synagogue and pushed the Chovevei Zion group in England. He attended the Basel Congress of 1898 as part of its presidential council. He also organized the Maccabean Pilgrimage to Palestine in 1897. Later he parted from the English Zionist Federation, and the entry names him an authority on copyright.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernal-maestro-: Maestro Bernal was a Marano who sailed as ship's physician on the first voyage of Columbus to America. He had lived at Tortosa and done public penance in October 1490 as a follower of Judaism. The entry says Columbus, by his overbearing conduct, made an enemy of the physician. Bernal then stirred a plot against the admiral in Jamaica. That plot, the entry adds, weighed heavily on Columbus and his fate. Two points of a book on Columbus are cited as the source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-jeshimoth-: Beth-Jeshimoth was a town east of the Jordan. Numbers and Joshua assign it to Reuben. Ezekiel instead calls it a Moabite city. Josephus named the place Besimoth. Eusebius put it on the Dead Sea. He set it 10 Roman miles southeast of Jericho. Its site was a sandy hill near Beth-haran. The entry also corrects a Talmudic distance. Twelve miles from Abel-shittim, it says, is wrong.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bing-meyer-herm: Meyer Hermann Bing was a Danish art publisher. He was born at Copenhagen on June 4, 1807. He died there on September 15, 1883. As a boy he worked in his father's bookshop. At his father's death he took charge of it. In 1846 he set up on his own. He also manufactured goods himself. In 1856 he presided over Scandinavian booksellers. He served as town councilor from 1858 to 1871. He directed Copenhagen's two Jewish free schools until death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blood-money-in-:
Blood-money in Rumania fell on whole villages. Moldavian and Wallachian law fined murderers heavily. If the killer was unknown, the nearest village paid. Unpaid fines could depopulate a whole village. Jews bore the levy in common with others. Traveling peddlers faced mortal danger on the roads. A 1553 decree records one huge fine.

The village of Vianul owed 40,000 aspers. A murdered Jew's family had complained. The prince paid when villagers could not. To dodge fines, villagers hid found corpses. That hid husbands from their widows too. The law of 1831 abolished the fines. Murders of Jewish travelers continued anyway.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bondi-abraham-b: Abraham ben Yom-Tob Bondi was a Bohemian Talmudist who died in 1787 at Prague. His book Zera Abraham was printed after his death by his son. It holds essays on Talmud treatises and on later writers on marital questions. The son added an appendix when it came out at Prague in 1808. Another work by Abraham, on the investigation of the law, stayed in manuscript. The entry gives no birth date for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bukki-3810: Bukki is a Bible name borne by two men, and the entry treats both in a few lines. The first Bukki was a son of Jogli and prince of the tribe of Dan. He represented his tribe in the division of the land, as told in Numbers. The second Bukki was a son of Abishua and father of Uzzi. He was a priest, fourth in line from Aaron, and an ancestor of Ezra. The entry adds his name forms in the Apocrypha, Boccas and Borith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calahor-r-a-391:
Calahorra was a family of Spanish descent settled at Cracow from the sixteenth century onward. The entry profiles three men. Israel Samuel, a writer, finished a lexicon to the four ritual codes in 1624. It was printed at Cracow in 1626 and again at Amsterdam in 1693. His other Bible and prayer works stayed in manuscript.

Mattithiah, an apothecary, held a religious dispute with a Dominican and was burned at the stake in 1664. Solomon, a physician at Cracow from 1559 to 1586, likely came from the Spanish town of Calahorra. Kings Sigismund Augustus and Stephen Bathori granted him privileges, and he served the first as court physician. Leading rabbis of his day prized his medical skill.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-captain-4010:
Captain in the Bible versions renders a wide set of Hebrew and Greek words for chiefs and officers. The title stays vague because early Israel had no fixed army order. No standing force existed before the kingdom. Levies formed along tribe and clan lines, and each band's captain was as a rule its tribal chief.

Change came under Saul and David. Saul picked three thousand men and kept a guard about him, with Abner as the first named captain in chief. David, once a freebooter leader himself, built his followers into a standing force. The article sorts captains of the host, of the bodyguard, and of the palace runners. Later kings show fuller ranks, yet the word still covers many unlike posts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cassel-4110:
Cassel is a city in the Prussian province of Hesse-Nassau. Jews near Cassel suffered in the Black Death persecution of 1348 at Wolfshagen. In 1610 Landgrave Moritz granted Cassel Jews protection for 1,000 reichsgulden. By 1635 only one Jew, Benedict Goldschmidt, lived in the city.

Hard rules followed. In 1649 Jews had to attend weekly conversion sermons at the town hall. Later rules charged unprivileged Jews a ducat per night of stay, barred house buying outside one quarter, and named streets where Jews might live. A Jews' street was laid out in 1773. Open shops were allowed in 1775. A new synagogue was dedicated in 1839. The entry counts 2,200 Jews at Cassel in 1902 and notes a teachers' seminary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chernobyl-4310: Chernobyl is a town in the government of Kiev, in Russia. In 1898 it held 10,759 people, including 7,189 Jews. Of those Jews, 651 were artisans, and tailoring led the trades with 165 persons. About 167 Jews worked as journeymen, and 120 in a paper mill. Schools were only ḥadarim and a Talmud Torah with 45 pupils. Two Jewish colonies, Bobrik and Bobry, stood 40 English miles away. There 47 families farmed 618 deciatines of land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cleif-daniel-ha: Daniel Hayyim Cleif, a Russian rabbi, was born in Amsterdam in 1729 and died there on May 14, 1794. He settled at Hasenpoth in the government of Courland. He began there as a jeweler. Later he served as rabbi in that town for many years. In those years he wrote Arugah Ketannah, a small book that sets the 248 binding precepts in rhyme. It came out at Altona in 1787 and was reprinted several times. He also left a manuscript commentary on the Pentateuch. One son became a Russian state physician.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-lipschutz: Ephraim Cohen Lipschutz was an Italian rabbi and author of the later seventeenth century. He served as one of the rabbis at Modena. Contemporaries knew him as a keen Talmudic scholar, the entry says. His own book does not survive as a separate volume here. Instead, his responsa on Talmudic topics appear inside other men's works. They stand in Isaac Lampronti's Pahad Yizhak, in Joseph Ergas's Dibre Joseph on ransom law, and in Samson Morpurgo's Shemesh Zedakah. Nepi names him as teacher of Ishmael Cohen and of Samson Hayyim Nahamani.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-conrat-mase-461:
Max Conrat, also printed as Mase Conrat, was a professor and writer on Roman law, born in Breslau on Sept. 16, 1848. His birth name was Cohn, changed to Conrat in 1882 when he embraced Christianity. He took his doctorate at Berlin in 1870, taught Roman law as privat-docent at Heidelberg in 1873, and became professor at Zurich in 1874.

In 1878 he took the Roman law chair at Amsterdam. Early work treated ancient Roman law; twenty later years went to Roman law of the Middle Ages. The entry lists a dozen books, from a study of Roman public associations in 1870 to a history of the sources of early medieval Roman law in 1891. A late work of 1897 views the persecutions of Christians through a jurist's eyes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-curiel-4810: Curiel was a wealthy Marano family that settled in the Netherlands and at Hamburg. It settled there about the sixteenth century. The family intermarried heavily with the Da Costa family. In 1682 Antwerp was stirred by a forced baptism attempt. The rector of Saint George tried to baptize the son of Diego Curiel by force. The effort was frustrated. Moses de David Curiel, at the start of the eighteenth century, was a well-known London Jew. Three sources are cited at the close.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-desecration-511:
Desecration is the act of turning something sacred to a common use. Jewish law forbade using the sanctuary's anointing oil for ordinary purposes, or even making oil or incense like it. The punishment was excision, being cut off from the people of Israel. Every object of the Temple service counted as sacred.

A person who knowingly used such an object for himself faced stripes. If he acted by mistake, he brought a sacrifice and paid the object's value plus one-fifth. Sacred things could not even be exchanged. A consecrated animal swapped for another left both animals sacred, whether the trade was better or worse. Animals unfit for the altar could be redeemed for their value plus a fifth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-diodatus-surnam:
Diodatus, surnamed Trypho, ruled Syria from 141 to 138 B.C. Born at Kasiana near Apamea, he began as an officer under Alexander Balas. He backed Alexander's young son Antiochus against Demetrius II. With help from deserters, he took the city of Antioch.

Fearing Jonathan the Hasmonean, Diodatus lured him to Ptolemais and had him put to death. He then killed the young Antiochus and took the crown of Asia for himself. Simon Maccabeus turned to Demetrius and won independence for the Jewish state. Antiochus VII later shut Diodatus up in Dora. He fled to Orthosia and, besieged at Apamea, took his own life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-drawer-of-water: Drawer of water is a stock phrase in the Bible, always paired with hewer of wood. The entry ties it to the Gibeonites. Caught in a fraud, they were spared by oath but set to low tasks. They drew water and cut wood for the Tabernacle, and later for the Temple. Water went from the well into goatskins for carrying. A man with a donkey could sling two goatskins across its back. The entry closes by noting the water drawer is still a familiar figure in the Orient.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-el-asah-5510: El'asah was an amora whose exact period is uncertain. The entry knows him mainly through a debate he held with a man named Philippus, who is also called a philosopher. Philippus pointed to a verse in Malachi about Edom. He argued that Edom still stood, though the prophet said God would throw down its building. El'asah replied that the verse meant plots and schemes, not stone and timber. Philippus admitted the point, saying that plots against the Jews often failed when an elder stepped in.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-d-itali: Eliezer d'Italia was a printer of Hebrew books at Mantua. He worked at the start of the seventeenth century. In 1612 he set up a print shop in that town. No Hebrew press had run there for fifteen years before him. In his first year he put out three books. One gathers prayers by Mordecai Yare. One is a Purim poem by Moses of Corfu. The third is a work by Abraham Portaleone. The entry gives no facts of his life beyond the press.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elvira-5710: Elvira was an old town in Spain, the Illiberis of old. It stood on a hill northwest of Granada. The town now lies in ruins on that hill. Men call it the cradle of the church in Spain. A famed council met there in early church days. That council first set a wall between Jew and Christian. It met in 303 or 304, in a time of persecution. It banned Christians from wedlock with Jews on pain of casting out. It also banned meals and all contact with Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephraim-vidal-k: Ephraim Vidal, also known as Ephraim Blasom and Vidal Blasom, studied under R. Nissim of Gerona. He served as rabbi in Palma and taught Simeon Duran. Isaac ben Sheshet held him in great esteem. The entry also notes his skill in mathematics. It ends by saying he died a martyr to his faith. No dates, places of birth, or writings are given for him in the entry. His record rests on responsa by Isaac ben Sheshet and Simeon Duran.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eurydemus-ben-j: Eurydemus ben Jose was a son of the tanna Jose ben Halafta, and his entry is mostly about his name. The name survives in mixed forms: Awradimus, Abirodimus, Abdimus, and Wradimus. Bacher takes Eurydemus as the base form, a name also found in Herodotus. Levy and Kohut favor Eudaimon instead. Others read all the forms as Abdimus and merge him with Menahem ben Jose. The entry closes with one content note: the few sayings under his name urge kindness. No dates or life events are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fochs-anton-621:
Anton Fochs was a Hungarian philanthropist who died at Budapest on May 31, 1874. A few years before his death he sent an unsigned letter to the Jewish community there. It gave 43,000 florins to found an orphan asylum. Suspected as the donor, he denied it in the press. Only his will showed the truth. It asked that the asylum bear his parents' name.

Fochs left a fortune of more than 1,000,000 florins. Most of it went to humane bodies with no bar of faith. About 60,000 florins were set aside for the schooling of his orphans with a gift for letters or science. A sum of 300,000 florins founded a deaf-and-dumb institute for Hungary and Transylvania. He himself was unmarried, silent, thrifty, and a recluse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fubini-simone-6:
Simone Fubini, an Italian physiologist born on May 26, 1841, at Casale Monferrato, died at Turin on September 6, 1898. He earned his medical degree at Turin in 1862 and trained further in Paris. Back in Turin he aided Moleschott in physiology. In 1881 he became professor of physiology at Palermo. In 1888 he took a chair in materia medica and pharmacology at Pisa.

After Moleschott died in 1893, Fubini edited his journal on the study of man and animals. His many papers treat the cornea, the weight of the central nervous system, opium alkaloids and breathing, and skin absorption. The entry calls him one of the leading physiologists of Italy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gaon-6510: Gaon names a strong Jewish family of Vitoria in Spain. Don Gaon farmed taxes for Henry IV of Castile. In 1463 the king sent him to Guipuzcoa to gather tribute. Local nobles saw the demand as a breach of old rights. They murdered Gaon when he reached Tolosa on May 6, 1463. The king marched to avenge him and spared the town only when its leaders gave up their prized rights. His son Eliezer later farmed taxes at Vitoria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gerondi-moses-b: Moses ben Solomon Gerondi, a Hebrew poet and kin of Moses Nahmanides, lived at Gerona in Catalonia in the late thirteenth century. In a letter home from Jerusalem, Nahmanides sends him warm greetings. Nahmanides calls him my son and my pupil. He tells his son that he read Gerondi verses with bitter tears on the Mount of Olives. The poem was likely a dirge for ruined Jerusalem. Only two religious poems of his are firmly known.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-glogauer-judah-: Judah ben Ḥanina Selig Glogauer was a German Talmudist of the early eighteenth century. His one named work is "Ḳol Yehudah," printed at Amsterdam in 1729 and often reprinted. It gathers notes on the Talmud by various rabbis of his own time, with some remarks of his own mixed in. The entry says nothing more about his life, posts, or family, and points readers to Fürst's "Bibliotheca Judaica" and Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue for the record of the book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gordon-david-b-:
David Gordon, son of Dob Baer, was a Russian journalist. He was born at Podmerecz, near Wilna, in 1826. He died at Lyck, Prussia, on May 21, 1886. He studied in Wilna's yeshibah from age ten. After years in England and teaching in Liverpool, he joined the Hebrew weekly "Ha-Maggid" in 1856. He became its assistant editor at Lyck in 1858.

He helped Silberman found the Meḳiẓe Nirdamim society in 1864. It published old and valuable Hebrew works. On Silberman's death in 1882, Gordon took over "Ha-Maggid" as editor. He was a pioneer Zionist and a leader of Chovevei Zion. His translations cover travels in Asia and Africa and Montefiore's journey to Jerusalem. His 1881-82 narrative in the Jewish Chronicle records the Russian persecutions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grunhut-lazar-6:
Lazar Grünhut was a Hungarian rabbi and writer. He was born at Gerenda, Hungary, in 1850. He earned his rabbinical diploma while still a youth. In Berlin he heard Israel Hildesheimer at the seminary and lectures at the university. He took his doctorate at Bern. For eleven years he served as rabbi at Temesvár. In 1892 he became director of the Jewish orphan asylum at Jerusalem.

His works study Midrash and classic texts. They include a critical study of Kohelet Rabbah and editions of Midrash Shir ha-Shirim. He wrote on Saadia Gaon and on Ezra and Nehemiah. He also published Benjamin of Tudela's travel accounts from manuscripts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halleluiah-or-t: Halleluiah is a cry of praise meaning "Praise ye the Lord," the holy name clipped to its first two letters. Save for Psalm cxxxv. 3, it comes only at the starts or ends of psalms. In some psalms the words that follow grow out of it. In others it looks tacked on by Temple authorities to fit a psalm for public worship. The Hebrew words passed through the Vulgate into Christian psalters and modern hymns. English versions always render them "Praise ye the Lord."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hazael-7410:
Hazael was the strongest of the kings of Damascus. Elijah had been told to anoint him as a coming king while Ben-hadad still ruled. When Ben-hadad fell sick, he sent Hazael to ask Elisha about his health. Elisha said the king would die and that Hazael would rule and war cruelly on Israel. Hazael went home, killed Ben-hadad, and took the throne.

His wars hurt Israel badly. He took Bashan, Gilead, and all the land east of the Jordan. He wrecked Gath and drew rich spoil from Jerusalem's palace and temple. Yet he also stood firm against Assyria. Shalmaneser fought him twice and could not take Damascus. The entry calls that stand a shield for the whole coast land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heinefetter-sab: Sabine Heinefetter, born on Aug. 19, 1809, at Mayence, was a German soprano. She began life as a wandering harpist. A Frankfort musician noticed her and taught her music. She later studied at Cassel under Spohr and in Paris under Tadolini. In 1829 she sang at the Paris Italian opera beside Sontag and Malibran. In 1835 she took a post at the Dresden court theater. Her big roles included Romeo, Norma, and Rosine. She last sang at Frankfort in 1844. She died insane on Feb. 18, 1872.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herrmann-leo-76: Leo Herrmann, born in Paris on July 12, 1853, was a French painter trained at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris. He showed his first picture in the Paris Salon of 1875. A second followed in 1876, and he then exhibited in the Salon steadily. The entry lists four later paintings by their French titles, dated 1877, 1887, 1889, and 1896. No death date, family detail, or account of his style is given beyond the exhibition record and a single cited source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hiller-ferdinan:
Ferdinand Hiller, born at Frankfort-on-the-Main on Oct. 24, 1811, was a German composer and musical writer. He played a Mozart concerto in public at ten and began composing at twelve. After study under Hummel at Weimar, he toured to Vienna and saw Beethoven near death.

In Paris from 1828 Hiller taught and gave concerts, first bringing a Beethoven concerto to that public. His opera Romilda failed at Milan in 1839, but his oratorio on Jerusalem's destruction succeeded at Leipsic. He later led music at Düsseldorf and Cologne. His books treated Beethoven, Mendelssohn, Goethe's music life, and harmony exercises. He died at Cologne on May 10, 1885.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hohenems-7810:
Hohenems is a town in Vorarlberg, Austria, between Tyrol and Lake Constance. In 1890 it held a total population of 3,988, of whom 118 were Jews. At its height in 1862 the community counted 564 souls. Jews driven from Burgau found shelter there in 1617, in the period when the town still belonged to its own sovereign counts.

Each family paid a yearly protection fee, first ten florins plus two fattened geese, and the fee later rose. Expulsion came in 1676, readmission in 1688. Austria gained the town in 1765 and set fresh limits in a protection writ of 1769, capping trade and land buying. From 1849 to 1878 Jews formed their own political community. Their large synagogue dates to 1772 and their German school to 1785. A poorhouse followed in 1871, and the cemetery dates to 1617. The community tends liberal and lists named rabbis of note.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-houbigant-charl:
Charles Francois Houbigant was a French Christian Hebraist born in Paris in 1686. He died there on October 31, 1783. In 1704 he joined the Congregation of the Oratory. He taught at several towns, then lectured in Paris from 1722 until deafness forced him to retire.

His Hebrew roots book of 1732 argued that vowel points are useless in Hebrew. His Prolegomena of 1746 held that copyists had badly altered the Old Testament text. His chief work, a Hebrew Bible of 1753, printed the text without vowel points and corrected it freely, chiefly from the Samaritan Pentateuch. Scholars such as Michaelis attacked his method as careless and arbitrary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-b-reuben-:
Isaac ben Reuben Albargeloni, Spanish Talmudist and liturgical poet, was born at Barcelona in 1043. He served as judge in the important community of Denia and became connected, probably as son-in-law, with ibn Alhatosh. Nahmanides was among his later descendants. Contemporaries held him in such regard that he is simply called "Ha-Rab Albargeloni," the rabbi.

At thirty-five, in 1078, he translated Hai Gaon's work on buying and selling from Arabic into Hebrew. His fame rests on his Azharot, 145 strophes of three verses each ending in a biblical quotation, which entered the rituals of Constantine, Tlemcen, Tunis, Morocco, Algeria and Oran. Al-Harizi praised how he fitted the laws to the verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-benja:
Jacob ben Benjamin Ze'eb Sak was a Lithuanian Talmudist born at Wilna in the first half of the seventeenth century, who died at Jerusalem. The Chmielnicki persecutions drove him from his city. He fled with his father-in-law, Ephraim ben Aaron, but their pursuers split them apart on the road. After months of wandering, barely escaping death, he found Ephraim again at Trebitsch, in Moravia.

About 1665 Jacob became rabbi of Trebitsch, then of Ungarisch-Brod, and after Ephraim's death, of Ofen. There his luck failed again. Imperial troops took the city in 1686, and Jacob was carried off captive to Berlin. The Jews of Berlin ransomed him. He lived some years with his son Zebi Ashkenazi at Altona, then went on to Jerusalem, where he died at seventy-three.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jeshua-ben-juda:
Jeshua ben Judah, known in Arabic as Abu al-Faraj Furkan ibn Asad, was a Karaite Bible student and thinker of the second half of the eleventh century. He probably lived at Jerusalem and studied under Joseph ben Abraham ha-Roeh. Karaites called him the great teacher and ranked him among their highest authorities. His public talks on Karaism drew many inquirers, including a Spanish Rabbinite who carried his writings home.

His chief service to Karaism was a reform of the laws on forbidden marriages, a change his own master had urged. He also turned the Pentateuch into Arabic and wrote a huge commentary on it, with a short form made in 1054. Parts of both survive in manuscript, and later writers quote him often.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-abra: Joseph ben Abraham Issachar Barman was a Dutch scholar of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. His one known work is a translation into Judaeo-German of the Targum to the Song of Songs. It was printed at Amsterdam in 1711. The translation was placed inside Jacob b. Isaac's Ze'enah u-Re'enah, the well-known retelling of the Pentateuch for home reading. The entry is very short and rests on two catalogues of Hebrew books. Nothing is told about his life, family, or other writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joshua-b-abin-8: Joshua b. Abin was a Palestinian amora of the fourth century whose name is tied chiefly to haggadot, the non-legal tales and teachings. He passed on a haggadah of Levi and a legal ruling of Anani b. Sason. Some of his own haggadic sayings also survive. So do his rewordings of Bible verses in plainer form. The entry is only a few lines long and rests on Bacher and on Heilprin's Seder ha-Dorot. No birthplace, teacher, or death date is given for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-leone-b-i:
Judah Leone b. Isaac Sommo, called Leone Ebreo, was an Italian writer, drama critic, and stage manager who died after 1591. Of the Portaleone family of Mantua, he lived at Ferrara and then at Mantua. At the wish of the ducal court he gave himself wholly to the stage, teaching the theory and craft of drama.

His Italian writings fill sixteen volumes in manuscript at Turin: plays, poems, and dialogues on acting. Those dialogues treat the roots of drama, the five-act form, delivery, dress, the actor, and scenery. He held Moses, as reputed author of Job, to be the first dramatist. For Jewish letters he rendered forty-five Psalms into Italian verse and wrote Magen Nashim, a defense of women, in Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-low-ben-o: Judah Low ben Obadiah Eilenburg was a Russian rabbi of the sixteenth century. About the year 1570 he followed Naphtali Herz as rabbi of Brest-Litovsk. His name stands on the rules passed by the Council of Four Lands at Lublin in 1587. Those rules banned, among other things, the buying of rabbinic posts. His book Minhat Yehudah gives notes on Rashi's commentary on the Pentateuch. It mixes his own remarks with extracts from Solomon Luria, Mordecai Jaffe, and Elijah Mizrahi. Editions came out at Lublin and Prague.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaddish-lit-hol:
Ḳaddish, a word meaning "holy," names a doxology said at the close of prayer. The congregation answers aloud as it is read. It is also said after readings from Scripture. It follows talks on religion as well. All of it but the last clause is in Aramaic. The entry gives the full text in English.

The long article traces the prayer's past. It began as a teacher's closing words after a discourse. At first it had no link to prayer or to the dead. The article then sets out the five forms of Ḳaddish. It gives rules for which mourners say it first. It notes the custom of sons saying it for eleven months. It ends with the tunes used for it in the service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kara-simeon-921: Simeon Ḳara was a French rabbi who lived at Mans in the eleventh century. He was the brother of Menahem ben Ḥelbo. He was also the father of Joseph Ḳara. One early list counts him among the leading French rabbis. No work of his has survived. Rapoport once named him as the maker of the Yalḳuṭ Shim'oni. Abraham Epstein later showed that the manuscripts do not bear his name. In some copies the name reads "Simson" instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kiddushin-betro:
Ḳiddushin is a treatise on betrothal. It stands in the Mishnah, the Tosefta, and both Talmuds. It is the seventh and last treatise of the order Nashim. It holds four chapters and forty-seven paragraphs. A wife is gained, it opens, in three ways: by money, by a written note, or by union. She goes free by divorce or by her husband's death.

The entry outlines each chapter in turn. Proxy marriage takes much of the space. So do hard cases where a father betroths a young daughter without naming which one. The last chapter lists ten families that came up from Babylonia. It also sets rules of decent conduct. The Talmud parts add tales and maxims. One warns that a father who teaches his son no trade teaches him robbery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-koenen-hendrik-: Hendrik Jacob Koenen, born at Amsterdam on Jan. 11, 1809, was a Dutch historian of the Jews who died at Buitenrust, near Haarlem, on Oct. 13, 1874. Trained for the bar, he took his doctor of law degree in 1831 and sat for years on the common council of Amsterdam and on the provincial states of North Holland. His prize-winning history of the Jews in the Netherlands appeared at Utrecht in 1843. The entry notes it was the first history of the Jews in Holland and that it cited many sources not known before.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kremnitzer-joha: Johanan ben Meïr Kremnitzer, a Polish rabbinical author who lived at Kalisz in the seventeenth century, wrote a work called Oraḥ Mishor. The first book with that title, printed at Sulzbach in 1692, comments on Moses Isserles' guide to Yoreh Deʿah. A second Oraḥ Mishor, printed at Berlin in 1724, gives new readings on the tractate Nazir. It corrects the text of the Gemara, Rashi, and the Tosafot. The two works were later issued together, and a third edition of the first appeared at Fürth in 1766.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-laguna-daniel-i:
Daniel Israel Lopez Laguna, a Spanish poet born in Portugal about the middle of the seventeenth century, came from Marano parents. The Inquisition jailed him for years as a Marano before he escaped. At Jamaica he openly confessed Judaism. There he finished a Spanish verse paraphrase of the Psalms begun in prison.

London gave the work its printed form in 1720, after twenty-three years of labor. Praise poems in Spanish, Latin, and English fill the front matter. Laguna then went back to Jamaica to his wife Riki and three sons. He died at age seventy, though the entry gives no year for his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-landau-leopold-: Leopold Landau, a German gynecologist born at Warsaw on July 16, 1848, studied at Breslau, Würzburg, and Berlin. He graduated in 1870 and served as assistant surgeon in the Franco-Prussian war. Breslau hospital work and teaching followed to 1876. He then moved to Berlin and joined its medical faculty. A professor title came in 1893. In 1892 he and his brother Theodor opened a private hospital for women's diseases. His books treat wandering kidney and liver in women and radical surgery, dated from 1881 to 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lefmann-salomon: Salomon Lefmann, a German scholar of language born at Telgte in Westphalia on Dec. 25, 1831, studied at Münster, Heidelberg, Berlin, and Paris. His Berlin doctorate came in 1864. Heidelberg made him lecturer in 1866 and assistant professor in 1870; he is now honorary professor of Sanskrit there. Small Westphalian communities knew him as tutor and schoolmaster on the way up. His chief works give a history of ancient India dated 1879-90 and a life of Franz Bopp in two volumes, dated 1891-97.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-david-9810:
David Levi, an Italian poet and patriot, was born at Chieri in 1816 and died at Venice on Oct. 18, 1898. He studied law at Parma and Pisa. He had to leave Pisa after a duel. He had challenged a fellow student who had insulted the Jews, and wounded him.

In Paris in 1839 Levi joined the circle of Italian patriots. Back home he led the push to free northern Italy from Austria and unite all the Italian states. He fought in the Lombard revolt of 1848-49. From 1860 he sat in the national assembly and spoke for equal rights and free worship. He stayed in politics until 1879. His poems and war songs run through his career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-uriah-phil:
Uriah Phillips Levy, an American naval officer, was born in Philadelphia on April 22, 1792. He died in New York on March 22, 1862. He went to sea as a cabin boy before he was eleven. By 1812 he held a share in a schooner and sailed as its master. That year the navy made him a sailing master.

Levy served on the "Argus," was taken prisoner, and spent sixteen months in England. His navy path was rough: a duel, six courts-martial, and removal from the list. A court of inquiry in 1855 cleared him, and he rose to commodore. He bought Jefferson's Monticello and gave a statue of Jefferson to the nation. His stone calls him father of the law that ended corporal punishment in the navy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lippe-lippe-det:
Lippe, also called Lippe-Detmold, was a small sovereign principality in northwest Germany. In 1895 it had 123,515 people, including about 750 Jews. The entry traces Jewish settlement there from the early fourteenth century. Jews there seem to have had more safety and rights than in many other German states.

A Jewish community formed in Detmold in the late seventeenth century. After a split, the group reunited and in 1742 turned a barn into a synagogue that was still in use. Jews received family names in 1810. Laws in 1858 and 1879 reset civic rights, schools, and synagogue rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyon-leoni-myer:
Myer Lyon, known on stage as Leoni, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 as both opera singer and cantor. He began as a chorister at London's Great Synagogue, alongside his nephew John Braham. His voice was said to surpass his nephew's in sweetness. He first sang at Covent Garden in 1775, in Artaxerxes. He died at Kingston, Jamaica, about 1800.

The article traces his double career across the Atlantic world. He helped manage an English opera house in Dublin and sang at the Royalty Theatre. He ended as cantor of the synagogue in Kingston, the first trained cantor in the English colonies. He composed music for theater and synagogue alike. His name survives in the hymn tune Leoni, taken from his singing of the closing hymn Yigdal. A Wesleyan minister set it to The God of Abraham Praise, and it spread through English hymnals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-majority-10310:
Majority is treated in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia under two meanings in Jewish law. The first is a legal principle: doing the greater part of an act can count as doing the whole. Cutting most of the throat passages in slaughter, for example, makes an animal fit for food. A child mostly born is counted as born.

The article sets the principle's limits and its second sense. Majority beats the rival principles of presumption and proximity. It never applies in money cases, and witness numbers do not settle testimony. A hundred witnesses can be undone by two. The second meaning is the age of maturity. The Bible sets no single age, though army service and the half-shekel began at twenty. The rabbis tied adulthood to puberty, about thirteen for girls and fourteen for boys. The entry is a compact guide to a rule that runs through ritual and civil law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-margulies-samue:
Samuel Hirsch Margulies, a rabbi of Florence, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Brzezan, Galicia, on October 9, 1858, he descended from Rabbi Ephraim Zalman Margolioth. He was educated at the theological seminary at Breslau. His career then moved steadily west and south.

The article lists his pulpits in order. From 1885 to 1887 he served Congregation Newe Shalom in Hamburg. Weilburg in Hesse-Nassau followed until 1890. Since 1890 he had been chief rabbi of Florence. In 1899 he also became principal of the Italian rabbinical college, later moved to Florence. His writings include a study of Saadja's Arabic translation of the Psalms, printed at Breslau in 1884. Two Passover sermons and a work called Poet and Patriot followed. By 1904 he was editing the Rivista Israelitica. The entry shows a Galician scholar heading Italian Jewry's rabbinate and school.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maybaum-siegmun:
Siegmund Maybaum, a rabbi in Berlin and a leader of Germany's rabbis, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman. Born at Miskolcz, in Hungary, on April 29, 1844, he studied at the yeshivot of Eisenstadt and Pressburg, at Breslau's university and Jewish seminary, and took his doctorate at Halle in 1869. Pulpits at Alsó-Kubin and at Saaz led in 1881 to Berlin, where he also taught at the Lehranstalt, the college for Jewish scholarship.

Maybaum founded the rabbinical society of Germany and, as its president, called the first congress of German rabbis at Berlin in 1884. The entry calls him one of the most eloquent rabbis in the country and notes the professor's title granted in 1903. His books trace his pulpit scholarship, from studies of anthropomorphism in the Targum to histories of the priesthood, prophecy, and the Jewish sermon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-melville-lewis-:
Lewis Melville was the pen name of Lewis S. Benjamin. Benjamin was an English man of letters born in 1874. Joseph Jacobs and I. L. Bril enter him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His whole short list of books circles one novelist. It holds a "Life of Thackeray" in 1899. It holds "Thackeray's Stray Papers" in 1902. It holds an introduction to Thackeray's works too. That piece was issued in 1903 and 1904.

His one trip away from that devotion was "In the World of Mimes," also of 1902. He also wrote for the "Fortnightly Review," "The Bookman," "Temple Bar," and other English periodicals. The notice is among the briefest in the volume. It rests on one source, the Literary Year-Book for 1904. It catches him at the start of a career spent editing and championing Thackeray.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-d:
Meshullam ben David was a German tosafist of the twelfth or early thirteenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 notices him through the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn. He was the son of David ben Kalonymus of Münzenburg. His father was himself a tosafist and liturgical poet. Meshullam's scholarly world is mapped by his correspondents. They were R. Baruch, Simhah of Speyer, and Isaac Or Zarua. His name and opinions appear in their responsa. They appear in the "Mordekai" too.

The notice ends with a caution typical of these entries. In the "Mordekai" on Hullin, a Meshullam is cited. Gross, in his "Gallia Judaica," thinks that Meshullam is another man. He thinks it is Meshullam of Melun. The trail of a glossator who wrote no surviving book runs through other men's footnotes. The encyclopedia leaves the identification honestly unsettled.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-modon-simson-ha:
Simson ha-Kohen Modon, a Mantuan poet born on August 1, 1679, was his congregation's polished face to power, as Isidore Singer and S. J. Levinson tell it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. An accomplished linguist, he was sent to Vienna to do homage to Emperor Charles VI and came home with the emperor's goodwill. Rabbi David Finzi then steered him to poetry.

His collection Ḳol Musar appeared at Mantua in 1725, with some of Finzi's own poems inside, and Venice printed his Keter Torah and an elegy for his teacher Judah Brill. The tour de force was Shigyon Shimshon, three hundred lines each beginning with the same letter. He also compiled an alphabetical rabbinical encyclopedia, Sefer Zikronot — which, like the poem, never left manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordo-lazare-11:
Lazare Mordo, born in 1744, was physician and honorary rabbi of Corfu. That combination tells its own story, as a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco shows in 1906. He studied at Venice and Padua. In 1814 he was appointed chief physician of the island. He was esteemed by government and populace alike for learning and philanthropy.

When he died in 1823, the Corfiote poet Delviniotti composed an elegy in his honor. Mordo left numerous works in manuscript. The one that reached print was his Nozioni Miscellanee Interno a Corcira of 1809. It was dedicated to the Senate's president. It preserves the names of the physicians who had served Corfu before him, several of them Jews. Civic memory was kept by the island's doctor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-judah-lob:
Moses Judah Löb ben Samuel was a Russian rabbi and author born at Turetz in the government of Minsk. Herman Rosenthal and N. T. London wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He married into the family of Rabbi David Tebele of Minsk. When David died, Moses succeeded him and held the Minsk rabbinate for thirty years.

With his brother-in-law Saul Hayyim he prepared the Bet Dawid for the press. His own treatises, Mille di-Berakot and Mille di-Nezikin, treat the laws of blessings and the recovery of damages. Some responsa of his remain in manuscript. He died at Minsk in 1889, and his son Jacob followed him as rabbi there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-muller-david-he:
David Heinrich Müller was an Austrian Orientalist born at Buczacz in Galicia on July 6, 1846. Isidore Singer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Trained at Vienna, Leipsic, Strasburg, and Berlin, he became professor of Oriental languages at Vienna in 1885. He also taught Hebrew and religious philosophy at the Vienna Jewish seminary.

Müller's long list of works centers on South Arabia: its castles, its inscriptions, and its old language. He edited the versions of Eldad ha-Dani and wrote on Ezekiel and on the meter of the Prophets. His 1903 book compared the laws of Hammurabi with the legislation of Moses. In 1897 he led a learned expedition to South Arabia and Socotra.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naphtali-tribe-:
The Tribe of Naphtali numbered fifty-three thousand four hundred men at Sinai, the Jewish Encyclopedia article records. Written by the editorial committee and J. F. McLaughlin, it follows the tribe's land and wars. In the march Naphtali camped with Dan and Asher as the rear guard. Its lot in Canaan was among the fairest, running from the Jordan lakes northward.

Josephus calls that country the very ambition of nature, an earthly paradise. From Naphtali came Barak, who led ten thousand men against Sisera at Deborah's call. The tribe also rallied to Gideon and sent David a great host at Hebron. Assyria deported its people early, yet Isaiah foresaw the same region seeing the dawn of deliverance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-necho-and-11410:
Necho ruled Egypt from 610 to 594 B.C. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and George A. Barton for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was son of Psammetich I, of the twenty-sixth dynasty. Herodotus credits him with a bold canal project. He tried to join the Nile to the Red Sea.

Phoenician sailors for Necho circled Africa in three years. In 608 he marched into Asia for spoil. King Josiah tried to stop him at Megiddo and died. Necho chained Jehoahaz and set Jehoiakim in his place. Judah paid him a heavy tribute in silver and gold. Four years later Nebuchadnezzar crushed him at Carchemish. He fled home and never regained Asia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-newport-11510:
Newport was Rhode Island's capital and a colonial trading giant. Joseph Jacobs, L. Hühner, and Max J. Kohler wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Roger Williams founded it on broad religious toleration. Fifteen Jewish families arrived from Holland in 1658. Their congregation took the name Jeshuat Israel.

Portuguese Jews after 1740 made Newport rich and busy. Jacob Rodrigues-Rivera brought sperm-oil making to America. Aaron Lopez became New England's great merchant prince. He owned thirty vessels when the Revolution began. The town's synagogue, finished in 1763, still stands today. Its cemetery was bought in 1677 by two merchants. The Revolution ruined Newport's trade and scattered its Jews. In 1790 the congregation addressed President Washington in friendship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novoaleksandrov: Novoaleksandrovsk is a Russian city in the Kovno government. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The census of 1897 counted 6,370 people there. No fewer than 4,277 of them are Jews. Artisans number 445 among the Jewish residents. Sixty pupils study in the Talmud Torah. Thirty small ḥadarim teach 240 more children. A private Jewish school opened in 1897. Two charities aid the sick and the poor. One synagogue and five prayer houses serve the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-onias-from-hebr:
Onias was the name of high priests of the Second Temple. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The order here rests on the works of Josephus. Those works are not sound on all points, the piece warns. Josephus lacked good sources for this span of time.

Onias the First was son of Jaddua, by that account. Some link him to Areus, a king of Sparta. That link may rest on a forged set of letters. Onias the Second was son of Simon the Just. He was a boy when his father died young. His uncles held the high priest's post till he grew. Josephus calls him a man of greed and small wit. He would not pay the tax due to Egypt's king.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottinger-jacob-: Jacob Joseph Öttinger was a German rabbi at Berlin. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Glogau in the year 1780. He died at Berlin on November 7, 1860. He read with Hirsch Samose and learned the rabbis' books well. In 1820 he was called to Berlin as a help rabbi. Five years on he was made the town's acting rabbi. His firm stand on Reform is stressed in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pentapolis-i-e-:
Pentapolis is a Greek word for a group of five cities. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Bible world knew three such groups. Each group lay in a different land. The name works like Decapolis, a group of ten.

The first group is the cities of the plain. Sodom and Gomorrah head that famous list. The second group is the five Philistine cities on the coast. Gaza and Gath belong to that group. The third group stood in Cyrenaica, in north Africa. Jews carried their war of 70 there as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-sir-be:
Sir Benjamin Samuel Phillips was lord mayor of London. He was born there in 1811 and died there in 1889. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He began as a tailor's son in the family firm.

Phillips built Faudel, Phillips and Sons with his brother-in-law. He served the Board of Deputies for thirty years. He fought long to lift the legal bars on Jews. London made him alderman, then sheriff, then lord mayor in 1865. He raised a vast cholera fund in that term. Queen Victoria knighted him for his service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-plock-plotzk-12:
Plock was a government of Russian Poland, on the Vistula. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1897 it held 50,473 Jews among 553,094 souls. No Pale government held fewer Jews in all. Its towns each get their own short notice.

The capital, also called Plock, held 10,000 Jews. They formed over a third of the whole city. Synagogues, a Talmud Torah, and a hospital served them. Hasidic feeling kept the rabbinate changing hands. Seventeen years in the chair counted as very long. Mlawa and Przasnysz held thousands of Jews each.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-posquieres-or-o:
Posquières, also called Vauvert, is a town in the Gard in France. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews are known to have lived there since the twelfth century. Benjamin of Tudela came to the town about 1165. He found a community of forty members there.

At the head of the town stood Abraham ben David. His school drew students from lands far away. He gave them a warm welcome in his own home. In 1172 he spent a short time in prison. His foe had him seized on a charge. The entry follows the town through those years of fame and strain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-psalms-midrash-:
Midrash Tehillim is an old Jewish tale-note on the Psalms. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It has been known since the eleventh century. Nathan of Rome cites it in his word book. Isaac ibn Ghayyat cites it in his law book as well.

Rashi cites the work on many Bible verses. It is called Agadat Tehillim in some of those places. From the twelfth century men called it Shoher Tob too. That name caused mix-ups with a like work on Proverbs. The article sorts out the names, the age, and the prints. It shows how the tales gloss the psalms verse by verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinovitz-josh:
Joshua ben Elijah Rabinovitz was a Russian rabbi of the Minsk land. Isidore Singer and Benzion Eisenstadt wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Shat near Kaidan in 1818. He died at Nesvizh in 1887. His father, known as Elijah Ragoler, taught him Talmud. That home schooling made him a rabbi in his teens.

At eighteen Rabinovitz wed the daughter of a rich man of Kletzk. He then led the yeshivah of that town. In 1847 he became its rabbi as well. Twenty years on, Nesvizh called him to its rabbinate. He served that town for the rest of his life. The entry keeps the bare bones of a rabbi's career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rebekah-12610:
Rebekah was the wife of Isaac and daughter of Bethuel. Emil G. Hirsch, M. Seligsohn, and the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Genesis tells how Abraham's servant found her at a well. She drew water for him and his camels.

The article follows her life after that meeting. She stayed childless for nineteen years, then bore twins. Those twins were Jacob and Esau. At Gerar she and Isaac claimed to be siblings. Later she helped Jacob win the blessing meant for Esau. She urged Jacob to flee to her brother Laban. A rabbinical part debates her age at marriage. The entry joins a Bible story to later debate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reuss-eduard-wi:
Eduard Wilhelm Reuss was a Protestant theologian born on July 18, 1804. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Strasburg. He died there on April 15, 1891.

The article says he studied Oriental languages at Halle and Paris. Gesenius and Silvestre de Sacy were his teachers. In 1834 he became a professor in his native city. He claimed his first lectures set out a bold thesis. The Priestly Code was the latest layer of the Pentateuch. Graf and Wellhausen later won fame for that same view. Reuss translated the whole Bible into French. That work filled sixteen volumes from 1874 to 1888. He also wrote a history of the Old Testament.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romanelli-samue:
Samuel Aaron Romanelli was a Neo-Hebrew poet born on September 19, 1757. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Mantua. He died at Casale Monferrato on October 17, 1814.

The article calls him gifted but unsteady in habits. He traveled early, spending four years in Morocco. His popular book describes those experiences in Barbary. He later lived in Berlin, Vienna, London, and Lille. He supported himself by teaching and occasional poems. Weddings and patriotic feasts commissioned much of that verse. His scoffing at religion made him many enemies. He lived in great poverty for most of his life. He translated plays and the prayer book between languages. The entry paints talent without stability or ease.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rothschild-davi:
David Rothschild was a German rabbi and author born at Hamm, Westphalia, on November 16, 1816. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He began as a preacher in his native town of Hamm.

In 1850 Rothschild was called as rabbi to Aachen, and in 1862 to Alzey. He stood with the Reform movement in German Judaism. His first book, from 1847, examines the oath of the Jews theologically. He published the Psalms with reflections and prayer, plus an Aachen prayer book. A late work, from 1877, defends the philosophy of Spinoza.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jaco:
Samuel ben Jacob ibn Jam' was rabbi of a North African community in the twelfth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He stood on intimate terms with Abraham ibn Ezra.

Ibn Ezra dedicated his Hai ben Mekiz to Samuel in friendship. He also praised Samuel's three sons, Judah, Moses, and Jacob, in the dedication. Samuel wrote a supplement to Nathan ben Jehiel's great dictionary, the Aruk. Extracts of it were printed from a Parma manuscript centuries later. Two Arabic works, on slaughtering law and on ethics, are credited to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schottlander-ju:
Frederick T. Haneman joined Isidore Singer to write this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Julius Schottländer. He was a German merchant. Schottländer was born at Münsterberg, in Silesia, on March 22, 1835. He set up there as a wool and grain merchant. In 1859 he moved his business to Breslau. From 1864 to 1869 he leased the Mittel mill from that city.

Schottländer supplied armies in two wars. He contracted for the sixth Prussian corps in 1866. He served the third German army in 1870 and 1871. Later he worked in milling, mining, cement, bricks, and sugar. He also dealt in real estate. In 1890 he retired to a large farm in Silesia. He gave largely to charities in Breslau and Münsterberg. He also spent much to beautify his home town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semalion-13410:
Semalion is a puzzling name found in a passage about the death of Moses. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Ancient commentators disagreed over whether the name meant a man or an angel. Modern scholars link it to a Greek word meaning giving a sign.

Rashi took Semalion for a scholar, while others made him an angel. Later sources name an angel Semalion who rules a month and a season of the sun. The entry also notes a Greek use as a title of Zeus. Short as it is, the piece shows how one unclear word drew centuries of debate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shaving-13510:
Shaving covers the Bible's rules and customs about cutting hair and beards. Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the topic. Mosaic law bars shaving the corners of head and beard. Priests get a special warning not to break that ban.

Ezekiel tells priests neither to shave bare nor let locks grow long. They should only poll, or clip, their heads neatly. The Talmud describes a costly layered cut worn by nobles. High priests had it done each Friday, and kings each day. Common folk shaved close, keeping only ear-locks and beard ends. The entry shows how hair marked rank, cost, and holiness in ancient Israel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-nethan:
Simeon ben Nethaneel was a tanna of the first generation, pupil of Johanan ben Zakkai. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He married into the family of Gamaliel the First. His own family was a noble priestly line.

His teacher praised Simeon for piety and fear of sin. Simeon taught that man's best habit is foresight. One should weigh the outcome of each deed carefully, he said. The worst practice to shun is failing to pay debts. No legal rulings by Simeon have been preserved at all. One sentence on prayer shows his deep piety clearly. Never neglect the Shema and daily prayer, he urged. Beg mercy in prayer, and let conscience accuse you of nothing. The entry keeps a moral teacher's voice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-smol-von-derenb:
Smol von Derenburch, or Samuel of Derenburg, was a court banker. Isidore Singer and Abraham Lewinsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He served the archbishops of Magdeburg in the fourteenth century. He died after October 5, 1382. Two brothers, Marquard and Ephraim, helped him in his deals.

Records show Smol acting for the archbishop in many matters. In 1365 he sat on a commission over a salt mine dispute. In 1366 his name stood on the archbishop's bond. Archbishop Peter gave Smol and his children special privileges in 1372. Pope Gregory XI rebuked that favor in a letter from Avignon. Smol had set up a synagogue in a former chapel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinberg-samue:
Samuel Steinberg was a Hungarian historian born at Güssing on December 16, 1857. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at Gratz, where he earned his doctorate in 1882. In 1895 he became a lecturer at the University of Vienna.

In 1901 Steinberg was appointed professor of history at the German University of Prague. He wrote essays for historical journals on many topics. His work focused most on the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries. In 1897 he published a book of German diplomatic reports. The short entry gives readers his career path and main field of study. It shows how Jewish scholars held posts at major universities of the time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-summons-14110:
A summons is a court order that calls a defendant to appear. Wilhelm Bacher and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. A court messenger carried the writ for the rabbis. Ignoring it counted as contempt of court. Village servers had to try at least three times.

Court sat on Mondays, Thursdays, and the Monday between. If the messenger missed the man, his wife could take the notice. A neighbor could receive it as well. A defendant who skipped three court days faced contempt. He then had thirty days to apologize. Failure meant excommunication by the court. The entry quotes a sample contempt order in full. Readers see how rabbinic courts enforced their authority in practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tallit-14210:
The tallit is the fringed prayer shawl of Jewish worship. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Men wear it over their clothes at prayer. Custom once limited it to married men. Modern practice adds boys after their bar mitzvah.

A tallit spreads out flat like a sheet. Weavers make it of wool or silk in white. Black or blue stripes mark its ends. Fringes called zizit hang from its four corners. Numbers commands those fringes in the Mosaic law. The pious prefer coarse wool from the Holy Land. Such a shawl is nicknamed the Turkish tallit. Russian wool runs finer and almost pure white. American silk mills at Paterson now supply most silk ones. The entry details a garment's cloth, bands, and making.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-temple-of-solom:
Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem, the first Temple, is the subject here. George A. Barton wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It follows the accounts in Kings and Chronicles. Solomon built for seven years, starting in his reign's fourth year.

David had bought the site and stored materials for the building. Hiram of Tyre sent skilled workmen and timber from Lebanon. The stone house stood sixty cubits long and was overlaid with gold. Its innermost room, the Holy of Holies, held two huge cherubim. Their wings met in the center and touched both walls. The article walks through the porch, side chambers, and courts in detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-titles-of-hebre:
Hebrew books are known by their titles, not their authors' names, this article notes. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Students cite Pene Yehoshua without knowing who wrote it. Bibliographers therefore list Hebrew books by title first.

Tradition credits the Great Assembly under Ezra with Bible titles. Torah, Prophets, and Writings named the three great parts. The five books of Moses later took their opening words as names. Bereshit, Shemot, and the rest came from first key words. Talmud sections took titles from their contents instead. Geonic works followed the same habit. Saadia's Book of Creeds and Opinions is one example.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trier-frederik-:
Frederik Jacob Trier was a Danish physician of high standing in Copenhagen. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born there in 1831, he died there in 1898. He took his medical degree in 1860. His essay on duodenal ulcer won early notice.

From 1861 he edited a leading medical weekly for thirteen years. He also co-edited a Nordic medical archive journal. His university named him professor in 1881.
