A patchwork layout changes how scientists picture energy production: output may depend on where the machines cluster, not just how many exist. That view matters when explaining why disturbed mitochondrial movement leads to disease.
plos-pone-0012010:
Hideo Matsumura and colleagues combined in 2010 a digital gene-counting method with next-generation sequencing to handle many samples at once. The base method, SuperSAGE, cuts a short tag from each gene message, and counting tags gives a digital readout of gene activity. Sequencing had become fast enough to count tags for whole sets of samples in one run.

Their high-throughput version keeps the counting honest while scaling up to multiple samples. Digital counts avoid some distortions of older analog measures of gene activity. For projects comparing many tissues, treatments, or patients, a scalable counting method is the difference between a pilot and a real study.
plos-pone-0012210:
Scott Heron, Bette Willis, William Skirving, and co-authors modeled coral disease outbreaks on the Great Barrier Reef in PLOS ONE in 2010. White syndrome, a tissue-destroying coral disease, has struck the reef in waves, and hot water stress was already suspected as a trigger. Their model added the other half of the year, asking how winter conditions set the stage for summer outbreaks.

Linking hot snaps with the cold season before them gives forecasters a longer lead time on outbreak years. Reef managers could then watch the most at-risk areas closely or cut other stresses, like pollution, ahead of a predicted outbreak. For a reef under climate pressure, advance warning is one of the few tools left.
plos-pone-0012310:
Jean-Philip Truman, Mónica García-Barros, Matthew Kaag, and co-authors studied how precise radiation treatment interacts with vessel-blocking therapy, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Combining anti-vessel drugs with radiation was a popular hope, yet trials had gained little, mostly because nobody knew exactly how vessel blockade changes radiation's effect. Their setting was radiosurgery, the tightly focused high-dose radiation used on small tumors.

They found the tumor's vessel lining must remodel its membranes for the anti-vessel drug to sensitize the tumor to radiation. A required step like this explains uneven trial results and tells doctors which tumors and timings should benefit. It turns a failed combination into a recipe with conditions attached.
plos-pone-0012410:
Marc Pearton, Sang-Moo Kang, Jae-Min Song and colleagues examined skin immune cells after a flu-like vaccine shot, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Langerhans cells sit in the skin and are first responders when a vaccine enters through it. How they change shape and move right after vaccination in human skin was largely unknown, a gap for teams designing needle-free skin vaccines.

Using human skin samples given virus-like particle vaccines, the team tracked early changes in these cells. The particles stirred the cells and set them moving, a good sign for skin delivery. The work gives vaccine designers concrete early readouts to compare delivery methods before large trials.
plos-pone-0012510:
Jianzhong Ma and Christopher Amos set out the math behind a key fix used in gene studies, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. When scientists hunt for genes tied to a disease, they compare large groups of people. If the groups differ in ancestry, that gap alone can fake a gene link. A method based on principal components, a way to sum up big data sets, is used to spot and remove that bias.

The authors give the firm math base for how the fix works and when it can be trusted. Gene hunts now use the method as a matter of course, so its limits matter a great deal. Their work helps study teams choose how strong a fix to apply, and when a weaker or stronger one is the right call.
plos-pone-0012610:
Loebig, Klement, Schmoller and co-authors tested a link between body weight and a growth factor called VEGF. VEGF helps blood vessels grow, and its blood level may shift with body mass. Their 2010 study used healthy young men of similar background to keep the test clean.

Each man went through a glucose clamp, a careful lab method that holds blood sugar steady while insulin response is measured. Even after that control, VEGF still tracked with body mass index. That points to a weight link that does not run through insulin alone, a clue for obesity research.
plos-pone-0012710:
Yu, Zeng, Xiong and co-authors warned that some epigenetic cancer drugs may also help cancer spread. Ezrin is a protein raised in many tumours, where it helps them invade new tissue. Their 2010 study asked whether drugs that change gene tags, used to wake silenced genes, also wake ezrin by mistake.

They found such drugs can raise ezrin through changes to its gene control region. A treatment that fights a tumour while feeding its spread would be a bad trade. The warning tells drug developers to screen for this side effect early.
plos-pone-0012810:
Yen, Le, Bansal and co-authors compared ways of measuring fat in the tiny worm C elegans. The worm is a stand-in for human obesity studies because its energy pathways match ours closely. Judging a worm's fat stores, though, needs methods that are exact and fair.

Their 2010 study ran dye-based methods, which stain fat, against label-free methods that need no stain. Stains can mislead, so a checked label-free option strengthens every obesity screen done in worms. The comparison gives labs a clear guide for measuring worm fat.
plos-pone-0341210:
Xiaocui Yuan and colleagues built an automated system that both finds defects in railway fasteners and measures their parts precisely. Fasteners hold rails in place, and worn or broken ones threaten train safety. Inspectors can spot defects with cameras, but careful measurement of each part still relies on slow hand work.

A 3D line laser scanner captures color images and matching depth maps of each fastener. One neural network spots defects and locates sound fasteners, while a second segments the parts so the system can compute block sizes, pad thickness, and bolt height. In tests the defect finder reached very high precision, pointing toward faster and more consistent track inspection.
plos-pone-0342410:
Sabine Pur, Stefan Huesig, and Christoph Schmidhammer trace how online lending marketplaces in three countries grew alike, in this 2026 PLOS ONE case study. These platforms match borrowers with lenders directly online. The authors followed the market leaders in Britain, the United States, and Germany from 2005 onward, comparing who they served and what they promised customers.

All three drifted toward the same shape: funding from institutions rather than small savers, aimed at underserved borrowers such as small firms and the self-employed. Regulation, technology, and institutional money drove the sameness. The authors turn the pattern into a general model of how platform business models standardise across borders.
plos-pone-0343610:
Ada R. Miltz and her team tested a chain of harm for people with HIV in the UK. The chain runs from slights in daily life to shame, then to lone days, then to low mood. They used a UK-wide survey from 2022 and 2023. It held more than twelve hundred straight men and women with HIV.

More than half felt shame about their state. Slights in health care fed that shame the most. Next came fear of public spots and slights from kin. Lone days were the top link to low mood. Cash strain hurt too, while grit helped. The chain fit the data well, the team says.
plos-pone-0345710:
Jorge Quiroga-Canaviri and colleagues argue that standard measures of output misjudge Latin American economies. Those measures ignore the limits of nature. They also ignore the slow loss of natural wealth. The team proposes a bioeconomy frame rooted in Andean and Amazonian thought. It joins an entropy-aware view of production with ancestral knowledge. Six countries were studied across three decades. Human development stood in for well-being.

The new model explained far more of the well-being pattern. It also surfaced a paradox. Saving the shared fund of ecosystems and cultures predicted higher well-being. Normal accounts book that saving as a pure cost. In these results, care for nature reads as an investment that pays in human development.
plos-pone-0345910:
Xia Li and Maho Niwa examined how the fat makeup of cell membranes affects stress control in yeast cells. They focused on the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell structure that folds proteins and must pass intact to new daughter cells. Their 2026 study changed membrane fat saturation in a controlled way and watched three linked safety systems.

Changing fat saturation affected whether the stressed reticulum was passed to daughter cells. Yet it affected the other two systems, which repair the reticulum and destroy bad proteins, in different ways. A fat signal also helped trigger the checkpoint that pauses cell division under stress. The findings suggest membrane fats help coordinate how cells protect this key structure during division.
plos-pone-0347210:
Zhichao Jiang, Xiaorun Wang, and Pengling Liu ask whether digital tools can raise the quality of farm goods that China sells abroad. Their 2026 study uses yearly data from thirty-four Chinese provincial regions covering more than two decades. They build an index of farm digital growth and track how it lines up with export quality over time.

Digital growth did go with better export quality, and the link held up under extra checks. The gains ran through faster farm technology, better trained workers, and smoother shipping. Effects were stronger in eastern regions, big grain areas, and places with more open markets. Government support and trade openness made the link stronger still.
plos-pone-0347410:
Long Zhou, Litao Zhu, and Faming Zhang ran pot experiments to free phosphorus locked in iron-rich red soils, where maize often starves despite fertiliser. They combined organic phosphorus with two helpers: phytase, an enzyme that releases phosphorus from plant residues, and bacteria that dissolve mineral phosphorus. The 2026 study measured plant growth, root shape, and how much phosphorus the maize actually absorbed.

The combination outperformed either addition alone, and the enzyme proved the stronger partner, raising phosphorus uptake by more than half in one comparison. Roots grew longer, thinner, and more branched where phosphorus flowed better. The authors offer the recipe as a sustainable way to farm phosphorus-poor red soils.
plos-pone-0347810:
Hyeonji Song, Yusik Lim, and Jaechul Lim describe a laboratory panel that can tell apart dozens of mouse cell types in one run, in this 2026 PLOS ONE methods paper. Flow cytometry sorts cells by fluorescent tags, but overlapping colours and scarce mouse-ready reagents have limited how much can be measured at once. Their panel uses twenty-seven colours across three lasers.

The panel resolves sixteen immune cell families plus several non-immune cell types, and it works across spleen, blood, gut, and other tissues. In a test inflammation model it tracked body-wide shifts in white blood cells and spotted a previously unnoticed cell subset. Such panels speed up immune research in mice.
plos-pone-0348110:
Yangyang Chen leads a team of eight reading ten thousand years of climate from a pillar of black soil in northeast China, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The Songnen Plain holds one of the world's three black soil belts, vital to national grain supply, yet how its rich layer formed is still debated. The team sliced a sediment profile and combined grain size fingerprinting, chemical weathering measures, and luminescence dating to build a dated history of the whole Holocene.

Five stages emerged. Dust piled up fast in the early Holocene, then a cooling spell arrived near the transition to the middle period, echoing a known global cold snap. The middle Holocene optimum, warm and humid, did the decisive work: weathering peaked and the black soil began in earnest. Late Holocene cold and dryness then slowed the process. The profile ties a farming treasure directly to an ancient climate window.
plos-pone-0348510:
Aboa Paul Koffi and co-authors carried out a huge hunt for yaws, a poverty-linked skin infection that mostly strikes children in the humid tropics, across fifteen districts of Côte d'Ivoire. The country is one of the few where yaws remains endemic, and planners needed its true extent before attempting eradication. Their 2026 campaign visited nearly four thousand villages and targeted close to half a million children in schools and homes.

About fifteen percent of examined children had skin lesions of some kind. Blood tests flagged two hundred ninety-one possible yaws cases, and a confirmatory test verified about half, mostly in children aged five to fourteen. Confirmed cases received a single antibiotic dose. Teams also catalogued other common skin conditions, giving health authorities a fuller map for the eradication push.
plos-pone-0348610:
Zhiqi Huang, Yizhang Jiang, and Kaijian Xia present a fuzzy logic classifier that learns from several views of the same data at once. Fuzzy systems sort items by degrees of belonging rather than hard lines, which suits messy real-world data. Their 2026 model lets each rule's center shift to fit the data and weighs rules by importance for each new sample.

Across five public datasets, from handwriting to brain signals, the model beat strong rivals at sorting accuracy. Removing either new part hurt results, and using both helped most. Brain signal sorting gained the most from the pairing. The design offers a clearer, more flexible way to classify when information arrives from mixed sources.
plos-pone-0349110:
Yingjie Kuang and co-workers train machine learning models to predict which leg vein clots confined to the calf will fail to clear. Such clots are common, and doctors lack good tools for judging their course. Their 2026 study gathers records for sixteen hundred patients, builds six competing models, and tests the best on patients the models never saw during training.

All six models sorted outcomes acceptably to strongly. A boosted-tree model won overall, pairing high accuracy with honest probability estimates. An explanation method then ranked which patient features drove its calls. A tool like this could help doctors decide who needs closer watching or longer treatment, and who can safely be left to heal.
plos-pone-0349310:
Jean-Marc Perone and colleagues mined data from a large cataract surgery trial to learn why eye pressure falls after the cloudy lens is removed, even in eyes without glaucoma. The drop is well known but unexplained, and knowing its drivers could sharpen glaucoma care. They tracked pressure at one, three, and twelve months, sorting eyes by starting pressure into high, middle, and low bands.

A wide set of eye measurements and surgical details was tested for what predicted the size of the drop at three months, in the whole group and each band. A literature review checked the regression approach against prior traps in this kind of analysis. Since cataract surgery is the world's most common operation, its pressure side effect is a therapeutic lever hiding in plain sight.
plos-pone-0349410:
Breast cancer that starts young tends to behave worse, and Le-Wei Zheng and colleagues searched tumor DNA for why, focusing on the hormone-sensitive luminal type. Their 2026 PLOS One study combined gene fusions, mutations, and missing DNA segments across many tumors.

One pairing stood out: a fused gene joining two partners, together with deletion of a gene called KDM6B, marked tumors with aggressive traits and shorter survival. Young patients' tumors also carried more fusions overall and distinct mutation patterns. The authors propose the pairing as a warning marker that could help doctors single out young patients needing closer watching and stronger treatment.
plos-pone-0349510:
Kaleab Fikre, Abeje Berhanu Kassegne, and Getnet Tadele interviewed forty one people in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia: cancer patients, family caregivers, and religious leaders. In depth talks explored how faith shapes what cancer means and what care people seek. Beliefs in Ethiopia had drawn little study despite their central place in daily life.

Illness was often read as divine or supernatural in origin: a punishment, a test of faith, Gods will, or spiritual attack. Views shifted over time with teaching, custom, and reflection. Faith brought comfort and strength while also steering treatment choices, sometimes toward prayer first. Clinicians who grasp those frames, the authors argue, can plan care patients will actually follow.
plos-pone-0349610:
Alba Roldan and colleagues examined how shaky movement affects learning in adults with severe cerebral palsy of the athetoid or ataxic types. Thirteen adults with the condition and eighteen without practiced motor tasks that taught through two channels: correcting errors and chasing rewards. Extra movement noise might open exploration, or it might drown the signals learning needs.

The cerebral palsy group moved far more variably, made larger absolute errors, and adjusted less precisely within tasks. Yet the two teaching channels were not equally blocked. Error-based practice produced substantial improvement after training, while reward-based learning lagged further behind. For therapists, the split is practical guidance: build drills around clear error feedback, where these learners demonstrably gain, rather than around reward signals their motor noise obscures.
plos-pone-0350010:
Xue Zhang, Xiaoya Ba, and Bo Li studied seven major cyberattacks that spread through supply chains, hitting sectors from retail and logistics to energy and health care. Attackers in these cases slipped in through trusted third-party connections instead of breaking front-door defenses. The team mapped how each attack entered, spread inside, and was eventually stopped.

Across the cases, four spread patterns kept recurring, including flattened networks that let intruders roam and alert overload that paralyzed defenders. Damage grew worst when systems were tightly linked and teams failed to coordinate. Recovery worked only where firms shared information early and were organized before the crisis, which the authors call synergy dependency.
plos-pone-0350110:
Marleen G A M van der Velde and co-authors introduced a new Dutch registry tracking urgent internal medicine care in 2026. The registry follows how hospitals handle urgent medical admissions, so units can compare themselves with a shared benchmark and find bottlenecks.

The report covers a single centre pilot at one teaching hospital, drawing records for more than six thousand emergency patients aged sixty-five and over between late 2019 and mid 2023. Data cover complaints, ward organisation, and measures like time in the emergency department. The pilot proves the dashboard works locally before national use, and shows the case mix such registries must handle.
plos-pone-0350510:
Chidozie Ezechukwu and colleagues interviewed the people charged with delivering Nigeria's new HPV vaccine in Kano, Kaduna, and Lagos states, asking what keeps the program from running steadily. The vaccine prevents cervical cancer, and Nigeria added it to the national schedule recently, but early rollout stumbled. Policymakers, immunization officers, agencies, community groups, and partners described the friction from their seats.

The analysis organizes the barriers by the machinery of delivery: how policy is implemented, how the program is financed, and how services reach girls in practice, with community-level obstacles woven through each. Interview studies like this cannot weigh the barriers, but they name them in the words of the people hitting them, which is where fixes start. Sustaining a vaccine program is a systems problem, and this is a systems map.
plos-pone-0350610:
Ika Saptarini and colleagues in Indonesia followed dengue patients through fever and early recovery in 2026, measuring immune signals in blood. Severe dengue often declares itself as fever fades, and doctors lack early warnings of who will worsen.

Paired blood samples from more than one hundred patients at five hospitals were tested for a set of messengers and complement parts. Two signals ran higher in the severe form during early recovery, while none separated the groups during fever. Links among the signals also shifted. Tracking how immune signals move, not just their level on day one, may sharpen dengue care.
plos-pone-0350810:
Medical students in Tunisia will soon treat people living with HIV, and Imen Mlouki and colleagues tested whether hands-on workshops can cut the stigma those patients face from health workers. Their 2026 PLOS One study covered all fifth-year students at the Monastir medical faculty across two academic years.

Two hundred sixteen students completed anonymous questionnaires before and after each workshop, using validated knowledge and stigma scales. Most already knew the facts about HIV well. The team measured how far attitudes moved after active sessions, and which student traits traveled with lingering stigma. Findings should help faculties design training that changes behavior, not just knowledge.
plos-pone-0350910:
Vivat Keawdounglek, Anuttara Hongthong, and Warapon Paenkhokuard built a community-run food safety system in Wiang Kaen District, a rural area of northern Thailand, and documented its first steps in 2026. Their mixed-method study surveyed 204 households, interviewed local stakeholders, and tested food from eight establishments for chemical and microbial contamination while residents co-designed the management approach.

Testing found contamination generally low, though pesticide traces turned up in garlic bought from outside markets, beyond local control. Food safety knowledge varied with gender, age, and rice growing. The process's concrete product was a standing Community Food Safety Committee linking households, vendors, and officials. The authors present the model as a workable template for rural districts with informal food systems.
plos-pone-0351110:
Jaya Kshatri and colleagues lay out a planned trial of joined-up primary care for older adults in urban India. The patients live with several chronic diseases at once, plus growing frailty. Indian primary care still tends to treat one disease per visit. Ten public health centers in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, will take part. Whole clinics will be assigned by lot. Half will give a monthly package of combined care. Half will give standard care as usual.

The trial will judge health-related quality of life and well-being. It is built from parts a public system could truly staff and fund. As a protocol, it reports no results. If the package works, its design is the point. It shows other cities a model that does not depend on private money or rare specialists.
plos-pone-0351210:
Olanrewaju Onigbogi and four co-authors study how depression drugs link body weight and smoking in American adults. They used a 2023 national health survey. Their model asked whether taking drugs for depression helps explain smoking habits. They compared adults who were underweight, normal weight, overweight, or obese.

Use of depression drugs played the largest connecting role in underweight adults. It played the smallest role in obese adults. Underweight adults on such drugs were more likely to smoke than obese adults were. Obese adults on the drugs also showed raised odds of smoking, compared with underweight peers. The authors say weight group should be part of the picture. Clinicians should weigh it when they design quit-smoking support for people treated for depression.
plos-pone-0351310:
Jingjing Ma refines how forecasters combine predictions about a country's energy mix. The 2026 study works with compositional data: shares of coal, oil, gas, and renewables that must sum to a whole. Single forecasting models shine at different times. Combining them helps, but only if the weights adapt. Ma proposes an aggregation method built on an ordered weighting operator, informed by each model's recent accuracy. A genetic algorithm searches for the weight set that minimises error against the real series.

Two combination schemes resulted: one with time-varying weights, one built on the new operator. Both were tested on China's primary energy production structure. The varying-weight model beat the benchmark on prediction accuracy. Energy planners live and die by share forecasts: grid investment, import contracts, and carbon budgets all hang on them. A demonstrably better way to blend rival forecasts is a quiet but consequential upgrade.
plos-pone-0351410:
American law reviews are edited by students who must pick a few articles from thousands, and they lean on the author's school as a quality shortcut. Chad M Topaz simulated that market with a computer model, in this 2026 PLOS One study, and compared it with centralized matching like the system placing medical residents.

More than sixty percent of top placements differed from what quality-based matching would give, and article quality lined up only loosely with journal rank. Partial fixes such as longer deadlines barely helped; the scattered structure itself caused the waste. The model also shows prestige bias persists even between equally strong articles, an inequity built into the system.
plos-pone-0351510:
Brittany Lee Vermeulen and three colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS One case study on short online courses, called microcredentials, inside university teaching. The setting was a large undergraduate science subject in 2024, where students also completed a brief sustainability course on thinking, caring, and acting. The authors focused on a smaller group of students and studied their final reflective writing.

Reading those reflections, the team found students understood sustainability more deeply, rethought daily habits, and saw their future science careers differently. Engagement with the self-paced course varied widely, as the authors expected. They offer the case as a workable model for universities that want to build sustainability literacy into existing subjects rather than adding whole new courses.
plos-pone-0351610:
Editorial Note: PLOS One corrects a greenhouse tomato study after data from another institution was included by mistake. This 2026 note replaces the wrong figure and fixes sentences describing the test of micro-fog systems, which cool greenhouse air by spraying fine mist during summer heat.

The corrected values describe midday conditions with and without fog: the fogged section ran cooler and far more humid, with much lower dryness stress on the plants. The original paper argued the gentler air improved leaf photosynthesis, growth, and yield. Readers should rely on the corrected figure and numbers given here rather than those first printed.
plos-pone-0352110:
Yu Zhao and six colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One nationwide study of colorectal cancer deaths in China's cancer registration areas from 2005 to 2018, with forecasts to 2035. The team combined trend analysis, an age-period-cohort model, and spatial statistics to separate the roles of aging, calendar time, and birth generation, and to locate high-risk regions.

Mortality rose, then fell significantly for several years, then flattened into a slight rise, with urban rates falling over the later years while rural rates crept up. Risk grew steeply with age, and hotspots concentrated in eastern coastal and northeastern provinces. The forecast shows a slow upward drift ahead. The authors offer the patterns as a basis for targeting screening and prevention where deaths cluster.
plos-pone-0352310:
Mengxuan Liu and five colleagues search public gene data for shared sparks between sepsis and diabetes. Their 2026 bioinformatics study concerns pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death that bursts cells open. Both diseases kill many people, and they worsen each other in practice. Two gene expression datasets supplied the raw material. The team filtered for genes that change in both conditions and belong to the pyroptosis machinery. Network and pathway tools then mapped their neighbourhoods.

Seven genes survived the sieve. Most specialise in killing cells or sounding immune alarms. Their pathways centred on cell bursting and an inflammatory signal family. A separate enrichment pass flagged another immune signalling route. Immune cell mixtures in blood correlated with the genes' activity too. None of this treats a patient yet. It nominates molecular markers where two major diseases overlap, giving laboratory researchers concrete suspects for the crosstalk clinicians see at the bedside.
plos-pone-0352810:
Josheil Boparai and seven colleagues test a simple fix for weak concussion teaching in medical school. Their 2026 study starts from a known gap. Concussion barely appears in undergraduate medical curricula. Poor knowledge then follows graduates into clinical practice. Students first completed a knowledge survey. Next came a single didactic lecture on concussion.

Knowledge scores jumped sharply right after the lecture. Students were surveyed again within two days. A final survey came two weeks later. Scores at two weeks matched the immediate scores, showing the learning had stuck. No extra teaching happened in between. One focused lecture, the authors argue, earns its place in a crowded curriculum. Better-trained graduates should then recognise and manage concussion more safely in real patients.
plos-pone-0353010:
Faith Logan and six colleagues published this 2026 protocol for a pilot trial helping teenagers who live with chronic muscle and joint pain stay active. Many such teens avoid movement for fear of hurting more, which can seed lifelong pain. Their program, called PREP-Y, builds confidence and motivation alongside activity for forty adolescents at a children's hospital in Ohio.

Surveys, activity measures, and pain scales will track functioning, fear of movement, and resilience. As a protocol, the study promises no results yet; Logan's team designed it to shape a later full trial.
plos-pone-0353110:
Amr Sobhy led a team of six authors on this 2026 randomized trial of pain control for young children having penis repair surgery. Thirty children aged one to five received either the standard caudal epidural block or a newer ultrasound-guided block near the sacrum, both using the same local anesthetic. Nurses recorded how long relief lasted and how much rescue medicine was needed.

Children with the newer block waited longer before needing extra pain relief and needed less of it, with similar safety and body readings. Sobhy suggests the technique as a dependable alternative for this surgery.
plos-pone-0353610:
Toqeer Ali Syed and four colleagues propose giving city infrastructure a self-managing digital twin, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. A digital twin mirrors bridges, roads, and water systems in software, fed by live sensors. Their design adds artificial intelligence agents that perceive problems, plan responses, and act through official city systems, while a permissioned blockchain seals every observation, approval, and action against tampering.

Eighteen thousand simulated incidents tested the framework across five designs and three difficulty levels. The paper characterises how the system behaves under stress rather than proving it in a real city. The stakes are accountability: when software orders a road closure or repair, someone must be able to audit why.
plos-pone-0354510:
Sabrina Al Bukhari and colleagues built a closed-loop pain therapy in which brainwaves drive a virtual reality healer. Their 2026 study trained lightweight machine learning classifiers on an open dataset where volunteers rated laser-induced pain. One-second slices of scalp signals became an eleven-step pain scale. The live prediction was then piped into a game engine, where a digital avatar responds with tailored therapy.

The best classifier sorted pain levels with accuracy in the high nineties in cross-validation. It beat comparable published systems. The avatar reacted in real time across slight, moderate, and severe bands. Nothing here treated a real patient yet; the work proves the loop runs. Drug-free, self-adjusting pain care is the stated destination.
plos-pone-0354610:
Fahimeh Alsadat Hosseini and three colleagues published this 2026 trial of positive psychotherapy delivered through virtual reality to people with major depression. Seventy-eight patients were split between headset sessions and the same therapy face to face, three sessions each. Mood, life satisfaction, and suicidal thoughts were measured around every session, followed by interviews.

Both formats improved emotions, satisfaction, and suicidal thinking by similar amounts, and patients found the headset version workable. Hosseini calls the trial preliminary and asks for larger groups and longer follow-up before clinics adopt virtual delivery.
plos-pone-0354710:
Michael Getie led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of bloodstream infections at a public health institute in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia. Four full years of blood culture records, from 2020 through 2023, were reviewed to see which bacteria grew and which antibiotics still worked reliably, using standard lab methods.

Half the suspected cases grew true pathogens, dominated by hard-to-treat Gram-negative and notorious hospital bacteria, hitting males, newborns, and young adults hardest. Getie calls for immediate antibiotic stewardship, refreshed treatment guidelines, and stronger lab testing to track resistance.
plos-pone-0354810:
Yüksel Peker led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study linking a mixed sleep disorder to heart and blood vessel disease in Türkiye. The condition, called COMISA, pairs insomnia with sleep apnea. Drawing on a national sleep registry of nearly thirteen thousand adults sent for sleep testing, they compared four sleep groups.

The mixed disorder appeared more often in patients who had cardiovascular disease than in those without it, even after adjusting for many other factors. The link was modest, though. Peker treats COMISA as a distinct, burden-heavy pattern shaped by both body and behavior.
plos-pone-0354910:
Ziyang Luo led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of the HIV strain dominant in Ningxia, China. They analyzed just over two hundred local virus sequences of the CRF01_AE recombinant to trace where it travels and who drives its spread. The strain is known for faster disease progression.

Spread radiated strongly from the capital, Yinchuan, toward other cities, carried mainly by people in their twenties and thirties. Transmission remains above the level where the epidemic shrinks, while the virus's mutation pace stays steady. Luo urges prevention aimed at this strain's actual hubs and groups.
plos-pone-0355210:
Tonya Campbell led a team of eight authors charting deaths tied to benzodiazepines in Ontario, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. These sedative drugs are widely prescribed, and deaths involving their toxicity have been rising. The team ran a descriptive cross-sectional study of trends and patterns in those deaths.

Campbell's data give coroners and policymakers a clear picture of who is dying and how. Patterns by age, setting, and drug combinations point to where prevention can work, from prescribing rules to safer supply debates. Benzodiazepine deaths often hide inside wider drug toxicity figures, mixed with opioids. Separating them out, as this study does, is the first step toward policies aimed at the right problem.
plos-pone-0355410:
Rownak Jahan and colleagues check in 2026 whether fresh fruit skins in their study area carry a gut bacterium that can cause severe infection and resist many drugs. Washed samples from seven fruit types were cultured and tested for the bacterium, its harm related genes, its ability to form slimy layers, and its drug resistance.

More than three in five samples carried the bacterium, most often on oranges. Resistance was high to several common drugs and worrying even for last resort drugs, and most isolates resisted many drugs at once. Harm genes and slime forming were common. Thorough washing and wider monitoring are urged.
plos-pone-0355710:
Theres Mühlberg and three colleagues build a classroom observation tool for identifying which teaching principles a teacher is actually using, in this 2026 German study. Many observation instruments exist, but few are valid, reliable, subject-independent, and rooted in constructivist ideas about learning rather than simple evaluation. The team developed their protocol, called OPTIS, from a comparative review of teaching principles and refined it through expert rounds.

Piloting used both video-recorded lessons and live observation. Two independent observers reached almost perfect agreement with each other, and each stayed consistent over time, as measured by a chance-corrected agreement statistic suited to the data. Expert review supported the tool's foundations and its power to predict what it aims to capture. The authors present OPTIS as a psychometrically sound lens for researchers and school developers studying teaching quality across subjects.
plos-pone-0356910:
Xiaoxia Jia and colleagues model how city firms might cooperate to cut waste when the costs of doing so can be shared. Cities need industry to shrink its waste stream, but each firm weighs its own costs and gains. The study first maps material flows and life cycle impacts. That finds the nodes where cuts matter most. Then it runs a game model in software. Firms linked in a network copy or abandon cooperative moves over time.

Moderate penalties and positive spillovers between neighbors encouraged cooperation most reliably. Cost sharing and fair benefit splits also helped, but only within sensible ranges, and effects shifted with network size. Jia and colleagues advise cities to tune incentives to the local business network rather than copy one national recipe.
plos-pone-0357010:
María Carmen Martínez-González leads a team of eight testing whether needling a deep calf muscle changes how the foot bears weight, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The tibialis posterior, buried behind the shin, steers the arch when walking, and hidden trigger points in it may distort foot loading. Eighty-two adults with such trigger points were assigned to real deep dry needling or a simulated version, with foot pressure measured on a walking platform before treatment and at three points afterward.

Right after needling, pressure under the heel rose in the treated group. A day later, average pressure rose while contact areas shifted, including less forefoot contact. By seventy-two hours, every difference from baseline had vanished. The authors conclude a single session rearranges foot loading only briefly, which matters for clinicians deciding whether the technique can support longer term gait correction plans.
plos-pone-0357110:
Sarah Al-Rihaymee leads a systematic review of whether a little-studied mouth bacterium belongs on the list of gum disease suspects. Known gum pathogens do not fully explain why disease severity varies so much between people. The review gathered observational studies in healthy adults that compared the bacterium's presence in people with gum disease against people with healthy gums, in spit or in plaque below the gumline.

Across eight studies from three continents, the bacterium turned up more often, and in larger shares, in disease than in health, with enrichment clearest in advanced stages. The authors rate the certainty as low, since most studies were snapshots rather than follow-ups. Al-Rihaymee and colleagues call for stronger designs before the bacterium earns a firm causal label.
plos-pone-0357310:
Weirui Zhang and three colleagues studied what Chinese school textbooks teach about the nature of science, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. They read senior secondary geography textbooks in light of sustainable development, a theme the books are meant to carry. Textbooks shape whether students see science as fixed facts or as inquiry.

Zhang's team identified gaps between what the books claim about science and how they present it. They also pointed to reforms that would show science as argument and testing, not just lists to memorize. In a country teaching millions of students, textbook wording matters at huge scale. Better books can shape how a generation judges evidence on climate and resources.
plos-pone-0357410:
Rena Hidaka and fellow researchers pilot a monthly program in Tokyo that teaches children about mouths, chewing, and food at community cafeterias. These cafeterias serve local families, and the team added a chewy meal plus a short talk on teeth and balanced eating. About fifty children and thirty parents joined six sessions, answering surveys before and after the program.

Children looked inside their own mouths more often and used fluoride more after the program. Fewer children said they ignored balanced eating, and parents reported serving more meat, dairy, and root vegetables at home. Because there was no comparison group, Hidaka and colleagues treat the gains as promising early signs and call for a fuller trial to confirm them.
plos-pone-0357910:
Atefeh Allahbakhshian and three colleagues traced how uncertainty affects heart patients' lives, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. People with coronary artery disease live with gnawing doubt about their future. The team ran a pathway analysis linking quality of life in these patients to their coping strategies, perceived stress, and illness uncertainty.

Allahbakhshian's pathways reveal where support could break the chain from uncertainty to poor quality of life. If coping strategies carry much of the effect, teaching better coping becomes a concrete intervention. Cardiac care often stops at the artery; this work insists the mind's burden is part of the disease. Nurses and counselors gain a map of which link to strengthen first for each patient.
plos-pone-0359210: Aujla and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on gene copy changes in a national Canadian data bank. HostSeq holds genetic data from people across Canada. The team charted the full spectrum of copy number variation, places where chunks of DNA are missing or repeated. Such a spectrum gives doctors a baseline: which changes are common and harmless, and which stand out in disease.
plos-pone-0359310:
Jie Wang and co-authors set out a protocol in 2026 for comparing three sets of criteria used to classify antiphospholipid syndrome. This autoimmune condition makes blood more likely to clot and complicates pregnancies, and classifying it consistently is essential for research. The planned study is a systematic review with network meta-analysis, a method for comparing several options across many studies at once.

The criteria under comparison are the Sapporo criteria, their revised version, and the newer 2023 criteria from two major rheumatology bodies. The protocol fixes the questions and methods in advance, so the eventual results can be judged against a public plan. Which set performs best shapes who counts as a patient in every future trial of this disease.
plos-pone-0359810:
Kulthoom Qureish and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about dengue fever in Kenya. It tests vector competence, whether mosquitoes can pick up and pass on dengue-2 virus. The mosquitoes are Aedes aegypti sampled at selected sites in Lamu County, split into groups resistant or susceptible to the insecticide permethrin.

Comparing the two groups matters because spraying programs assume resistance only affects survival, not virus spread. If resistant mosquitoes also differ in how well they carry dengue, control plans need rethinking. Malaria and dengue control teams in coastal Kenya are the readers who must weigh insecticide choices against disease transmission.
pmc-10653410:
Salleh and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-three translating an implementation survey into Malay. Programs need measures of whether communities accept and can use them. Malaysia lacked such tools in its national language. The team translate and adapt a three-part outcome questionnaire. Two samples, of one hundred seventy and two hundred thirty-five people, test it. The Malay version settles into one factor with seven items. Content checks and reliability scores run strong.

The single scale fits the data well by standard indices. All items load cleanly on the one factor. The authors back it for community program evaluation. Dialect variety across states merits more testing, they note.
pmc-10654810:
An EFSA expert panel assessed a food enzyme called catalase in 2023. The enzyme comes from a fungus strain. That strain was not genetically modified. Food use requires a safety verdict first. Production and exposure were examined closely. Allergen matching was also performed.

One match with known allergens was found. Allergy risk could not be fully excluded. Likelihood was judged low, though. Genotoxicity results raised unresolved questions. Absence of living production cells was unproven. Safety could therefore not be established. The panel withheld a clean verdict. More data would be needed.
pmc-10655310:
Dazhi Fu and co-authors map the father-line genetics of the Hui people in Liaoning Province, China, in a 2023 paper. The Hui are China's second-largest ethnic minority, spread across the whole country, yet earlier work on their paternal lines had skipped Liaoning. The team typed 282 unrelated Hui men at two sets of markers on the Y chromosome, the piece of DNA passed from father to son.

The men's lineages proved highly varied, sorting into 46 branch groups. Comparing marker patterns with other regions split China's Hui into three broad clusters. The Liaoning Hui grouped with those of the northwest, apart from groups in the southwest and in two other provinces. Measured against other Chinese peoples, the Hui showed the closest kinship with the Han, the majority group. The authors offer the data for both population history and forensic work, where such marker profiles help identify people.
pmc-10669010:
Alexandra Louise Møller and co-authors test whether pairing two drug classes lowers a scarring signal in people with type 2 diabetes, in a study from 2023. The signal, endotrophin, reflects the building of a stiff collagen type and marks risk for kidney decline. It was measured in blood from nearly three hundred patients in a kidney-focused project.

Among all blood markers tested, this signal best predicted later kidney function loss. Patients on both drug classes together showed a clear drop in the signal, compared with one class alone. Higher starting levels of the signal also meant higher risk of kidney decline. The authors suggest the paired treatment may slow kidney damage, with the signal as a way to watch it.
pmc-10669310:
Horațiu Roman, Adelina-Gabriela Niculescu, Veronica Lazăr, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It tests tansy essential oil against the ESKAPE gang, the hospital superbugs most notorious for dodging antibiotics, and checks whether the oil makes standard drugs hit harder.

Drug-resistant infections are among medicine's worst problems, and multi-target plant compounds are promising allies. The team distilled the oil and charted its chemistry by gas chromatography. Its main components include thujones, eucalyptol, camphor, and germacrene. Standard disk and dilution tests measured killing power against resistant Gram-positive and Gram-negative strains on the ESKAPE list. The authors tied activity back to the isolated compounds. Pairing the oil with antibiotics showed synergy in the study's framing. The paper builds the case for tansy as an adjunct worth developing, not a folk remedy to shrug off.
pmc-10687210:
Kangjie Li, Jielian Deng, and four colleagues untangle a confound in HIV research, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-three. Gut microbe changes blamed on the virus may partly belong to the study population instead. Many HIV gut studies enroll men who have sex with men, whose microbiomes differ from other men's even without infection.

The team gathered the published changes linked to HIV and to this population separately, using databases of microbe genes and metabolites. They then asked, with bioinformatics and single-cell data, what the population-linked changes do to immune balance. Their synthesis argues that dysbiosis tied to this group can itself disturb immune homeostasis and raise HIV infection risk. That reframes a literature: some effects credited to the virus may precede it. Untangling cause, consequence, and coincidence is essential before microbiome therapies for HIV can be designed honestly.
pmc-10692110:
A team of researchers maps the microbes living in the bladders of baby boys in a paper from 2023. Doctors once thought urine held no germs, but the bladder hosts a small community now called the urobiome. Samples were taken with a thin tube during care, so they stayed clean. The team used both lab growth and gene reading to name the microbes present.

Many microbe types appeared in all samples, which points to a shared early pattern. Birth type and past antibiotic use did not change the mix. The team also grew nine strains of one germ linked to infections in older men. Their gene maps add a base for later health studies.
pmc-10693410:
Wang, Chen, Deng, and Jiang study second cancers after prostate radiotherapy in work from twenty twenty-three. Radiation can cure prostate cancer, but it may raise the later risk of new cancers in the pelvis, such as bladder or rectal cancer.

The team used a large United States cancer database that spans decades. They picked men whose first cancer was prostate cancer treated in the pelvis region. Standard risk models weighed the chance of a second pelvic cancer against other causes of death. A hospital group in Nanchang gave an outside check. Knowing who faces the most risk can guide long term checks after treatment.
pmc-10697810:
Oscar Delaney, Andrew Letten, and Jan Engelstädter rethink a lab staple: growing microbes in cycles, each time keeping only a small share to seed the next round. Tight cuts risk losing good new mutants, while long growth rounds force tight cuts. The standard daily cycle with a harsh cut has little theory behind it, the authors say.

Their math flips the usual answer. Measured per hour of experiment, not per round, adaptation runs fastest with very frequent, very gentle cuts, near steady growth in the limit. Adding food limits and rival mutants did not change the verdict. They suggest robots or steady-flow vessels to put the idea to work.
pmc-10698910:
Bigirinama and co-authors probe how lead works at ward tier in long-crisis Congo. Care webs in low and mid lands strain to give good care to all. Lead aids web grace and true change in past tales. Yet lead in the Congo had thin print till this work. Eight farm health zones in east Congo ground the work. Facts came in 2021 by deep talks and plain watch runs.

Key health hands in each zone gave the talk facts. Six lead themes frame the hunt in a bent set form. That form stems from a known lead frame in the text. Talks span how lead is lived and seen by zone hands. Watch runs add what talks can't catch in the zones. The work is one-cut and word-based in its build.
pmc-10699410:
Vicky Chang leads an eleven-author team testing whether a common herbicide damages farmers' chromosomes, in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. Glyphosate is the world's most used herbicide and is suspected in some blood cancers. Human evidence for its genotoxicity was scarce.

The marker studied is mosaic loss of chromosome Y in blood cells, a measurable sign of genomic damage. DNA came from 1,606 farmers aged fifty and over in an agricultural health cohort. Lifetime glyphosate use was reconstructed from self-reported spraying histories. Men who spray more can be compared for Y loss rates. Such biomarker studies probe possible mechanisms long before cancer counts could settle the question either way.
pmc-10699610:
Yakup Yildirim and Yeşim Yilmaz gather teacher views on fostering creativity in preschool. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, works in Alanya, Turkey. Twenty-five working preschool teachers and twenty-five trainees took part. All answered open-ended questions about the current preschool program.

Both groups prize creative thought that lets a child express feelings well. Problem solving and cause-and-effect thinking also rank high. A fresh viewpoint on events rounds out the valued traits. For growing creativity, trips out of class lead the suggestions. Art, drama, science, and math activities follow close behind. The findings can steer teacher training.
pmc-10700210:
Lucia Brodosi and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-three, the risk of binge eating disorder in patients with fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction. Few data link the liver disease to eating disorders. The team assessed one hundred twenty-nine patients sent by general doctors to a hospital metabolic unit. Most had obesity, with a mean body mass index in the mid-thirties. A standard binge eating scale scored risk: mid scores meant possible disorder, high scores meant probable disorder. Liver fat and scarring were checked with blood markers and scans.

About eighteen percent scored as possible cases and about eight percent as probable cases. Those rates did not link to sex, obesity class, diabetes, liver fat, or scarring. Daily calorie intake did link to possible cases.
pmc-10700610:
Jun Suzuki and fourteen co-authors present a 2023 study of a fat handling protein and noise caused hearing loss in mice. The protein helps cells take in and move fatty acids in the nervous system. Whether it shapes the ear's response to loud noise was unknown.

The team bred mice that lack the protein and compared their hearing with normal mice. Hearing was tested before noise, a day after a loud blast, and two weeks later. At the start, the groups heard alike. After noise, the mice without the protein kept lower hearing thresholds and more of their sound sensing cells survived. Gene and chemical readouts from the inner ear filled in the picture.
pmc-10702410:
Winter Roth, David Dadiomov, and Michelle Chu audit off-label antipsychotic use at a large teaching hospital. Their review from twenty twenty-three covers one year of quetiapine dispensing. The drug is often prescribed outside psychiatry at low doses. Side effects include weight gain, blood sugar rises, and falls.

A safe-use protocol was drafted from labels and guidelines first. Every dispensed strength over the year entered the review. Charts were then checked against the protocol criteria. Inappropriate uses were counted and their harms costed. The audit tests whether a stewardship programme is needed. Antipsychotic stewardship mirrors antibiotic stewardship logic. Hospitals can target the commonest misuse patterns found.
pmc-10707010:
Emanuele Piccinno and co-authors track a small RNA that controls cell joining in colorectal cancer, in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. Desmosomes are the rivets that hold surface cells together, and they fall apart as this cancer turns disordered. The team focused on miR-195-5p, a tiny RNA that tunes gene use, and on JUP, a gene that codes for a rivet part called gamma-catenin.

Restoring the small RNA in colon cells lowered JUP output and shifted two partner proteins of the rivet system. It also changed key parts of the Wnt signal path, which drives growth in this cancer. The work names a fresh control route over cell adhesion in the gut lining. The authors suggest the small RNA could one day serve as a base for treatment.
pmc-10708410:
Patrizia Picerno and a large team of co-authors turn almond skins into a health extract, in a paper dated twenty twenty-three. Sicilian almond peels, a food industry waste, are rich in plant compounds that fight free radicals. The team made a dry water extract and coated it with a natural polymer.

Tests showed strong antioxidant action and a clear block on nitric oxide. The extract also curbed an enzyme that breaks down tissue and slowed sugar damage. The coating helped the powder dissolve and release better. A food supplement with added health value came out of the work.
pmc-10709610:
Maristella Canovai and ten colleagues showed that resistant prostate cancer cells can export their drug resistance to neighbors. Docetaxel failure is a main reason metastatic prostate cancer treatment collapses. The team found that resistant cell clones release three specific microRNAs into their surroundings. When other cancer cells take up these molecules, the chemotherapy works less well on them too. The twenty twenty-three study traced this sharing mechanism in cell experiments.

Computer analysis and lab tests identified genes the microRNAs suppress, including FOXO1 and PDCD4. Two further genes, PPP2CB and INSIG1, carried much of the resistance effect. Tiny vesicles called exosomes ferried the microRNAs between cells. Blocking this traffic could be a future strategy for keeping docetaxel effective longer in advanced prostate cancer.
pmc-10709910:
Novika Purnama Sari and co-authors published this study in 2023 on autistic traits in mothers and children. Past work showed the two run together in families. The team asked whether a mother's weight before pregnancy changes that link. They drew on two cohorts: a Dutch one with 4,659 members and a Cambridge one with 179. Traits were scored in mothers and in children from toddler age to the early teens.

Higher traits in mothers went with higher traits in children at every age checked. Higher pre-pregnancy weight also tied to higher child traits in the Dutch cohort. But weight did not change the strength of the mother-child link in either cohort. Children of underweight and overweight mothers scored higher than those of healthy-weight mothers. The authors say the family link stands on its own, and the brain paths behind it still need work.
pmc-10710310:
Ann-Elin Synnes and co-authors compared fish communities under different protection regimes in Norway in two thousand twenty-three. When top predators vanish, mid-level predators can multiply and reshape the food web, an effect called mesopredator release. Cod is a likely top predator in these coastal waters.

They sampled fish with fyke nets over three seasons in national park waters open to fishing and in a nearby seascape with protected zones. Cod in the protected seascape were much larger on average. Open waters held more mesopredator fish. The pattern fits the release hypothesis: protecting top predators helps them control mid-level fish. The authors link today's coastal fish state to long fishing pressure on large predators.
pmc-10711910:
Daniel Freeman leads a large team presenting the protocol for the Phoenix trial of automated virtual reality therapy, in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Young people with psychosis often have low confidence and heavy negative self-beliefs. Many pull back from day-to-day life. And a lack of therapists means few of them get psychological help at all.

The therapy was built with young people who have lived experience of psychosis. A virtual coach inside VR gives the treatment. Staff help the user, in place of a full therapist. The randomized controlled trial will test if it lifts positive self-beliefs and psychological wellbeing. This protocol paper sets the design out in advance. If it works, automated VR could widen access to therapy that builds confidence, and by a lot.
pmc-10712110:
Dalia H El-Kashef and Mona Abdel Rahim tested whether an allergy drug can protect rat lungs from a harsh cancer drug, in a study published in 2023. The cancer drug is used worldwide but can badly damage the lungs. The allergy drug is known to calm swelling and allergic responses, which made it a candidate shield.

Rats given the cancer drug alone showed clear lung harm: more swelling signals, more damage markers, and worse tissue under the microscope. Rats that also received the allergy drug for two weeks, starting a week before, showed much less of each harm. The authors credit the drug's mix of calming, protective, and anti-scarring effects. The work is early, animal-only evidence, but it points to a possible guard for patients who need the cancer drug.
pmc-10716410:
Cezary Grunwald and twelve co-authors published a 2023 case-control study of an immune gene variant and multiple sclerosis risk in Poland. Earlier work on the IL-13 variant rs20541 and MS had clashed. The team genotyped 94 relapsing-remitting MS patients and 160 healthy volunteers. One allele, A, and the genotypes carrying it appeared significantly more often in patients.

Carrying A raised the odds of MS by about 1.7 times per allele. The variant showed no link, though, to age at onset or disability scores. The authors conclude the variant may predispose Poles to MS without shaping its course. They frame the result as one piece of the disease's genetic puzzle, needing replication in larger cohorts.
pmc-10716810:
Longwu Wang and co-authors present a 2023 study on why cuckoos remove host eggs from nests they parasitize. Cuckoos lay their eggs in other birds' nests and let the hosts raise the chicks. A female cuckoo usually removes one or two host eggs as she lays, and the benefit of that habit has long been debated.

One idea says biting an egg speeds up her laying, shrinking the time she is exposed to host attack. The team timed common cuckoos laying in empty nests, nests with host eggs, and nests with blue stick models. Biting an egg or a stick cut laying time by about thirty-seven percent. This is the first direct experimental support for the speed hypothesis.
pmc-10717810:
Majid Mokhtari, Samane Khoshbakht, Mohammad Esmaeil Akbari, and Sayyed Sajjad Moravveji published a precision medicine study in twenty twenty-three presenting a protocol that picks drug combinations patient by patient. Cancer drug screening for individuals is slow and costly. Their bioinformatics system instead reads each patient's disturbed gene pattern like a fingerprint and matches drugs against it.

Data covered over six thousand breast cancer patients, healthy controls, and nearly seven hundred drugs. Combinations mixing cancer and non-cancer drugs outperformed cancer-only sets in their analysis, a win for drug repurposing. Every patient's perturbed pattern proved unique. The protocol is offered as the front end for laboratory platforms that validate personalized combinations before treatment.
pmc-10720010:
Muhammad Ali and co-authors test a common blue dye as a tool to free trapped oil from sandstone in Pakistan, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Much oil stays stuck after standard recovery, and rock soaked in organic acids repels water. The team aged rock samples in acid, then soaked them in dye solutions.

Heat, pressure, and salt all pushed the rock toward oil-loving behavior. Dye soaks flipped the rock back toward water-loving, which favors oil release. The strongest dye bath gave the biggest flip. Since the dye is a waste product in huge amounts, the authors pitch it as a cheap recovery aid.
pmc-10720210:
Sengo and six co-authors study eye strain from screens in Mozambique, in work from twenty twenty-three. Computer vision syndrome is a set of eye and vision problems tied to screen use. Screen use surged for students and teachers during the pandemic.

The team surveyed students and teachers at a university in Nampula in late twenty twenty and early twenty twenty-one. They used a tested eye strain survey plus questions on desk setup and habits. More than three in four people met the mark for the syndrome in their results. Odds tests linked risk to certain work conditions. The study gives local proof for eye health steps in schools.
pmc-10730010:
Ruszkowski and Pfrommer give a teaching-style review of cosmic rays in galaxies and galaxy clusters. Knowing what shapes galaxy growth is a core problem in astrophysics. Recent work suggests cosmic rays, fast charged particles, may play a far larger role than once thought in that story.

Cosmic rays cool slowly and couple strongly to gas, so their pressure can rival heat, magnetic, and turbulent pressure in interstellar space. They can drive large galactic winds that reshape whole systems. The review covers how cosmic rays are sped up, how they travel, what telescopes see, and how they push back on galaxy growth.
pmc-10731310:
Rachel Deere and colleagues ran a small crossover trial in 2023 on exercise and long-term knee pain. Many people with sore knees find that leg exercise makes pain worse for a time, which can push them to stop exercising. The team asked whether arm exercise could ease knee pain without working the painful joint. Volunteers with knee pain lasting at least three months each did one session of arm cycling and one of leg cycling, a week apart, and rated their pain for days afterward.

Arm exercise lowered knee pain the next day, while leg exercise did not. Both kinds of exercise changed how pressure felt at test spots, and responses to light touch varied widely. The authors say the reason for the arm effect is not yet clear. Still, they suggest arm exercise may offer a useful extra option for people whose knees limit leg workouts.
pmc-10736310:
Dianne Oladejo, Joyce Chapman, Tonya Roberson, and Rachel O'Conor describe work with Black dementia caregivers in two thousand twenty-three. Their team joined two local groups and a medical center on Chicago's Far South Side. Black families face gaps in diagnosis and health that add to the load of care. Few care programs fit their needs or their culture.

The local groups helped design interview guides and spoke with thirty caregivers. Most cared for a parent or grandparent and shared tasks with kin. They named stress, the need to learn how dementia changes, racism, family duties, and a wish for rest and local help. Their views will shape a new family care program.
pmc-10736910:
Emily Heilbrunn and co-authors present a 2023 study of mood in nursing home residents across the COVID-19 years. Lockdown rules cut visits and group life to curb spread, with loneliness as the feared side cost. The team mined the national care data set, scoring low mood with a standard nine-item form. Scores were set beside the home's four-week case counts in bands from none to heavy.

Odds of low mood ran higher in every band with cases than in case-free spans. The lift was largest in the lightest band, a third higher, and stayed raised in heavier ones. The pattern hints that fear and disruption, not just illness counts, weighed on minds. Pandemic playbooks should budget for mood care, the data suggest.
pmc-10737310:
Rafael de Cabo reports in 2023 on how daily fasting and calorie cuts affect health in female mice. Earlier work of this kind used mostly males, leaving a gap. A carousel feeder let the team control how much food mice got, and when.

Mice on calorie restriction responded strongly: cancers progressed less and lung inflammation eased, compared with mice that only ate in a set time window. Blood chemistry after an overnight fast also differed between the two regimes. Late-in-life daytime feeding with long fasts helped most when paired with lower energy intake. The study guides how diet timing studies should be designed.
pmc-10737910:
Jingwen Liu wrote this research paper, published in 2023, on how often middle-aged and older Americans take part in religious life. It tracks how attendance changes with age and across birth cohorts, and whether the pattern differs by race and ethnic group.

Liu used survey data from 2004 to 2020, covering more than 130,000 person-years. Attendance followed a reversed U shape over life, and newer cohorts attended less and dropped off faster. Black and Hispanic older adults attended more often than White older adults but declined faster in late life. Among Hispanic immigrants, longer exposure to strict immigration policy went with higher attendance. The paper shows faith habits shift with both age and the times people live through.
pmc-10738510:
Breder and three co-authors ask how old queer folks used tech for friend webs in the plague years in this twenty twenty-three study. Such folks oft live lone and lean on peers for care. Far rules in the plague cut those webs at their most frail hour.

Inside, deep talks with a mixed crew of old folks feed the checks. Three themes rose: a want for true touch, web bound rules, and age gaps. Touch lack topped the list, with screens a poor fill for hugs. Web bounds took care as folks set who could reach them there. Age-gap tech skills barred some from care calls and meets.
pmc-10738910:
Eunju Lee and Kyungmin Kim studied married couples in Korea in a research paper from twenty twenty-three. Their subject is whether husbands and wives agree on moving home after they retire. The authors note that where a couple lives can shape health and well-being in later life.

Most couples in the large sample agreed with each other, either both wanting to move or both wanting to stay. Couples were more likely to agree when they solved problems together as a team. Agreement was also more common when the wife felt happier in the marriage. Talking about life after retirement also helped couples agree to move.
pmc-10739010:
Michelle Paulsen and three co-authors test whether a drug burden score helps cut risky medicines in older veterans in a 2023 paper. Many medicines raise fall risk by sedating patients or scrambling balance. A burden index totals a patient's exposure to those drug classes.

A pharmacist reviewed fall-risk medicines for veterans in a prevention program, in two rounds. In the second round, the burden score was shared with each patient's main prescriber. Three months later the team counted medication changes and score drops. Nearly every participant, ninety-five percent of forty-four, took at least one risky drug. The comparison asks whether one extra number in the chart moves prescribers to act. Safer prescribing for fall-prone elders is the practical prize.
pmc-10740510:
Serena Dattola and co-authors map brain activity during mental arithmetic in a 2023 paper. Most prior work used fMRI scans, but this team used EEG signals instead. They rebuilt source activity with a method called eLORETA.

Thirty-five healthy young adults performed a serial subtraction task. The team split them into good and bad counters by score and compared brain activity. A clear difference appeared only in the beta band. The left limbic lobe was more active in the better counters. That region links to memory, fact retrieval, and emotion. The authors offer the finding as a start for deeper study.
pmc-10741510:
Małgorzata Knapp and colleagues reviewed in 2023 what myostatin, a protein best known for limiting muscle growth, does to the heart. Myostatin is secreted mainly by skeletal muscle, with smaller amounts from heart muscle and fat. It switches on signaling pathways that restrain growth. Animal studies show the heart shrinks when myostatin is overproduced and enlarges when the protein is removed.

The review gathers evidence on myostatin's diagnostic and prognostic value across heart conditions. It discusses how myostatin-null mice develop larger ventricular chambers and volumes, and how the heart may release myostatin as a brake on its own growth signals. For clinicians, a circulating factor linking skeletal muscle and heart size could become a blood marker of disease or a drug target. The authors weigh that promise against what is still unknown.
pmc-10742410:
Wenqiu Lin and co-authors traced how a spray forces pineapple plants to flower in a 2023 study. Growers spray ethephon, which sheds ethylene gas, to make a whole field bloom at once for a timed harvest. The gene and chemistry shifts that the gas sets off inside the plant tip were not well mapped.

The team read both the gene activity and the small-molecule mix in shoot tips across the days after spraying. Samples ran from day zero to the first bud parts. Joined maps show which genes wake and which pathways shift as the tip turns to bloom. The map may help breeders time or boost flowering.
pmc-10742510:
Katherine Quispe-Medina and co-authors map lung microbes in critically ill patients in southern Peru in two thousand twenty-three. Gene reads of the 16S marker can chart whole microbe communities. Whether the lung mix marks who will recover was the pilot question.

Patients on breathing machines for non-lung reasons gave airway samples, read by next-generation sequencing. Three phyla led the mix: Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, and Bacteroidata, with the order shifting between those who lived and those who died. Friendly resident microbes fell in the group that died, while hospital germs rose over time. The team frames the profile as a candidate early marker, pending larger studies to confirm it.
pmc-10742710:
A team of co-authors presents a trial from two thousand twenty-three on diet and premenstrual syndrome in Omani teenagers. The syndrome affects mood and well-being in women worldwide, and evidence on diet's role conflicts. The trial tested a healthy diet plus motivational support.

Two schools in the Muscat region took part. Students in grades ten and eleven with regular cycles and PMS symptoms were split between groups. The diet group got a personal face-to-face consultation and follow-up motivational phone calls. The study tracked symptom severity and quality of life, asking whether eating advice can ease the monthly burden.
pmc-10742810:
Bailing Chen, Huilin Lai, Chuandong Lin, and Demei Li model how a tilted boundary between two fluids changes a classic mixing instability, in a twenty twenty-three paper. The Rayleigh-Taylor instability grows when a heavy fluid sits over a light one. Most studies start with a flat boundary. This team started with an inclined one and used a particle-based flow method that tracks effects beyond normal fluid theory.

They found several measures of imbalance first rose and then fell as mixing grew. A steeper starting tilt made the density gradient, the out-of-balance strength, and the affected region all larger. Three rival effects explain the pattern: the growing wavy boundary spreads contact, waves fade with time, and the fluids blend. The work aids designs where tilted fluid layers mix.
pmc-10748010:
Yang and co-authors test computer models that predict how pregnancy and cancer together change the handling of cancer drugs, in a study from 2023. Treating cancer in pregnancy is hard because pregnant patients are rarely in drug trials, so dose and safety data are thin. Body-based models can fill part of that gap.

The team checked a pregnancy population model against real data for two drugs, paclitaxel and docetaxel, in pregnant patients with cancer. The model fit docetaxel well, while paclitaxel needed a boost to one liver enzyme that rises in pregnancy. Changes in blood protein binding in cancer had little effect. The model then forecast much lower exposure to a third drug, acalabrutinib, in pregnancy. The authors urge wider checks with more drugs.
pmc-10749410:
Mohammadi, Hadian, and Olyaei test whether Wii game training improves brain-based skills in athletes with unstable ankles. Ankle sprains lead to lasting instability in about 80% of cases. Standard rehab often skips the thinking and reaction problems that come with the injury. The trial enrolled 25 athletes with instability in one ankle and 25 without. Athletes were split at random into training and no-training groups.

The training group played balance and strength games three times a week for 12 sessions. A computer test measured reaction time before and after the program. The study asks whether game-based rehab can restore mental sharpness along with ankle control. Results bear on how sports rehab should be designed.
pmc-10750410:
Izuhara and co-authors test whether how long people sleep affects antibody gains after COVID-19 mRNA shots. Sleep is known to boost vaccine responses, but data for mRNA vaccines were thin. The study followed 48 healthy adults who got one of two mRNA vaccines in 2021 and 2022. Sleep was tracked with wrist devices and written diaries. Tracking covered the first shot and the booster periods.

After accounting for other factors, longer measured sleep after the booster linked to stronger antibody levels. The link showed at both three and seven days after the booster. Self-reported sleep showed a weaker pattern than device data. The findings suggest sleep in the days after a booster matters for immunity.
pmc-10753810:
Rakshyakar Giri leads a team on charge states of diamond NV centers. Their study from twenty twenty-three deals with shallow nitrogen vacancy centers. Spin based uses need an efficient spin readout.

One route maps spin onto charge states for reading. Stable charge allows long measures with less noise. Sensing needs centers just nanometers below the surface. Surface effects there can harm charge stability. Four shallow centers passed the conversion protocol tests. Readout noise fell well below fluorescence based reads. Initialization of charge states was also shown.  Charge starts were shown on the same centers.
pmc-10753910: The editors of Open Forum Infectious Diseases thank the peer reviewers who read and judged papers for the journal. The thanks cover one year of work, from the start of November 2022 to the end of October 2023. The notice names each reviewer in one long list. It notes that the quality of the journal rests in large part on their skill and unpaid time.
pmc-10756910:
Qiu and five co-authors set two reed kin side by side in mixed soils in this twenty twenty-three study. The two reeds grow side by side in salt meadow and in sand on one plain. Mixed ground can push kin apart in form and gene code as time runs on.

Inside, gene proof backs the pair as two true split species, not one loose kind. One reed reads as a broad guest that shifts form a lot from soil to soil. The other reads as a soil-bound type with tighter form shifts across ground types. Small gaps in shape, code, and soil use add up to let both reeds thrive in harsh ground.
pmc-10768410:
Marija Kocic and eight co-authors review the causes of upper gut bleeding in children by age. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. The cause shifts a lot from newborn to teen, though some causes span all ages. Where a child lives also shapes the most likely cause.

Some causes bind to one age band, such as vitamin lack in newborns or milk protein allergy in infants. Others, such as a sore food pipe or stomach lining, can show at any age. The worst bleeds come from swollen veins, ulcers, or a blood clotting crash. Care starts with a fast check of how grave the bleed is, then a scope. Surgery is held for the worst cases.
pmc-10773810:
Zhaoliang Geng and five co-authors measure the aroma precursor chemistry of cigars across tobacco parts and origins, in a two thousand twenty-three food chemistry paper. Which leaf and which terroir produce which flavors had not been systematically mapped.

Sixty-nine precursors were quantified in sixty-one tobaccos. Plant part mainly shifted amino acid content, while origin influenced amino acids, organic acids, fatty acids, and sugar alcohols. Middle leaves from different origins varied widely in style and quality, with woody aroma prominent. Dozens of precursors correlated strongly with flavor, style, and quality scores. The authors offer the map for steering blending and cultivation toward desired sensory profiles.
pmc-10786210:
