Sandeep Karna and Ki-Woon Kang review why fat around the heart grows too large in heart failure, in a twenty twenty-three article. This fat hugs the heart and acts like a hormone-making tissue, not a passive store. Too much of it is tied to heart disease and to worse heart failure. The authors set out to sum up each path that links the fat to the failing heart.

Their review covers fat-made hormones in excess, swelling signals, stem cell growth, cell stress from oxygen damage, and sugar harm. It also covers faults in the nerves that tune the heart. The fat serves as an energy store and talks closely with heart muscle. The authors argue this two-way talk helps drive the disease.
pmc-10809810:
Sayan, Kankoc, Valiyev, and Celik present cases in twenty twenty-four showing varied uses of a thermal camera in chest surgery. The camera maps temperature as colour in real time, with no contact, no radiation, and easy repeat use. Medicine has applied it to wounds, diabetic feet, and heart surgery checks, but chest uses were less documented.

In one case, the camera marked the boundary between blood-fed and starved lung tissue during cancer surgery, guiding where to cut. Measured temperatures confirmed the visual gap. In another, it checked whether palm temperature rose after a nerve-cut operation for sweaty palms, a sign the procedure worked. The authors argue the tool is safe and handy across chest procedures.
pmc-10811210:
Maria Tsagiopoulou and Ivo Gut wrote this review, whose text is dated 2023, on machine learning for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The blood cancer varies widely from person to person. New tools read many layers of cell data at once, from genes to proteins, a stack called multi-omics. The pair ask how learning models can turn that stack into care fitted to each patient.

They survey models trained on single data layers first, noting where each helps diagnosis or forecasting. They then turn to the newer work that fuses layers, and weigh its promise against its flaws: small cohorts, messy data, and hard-to-read models. The authors see real hope for precision care, if the field solves data sharing and proof in clinics. The review maps a young field for doctors and data scientists alike.
pmc-10825010:
Shun-Yao Liao and Yuan-De Tan present a new statistical method in a paper whose text dates to 2023. Their topic is haplotypes, the sets of gene variants a person inherits together on one chromosome. Studies often link haplotypes to complex diseases, but mixing between chromosome copies can distort the results.

The method pairs each haplotype with its sister copy, a matching form built by restating the gene data. It then checks whether the pairing pattern differs between patients and healthy controls. Applied to past data, the method confirmed a link between one gene region and Alzheimer disease. It also showed that some reported links to breast cancer and heart disease may have been artifacts. The authors argue their check should come before strong claims are made.
pmc-10854010:
Hannah Varkey and co-authors map research on screening baby movement in a study published in 2023. Disorders of brain development are often found only after age four, which delays help. Watching how infants move on their own can flag risk far earlier. A classic method, General Movement Assessment, scores those movements by eye. Digital tools that track movement with sensors have grown fast over two decades.

The team mapped close to three hundred papers with bibliometric software, charting keywords, co-authors, and citations. Observation still rules the field's standard method. A few classic groups have added digital tools, but few teams have gone fully digital. Sensor use stayed rare in the maps. The authors propose blending trained observation with digital tracking. That mix, they argue, could yield earlier diagnoses and earlier therapy for infants at risk.
pmc-11081110:
Megan Kennedy wrote this editor's message for the December 2023 issue of a Canadian journal for health sciences librarians. She had just taken over as editor. The message appears in both English and French, matching the journal's two working languages.

Kennedy thanks the outgoing editor for getting the journal indexed in a major citation database, which will bring it an impact factor starting in 2024. She also thanks the departing production editor and welcomes new staff. She describes the board's planned work on fair and inclusive peer review. The message closes by previewing the issue, which covers Wikipedia in health teaching, two book reviews, and a product review.
pmc-11532410:
Gao, Fu, Li, and He test a case based, staged teaching plan for jaw surgery students in twenty twenty-four. The plan walks each lesson through six steps, from a hook to a summary, with real cases at its core. Thirty-eight master's students were split by chance into the new plan or classic lectures. Scores for theory and clinical thinking were compared at the end.

The new plan group scored higher on theory and on case analysis. On a scaled clinic exercise, they led on four of five skills. Teachers also rated their own teaching as stronger after the switch. Students said the method sharpened their thinking, though some felt more pressure. The authors back wider use of the plan.
pmc-11535110:
Fatemeh Bamarinejad and seven co-authors look for predictors of a heart procedure complication in a study from two thousand twenty-four. After emergency stenting for a severe heart attack, blood flow through the reopened artery can stay slow or fail, a problem called slow flow or no reflow. It affected about thirty percent of their patients.

The study included four hundred sixty patients treated for ST-elevated heart attacks. Early analysis tied the problem to age, heart pumping strength, kidney function, and lesion traits. In the final adjusted model, three factors stood out on their own: long diffuse lesions, weaker pumping, and poorer kidney filtration. The authors say these markers can warn clinicians before the procedure.
pmc-11537410:
Jili Qu leads a team on zeolite and palm fiber in treated soil. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with cement treated soil strength. Additives may raise strength while cutting cement use.

Compression tests tracked strength across mix levels. Cement, zeolite, and fiber shares were all varied. Curing time also shaped the strength results. A best swap rate of zeolite for cement was sought. A best fiber share for strength and bend was probed. Regression models tied strength to the mix shares. All factors showed strong effects on strength.  Software aided the search for best shares.
pmc-11538510:
Xuequn Luo and six colleagues published a genome study in two thousand twenty-four on the Chinese grouse, a rare bird found only in China. Its subspecies boundaries were poorly settled, above all in Sichuan. The team sequenced the bird's full mitochondrial genome from a nature reserve population.

The Sichuan birds' mitochondrial structure and sequence closely matched birds from Gansu, suggesting one shared subspecies. A control region differed clearly in length from the hazel grouse, a close relative. Family trees built from the full data led the authors to propose splitting the hazel grouse group into two genera. The work is the first Sichuan sequence for the species and feeds conservation planning.
pmc-11540110:
James Vienneau, Camden Burns, Anto Boghokian, and Varun Soti compare two ways to repair a swollen abdominal aorta before it bursts. Open repair replaces the weak section through a large incision, while the endovascular method threads a graft inside the vessel through small cuts. The review gathers studies that compare the two head to head.

The inside method gave a survival edge for up to four years. After that the balance shifted toward open repair. Graft problems such as leaks led to more follow-up procedures and lifelong checks. Open repair patients more often needed breathing support and transfusions, and stayed longer in intensive care. They also recovered to normal life more slowly at first, though quality of life ended up similar. The authors stress that the choice should weigh each patient's health, anatomy, and odds of long-term success.
pmc-11548910:
Wendell Rodrigues Oliveira da Silva and four co-authors asked who really pays for basic medicines in Brazil in a 2024 paper. Brazil's public health system splits duties among federal, state, and municipal governments, but the money tells a messier story. The team analyzed spending from 2016 to 2020 across regions.

Municipalities spent more on medicines than the federal contribution in every year studied. Per-person municipal spending rose over the period, most steeply in poorer municipalities. A federal pharmacy subsidy program, meanwhile, mostly reached large, better-off cities. The authors conclude that inequality is widening: the places least able to fund medicines carry the heaviest load, raising illness and death risks in primary care.
pmc-11563210:
DNA origami folds a long strand of DNA into tiny shapes that can carry cargo, and placing each one exactly where it belongs is the hard part. Tingting Zheng, Caoimhe O'Neill, John Marshall, Thomas Iskratsch, and Matteo Palma use a heated scanning probe to pattern a surface so the folded shapes stick only at chosen spots. As a proof of concept they placed origami carrying gold particles and quantum dots, tiny light-emitting crystals.

The shapes landed at the planned positions in neat arrays, with control down to single molecules. The team says the method could build mixed arrays where different spots carry different cargo. Such platforms could serve in sensing and in the study of single molecules and new materials.
pmc-11566110:
Abrahams and co-authors introduce a microphone that hears sound in a completely new way. Most microphones track a membrane wobbling under sound pressure. Their device instead watches how sound pressure changes the stiffness of a thin trapped air film under a graphene membrane driven at resonance.

As sound waves shift the air pressure, the film's stiffness shifts, and the membrane's resonance frequency moves with it. A tracking loop follows that frequency, turning it back into sound, and the team used it to record sound and music. The graphene disc is over a thousand times smaller in area than the membranes in standard micro-electromechanical microphones. The authors see room for wider dynamic range and tougher, smaller devices.
pmc-11570810:
Peikai Ding and eight co-authors build a survival model for an aggressive breast cancer in a 2024 paper. This subtype lacks the usual hormone and growth receptors, so treatment options are few and outlook poor. The team focused on genes tied to a cleanup process that removes damaged mitochondria. Single-cell data from public databases helped find the relevant genes and build a risk score.

Nine genes formed the model, which split patients into high and low risk with clearly different survival. It predicted well across several independent cohorts. High gene levels also tracked with more immune cells in tumors and possible sensitivity to certain drugs, aiding personal treatment choices.
pmc-11574910:
Kazuki Ohashi and co-authors count, in a 2024 study, whether Hokkaido has enough clinics able to give a new Alzheimer's drug. Lecanemab was approved in Japan in 2023, but it demands brain scans and close monitoring, so only some hospitals qualify. Using map data, the team sorted hospitals into three scenarios by how fully they met the treatment rules. Then they measured how much of the population could reach one within thirty, sixty, or one hundred twenty minutes.

Coverage swung widely with the rules. Under the most workable scenario it reached fifty-six, about seventy-four, and eighty-eight percent at the three travel times. The far north and south were worst served, while Sapporo was flagged as likeliest to overflow. The authors call for new treatment centers placed where access and capacity are thinnest.
pmc-11575010:
Ming Liu and five colleagues published case reports in two thousand twenty-four on redoing root canal work in oddly shaped upper molars. Some upper molars fuse their roots into a C shape, hiding extra canals. Missed canals are a common reason root treatments fail.

The first case had three canals in the palate root merging into a C shape, a pattern not previously reported in a first molar. The second fused all cheek-side canals of a second molar into a C ending near an extra tooth. Both patients were free of symptoms at later checks, and scans showed healed tissue. In one case, sinus swelling from the tooth also settled. The authors stress scan and microscope use.
pmc-11575210:
Cynthia Henley-Smith and four co-authors test a plant-based blend against the bacterium that drives tooth decay. Streptococcus mutans colonizes enamel and starts cavities; stopping its adhesion is a prevention strategy older than modern dentistry, since plants like Heteropyxis natalensis have long treated oral infections. The study examined that plant, green tea, and tea tree and peppermint oils.

After forty-eight hours the blend cut bacterial load by about a hundredfold, while sparing a friendly Lactobacillus species much more. Microscope images of enamel blocks showed fewer attached bacteria, broken chains, and damaged cell shapes. Human macrophage tests found low to no toxicity for the mixture and its parts. The authors call it a selective first candidate for caries prevention.
pmc-11577810:
Ha Na Cho and co-authors present work from two thousand twenty-four on predicting how long sick patients stay in hospital after surgery. The patients studied needed general anesthesia, which puts them to sleep for the operation. Knowing the likely stay in advance helps hospitals plan beds, staff, and care.

The team used records from a very large group of patients treated between two thousand eighteen and two thousand twenty. They tested four kinds of machine learning models, and one called XGBoost gave the best results, with an average error within three days. The paper also shows which factors shaped each forecast, so doctors can see why a stay was predicted to be long or short.
pmc-11580310:
Yuna Uchi and co-authors read, in a 2024 study, the death records of a city hit by the Fukushima nuclear disaster. Deaths tied to a disaster can come late and by indirect paths: the stress and disruption of evacuation can kill months later. The team read all 520 certified disaster-related deaths in Minamisoma City, north of the plant, from 2011 to 2021.

Heart and vessel diseases led, at 27.7% of deaths. Lung diseases came next, at about a quarter, and cancers third. Older people bore the brunt of the heart and lung toll, which points to evacuation strain. Cancer led deaths for those in their fifties, a hint that evacuation cut screening and care. Self-harm led for the young and could strike years later. The authors urge better shelters, evacuee care networks, cancer care during evacuation, and long suicide watch.
pmc-11584810:
Yu and co-authors profile cervical tumors with joined gene and protein data from 139 Chinese women. Cervical cancer has fallen where vaccines and screening spread, but it still threatens women in poorer nations. Tumor samples got deep proteogenomic reads. The joined analysis links gene faults to the pathways they disturb. It also maps how HPV infection reshapes the tumor at many levels. One finding ties the protein EP300 to faster tumor growth through a partner protein.

Protein patterns split patients into three groups. The groups differ in outlook, gene faults, and likely drug response. The atlas aims to guide both biology and treatment picks.
pmc-11586610:
Supattra Changsuphan, Boonjai Srisatidnarakul, and Holli DeVon present a 2024 study that builds a short scale for nurses to judge when older patients can go home after hip surgery. Poor readiness can mean pain problems, weak movement, and too little help at home. A clear checklist could cut those risks and lower readmission.

The team drafted items from past research and from talks with experts and patients. They then tested the nine item scale in four large public hospitals with 200 older adults who had hip joint surgery. The paper reports how sound the scale proved: how well its items hang together and how well it sorts patients.
pmc-11587710:
Rubén Cuevas-Martínez and ten colleagues published a mouse study in two thousand twenty-four on intermittent fasting and rheumatoid arthritis. Fasting calms inflammation in several conditions, but its mechanism in arthritis was murky. Sixteen mice with induced arthritis were split between normal feeding and alternate-day fasting for four weeks.

Fasted mice developed milder, less frequent joint disease, confirmed by tissue and imaging checks. Gene activity shifted broadly: hundreds of genes rose or fell, with inflammatory pathways turned down. One mediator, IL33, stood out as central to the benefit. Gut microbe profiles changed too. Master metabolic regulators were implicated in the response. The authors propose fasting as a probe and possible adjunct in arthritis.
pmc-11591910:
Jessica Angelina Trejo Vazquez and co-authors show how lung tumor vesicles switch on nearby fibroblasts. Their 2024 study uses vesicles shed by lung adenocarcinoma cells. Lung cancer kills more patients than any other cancer, mostly through spread. The tumor's neighborhood helps drive that spread.

Vesicles were spun out of cell cultures and checked by standard methods. Resting lung fibroblasts then bathed in vesicles, a growth factor, or plain buffer. Vesicles woke the fibroblasts into a cancer-linked state, raising marker proteins. Their gene patterns partly matched the growth factor's effect. Vesicle-woken cells favored tissue remodeling and invasion-linked genes more strongly. Tumor messages in tiny parcels may recruit local help for growth.
pmc-11596210:
Jennifer Narro-Serrano and co-authors study scent chemicals in urine as possible signs of COVID-19, in this 2024 paper. Infection changes body chemistry, and urine carries volatile compounds that reflect those shifts. Past studies named varied candidate markers. This team wanted a firmer set, so they tested urine in several ways and compared the results.

They gathered urine from thirty-five hospital patients with the disease and thirty-two healthy people. A fiber-based method fed the samples into a gas analysis machine, with some samples dried or acid-treated first. Statistical models separated patients from healthy controls, and the split grew sharper with the treated samples. Yet treatments could also create or destroy compounds. The authors advise mixing methods when picking markers of viral illness.
pmc-11597410:
Lea Schuh and co-authors follow COVID-19 inside the body, asking what the antiviral drug remdesivir really does. Trials had suggested it speeds recovery, but only modestly. The team tracked 369 patients of all illness levels, treated and untreated, and used a process-based math model to reconstruct the infection's course in 88 of them.

Among untreated patients, those who ended up in hospital showed weaker early immune responses and higher total virus loads than those who stayed home. Among treated patients who died, hospital arrival came later after symptoms began than among survivors, a sign that timing matters. The model's verdict on the drug itself was restrained: its antiviral activity looked rather limited. The authors argue the findings point to a need for different or added treatment plans.
pmc-11599610:
Cosme Ayani and seven co-authors present a 2024 study of electrons in a flat material that normally traps them in place. Such materials, called Mott insulators, owe their behavior to strong pushes between electrons. Stacking a single layer of one on a metal base lets scientists watch how the layers sway each other.

The team mapped how electrons scatter in the stack as the temperature fell. Below eleven degrees above absolute zero, a sharp contour emerged in the maps. That signals electrons breaking free and moving as a coherent group, a state tied to a known lattice effect. Math models of the material backed the reading of the data.
pmc-11600910:
Shunqing Shu leads a team on whether a scope step is needed in colon checks. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with entry to the last gut part. That step proves a full check, but its worth is in doubt.

Records came from a large set of folks at one center. Half had the extra step and half did not. Odd finds in that gut part were quite rare. Rates of polyp and growth finds were compared by group. Score matching was used to make groups more fair. The team finds the step not needed as routine.
pmc-11604010:
Jingyan Sun and four co-authors examine how clashing work and family demands feed depression in Chinese prison officers. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Depression runs high in this workforce, and role conflict theory predicts stress is the bridge between the clash and the low mood.

Four hundred seventy-two officers completed standard scales for conflict, stress, and depressive symptoms. Mediation analysis tested whether stress carries the effect from conflict to depression. A network analysis then mapped which symptoms sit at the center and which link the three clusters together. Naming those bridge symptoms points to precise targets for support programs. The authors aim their findings at interventions built for this overlooked group.
pmc-11607310:
Yuanqi Wang and nine co-authors track how Arctic surface waters mixed as sea ice waned. Their 2024 study covers the Pacific Arctic shelves from 1996 to 2021. These seas feed rich ecosystems, yet ice loss is reshaping their upper layer. Ship data and model records gauged the summer mixed layer.

Before 2006, the mixed layer grew shallower as ice melted and surfaces warmed. After 2007 the trend flipped to deepening. Longer open water, stronger wind stirring, and less meltwater drove the change. Control thus passed from surface buoyancy to wind. The shift may explain odd fall plankton blooms and faster acidification. Ice loss, in short, now stirs the sea it once calmed.
pmc-11607910:
Parivash Jamrasi, Mia Tazi, Nur Afiqah Zulkifli, Jun Bae, and Wook Song review whether exercise can shield fertility during immune cancer therapy, in a 2024 paper. Checkpoint inhibitor drugs have transformed cancer care but can inflame glands and damage the gonads. Many patients are young enough for parenthood to matter. Exercise already helps patients feel better and may improve treatment response, and it supports reproductive health in other settings.

Direct evidence for the therapy pairing, though, is thin. The review gathers what is known about fertility-related side effects and the paths by which the drugs might harm reproduction. It then argues exercise is a plausible, low-risk shield worth testing. The authors urge that fertility counseling become routine beside these drugs.
pmc-11608210:
Zhifeng Wang and co-authors study an enzyme that helps liver cancer evade immunity in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The enzyme adds sugar units to cell molecules, and its levels are abnormally high in HCC tumors. High levels also mark a worse outlook for patients.

The team traces a chain from this enzyme through two signaling proteins to a secreted factor. That factor reshapes the immune cells around the tumor, favoring types that suppress attack. Silencing the enzyme in mice made an immune therapy work better at killing tumors. The authors propose the enzyme as both a prognostic marker and a helper target for immunotherapy.
pmc-11610310:
Xia Shan, Ruoyu Huang, Kuanyu Wang, and Pei Yang build a prognosis score for glioma brain tumors out of nineteen genes tied to reactive oxygen species. These molecules are double agents: moderate levels sustain cells, high levels feed tumors. Mining gene expression profiles, the team first split patients into two groups with distinct clinical features and survival.

The nineteen-gene signature predicted prognosis robustly in both training and validation datasets. High-risk tumors showed raised immune checkpoint and M2 macrophage markers, painting an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Functional analyses tied oxygen species levels to that immune landscape. The authors propose the score as an independent prognostic factor and a hint that redox biology helps gliomas hide from immunity.
pmc-11611510:
Evelyn Goicochea-Rios and three colleagues study which factors link to kidney disease in people with type two diabetes, in a twenty twenty-four paper. The team reviewed 371 diabetes patients seen in primary care between twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-four. Kidney disease harms quality of life and raises heart risk. Records covered age, sex, disease length, other illnesses, and lab values.

Being male, being over sixty, poor sugar control, and more than twenty years of diabetes all linked to kidney disease. High blood pressure was the most common extra illness, in seventy percent. The middle kidney stage was most frequent. The authors urge screening of older men with long, poorly controlled diabetes.
pmc-11612310:
Xie and four co-authors studied in twenty twenty-four how water weakens red mudstone, a soft rock in red beds. The rock is hard when dry and soft when wet, which can shake slope safety. They ran shear and fine-view tests across the full range of wet levels.

Strength and stiffness fell along a smooth S curve as water rose. Stick force fell more than rub force, then both leveled off. Cracks from swelled grains drove the fast fall in the mid range. Their harm model, with load and start harm joined, fit that fall well and can shift form by its parts.
pmc-11613410:
Peng Bao and seven co-authors ask whether food state before heart bypass surgery forecasts grave kidney harm after it in older patients. Kidney harm is a common and grave side issue of this surgery. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

Records came from a large US care database and held about a thousand older bypass patients. Two scores rated food state from blood protein and body measures. Over half the patients had mid to grave kidney harm after surgery. Worse food scores linked to higher harm risk after other factors were weighed. The authors also test how well the scores alone can flag who will be harmed.
pmc-11615510:
Yuki Suzuki leads a team on how a transplant drug is absorbed. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with kidney transplant patients. The drug, mycophenolic acid, varies a lot from person to person.

Data came from a small group of transplant recipients. Models of uptake were tested with a mixed effects tool. A two part model with two uptake steps fit the data best. Weight, kidney work, and days since surgery shaped drug levels. The last model was used to work out dose advice. Good models help keep drug levels safe.
pmc-11615810:
Faten Moassass and co-authors study a gene mutation that marks a distinct form of acute myeloid leukemia. Their 2024 paper covers Syrian patients whose leukemia cells had a normal chromosome picture. The gene, NPM1, is mutated in a large share of such cases worldwide and shapes how the disease behaves.

The team sequenced samples from one hundred newly diagnosed adults. About a fifth carried the mutation, most of a common type, with a few new variants found. They also tracked two partner mutations that often travel with it. The mix of mutations shapes prognosis and treatment choices for this leukemia subset. Local data matters because mutation rates and pairings can differ between populations, and care plans borrow strength from pooled global figures.
pmc-11618510:
Qikun Hu and colleagues recycled polyethylene plastic chemically in two thousand twenty-four. Breaking plastic down with hydrogen yields fuels and waxes. High hydrogen pressure usually suppresses unwanted methane gas. Their catalyst mixes a little ruthenium into platinum. This dilute alloy changes where bonds break. Plastic sticks to both metals on the surface.

Bond cutting runs faster on ruthenium sites. Isolated sites prevent repeated end-cutting of fragments. Methane stayed very low even at ambient pressure. Fuels and lubricant oils formed instead. Low-pressure hydrogen sources could feed such plants locally. Decentralized plastic upcycling becomes more feasible. Spectroscopic studies backed the mechanism proposed.
pmc-11619210:
Jinbo He and co-authors study what people with eating disorders in China see as the causes of their illness, in a paper from 2024. These disorders are common in China yet often go unnamed and untreated for years. The team read posts on a large question-and-answer platform. They kept more than two thousand posts from users who reported an eating disorder.

Coders sorted the claimed causes into personal and social groups. More than nine in ten users named a personal cause. Worry about body image and food was the most named cause, with mood problems close behind. A third to a half also named social causes like media ideals. Trauma, genes, and sports were named far less. The mix of causes shifted by disorder type. The authors say the patients' own views can guide better care.
pmc-11624210:
Raúl Mateos and a team of co-authors built a test to spot when a cell stress system is stuck on. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, deals with the KEAP1-NRF2 system. This system guards cells against harsh chemical stress. When it breaks, genes below it run too high, a known mark of cancer. A good test for this stuck state can guide both study and care.

Their test reads splicing joints in gene reads, since overactive genes leave extra odd joints. A simple Bayes based sorter reads the pattern. It held up well across large data sets. Readers who study cancer get a new way to flag this state from gene data they may already hold.
pmc-11626110:
Fatema Hashem Rupa and Mosharop Hossian map the health fallout of the August two thousand twenty-four floods in Bangladesh in two thousand twenty-four. The floods hit over five million people, swamping latrines, sewers, and farm land. Dirty water then raised the risk of cholera and other gut diseases, while still pools bred mosquitoes that spread malaria and dengue.

Broken clinics slowed emergency care, and fear, grief, and stress spread through displaced communities. The authors call for fast steps: restore clean water, watch for outbreaks, and repair health sites. Longer work should brace the system for the next flood. The piece is a perspective, blending impact data with a review of risk factors.
pmc-11627110:
Adel Moalwi led a large team making wound-healing particles from a plant in a 2024 study. They used water extract of a high-altitude flower to make zinc oxide particles in a green way. Such particles are cheap, easy to make, and known to fight germs. The team measured the particles and tested them on cells and rats.

The particles were tiny and killed a broad range of bacteria plus a fungus. In cell tests, treated wounds closed far faster than untreated ones. In rats, treated wounds shrank much more than untreated wounds, matching a standard iodine treatment. The authors see promise but call for more work on how the particles act and their long-term safety.
pmc-11629010:
Zongshi Qin and seven co-authors present a free software macro that checks whether trial patients truly stayed blind to their treatment, in a 2024 methods paper. Blinding keeps patient and staff guesses from skewing trial results. Bang's Blinding Index turns guess counts into a score for each trial arm. The macro, built for the SAS statistics package, computes the score and draws it as a chart.

Users need no ready data set; they just type in how many people guessed right, wrong, or were unsure in each group. The tool covers two-arm, three-arm dummy, and four-arm factorial designs. The team shows it on guess data from three past trials, on topics from weight gain to depression care. Charts make the success or failure of blinding plain at a glance. The authors aim the tool at trial teams of all sizes.
pmc-11630610:
Liu, Ma, Wang, Cui, and Shen study risk spillovers among Chinese financial sectors, in work from twenty twenty-four. Shocks in one sector, such as banking, can spread to insurance, securities, and multifinance. COVID was a sharp test of those links.

Daily closing prices from mid twenty seventeen to the end of twenty twenty-three fed a time varying model. Three stages were split: before, during, and after the epidemic. Total spillover rose then fell, with far bigger swings during the epidemic. The securities sector was most exposed both ways, while banking stayed most stable. Regulators can use such maps to watch the weakest links.
pmc-11631810:
Podgorska asks if plant flags for old iron mines flag old lead mines too. The field is a left mine plot from the 16th age in age. Heaps from lead ore digs still scar the plot's face. The team set 41 plots: 21 on heaps, 21 off the heaps. Each plot got a full list of leaf plants with cover shares. Soil bits from each plot went to lab checks for traits.

Checks read soil sour marks and the stock of key salts. Lead, lime, and three food salts got counts in the lab. Soil shifts drove the plant mix split twixt heap and field. On the heap plots, 18 leaf-wood flags for iron plots showed up. Those flags lean hard to heap soil in the counts. The flags thus serve for lead heaps as well.
pmc-11636010:
Fabiana Vieira Duarte de Souza Reis and colleagues, with the Diamater Study Group, ask whether gestational diabetes diagnosed early in pregnancy harms newborns in a different way from the usual late diagnosis. Terms and diagnostic rules for pregnancy hyperglycemia are being made standard. Women diagnosed by twenty-four weeks or earlier face higher risk of postpartum prediabetes. But the link to bad newborn outcomes was disputed.

The look-back cohort ran at a perinatal diabetes research center in São Paulo state, Brazil. Early-onset women had fasting glucose in the diabetic range, below the line for overt diabetes, before twenty weeks. Late-onset women screened negative in the first trimester. They tested positive on the standard glucose tolerance test at twenty-four to twenty-eight weeks.
pmc-11636310:
Hanna Poulsen and five co-authors study gum disease in women who once faced a high risk of diabetes in pregnancy, in a 2024 paper. Both gum disease and metabolic syndrome involve inflammation, and each may feed the other. The team checked whether women with the syndrome show worse mouth health years after delivery.

They examined 112 women from an earlier group of 348, four to six years after their pregnancies. About a fifth had metabolic syndrome by standard criteria. Full mouth checks, X-rays, and questionnaires measured gum bleeding, pocket depth, plaque, and tooth loss. The authors compare these signs between women with and without the syndrome. Links found here could push joint care of teeth and metabolism after high-risk pregnancies.
pmc-11638710:
Pham and six co-authors report a new record and diet study of a poorly known treefrog in Vietnam, in work from twenty twenty-four. The white lipped treefrog Zhangixalus pachyproctus was described only in twenty nineteen. It had long been confused with a similar species across China, Vietnam, and Thailand.

Misidentified records were corrected when the new species was named from form and DNA evidence. The Vietnamese record extends its known range. Dietary ecology, what the frog eats, was documented from field samples. For a species known from few specimens, each record sharpens range maps and conservation assessments.
pmc-11641610:
Xiaolan Zhang, Lingbo Liu, and Antonio Campese review, published in 2024, whether worn-out T cells quietly drive acute myeloid leukemia forward. This fast blood cancer kills through relapse and drug resistance, and immune therapy often fails against it. The review gathers signs that T cells in the marrow age early: they slow, change their surface marks, and stop killing well. Leukemia itself seems to push that aging. Aged T cells then shield the cancer instead of fighting it.

The authors chart the signals that drive the aging and the traits that mark it. They also weigh treatments meant to slow, dodge, or reverse the wear. Options range from drugs that clear aged cells to ways of shielding fresh immune cells. The piece is a map for trial designers rather than a trial itself. Its claim: fixing T cell youth may be the missing half of leukemia immune therapy.
pmc-11641710:
Niti Sharma, Seong Soo An, and Sang Yun Kim published a review in 2024 on common drugs and dementia risk. Older adults often take many drugs for long-term ills like high blood pressure, diabetes, and poor sleep. Some drugs may harm thinking or speed decline, even as they help the body.

The review covers five drug classes: pain drugs, drugs that block a nerve signal, sedatives, stomach acid drugs, and cholesterol drugs. It sums up cohort studies, trials, and past reviews for each class. The findings clash across studies, so no clear verdict on risk emerges. Blood tests for early disease signs may help future work, the authors note. They call for open weighing of gains and harms for each patient.
pmc-11642210:
Sadettin Uslu and co-authors report a 2024 study of a biosimilar drug in spine arthritis. Ankylosing spondylitis stiffens the spine through inflammation. CT-P13 is a biosimilar copy of infliximab, a proven antibody drug. The team asks how well it works and how long patients stay on it in real practice. Data come from a national Turkish registry of biologic drugs, covering 2014 to 2021. Patients split into first-line users and those on it after other biologics.

Drug persistence, safety, and effect are tracked in both groups. Registry data answer questions trials cannot: what happens over years, in mixed patients, after switches. Rheumatologists get persistence numbers that guide counseling when a cheaper biosimilar is offered. Payers care too, since biosimilars cut costs only if patients stay on them. First-versus-later line splits show whether prior failures dim the copy's value.
pmc-11642710:
Esra Kayacan Erdoğan, Hakan Babaoğlu, and Eugen Feist published a pilot study in two thousand twenty-four pitting trainee doctors against AI on rheumatology cases. Ten junior residents and two GPT-4 models, one specially trained and one not, worked ten cases of inflammatory arthritis.

Cases were scored for reasoning quality and staged management choices. The trained model beat the residents at every stage, from first impression to second-line treatment. Residents then reviewed its answers and answered attitude questions. Sixty percent favoured AI as a support tool, expecting gains in competence and relief from fatigue and burnout. The authors frame AI as an assistant, not a replacement. The study was small and single-specialty.
pmc-11643510:
Sergio Caprara led a team that tested, in two thousand twenty-four, a new view of cuprate superconductors. Cuprates are copper oxide wares that carry current with no loss at quite high heat. How their electrons act just above that point is still in dispute.

One view is the marginal Fermi liquid. The team's own view is the shrinking Fermi liquid. In their view, near a quantum critical point, swings of the order term scatter electrons near evenly across the Fermi surface. That gives the odd metal act seen in tests. Past light tests were read as a win for the first view. The team shows the heat range was too slim to split the two views. At high wave rates, their view fits the light data just as well.
pmc-11643610:
Bunka Son and three co-authors built a way to grade earthquake damage in concrete columns from crack photos in a 2024 paper. The columns are a resilient type, reinforced with weakly bonded ultra-strong bars, meant for quake-prone regions like Japan and China. Judging their damage by eye is slow and uneven.

The team photographed cracks on eight tested columns and measured each pattern's fractal dimension, a number for how wiggly and branched the cracks are. The number rose in step with how far the columns had drifted sideways in testing, and one column property, the shear span ratio, shaped the link. They fit simple equations tying crack pattern, past drift, and leftover drift together for quick assessments.
pmc-11644710:
Andreas Economides, Md Niamul Islam, and Konstantinos Baxevanakis study 3D printed plastic parts strengthened with short carbon fibers, in a 2024 paper. They varied how the parts were printed, including the internal pattern, the amount of empty space, and whether parts were heat treated after printing. They then tested stiffness, strength, and response to vibration.

Empty space inside the part had the largest effect on most traits, while the internal pattern mattered most for stiffness under pulling. Heat treatment raised stiffness in all samples tested. Microscope images showed fibers pulling out of the plastic, which points to weak bonding, but also showed better bonding between printed lines after heat treatment. The findings can guide design of printed parts for specific loads.
pmc-11644810:
Zhipeng Li and six co-authors study a display flaw called friction greening in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Polyimide is a flexible base used in foldable OLED screens. After long use, friction can build charge in the base and shift green pixels, making the screen look green.

The team tested how heat during making changes the inner structure of the material. Higher heat made chain segments more ordered, raised conductivity, and made charge traps more shallow. Tests with X rays, light, and electric measures backed this up. With less charge stored over time, the voltage drift that drives the flaw fell. The work points to a clear fix in how the base is made.
pmc-11646210:
Frazer and a large team reviewed in twenty twenty-four when a single drug is the best first care for spread kidney cancer. Mix care with two drug kinds is now common, but it is not right for all. They focus on one drug, tivozanib, that blocks a growth switch for blood vessels.

For folks with a good outlook, long-term data back single-drug care with fair life and life quality. This drug matches peers on strength but has fewer off-target side harms. The choice turns on risk class, age, other ills, and what the patient values most. Guides still list single-drug care as a norm for the good-outlook group.
pmc-11646810: Mohammad Dehbozorgi and six co-authors report a severe fungal infection after COVID-19 in a 2024 paper. The mold invades nose, eye socket, and brain, and it can kill quickly. Their case report walks through one patient's full management. The authors stress keeping suspicion high in anyone with a recent COVID-19 history, even without the usual risk factors like uncontrolled diabetes. Fast diagnosis, aggressive surgical removal of infected tissue, and antifungal drugs together gave the case its successful course, and they urge the same bundle elsewhere.
pmc-11647810:
Md Asif All Azad and three co-authors check water and soil near a coal mine in Bangladesh, in this twenty twenty-four study. Mining can load water and soil with heavy metals and change their quality across seasons. Local people depend on that water for drinking and crops.

The team sampled nine spots in summer and winter, taking water and soil to labs for testing. Surface water was broadly fit for watering crops, though haze and chemical load meant it needed treatment before drinking. Metal build-up and soil fertility were scored with set indexes. The results give a base for guarding health near the mine.
pmc-11649710:
Hubert Hörterer and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on repeat surgery for a painful heel tendon problem. The tendon joins the calf muscle to the heel bone, and it can wear down where it meets the bone. First-time surgery for this problem follows a clear plan. Much less is known about what happens when that first surgery fails and a second one is tried.

The team tracked patients at one large center who had the repeat surgery and checked on them at least a year later. Nineteen of the twenty-four patients took part in the final check, about four to five years on. Their pain and function scores were far better than before surgery. Still, only about one third felt as well as healthy people do.
pmc-11649910:
Waqas Faridi and four colleagues work out exact wave solutions for a plasma system of ion sound and Langmuir waves, in a twenty twenty-four mathematics paper. The system describes an electric field and a density ripple shaped by a nonlinear force in a charged gas. The team used three forms of fractional math, which track memory effects in the medium. A newer algebraic method then built the solutions.

The solutions came in many shapes: bright and dark solitons, mixed forms, and sharp singular waves. Graphs made with a math software package compared how the forms behave under picked settings. The authors note the method is fast and simple and can serve other nonlinear systems.
pmc-11651910:
Amy Balanoff reviews the study of dinosaur brains and senses, in this 2024 paper. Fascination with what dinosaurs could do began with the first fossil finds. The field reads brain cases from fossils to infer sight, smell, balance, and behavior.

Balanoff argues the field is maturing but faces three limits: a stable family tree, better methods for building brain casts, and fossil experts trained in neuroscience. Progress on all three now lets the field feed findings back into brain science. Most examples come from meat-eating dinosaurs and the origin of birds and flight. The review maps where the science stands and where it can go.
pmc-11653910:
Hu and seven colleagues hunt for genes tied to a form of cell death in a kidney disease in twenty twenty-four. The disease harms the kidney's filters and is a top cause of kidney failure. The cell death form, called necroptosis, is planned by the cell and stirs inflammation. Its role in this disease was unclear.

The team mined public gene data from patients and healthy controls. They found seven hub genes that set patients apart and built a test from them. The test worked well on a second data set. Gene patterns also hinted at how immune cells act in the disease. Four known drugs were flagged as possible treatments to try.
pmc-11654410:
Dion Gajadin, Wouter van der Heijden, and Maarten van den Berg wrote a letter in two thousand twenty-four about an ultrasound score used in critical care. The VExUS score grades venous congestion from flow patterns in several veins. The authors respond to a report on how reliable that score is between observers.

They add a caution for patients on venovenous ECMO, a form of life support that moves blood outside the body. In one such patient, they saw a high-speed wave in a liver vein, which they name the B-wave. They think the wave comes from steady flow through the ECMO circuit. Its presence could mislead the congestion score, so vein choice and settings matter.
pmc-11655910:
Kim Cocks and co-authors review how cancer trials use time to deterioration of patient-reported outcomes, and how to do it better. Their review appeared in 2024. Such endpoints measure how long patients keep a given quality of life before it worsens. Trials define and analyze them in many ways, which muddies comparisons. The team gathered trials published from 2017 to 2022 and extracted every endpoint definition they found.

Seventy trials yielded 849 single endpoints across seventeen cancer types. Full definitions were often missing from reports. Choices about what counts as deterioration and how to treat side events changed results. The authors give best-practice advice: define the endpoint fully, state the assessment schedule, and report methods plainly. Their goal is trials whose quality-of-life claims can be trusted and compared.
pmc-11657610:
Huanyu Zhang and five colleagues published a 2024 cross-sectional study from China on parents of autistic children. Behavioral interventions work best when parents carry them out consistently at home. Sticking to the program improves children's behavior and parents' own outcomes, yet the burden on parents is heavy and multidimensional.

Earlier studies measured mainly health-related well-being, which misses much of that burden. This study instead used capability well-being, a broader measure of what a person is able to do and be. The researchers surveyed caregivers and tested how strongly adherence to the intervention was associated with this wider well-being. Their approach gives services a fuller picture of what supporting parents should achieve.
pmc-11657810:
Jianfei E and five co-authors test blood measures that might catch deep vein thrombosis early after a leg fracture. Their twenty twenty-four article deals with a common risk: clots in deep leg veins around the time of surgery for traumatic fractures. Ultrasound is the standard check, but a blood-based early flag would help.

The team reviewed patients from one year of admissions and split them by ultrasound proof of clots. Sixty-one had clots and one hundred ninety-one did not. Several clot-related markers and a clot-strength test ran higher in the clot group. A risk model kept eight factors, among them hip fracture and a clinical risk score. The markers showed real diagnostic value.
pmc-11658410:
Zhigang Li, Siqi Peng, Decong Zhang, and Lulin Liu present a 2024 study on heavy metals in the blood and fecal incontinence in American adults. Losing bowel control is common and distressing, and metals are known to disturb gut microbes and the gut wall. Whether blood metal levels track with the condition was unknown.

Data came from national health survey cycles between 2005 and 2010, covering 12,142 adults. Bowel health answers were paired with lab measures of cadmium, lead, and mercury. Higher cadmium and lead each linked to more incontinence in raw models. After full adjustment, both links stayed significant, with the top cadmium group at notably higher odds. Mixture methods checked the metals acting together.
pmc-11659210:
Taizhi Lin, Qianhui Wang, Zixuan Tan, Wen Zuo, and Rong Wu analyze how neighborhood social life affects older adults' mental health in China. Older adults' living space shrinks as physical function declines, making the neighborhood social environment a major influence. Using the twenty eighteen China Labor Dynamics Survey, the authors modeled neighborhood ties, trust, and security as the social environment. Subjective well-being was the mediator and green space the moderator.

Structural equation modeling found social trust and community security directly and positively associated with mental health. All three social factors also promoted mental health indirectly, by raising subjective well-being. Green space strengthened the link between neighborhood ties and mental health. The mechanism matters for policy: neighborliness works partly by making older people feel their lives go well, and greenery amplifies the social benefit. Community investment should be social and spatial together.
pmc-11659510:
In twenty twenty-four, de Lorenzo reported a science outreach effort that brings microbiology lessons into Spanish prisons. The effort is run by Spain's National Research Council with a development charity. It aims to raise inmates' grasp of microbes and their weight in daily life. It follows a world drive for microbial literacy.

Talks use plain metaphors to turn inmates from passive listeners into people who join in. The core points are simple. Earth is a microbial planet, and each body hosts vast microbiomes that shape health and social life. Microscopes open up the hidden microbial world and spark curiosity. Cases from microbial biotechnology, like bioplastics and skin bacteria bred against acne, show the useful side of microbes. The author argues such literacy helps shut-out groups bear their time inside and rejoin life outside.
pmc-11663710:
Jitka Široká led a large team on a plant study in twenty twenty-four about how plants keep a stress hormone's raw stock in check. The raw stock, called cis-OPDA, can act on its own, apart from the main hormone path. Years ago, one tagged form of it was found in hurt leaves. The team went looking for more.

They found five tagged forms in a small lab plant, each built by linking the stock to a common building block of proteins. The tagged forms piled up when the plant faced attack or harsh stress. Their levels rose and fell through the work of two enzyme groups, one that tags and one that frees. The tagged forms acted much like the raw stock itself. Plants, it seems, bank the signal for later use.
pmc-11668610:

pmc-11672510:

pmc-11672910:

pmc-11673010:

pmc-11673710:
Mijun Noh and Jaehong Kim compare two ways of making thin zirconia veneers for teeth, in a 2024 study. One way mills the veneer from a solid block. The other prints it with a light-based printer. pmc-11674310:

pmc-11674610:

pmc-11675410:

pmc-11675910:

pmc-11677010:

pmc-11677110:

pmc-11678210:

pmc-11680110:
Marzia Cino and co-authors published this review in 2024. It surveys what is new in a dog cancer called AGASACA, a tumor of the anal sac glands. The tumor invades nearby tissue and spreads early. pmc-11689310:
Rahul Malhotra, Ha-Linh Quach, and Jeremy Lim-Soh published this study in 2024. It looks at sleep among family caregivers of older adults in Singapore. pmc-11689610:

pmc-11689910:

pmc-11690310:

pmc-11690610:

pmc-11691510:

pmc-11691610:

pmc-12662210:
