pmc-12663310:
Anas Arafa and five co-authors solve a fractional wave equation, the Fornberg Whitham type, with a step by step method that stays partly in closed form. Fractional forms let the math hold a memory of past states. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

The method is built for two senses of the fractional step, one of Caputo type and one with a broader kernel. The authors prove that a solution exists and is the only one, and they check that their steps converge. At whole order, results match known exact solutions. The broader kernel form held memory effects more strongly and settled faster, they report.
pmc-12666210:
Linge Jian and co-authors link a blood sugar control score to eye disease risk in a large cohort study from two thousand twenty-five. Lower scores mean the body resists insulin more. The cohort held over two hundred thousand adults in the United Kingdom with early stages of a heart, kidney, and body-chemistry syndrome.

Higher scores went with lower risk of two eye diseases in a straight-line way. Cataract risk formed a U shape, and one diabetes eye disease formed an L shape. Top versus bottom score groups split risk most for that diabetes eye disease. Links grew stronger at later syndrome stages.
pmc-12682910:
Kamil Rapacz, Jaroslaw Szymanski, Armour Forse, and Tomasz Rogula published a 2025 comparison of robotic and standard keyhole gastric bypass in patients with very severe obesity. A body mass index of 60 or more makes weight-loss surgery riskier and technically harder. Robots give surgeons steadier, more precise movements, but their value at this size was unproven.

The study drew on a national database covering 233,828 bypass patients from 2020 to 2023. Patients at the highest weights had more complications and more emergency visits than lighter patients. Within the heaviest group, robotic and keyhole surgery had the same 30-day complication rate. Robotic operations took longer, but patients left hospital sooner. The authors call for careful multi-centre trials to settle which approach is best.
pmc-12684110:
Ezgi Ulas and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 on what adding immunotherapy does to the lymph nodes that drain a lung tumor. Those nodes teach the immune system to attack the cancer, yet they sit near the tumor and often catch radiation. The team compared nodes from twenty-five patients who got chemo-radiation plus two immune drugs before surgery with nodes from twenty-five matched patients who got chemo-radiation alone. Nodes were sorted by the radiation dose they had absorbed.

The immunotherapy group's nodes showed strong type I immune responses and more killer and regulatory T cells, at every dose level. The effect ran strongest in the hardest-hit nodes. High-dose nodes also showed scarring and long inflammation signatures, which the drugs partly softened. The authors stress the surprise: heavy radiation did not blunt the nodes' immune work.
pmc-12686410:
Kun Lin and co-authors map the cells of joint lining tissue in hemophilic arthritis. The illness comes from repeat bleeding into joints in people with hemophilia. It wears the joint down, yet its cell profile was largely unknown. The team read single-cell gene activity in lining tissue taken during knee replacement surgery. They compared the map with maps from two other joint diseases.

The hemophilic map stood apart from both other diseases. Mast cells, rare in the others, were active here and may start leaks from vessels. Iron left by blood drove a cell death form called ferroptosis in vessel and support cells. One vessel cell type may steer support cells toward easing that death. The map names fresh targets for gene-based care.
pmc-12687510:
Rogate Phinias, Mikidadi Muhanga, and Joshua Malago studied health data quality in Tanzania in a 2025 paper. Good care depends on records that are accurate, complete, consistent, and on time, yet the workers who type in patient data can introduce errors. The team asked which traits of those workers predict better data.

They surveyed 336 data-entering health workers at eight regional referral hospitals between August and October 2024. Older workers produced more accurate, complete, and timely records. Sex and schooling also mattered, with education linked above all to accuracy and completeness. The authors suggest training and support should be shaped with these patterns in mind, since errors in patient data can put lives at risk.
pmc-12694910:
Pengxu Wang and co-authors present a 2025 study of gene marks that may shape pancreatic cancer risk. Chemical marks on DNA can change gene work without changing the code. The team used a gene based method that mimics a trial to test if such marks in blood track with this cancer.

They scanned marks across the full mark set, then ran checks with changed rules and in fresh data sets to test the strength of each hit. Hundreds of marks passed the checks, and a large share held up in at least one repeat test. A final pooled test kept a core set, with four marks backed most strongly. One top mark sits in a gene known from past cancer work. The authors offer the marks as leads for study.
pmc-12698710:
Xiaoyan Wang and a team of co-authors knit a smart hydrogel patch that tracks heart and breath through marathon misery. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Sweat, heat, and motion wreck most wearable sensors long before the finish line.

The gel mixes a common polymer with plant nanofibers, laced with MXene sheets and borax. It stayed stable for thirty-five days in storage and stretched to eight times its length with keen sensitivity. The MXene also killed over ninety-nine percent of bacteria. In simulated marathon heat and humidity, the patch held steady for six hours. Heart rate and breathing read cleanly throughout. The authors target early warning of heart and lung trouble in endurance sport.
pmc-12701210:
Paris Liokatis and nine colleagues wrote a surgical study in twenty twenty-five on rebuilding the mandibular condyle, the knob at the jaw joint, after a break healed in the wrong place. Such bad unions can spoil a patient's bite and make chewing hard, and surgery to fix them was long seen as hard to predict. The study tested whether digital planning changes that.

Each patient got a plan made on a computer and implants made for them alone by CAD/CAM methods. The team then set the planned joint surface against the real one after surgery. The gap between plan and result averaged 2.27 millimeters by one measure. Most patients ended with good jaw movement, opening their mouths about thirty-seven millimeters on average, and no lasting loss of feeling was reported. Close agreement of this kind turns a once wayward fix into a precise one.
pmc-12704310:
Sebastian Bogner and three colleagues published a review and combined analysis in two thousand twenty-five on suicide risk in colorectal cancer. A cancer diagnosis is known to raise suicide risk, but past studies on this cancer type disagreed. The team gathered the world evidence to settle the picture.

They searched six databases for studies comparing patients with people free of cancer. Forty-four studies qualified, covering more than nine million patients. Most reported standardised death ratios, which the team pooled in a combined analysis. The review weighs how factors like disease stage may shape risk. It gives clinicians and planners a firmer base for spotting patients who may need mental health support.
pmc-12706910:
Joseph Kwon and co-authors present a 2025 study checking a widely used children's quality-of-life questionnaire in Australian children. The tool has twenty-three items across body, feelings, social life, and school, and children answer it themselves. Before scores can be trusted for policy or care, the tool's measurement quality must be proven in the local population.

The team drew a random sample of five hundred children aged eleven to twelve from a long-running national study. Using a strict measurement model from Rasch theory, they tested whether each item behaves as a proper ruler should. The work shows whether the child self-report version measures one clean trait in this group.
pmc-12709710:
Meghan Hill and six colleagues publish the design of a New Zealand trial testing whether a familiar abortion drug can help people with a previous caesarean start labor naturally. Spontaneous labor is safest after a uterine scar, because the standard induction drug raises rupture risk. Mifepristone blocks progesterone and may make the uterus responsive to its own signals.

Participants with one prior lower-segment caesarean are randomized to a single dose of mifepristone or placebo near term. The trial needs at least 168 participants to detect labor starting within forty-eight hours rising from ten to thirty percent. A positive result could change how post-caesarean births are managed.
pmc-12714410:
Xiu Feng and colleagues surveyed the genetics of snow trout relatives, a group of fishes found only in the upper Yellow River and nearby waters on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. These high-altitude fishes are sensitive to human pressure and climate change, yet their population health was unmeasured. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team sequenced two mitochondrial gene stretches in hundreds of fish from many sites. The sites cover a great lake, canyon and source stretches of the river, and two neighboring drainages.

Diversity ran highest in the lake and the main river stretches and lowest in one isolated drainage by one measure. Dam-affected populations with little restocking showed thinned diversity, while stocked ones matched undisturbed levels. All fish sorted into three deep lineages with distinct geographic homes. The authors offer the map as a base for conservation planning.
pmc-12714710:
Tirthankar Bandyopadhyay, Baidehi Basu, and Pabitra Parua study how a chemical tag on a DNA-packing protein times the end of gene reading. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five, using fission yeast as the model.

Gene reading runs through start, stretch, and stop phases, and the handoff to stopping was murky. The team tracked proteins along genes with a binding-and-reading method. A driver protein left the reading complex near the stop signal, while a partner that resets tags grew beyond it. The histone tag steered that swap: it drew the driver in during the stretch phase and let it go at the stop signal. Upsetting the tag flipped the pattern of the reset partner and of several reading marks. The work clarifies a switch that ends messages cleanly.
pmc-12716510:
Anna Kalbarczyk leads a ten-author team studying women leaders' influence on health policy across sub-Saharan Africa, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Women form seventy percent of the region's health workforce but hold only thirty-eight percent of ministry leadership posts. Evidence about what women leaders actually change has been thin.

The mixed-methods study combined a multicountry online survey with in-depth interviews. Leaders of all genders answered the survey; a subset of women leaders sat for interviews. Fields covered reproductive, maternal, child and adolescent health, nutrition, and immunisation. The authors explore how women leaders are perceived to shape policy and gender equity. Their aim is evidence that can support widening women's path into health leadership.
pmc-12717310:
Zhenzhen Zhang and co-authors compare two ways of delivering a triple therapy for advanced bile duct cancer inside the liver, in this 2025 study. Sixty-seven patients with inoperable tumors got either liver-artery infusion chemotherapy or standard body-wide chemotherapy, each paired with the same targeted drug and immune drug. The infusion route bathes the liver in high drug levels while sparing the rest of the body.

Infusion patients responded far more often and shrank their tumors more. After statistical balancing of the groups, they also lived longer overall and stayed progression-free longer. Local and distant control both favored the infusion arm. Side effects stayed manageable, and immune side effects tracked with slower progression. The authors back the infusion route for this cancer when the team and tools allow.
pmc-12717810:
Bin-bin Zhao, Hui Wang, Nan Luo, and Zhuan-Zhuan Zhang interview parents of children with strabismus in a 2025 study. Crossed or wandering eyes affect family life well beyond vision. Twelve parents of children aged four to eleven took part in deep interviews in early 2025, framed by family systems theory, which treats the household as one interlocked unit. A seven-step method distilled the transcripts into themes.

Four themes emerged. Parents described raw emotional distress, from anxiety to guilt, and the family's adjustment strategies, like sharing labor. They also named a pile-up of challenges, including conflict between relatives, and the support they say they need. Services that treat only the child's eyes miss the household strain the interviews expose.
pmc-12718510:
Gang Chen and colleagues published a 2025 study hunting breast cancer prognosis markers in genetic data. Immune activity shapes how breast cancer progresses. The team combined several genetic databases. A method using inherited variants tested causal links. One gene, involved in cell shape, rose to the top.

Lab work checked the gene in patient tissue. Its levels related to immune cell infiltration. Cell experiments tested growth, sticking, and invasion. Changing the gene altered cancer cell behavior. Protein tests traced its working pathway. A validated marker could help predict outcomes. It might also suggest new treatment angles for aggressive cases.
pmc-12719610:
Gong and co-authors study how the plant compound dauricine affects bladder cancer through the immune cells around the tumor. Macrophages of the M2 type help tumors grow and spread. Dauricine, from a Chinese herb, can slow several tumor types. Its effect on the tumor setting was unclear. Lab tests showed dauricine blocked M2 shifting in macrophages. It also pushed those cells toward an iron-driven form of cell death.

The effect ran through a protein called HCK and its downstream partner IDO1. Cancer cells under treatment also showed more ferritin breakdown. Together the changes slowed tumor progress in the models. The work names a pathway that future bladder cancer drugs might target.
pmc-12723410:
Augusto Cesar Hunt-Serracin and five co-authors study how a germ that causes lung disease builds its wall. Their work from twenty twenty-five looks at two proteins, MurA and CwlM. MurA helps make the wall, and CwlM can turn it on.

The team used a computer model to find where the two proteins meet. That spot has charge and sits far from a known switch site. Tests with changed proteins showed the boost needs this spot. In live cells, though, the harm from change was mild. Other unknown parts may help MurA work.
pmc-12724010:
Lei and co-authors track plant strategy shifts as karst vegetation recovers. The CSR frame sorts plants by competition, stress tolerance, and disturbance use. Five recovery stages ran from herbs to tree forest. Each stage held five large plots with four subplots each. Leaf traits came from 2,503 plants of 160 woody species.

A strategic trade-off showed as succession advanced. Early stages leaned one way, and later stages leaned another. Diversity and leaf traits both tied to the shift. Random forest and redundancy tools mapped the links. The authors say strategy mix marks recovery stage in karst lands.
pmc-12728210:
Sharafeldin, Marzouk, and Abdelghany pulse water through a solar heater and count the gains in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Flat plate collectors are a workhorse of solar heat. Pulsing the flow, rather than running it steady, may stir heat transfer. The team built a full test rig outdoors. They measured pressure, flow, sunlight, and temperatures in and out.

They scored the setup three ways: energy quality, money, and emissions saved. Pulsing at the best setting pushed the top efficiency figure well above steady flow. Disorder measures fell too. The cost of the heat produced was worked out per unit. Such triple checks help buyers judge a tweak beyond raw heat. Solar engineers are the readers.
pmc-12729010:
Yan Chen and ten colleagues sorted septic shock patients into blood-flow subphenotypes and asked who benefits from fluids. Aggressive fluid resuscitation is standard, yet evidence on which circulation patterns gain most is thin. The twenty twenty-five retrospective study covered 691 patients monitored with PiCCO devices at a Chinese tertiary hospital. Latent profile modelling grouped patients using all measured hemodynamic parameters.

A four-profile model fit best. One group was hyperdynamic, with high cardiac output and low vascular resistance. Another carried the highest preload, and a third was hypodynamic with low output and high resistance. The team then tested how forty-eight-hour fluid balance related to intensive care death within each group. The approach aims to match fluid strategy to a patient's circulation pattern rather than treating all shock alike.
pmc-12729310:
Elisabetta Tumminelli and co-authors present a 2025 study on using whole olive pruning waste, branches and leaves together, as a source of healthy compounds. Olive growing makes heaps of prunings, but most recovery efforts chase leaves only, and sorting leaves out is costly. The team asked whether the unsorted mix gives extracts as strong as leaf-only ones.

Using a designed set of thirteen extraction runs, they tuned solvent mix, heat, and time. Scaled-up extracts were then tested in chemical assays and on skin cells facing oxidative stress. The mixed-waste extracts matched leaf extracts in antioxidant strength. The authors present unsorted waste as a simpler, greener feedstock.
pmc-12731110:
Wang and three co-authors probe how speech and reading link in the brains of three-tongue speakers in this twenty twenty-five study. The group spoke Uyghur first, then Chinese, then English, a mix that pulls apart age of learning from daily use. That split lets the team test which force shapes each skill.

Inside, one hundred forty-four speakers named pictures in one tongue, then judged words in a second tongue. Words heard in speech sped word calls across tongues, which shows a shared word store. Speech pull was ruled by how early a tongue was learned, with the first tongue on top. Word uptake was ruled by how much a tongue is used, with the town-dominant tongue on top.
pmc-12731310:
Jinghui Zhang and seven colleagues run a randomized trial of ultrasound-guided lung treatment for early-born babies, in a twenty twenty-five study. Babies born before thirty-two weeks often lack lung surfactant, a soapy layer that keeps air sacs open. Standard guides dose it by symptoms and oxygen need. The team instead dosed by lung ultrasound scans and a scan score in eighty-nine infants.

The scan group needed breathing machines less often and for fewer days. They also used less surfactant, got the first dose sooner, and faced fewer X-ray exposures. The authors say scan guidance sharpens both diagnosis and dosing for this common newborn problem, sparing babies radiation and drug.
pmc-12731410:
Natassia Rodrigo and colleagues study how weight loss before pregnancy shapes the placenta in obese mice. Obesity in pregnancy can harm how the placenta handles food and signals for the growing young. Female mice fed a rich diet lost weight either by a switch to plain food or by a drug that curbs hunger. The team then read the chemistry and gene activity of the placenta late in pregnancy.

The rich diet lowered key building blocks for protein and raised signs of stress and inflammation. The plain-food switch eased both. The drug eased signs of metabolic stress but not inflammation. The paper weighs how each route to weight loss lands on the placenta.
pmc-12732110:
Taein Lee and co-authors test a gene-silencing strategy against kidney cancer in mice in a 2025 study. The target is EphA2, a receptor that helps tumor cells behave badly. The team grew kidney tumor cells with the gene knocked down and implanted them under the kidney capsule of mice, the organ's true site.

Tumors with the gene silenced grew far less than controls, weighed much less at harvest, and showed more cell death. Two partner signals that drive malignant behavior, FAK and RhoA, also quieted. The authors read the pathway as a promising drug target for renal cell carcinoma and call for work toward treatments that block it.
pmc-12735410:
Hongyan Cheng and co-authors published this study in 2025. It follows soil microbes across forty-five years of tree planting on once-open land. The focus is carbon use efficiency: how much carbon microbes keep for growth versus breathing out. That balance helps decide whether soil gains or loses carbon. The team paired a tracer method with gene surveys along the planting timeline.

Efficiency rose as the forest aged, and it rose alongside soil carbon stores. Gene patterns explain part of the shift. Microbes rich in resource-gathering genes used carbon more efficiently. Those rich in stress-tolerance genes used it less so. The authors read this as a strategy shift: as conditions ease, microbes spend less on defense and more on growth and yield. That shift may help planted forests lock carbon away.
pmc-12736010:
Ewa Skała and Agnieszka Kicel published this study in 2025. It grows shoots of maral root, a Siberian medicinal plant, in a temporary-immersion bioreactor and measures their output of caffeoylquinic acids, antioxidant compounds prized from the plant. Wild supply is limited, so bioreactor production matters.

Two dials were tested: growing time, three versus five weeks, and how often the shoots were dunked in nutrient fluid. Five weeks with ninety-minute dunk cycles gave the most biomass. Three-hour cycles gave the best compound yield per reactor, led by chlorogenic acid, the family's best-known member. The extract scavenged three kinds of damaging radicals in test-tube assays. The authors conclude the PlantForm bioreactor suits this species well, and that immersion rhythm is a real production variable, not a detail. Tuning it lets growers trade bulk against potency for the market they serve.
pmc-12738610:
Bingxin Zhong and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on tar-like pollutants in the mud of lagoons in Lingshui County, Hainan. The lagoons form the island's first marine special reserve, yet little was known about these pollutants there. The team sampled surface mud in spring and sorted out where the pollution comes from and how much risk it poses.

Levels ran from low to middling, with six-ring forms making up over half the total. Math models pointed to burning of fossil fuels and plant matter as the main sources. Risk scores came out low to moderate for lagoon life. The study gives local managers a baseline and a source map for keeping the reserve clean.
pmc-12746010:
Ahmed Abdirahman Ahmed, Gökçen Yıldız, and Adadi Parise test ways to dry mango into powder faster without losing its good traits. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Drying method shapes both the cost of the powder and how much of the fruit's value survives.

The team paired ultrasound pre-treatment with three drying routes: hot air, microwave, and a mix of both. Thirty minutes of ultrasound plus the mixed route cut drying time by eighty percent. Plain microwave drying kept the most health-linked compounds, while hot air alone gave the powder the best handling traits, like density and flow. Ultrasound also made the powder dissolve and swell better. The authors frame the choice as a trade-off by goal.
pmc-12748610:
Moh Sofi'ul Anam and colleagues pool thirty-six trials on feeding microalgae to laying hens, in this meta-analysis from twenty twenty-five. Microalgae bring omega-3 fats, pigments, and antioxidants to the feed bag, but trial results have been patchy. The pooled verdict sorts the real effects from the noise.

The hens ate no more or less, yet laid more and heavier eggs, with stronger shells and better internal quality scores. Yolks turned deeper and redder in color. Their fat profile shifted the way nutritionists hope: more of the prized omega-3s, including EPA and DHA, and less omega-6, cutting the ratio between them. Blood cholesterol and liver enzymes fell, suggesting healthier livers. The authors conclude microalgae earn their place as a functional feed additive that upgrades both hen and egg.
pmc-12749210:
Feng Zhou and co-authors build a language model tool that finds viral traces in tumor gene data, in work from twenty twenty-five. Viruses may help start or drive some cancers, so finding them in tumor samples matters. Older tools align sequences, but fast viral change and gaps in viral genomes limit them.

The tool, called ViTrace, learns from DNA context, position links, and protein code data at once. It trained on just thirteen species yet recalled most strains from hundreds of unseen species in tests. Applied to single cell data from two throat area cancers, it showed virus patterns by tumor, cell, and patient. Some viruses found were not reported before. The frame could guide precise cancer care.
pmc-12749610:
Israel and Parnas build a fruit fly system to study how nerve circuits remodel as the animal grows in twenty twenty-five. One named neuron drives backward walking in adults. The team shows its circuit persists from larva to adult in conserved form. That span lets them watch remodeling live across life stages.

A gene control mechanism for outgrowth is described in the system. A causal link from remodeling to behavior is also shown. The circuit is small, well mapped, and tied straight to motor output. Driver lines give precise access to its cells. The authors offer it as a clean lab bench for circuit change.
pmc-12750610:
Luciana Sobral and a large team track tuberculosis spread to children and teenagers living with lung TB patients in Brazil. Their prospective cohort study was published in twenty twenty-five. Young contacts are prime targets for preventive treatment, if infection is caught.

Five hundred and sixty-two close contacts aged eighteen or under were followed for six months across several centers. Checks included exams, chest imaging, and a blood test for TB infection. A positive test at start or a switch to positive by month six counted as infection. About three in ten contacts were infected. Models then weighed which household and patient traits raised a child's risk.
pmc-12751010:
Vikas Ashokrao Sadaphal, Hsin-Ru Wu, and Rai-Shung Liu report a gold-driven reaction in this twenty twenty-five chemistry paper. They joined two kinds of starting material: a chain with both a double and a triple bond, and a nitrone, a nitrogen-oxygen compound. Gold steered the joining.

The reaction adds carbon and nitrogen groups side by side along the chain, then cuts the double bond. Tracing the steps, the team found an early attack by a nitrogen partner, followed by a cascade with the nitrone before the cut. Such routes can build complex molecules for drug and material research in fewer steps.
pmc-12751410:
Yang Liao and co-authors set out a trial protocol testing calligraphy training for stroke recovery in a 2025 paper. Stroke often leaves lasting problems with thinking and arm movement. Standard rehabilitation helps but can be costly, hard to reach, and easy to drop. Calligraphy practice combines fine hand movement with attention and memory, which may aid both domains at once.

The trial will enroll ninety-three patients in early recovery at one Shanghai hospital. Patients are assigned by chance to calligraphy plus routine care, a reading control, or routine care alone, over four weeks. A light-based brain imaging method will track activity changes in the cortex. Thinking, arm function, grip, and daily living skills are also measured. The authors aim to reveal both whether the training works and how the brain changes with it.
pmc-12756110:
Felipe de Sousa and co-authors lay out in 2025 how to diagnose the most common heart disease of cats. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy the heart wall thickens, sometimes silently, sometimes ending in heart failure. No single blood test proves it, so vets must combine several kinds of evidence.

The paper walks through that combination: history and hands-on exam first, then blood markers that support but cannot confirm the diagnosis. Heart tracings can hint at conduction trouble. Ultrasound of the heart remains the gold standard, confirming the thickening and guiding staging and treatment. The authors argue that an integrated workup prevents missed or wrong diagnoses and improves care for affected cats.
pmc-12757110:
Sathyaseelan Arumugam and four co-authors review surgery choices for two uncommon colon cancer sites in a 2025 paper. Cancers of the transverse colon and the splenic bend are rarer than other colon cancers. Surgeons still debate how much bowel to remove and how widely to clear lymph nodes.

The review follows standard reporting rules across seven databases through mid-2024. Seven studies covering hundreds of cases compared limited segment removal with extended removal. Robotic, keyhole, and open techniques all appear in the limited approach group. Safety around surgery and long-term cancer outcomes were weighed side by side. The synthesis helps surgical teams judge whether smaller operations cost patients anything in cure odds.
pmc-12764110:
Ye Li and eight co-authors build computer models to flag a thyroid problem in sepsis patients in a 2025 study. In severe illness the thyroid often slows even though the gland itself is healthy, a state called non-thyroidal illness syndrome. Finding which sepsis patients face this state, and which may die, could guide care.

The team drew records from 963 patients and trained eight learning methods. One method best predicted who would develop the syndrome, while another best predicted death among those who had it. Low thyroid hormone levels marked higher risk, and factors such as breathing machines and organ failure marked death risk. The authors warn that one hospital's data limits the findings.
pmc-12764210:
Tiara Resmi, Oki Suwarsa, and Irna Sufiawati report a rare case of a blistering form of lupus that struck mainly inside the mouth, in this 2025 case report. The disease, bullous lupus, affects fewer than five in a hundred lupus patients, and mouth involvement is usually mild. Heavy mouth disease as the lead sign is very uncommon and hard to pin down.

Their patient was a twenty-nine-year-old woman with a week of severe mouth ulcers, fever, and painful swallowing. Tissue samples showed the split-under-the-surface pattern of the disease, letting the team diagnose it without an advanced test they lacked. Treatment mixed mouth care with steroid infusions and an immune-calming drug. All lesions healed fully within four weeks. The case shows careful clinic work can both name and tame this rare presentation.
pmc-12772010:
Liying Wang and co-authors explore how women with ovarian cancer experience cancer-related thinking problems, in this 2025 study. Such impairment is among the most common and lasting symptoms these patients report. Thirty-one women at a Shanghai cancer center gave in-depth interviews about a year after diagnosis on average. The team coded the accounts using symptom management theory.

Four themes emerged. Women described subtle decline in memory and attention, though some barely noticed change. They blamed surgery anesthesia, chemotherapy, and tangled symptom clusters, while also withdrawing socially. Daily life disruption felt contained, but confidence in their own ability eroded. Coping meant cutting mental load, using compensating tricks, or passive acceptance. The authors call for culturally sensitive, patient-centered support for this symptom.
pmc-12772210:
Handuo Shi and co-authors model how a bacterial filament senses the shape of the cell surface it clings to in a 2025 paper. The filament, a relative of actin called MreB, guides wall building in rod-shaped bacteria and gathers where the surface curves in certain ways. Why it prefers those spots was not known.

Their model weighs the energy of twisting and bending a filament against the geometry of the surface beneath it. It predicts that a strongly twisted filament favors spots with lower values of two curvature measures. Simulations of the filament's stiffness gave length scales matching real cells. The preference held even without motion or rebuilding cycles. The findings suggest plain energy balance explains the pattern, and they offer design ideas for shape-sensing nano materials.
pmc-12775410:
Sudhakar and Muthucumaraswamy report a study from two thousand twenty-five on using machine learning to improve footwear production. Factories track defects, downtime, energy use, and output speed. The team asked whether tuning a prediction model could lift all of these at once on a real shop floor.

They refined a logistic regression model until its accuracy rose and it classified every defect-free output correctly. It beat rival methods such as support vector machines and naive Bayes on several scores. The gains in prediction led to real process gains: higher throughput, less equipment downtime, and lower energy use. The authors argue that tuned classifiers joined with live factory data can make shoe production both leaner and greener.
pmc-12783310:
Grahmm A Funk and co-authors compared two bone cements as local carriers for a cancer drug, in a study published in 2025. After a bone tumor is removed, cement fills the gap and steadies the bone. Loading that cement with the drug doxorubicin could attack leftover cancer cells right where they hide.

The standard cement weakened when the drug was mixed in, and drug released from it killed cancer cells less well in dishes. The likely cause is a clash between the drug and the cement's hardening chemistry. A newer cement based on different chemistry kept its strength with the drug aboard, and its released drug worked at full strength. The authors present the newer material as a strong candidate where bones must bear load and deliver treatment at once.
pmc-12785110:
Labeling cell types in single-cell data often means borrowing labels from a reference set, but batch differences between labs distort the patterns. Ming Zhang and co-authors present PLKD in this 2025 paper, a method that learns biological patterns instead of raw gene readings.

A large teacher model groups genes into sets that each stand for a biological function, then passes its knowledge to a small, fast student model. Working at the pattern level makes the labels steadier across batches, and the student stays robust to noise. Benchmarks show accurate annotation, and the design also handles data that mixes several measurement types.
pmc-12786610:
Krzysztof Żerdziński and four co-authors survey systematic reviews of artificial intelligence in intensive care and grade how ready the field is for real use, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Critical care is time-pressed and data-rich, fertile ground for AI support, but weak validation makes it risky too.

Thirty-four reviews across five ICU domains fed the overview. Prediction and early warning tools dominated, mostly in adults and built on health records. Reports touted accuracy ranges, yet calibration and bedside usefulness were rarely addressed. Readiness signals clustered at low to middling levels, with no sign of routine regulated deployment. The authors call for outside validation, real-world impact trials, fuller reporting, and governance work.
pmc-12790810:
Courage O Idahor and co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, radiofrequency ablation as a treatment for chronic pain. The method uses heat from radio waves, sent through a needle, to disrupt the nerve paths that carry pain. It serves pain from the spine, damaged nerves, and even cancer that resists other care. Many patients get too little relief from drugs, or suffer side effects they cannot bear.

It explains how lesions form, compares where each form fits, and weighs trial and guideline evidence. Newer tools such as live imaging, robotic help, and pairing with healing therapies are also covered. Safety risks and fair access close the authors' account.
pmc-12796410:
Nadezhda Sutormina, Inna Kalabina, Victoria Efimova, and Elena Nikolaeva studied brain links in young children and how they tie to memory and screen use, in twenty twenty-five. They recorded brain waves from thirty-one children aged five to seven, just before and just after a short smartphone game. They then gauged how brain areas link up, using graph measures of how tight and how spread the web is.

In faster waves, the stronger group also showed more local grouping. pmc-12797810:
Dingding Wang and co-authors study muscle loss risk across a combined syndrome spectrum in a 2025 paper. Sarcopenia, the steady loss of muscle, drives disability and raises death risk. Heart, kidney, and metabolic problems each feed it, but their joint effect was unmapped.

Muscle loss was judged by a standard national criteria set. Statistical models test how risk grows by stage and whether inactivity multiplies it. The multisystem view may help clinics spot high-risk patients earlier and target activity programs where they count most.
pmc-12804810:
Dongying Zhao and Maofa Jiang wrote a paper in twenty twenty-five on how steel plants can manage their energy loads with a fuzzy decision method. Making steel uses huge amounts of energy, so the choice among load plans shapes both cost and how green the plant is. The plans must be weighed on many points at once, and expert views are often vague.

The pair built a model on the Fermatean fuzzy FUCA method, which ranks options even when judgments are vague. They scored fifteen plans on gains and costs, with input from experts in the field. The model picked out the plans that work best and can be done, and dropped ones that cost too much or are hard to run. When they changed the weights, the rankings stayed much the same. Checks against like methods backed the model too.
pmc-12808310:
Tiwen Lu and co-authors report a new way to make a 3D-printed alloy stay strong and stretchy at very low temperatures, in a 2025 paper. Tiny hard particles can strengthen metals, but laser printing leaves little control over how they form. The team starts with powder grains of a cobalt-chromium-nickel alloy coated with nanoparticles of titanium carbide.

During printing, the first laser pass melts the coating into the alloy. Later passes reheat the metal, and the particles form again in place, small and evenly spread. At near-liquid-helium cold, the printed alloy pairs high strength with high ductility, and the team says the trick should transfer to other printed alloys.
pmc-12816610:
Zhou and a large team build a battery free, wireless patch and implant that tracks body pressure signals in twenty twenty-five. pmc-12817510:
Juan Izquierdo-Condoy and co-authors measure high-risk HPV infection in Ecuadorian women, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. HPV drives cervical cancer, and past Ecuador counts swung widely. Screening program data held over sixteen thousand valid tests from health centers across the land.

About eleven percent tested positive for the virus. Women in their thirties made up the largest share of positives. One pooled group of five types led the finds, at over forty percent of positives. About one in seven positive women carried several types at once. Rates sat below past national claims but above global norms.
pmc-12819410:
Tim Wehnes and co-authors present a 2025 study of mouth bacteria, body age, and thinking in the oldest old. The group held 311 adults aged 85 and up, most of them Chinese, living in the community. Body age was read from DNA marks by four known aging clocks. Mouth bacteria were typed by gene reads, and mind and body function were scored by standard tests.

People whose body age ran young for their years held a less varied mouth mix. No single germ kind passed strict proof bars. Still, germ kinds that make short fatty acids leaned with both age gap and marks on brain-linked genes. One such kind tracked with better mind scores. Mouth care may join the map of healthy late aging.
pmc-12820310:
Prince Paul and co-authors published a study in 2025 on concrete reinforced with waste natural fibers, such as jute, coir from coconut husks, and bamboo. They compiled 444 concrete mix designs from the literature, each described by seven input variables. Six machine learning algorithms were trained and tuned on the data. A gradient boosting model performed best, with the strongest fit and the lowest prediction error. Analyses of which variables drove the predictions named cement content, water, and coarse aggregate as the dominant factors. Fiber content and curing time played a smaller but real part. To test the modeling, the team cast ten fresh mixes with coir fiber. A fiber share near three quarters of one percent gave the best strength improvement.
pmc-12820610:
Dong, Bradford, Barnett, and Duvall found in twenty twenty-five that bite acts reset a mosquito's day plan to help it lay eggs. The Aedes mosquito spreads dengue and Zika and needs a blood meal to grow its eggs. After the meal the bug rests, then shifts to hunt for egg sites.

Bugs with ripe eggs move more and switch their peak acts to night, when they seek damp spots to lay. A clock gene is key to that shift in time. With-out it, the hunt is off time and egg yield falls when a search is needed. The shift backs strong brood growth.
pmc-12822310:
Sophie Witter and colleagues assessed in 2025 what is known about money control at primary care clinics in poorer countries. Governments increasingly give clinics more say over their own funds, assuming it improves performance. The authors build a typology and a conceptual framework from that material. Their conclusion is careful: financial autonomy can help when it fits local conditions and comes with clear accountability, purchasing rules, and public finance support.
pmc-12827510:
Ahmed Aldohbeyb, Jozsef Vigh, and Kevin Lear study why nerve spikes change shape during repeated firing. Their neuroscience paper from twenty twenty-six records three neuron types. A neuron can fire varied spike shapes to the same input. That variability complicates how signals encode information.

Four spike features were tracked across bursts of firing. First spikes in each burst looked alike regardless of stimulus strength. Later spikes drifted steadily, more so under stronger drive. Computer models tested which mechanisms reproduce that drift. A shifting reversal potential is the suspect named in the title. Matching model to data narrows how spike encoding works. The results matter for reading neural codes accurately.
pmc-12829010:
Congbo Yue and five co-authors published a machine learning study in twenty twenty-five on screening blood tests for the cervical changes that precede cancer. High-grade lesions need early catching, but HPV testing and colposcopy can be invasive or hard to reach. A routine blood panel would be a gentler first filter.

Four feature selection methods narrowed the predictors, and eleven learning algorithms competed to classify risk. Performance was judged with accuracy curves, calibration, and decision analysis, and the best model became a web calculator. The authors propose it as a triage step before colposcopy in low-resource settings.
pmc-12830510:
Lea Doppelbauer and co-authors test how best to show breast cancer patients their own outcome reports as pictures. Their study appeared in 2025. Patients regularly report symptoms and well-being, and charts of those reports can guide shared decisions. Yet little is known about which chart designs patients grasp best. The team had co-designed several designs with patients and clinicians during a large trial of symptom monitoring.

After the trial, patients received a paper survey with their own report in the new designs. They rated how clear and useful each feature was and named their preferences. The team compared answers between the trial's two arms and across chart features. The findings point to designs that patients can read at a glance, a step toward reports that truly inform care talks.
pmc-12837110:
Nathalie Ouare and co-authors published this malaria study in 2025 from Nanoro, Burkina Faso. Dams and irrigation fight hunger and thirst, but still water can breed the mosquitoes that carry malaria. The team ran monthly household surveys from March 2022 to February 2023 in five villages set three to forty kilometers from the Soum dam. Blood from 13,786 people was checked for the main malaria parasite.

Silent carriage, at 24.5 percent, beat frank illness, at 19.5 percent. The village by the dam ran highest, near forty-two percent, and the far village lowest. Teens carried the most infection in every village. Rain, oddly, tied to lower risk once other traits were weighed. The authors urge joint action across health, water, and farming to blunt the dam's malaria cost.
pmc-12838010:
Luyi Ying and co-authors published a 2025 case report of an eye infection blamed on human herpesvirus 7, a virus not known to affect the eye. The virus is a relative of the cold-sore virus family. It was known to target immune blood cells. No case in the cornea, the clear front of the eye, had been reported.

The patient was a thirty-two-year-old man who had received a corneal graft for a cone-shaped flaw. Twelve days later, a branching sore grew on the graft, the mark of the cold-sore virus family. Tear tests found the DNA of this virus, and none of its relatives. Drugs by mouth and drops cleared the surface in two weeks, as the viral markers fell. Pale bumps then appeared as he healed. At five weeks the virus was gone, and the eye stayed clear for eight months.
pmc-12844910:
Patricia Pérez-Pérez and a large team look for free-living amoebae in dry lands on a Spanish island. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. These tiny life forms live in soil and water all over the world. Some kinds can cause disease in people, so their spread near homes is a health concern.

They test soil and water samples from Fuerteventura with culture and gene tests. One genus ruled in soil, and one kind ruled in water. Gene tests were faster and cheaper, while culture proved the amoebae were alive and caught more kinds. Checks also found mixed germ loads in the water. The team urges care, since risky kinds live near people.
pmc-12849110:
Abi Crane, Juan Benito, Albert Chen, Daniel Ksepka, and Daniel Field use bird jaw bones to test fossil relationships. Their study from twenty twenty-five concerns the origin of crown birds. Fossils near that origin remain hard to place. Jaw bones hold useful clues, but their fused parts hid detail before.

Evidence from Asteriornis favoured gamebird-like relatives over primitive bird groups. Other fossils showed striking jaw similarities with each other. Those shared traits raise fresh questions about their placement. The work shows lower jaws deserve more weight in bird evolution studies.
pmc-12853910:
Fan He and colleagues profiled genes and proteins in myeloid cancers in 2025. Myeloid diseases overlap in their biology. Chronic forms can turn into acute leukemia. That turn brings poor prognosis quickly. Treatment options stay limited after transformation. Combined gene and protein data were analysed.

Shared features crossed disease boundaries clearly. A gene signature split prognosis groups. One growth pathway stood out strongly. That pathway looked druggable in models. A known inhibitor drug was tested. Animal models backed the inhibition effect. Risk sorting gains a new tool. Pathway therapy gains fresh rationale.
pmc-12875910:
Gabrielle Turcotte and co-authors wrote a study, dated 2025 in its text, on how horse competition organizers in Ontario handle biosecurity. Horses gather in large groups at events, where infections can spread fast. Organizers carry the duty of setting and enforcing the protective rules. The team interviewed ten organizers of English-style events, both sanctioned and not, about their experience.

Two themes emerged. First, biosecurity is a balancing act, weighed against cost, convenience, and the show's other demands. Second, the groups who share the duty, organizers, vets, riders, and governing bodies, often work at cross purposes. The authors note their sample may lean toward organizers already keen on the topic. Even so, they found broad willingness to cooperate on better practice. The study frames safer events as a shared project that needs every party's buy-in.
pmc-12882510:
Fatemeh Gabeleh, Mohammad Mahdavi, Mohammad Hadi Karbalaie Niya, and Mehrdad Ravanshad published this study in 2025. It tracks two common viruses in children who received heart transplants. Drugs that protect the new heart also weaken defenses, so dormant viruses can wake and cause harm.

The team followed twenty-eight children, testing blood at surgery and one and two months later, plus urine and donor heart tissue. Every child already carried antibodies to one virus, cytomegalovirus, and about two-thirds carried the other, Epstein-Barr virus. Active infection showed in roughly one in ten blood samples for the first virus. The second virus appeared in about a quarter of samples. Some donor hearts carried virus too. The authors urge long-term monitoring and preventive treatment for these children.
pmc-12895910:
David Wagaba and co-authors pool studies on brucellosis in people and livestock across Sub-Saharan Africa, in this 2025 paper. The neglected disease spreads from animals through milk, meat, and contact with birth materials. It burdens both health and farm incomes in the region.

The review searched six databases for studies from 2012 to 2024. Two hundred forty-two papers from twenty-five countries met the rules. Pooling their results gives a regional rate of past infection in humans and in farm animals. Such a map is a first step toward control plans that join human and animal health efforts.
pmc-12908310:
Masih Kameh Khosh and four co-authors describe a rare skin cancer that imitates breast cancer in this two thousand twenty-five case report. The tumor is a primary cutaneous apocrine carcinoma, a cancer of sweat gland type cells in the skin. It can look and stain under the microscope much like breast carcinoma. That likeness risks a wrong diagnosis and wrong treatment. Their patient was a sixty-year-old man who came to a breast clinic.

The team walks through the tests that separated skin origin from breast origin. Location, history, and marker patterns all played a part. The case warns doctors to keep this rare tumor in mind when a breast-like cancer appears in skin. Pathologists and breast specialists are the audience.
pmc-12913710:
Amelia Anshar and co-authors test a tropical fish as an early-warning species for plastic pollution in two thousand twenty-five. Stress gene reads tracked detox, antioxidant, and inflammation markers. The paired tissue and gene data judge both the harm styrene does at low doses and the fish's worth as a monitor for the region's waters.
pmc-12916410:
Rosa Eckert and eleven co-authors published a stroke study in twenty twenty-six on the dangerous hours after heart surgery, when a clot can fly to the brain. At a large academic heart center, thirty-nine patients received mechanical clot removal for major artery strokes following cardiac procedures between twenty eighteen and twenty twenty-two. The team charted who they were and how they fared.

Strokes clustered after assist-device surgery most often, then bypass grafting and valve replacement. Half the cases were wake-up strokes, found on waking rather than witnessed. pmc-13087110:
Bahari, Jazinaki, Asadi, and Golafrouz review curcumin and turmeric supplements for blood sugar control in twenty twenty-six. Curcumin is the main active compound in turmeric. They also lowered fasting insulin and a measure of insulin resistance. One measure of beta cell function did not change. pmc-13104410:
Van Niekerk, Cloete, Van der Kooy, and Hamman published in twenty twenty-six a study of cannabis compounds as possible migraine aids. Migraine can disable a person for hours at a time. Four compounds bound the receptor well in the screen. They then tested passage of those compounds across sheep nasal tissue in the lab. Some crossed about as well as mid-level standard drugs. pmc-13110610:
Loreto Lancia, Angelo Dante, Valeria Caponnetto, Cristina Petrucci, Vittorio Masotta, Leondino Mammarella, and Silvio Romano chart heart failure trends in a central Italian province in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Models weighed which traits forecast new cases and death. The work gives a local baseline for planning care as the population ages.
pmc-13128610:
Jose Castro and co-authors tally the public cost of Hansen's disease in Brazil in a 2026 study. National benefit records supplied the spending side. The overview shows how much of the disease's burden lands on the public purse, a figure that strengthens the case for finding cases early.
pmc-13130710:
Joseph Cornelius and Fabio Rinaldi test whether fake clinical notes can train software that scrubs real ones, in a paper dated 2026. pmc-13135510:
Oliver Kohl, Chetan Gohil, Matthias Sure, Alfons Schnitzler, and Esther Florin wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It studies how activity in a small deep brain region, the subthalamic nucleus, lines up with large brain networks in people with Parkinson's disease.

Recordings were taken with and without the patients' usual dopamine medicine. A model sorted the shifting brain states into large-scale networks. Links between the deep region and a motor-planning area grew stronger during two of those networks. pmc-13146210:

pmc-13147110:
Hyesun Jeong, Mi-Ae You, and Yoonju Lee track how happiness changes in early teens in South Korea. The early teen years bring fast shifts in body, feelings, and social life. Ties with parents set the starting level but not the slope of change. The authors urge help that starts near age eleven, built in schools and homes alike. pmc-13157810:
Şaban Melih Şimşek and co-authors measure artery stiffness across lung disease stages, in work published in 2026. Blood pressure traits stayed strongly tied to stiffness. Age was the top driver in the full model. The authors urge early heart checks keyed to pressure, not lung scores.
pmc-13162210:
Publication bias, the tendency for positive studies to appear in print more often, can distort meta-analyses. Simulations checked how well it adjusts for bias against rival methods, and several real data sets show its range across odds ratios and proportions with rare outcomes. The authors offer it as a practical way to gauge how much selective publication might be bending a rare-event meta-analysis.
pmc-13163710:
Jia-Wei Liu and co-authors test gene sequencing for stubborn skin infections in a 2026 pilot study. pmc-13163810:

pmc-13178910:

pmc-13180110:

One weight-loss drug and one vessel drug ranked highest by one method. Anti-inflammatory drugs appeared as a notable group too. Cancer drugs acted fastest, at about four months on average. pmc-13184010:
Hamad Algamaiah, writing alone, reviews a dental method that seals exposed dentin right after a tooth is prepared for a crown, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. The proof shows better bond strength and longer bond life than late sealing. Sealed teeth also let less fluid through and hurt less after care. Several glue styles and extra resin layers were weighed. Clinical studies report good comfort and lasting repairs. The author backs the method but notes study flaws and calls for longer trials.
pmc-13189010:

Younger patients use more of these services than older ones. The authors conclude referrals still come late in the disease course.
pmc-13190210:
Jiangping Fu and four co-authors set out a trial of heritage sport for health change in young adults. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The lead aim is to check a model that links class level, bodily skill, and a teach-practise-play path. Side reads map the mind traits that shift as habits change. Skill and mood facts are logged across set waves, with mixed models for the main read.
pmc-13192010:

pmc-13194210:
Masaki Iino, writing alone in 2026, proposes a concept called Integrative Intelligence, a way of describing how people judge well when time, roles, and body signals must be held together at once. The study uses self-ethnography, the author studying his own experience, drawing on mountaineering logs, body data, dialogues with an AI, and later reflections. Four linked lenses are developed, including an inner conference of viewpoints and AI as a reflective surface. Three mountain cases show the same constraint pattern producing distinct modes of judgment, supporting the claim that the mode is context-sensitive.
pmc-13194610:
Sihui Wen and ten co-authors trace a gene control chain behind age-related hearing loss in this two thousand twenty-six paper. This hearing loss is permanent and grows more common as populations age. That chain controls autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning process, in the ear's hair cells.

In aging models, the mark and the gene moved in opposite directions. Tuning the chain changed waste buildup and cell death in hair cells. A broad multi-omics scan mapped the wider effects. The work names a possible drug target for a condition with no cure.
pmc-13194710:

When virus was added as the balls formed, infection stayed trapped in the well-fed outer rim. When cells were infected first in normal air, the virus spread evenly through the ball. The pattern shows timing and oxygen together shape the attack. The authors urge that virus therapies be tested in such 3D, low-oxygen models. Flat dishes, they warn, flatter the virus.
pmc-13194910:
