Their method adds a robust cost function, Tukey Biweight, which down-weights wild data points, and models chaotic signal behavior with a Chebyshev-based generator. Monte Carlo simulations, repeated random trials, compared four variants. The combined chaotic and robust version consistently gave the best accuracy and resolution, especially at low signal-to-noise ratios and high signal correlation. The authors propose it for practical wireless and radar systems.
pmc-13197110:
Hiwot Abebe Haileslassie and colleagues report a 2026 pilot study of a pulse food toolkit for preschool children. Pulses are dry beans, peas, and lentils. Early tastes shape later eating, so the toolkit aimed to make pulses familiar in childcare centers.

The program ran three months in two centers in Saskatoon, with fifty children and eight staff. It mixed weekly lessons, new recipes, a food guide for cooks, and parent newsletters. Children got slightly better at naming chickpeas, beans, and peas, though gains were not firm proof. Children still ate more of the usual dishes than the pulse dishes. Staff views and food content checks round out the pilot's lessons.
pmc-13198510:
Jefté Peper-Nascimento and colleagues studied stress and sepsis effects on rat brain growth factors in a 2026 paper. Sepsis is a life-threatening body-wide response to infection. Long mild stress can reshape brain chemistry, so the team asked whether the two combine to lower nerve support proteins.

Rats went through a sepsis procedure, then thirty days of mild stress drills. Blood and two brain areas were tested for five support proteins and two stress hormones. Stress raised both hormones, while sepsis alone did not. Stress lowered four support proteins in both brain areas, with or without sepsis. Sepsis alone also lowered several, with strength by protein and region. No combined boost appeared.
pmc-13198610:
Xinpeng Zuo and six co-authors study gene control in a single-celled organism in this two thousand twenty-six paper. The organism, Paramecium tetraurelia, carries two kinds of nuclei in one cell. Small germline nuclei pass genes to offspring, while one big somatic nucleus runs daily life. During sex, the germline nuclei divide by meiosis and the big nucleus breaks apart. The team focused on a family of transcription factors called TFDP.

They found sixteen members of the family, a striking expansion. Two of them play double roles in the process. They guide meiosis in the germline nuclei and also steer the fragmentation of the somatic one. The work shows how one cell juggles two nuclear fates. Cell biologists who study reproduction are the readers.
pmc-13199410:
Christina Sauter and colleagues studied hidden neck spread in nose and sinus cancers across centers in a 2026 review. These cancers are rare, and no standard rule guides neck surgery when scans look clear. Doctors must choose between preventive neck dissection, removing neck nodes, and watchful scanning.

The study pooled 438 patients treated from 2012 to 2022. Hidden spread appeared in eight percent of patients whose necks looked clear on scans. One fourth got preventive neck surgery. Squamous cell type was the sole early risk flag for hidden spread. Patients with hidden spread had far worse five-year disease-free survival. Given the low spread rate, the authors question routine preventive surgery and urge case-by-case calls.
pmc-13200610: Yefei Zhang and colleagues are authors of a 2013 article retracted by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences, as recorded in a 2026 notice. The article claimed a small RNA molecule blocked cell death in vessel lining cells exposed to oxidized cholesterol. An inquiry found image editing and duplication shared with another paper submitted at the same time by a different group. The board lost trust in the findings and retracted the work. The authors were informed and gave no comment.
pmc-13201610:
Worries about fertility after cancer can weigh heavily on survivors, and a 2026 study headed by Shaimaa Mohamed Amin examines how a partner's support fits into that burden. The research article tests whether partner support carries part of the link between reproductive health concerns and psychological distress.

The cross-sectional study surveyed 202 married female cancer survivors, aged twenty to forty-nine, attending oncology departments at Tanta University Hospital in Egypt. Greater reproductive concerns came with greater distress, while stronger partner support came with less of both. Statistical mediation analysis supported a partial indirect effect through partner support, leading the authors to recommend couple-focused counselling in survivorship care.
pmc-13202010:
Removing excess fluid is delicate when septic shock has weakened the heart, and a 2026 study protocol by Jing-Chao Luo sets out to test a hormone treatment for that phase. The protocol describes a single-center trial of recombinant human brain natriuretic peptide in adults recovering from septic shock with cardiac dysfunction and volume overload.

Thirty patients will receive a bolus followed by an infusion lasting up to seventy-two hours, with monitoring already in place. The main measure is the within-patient change in a venous return pressure gradient shortly after treatment begins. Secondary measures cover heart function, tissue perfusion, and congestion, with blood pressure instability as the key safety endpoint.
pmc-13202710:
Negative skin tests do not always rule out drug allergy, and a 2026 case report by Nur Betül Baştuğ İnan shows that gap for the antibiotic teicoplanin. The article presents a patient whose skin prick and intradermal tests for teicoplanin were negative, yet who reacted during a supervised drug challenge.

The 66-year-old woman had been referred with suspected drug allergy after treatment that included teicoplanin a week earlier. During provocation testing she developed an immediate skin reaction despite the reassuring earlier test results. The authors note that reports of IgE-mediated teicoplanin allergy are rising, and they argue this case tempers claims that skin testing reliably predicts such reactions.
pmc-13204510:
Omar Alkathiri and Moishe Liberman review, in a 2026 paper, how doctors stage lung cancer by checking the lymph nodes between the lungs. That step decides who gets surgery and what treatment follows. The old standard, a surgical look inside the chest, has largely given way to ultrasound scopes passed through the airways or the food pipe. Each scope reaches different node stations. Used together, they sample more nodes with few complications.

The review explains where the combined approach shines and where it falls short. A negative result still needs surgical confirmation in some situations. The authors also fit the technique into the newest staging classification, which splits nodes into finer categories and makes tissue proof even more valuable. They discuss its role in molecular testing and modern treatment planning, and call the combined scopes central to today's lung cancer care.
pmc-13206610:
Beata Morak-Mlodawska and colleagues tested a family of sulfur and nitrogen ring compounds against melanoma cells in the lab in two thousand twenty-six. Melanoma needs new drug candidates, and these compounds were newly made. Growth tests covered four melanoma cell lines plus normal skin cells for comparison.

One compound stood out, stopping melanoma growth most strongly while harming normal skin cells less. Closer study showed it damaged DNA, drained protective cell chemicals, disturbed cell power stations, and pushed cells into programmed death. Chemists gain a lead structure whose multi-pronged attack could guide further drug design work.
pmc-13208710:
Jiraphorn Issara-Amphorn and co-authors profiled how immune cells respond to two forms of a bacterial molecule, in a 2026 study. Macrophages sense bacterial parts through a receptor called TLR4 and launch defense. Many bacteria slim down the sensed molecule to dodge that alarm. The team compared a full form and a slim form of the molecule, given outside cells or slipped inside.

The full form sparked strong inflammation, with alarm proteins released and a cell-death pathway engaged. The slim form barely stirred the cells and failed to trigger that pathway. Protein-wide scans showed the full form rewired energy use and defense programs in set patterns. Weak doses of slim forms never reached those patterns. The authors read this as a threshold effect set by shape and entry route.
pmc-13213710:
Priya Arya and colleagues present in 2026 two newborns with Williams syndrome whose vocal cords were paralysed, an unusual pairing. The syndrome, caused by a small chromosome deletion, already demands care from many specialties, and airway feeding problems add heavy complexity.

One early-term infant had both vocal folds paralysed and went home with a tracheostomy plus a feeding tube. The second had one-sided paralysis and likewise needed a feeding tube and feeding therapy. The authors link the problem to deletion of the elastin gene region, which weakens connective tissue. Their account documents each infant's hospital course and treatment, offering guidance for teams facing similar fragile newborns.
pmc-13214310:
Shu Aizawa, Hikari Ohno, and Yutaka Yamamuro study how a fatty diet changes gene marks in mouse testes, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Obesity is tied to poorer male fertility, but the molecular path is murky. Male mice ate a control diet or a high-fat diet for eight weeks.

Fat-fed mice showed lower levels of a chemical mark on one core DNA-packing protein. The mark on a sister protein stayed flat. One eraser enzyme for the mark rose at both message and protein levels. Other close eraser enzymes did not change. The authors link the diet to a skewed gene-mark balance in the testes.
pmc-13216110:
Michael Y Zhao and co-authors present a 2026 case series on outcomes after laser treatment for symptomatic retinal breaks, tears in the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye. Laser sealing is the standard defence against retinal detachment.

The series covered 600 eyes from 572 patients. Detachment followed in 43 eyes, and extra laser treatment was needed in 66 eyes, most often for the original break. Multiple breaks, a replaced lens, and bleeding inside the eye raised the detachment risk, while multiple breaks also predicted retreatment. Results were similar whether residents or senior doctors performed the first treatment. The authors recommend regular follow-up after the initial laser session.
pmc-13216710:
Koutarou Matsumoto and co-authors present a 2026 validation study from a Japanese emergency department, testing whether general-purpose AI chatbots can predict poor recovery after bleeding inside the brain. Fast prognosis shapes early decisions, and specialists are not always at hand.

Using admission data and CT images, GPT-4.1 and GPT-5 scored discrimination close to a purpose-built machine learning model, with areas under the curve around 0.84 to 0.85. Their predictions were highly reproducible across runs. Calibration, however, lagged: the chatbots systematically underestimated risk, and their overall accuracy measures trailed the specialist model. Feeding model outputs into the prompts helped modestly. The authors position the chatbots as explanation aids beside, not instead of, dedicated prognostic models.
pmc-13217210:
Ünal and colleagues test whether a chemical pathway in the blood tracks brain inflammation in children with ADHD. Attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorder affects school, social, and family life, yet its biology stays partly unclear. The team measured kynurenine pathway products, which are made when the body processes tryptophan, in children never yet treated with ADHD drugs.

Blood came from 51 such children and 36 healthy peers of similar age and sex. Comparing the products and their ratios let the team probe links between immune activity and the disorder. If certain patterns hold up, they could point to inflammation's role in ADHD and, one day, to blood markers that support diagnosis.
pmc-13217710:
Karin Cato and co-authors present a 2026 mixed-methods study of how routine needle procedures, vaccinations and blood tests, are softened for babies in Swedish child health care. The work is framed by Kolcaba's Comfort Theory, sorting findings into relief, ease, and transcendence.

Sixteen professionals, forty parents, and twenty-seven infants up to five months old took part. Practice that eased the experience included preparing parents with honest information about pain and relief options, and supporting them during the procedure. It also included keeping the setting calm and using comfort measures such as breastfeeding or sweet solutions. Safety handling of the infant and a sense of well-being afterwards also mattered. The authors distil the findings into practical steps clinics can adopt without drugs or new equipment.
pmc-13217910:
Yibo Chen and colleagues published a 2026 review on the host factors that shape Chikungunya virus infection. The virus spreads through mosquito bites and causes fever, rash, and joint pain that can linger for months or years. No approved antiviral drug targets it directly, so attention has turned to the human proteins the virus depends on.

The review maps how host factors control each stage of the viral life cycle, from cell entry and genome copying to assembly and release. It also weighs how these factors differ across cell types and drive inflammation and chronic joint disease. The authors judge which host targets look most druggable and survey drug candidates aimed at viral proteins and host dependencies alike. Because host-directed drugs sidestep the resistance that rapid viral mutation creates, the review frames them as a promising route toward treatment.
pmc-13219110:
Tejas Subramanian and Sravisht Iyer reply to a letter criticizing their study of frailty and outcomes after minimally invasive spine surgery in 2026 correspondence. Their work linked a high score on the five-item modified frailty index to worse outcomes and lower return to activities after one- or two-level fusion surgery. The letter writers raised concerns, and this response answers them point by point.

The authors accept several limits, including the small number of frail patients and bias in which patients received follow-up CT scans, and agree prospective studies are needed. They note the link between frailty and outcomes grew stronger across frailty levels, a dose-response pattern supporting the finding. Suggestions to model the index continuously, use time-to-event methods, and test removing one index item are welcomed as extensions. Confounders such as bone density and opioid dose matter but were not the study's target.
pmc-13220810:
Jin Yang and colleagues review risk prediction models for blood clots in multiple myeloma in a 2026 review and meta-analysis, and the verdict is unflattering. Myeloma patients clot at high rates, and models that flag the riskiest patients could target prevention, but clinicians had no account of whether the scores work. Four databases were searched to March 2026.

Fourteen studies covered seven assessment tools between them. Across the studies, 7.9 percent of myeloma patients developed venous thromboembolism. Pooled accuracy for the tools ranged from poor to modest, with areas under the curve between 0.57 and 0.68, and two related scores, IMPEDE VTE and its successor, performed least badly. Almost no study checked whether predicted risks matched observed ones, every study carried a high risk of bias on appraisal, and all models were published as formulas nobody has road-tested. The authors recommend updating and externally validating the tools rather than minting new ones.
pmc-13221510:
Lingyao Zhou and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 using genetic instruments to test whether blood metabolites and fats actually cause breast cancer, rather than merely travel with it. The method, Mendelian randomization, borrows nature's random gene shuffling to mimic a trial. Data came from large genome studies of diet tastes, blood chemistry, and breast cancer subtypes.

Several tastes and metabolites showed causal links to risk, differing by hormone-receptor subtype. One pathway stood out: liking curry seemed to lower risk through a membrane fat, while liking tomato raised risk through a vitamin-linked ratio. Reverse checks and mediation analysis probed direction and mechanism. The authors say metabolic pathways may offer prevention targets.
pmc-13222010:
Yaqin Xiong and Zhihui Li write a 2026 letter questioning how a study of sitting time and urinary leakage framed its mediation results. The original work used cross-sectional data, where exposure, mediator, and outcome are measured at one time point. Xiong and Li argue such a design cannot support the strong mechanistic reading the paper's language encourages.

Body mass, diet inflammation scores, and a blood ratio served first as adjustment variables, then as mediators, which blurs what each estimate means. No causal diagram or sensitivity checks were reported. Baseline patterns also cut against a simple inflammation story. The letter urges authors to present such pathways as associations consistent with a mechanism, not proof of one.
pmc-13222410:
Yihang Xu and co-authors evaluate a cell-surface protein called SDC2 as a marker in gastric cancer, in a 2026 multi-center cohort study. Survival analyses were combined with pan-cancer comparisons, tissue staining, and single-cell data to test how SDC2 expression relates to patient outcomes and tumor behavior.

High SDC2 expression tracked with shorter survival, confirming it as an independent risk factor in their models. Tumors with more SDC2 showed more varied microenvironments, lower mutation burden, and weaker predicted response to immunotherapy. Similar expression patterns appeared across several other cancers. The authors propose SDC2 both as an early detection aid and as a possible treatment target worth developing.
pmc-13222610:
Mahmut Onur Kulturoglu, Lutfi Dogan, and Mehmet Ali Gulcelik compare complication rates across oncoplastic breast surgery techniques used after drug therapy, in a 2026 records study. Five hundred fifty-six patients who had level II oncoplastic surgery following neoadjuvant treatment between 2019 and 2025 were grouped by technique, from racquet and vertical patterns to batwing and letter-shaped mammoplasties.

Racquet and vertical patterns removed larger tissue volumes than the others. Those two groups also suffered clearly more overall and major problems, including wound opening, infection, and fluid collections. Standard severity grades and a combined index ran higher there too. The choice after drug therapy, the data suggest, carries real consequences for recovery.
pmc-13222810:
Xiaoxi Dai and Qi Zhao review heart harm in spine-stiffening diseases, in work published in 2026. Ankylosing spondylitis and its kin inflame the spine over years. Proof now ties them to more heart attacks, strokes, and rhythm flaws, plus silent vessel and heart changes found on scans.

Lasting body-wide swelling, mixed with classic risk traits, drives the harm through vessel wall stress and plaque growth. Drugs that block one swelling signal may guard the heart as they calm joints. The heart effects of other drug classes stay murky. The authors urge joint care that pairs disease control with heart checks and risk repair.
pmc-13223710:
Yang Song and co-authors use microwaves to bond soy protein with fenugreek gum, aiming for a better food ingredient, in a 2026 study. Soy protein isolate loses solubility near its isoelectric point, limiting drinks and emulsions. Three minutes of microwave treatment at high power drove the grafting reaction between protein and gum.

Solubility in that problem range nearly doubled after treatment. Emulsifying activity roughly tripled, stability rose more than sevenfold, and antioxidant capacity climbed sharply too. Structural measures showed the protein unfolded and bound the gum covalently. Five minutes of treatment overshot, clumping the protein and erasing gains. A short microwave window, the work shows, can upgrade plant protein fast.
pmc-13225010:
Yisheng You and co-authors report a 2026 randomised trial comparing two ultrasound-guided nerve blocks for recovery after keyhole chest surgery. One block targets muscles along the back, the other the space beside the spine, and a third group received standard multi-drug pain relief only. In total, 129 patients were assigned across the three arms.

Recovery quality scores a day after surgery were significantly higher in both block groups than in controls. Block patients also reported less pain at rest and while coughing during the first hours, needed less opioid during surgery, and pressed their pain pumps less often. Nausea, vomiting, and dizziness were less common too, and the back-muscle block matched the established spinal-space technique.
pmc-13227810:
Madita Mühlhaus and a German research network measure a 2026 sepsis signal inside patients' blood cells: activation of toll-like receptor 4, the sensor that detects bacterial toxins and fires inflammation. Drugs blocking this receptor helped animals but failed in human trials, raising the question of whether the receptor is even active in most patients. Blood samples from one hundred sepsis patients were tested on day one and day four with a sensitive proximity assay.

Overall activation was strikingly low, usually under one signal per cell. A minority subgroup, though, showed clearly raised activation, and those patients died at significantly higher rates within thirty days at both time points. The link held after adjusting for severity, age, infection site, and sex, defining a high-risk subtype.
pmc-13231410:
Shanmugavelu, Palanisamy, Venkateshwaran, and Thiyagarajan report a jaw tumor that mimicked a failed root canal in twenty twenty-six. Dark areas near a tooth root usually mean infection needing retreatment. Rarely, a benign tumor causes the same picture. Their patient was a twenty-four year old man with swelling and pain near an upper front tooth.

The tooth had already had root canal treatment, yet the lesion persisted. Surgery removed the tumor while his orthodontic treatment continued. Regeneration used bone grafts, platelet rich fibrin, and guided tissue techniques. The root tip was preserved rather than cut away. The authors say bioactive materials plus conservative surgery rebuilt bone predictably. The tooth was saved despite active orthodontic forces.
pmc-13233010:
Isabella Zai and Adrian Zai published a 2026 cohort study asking whether common skin conditions raise the risk of later anxiety in young adults. Conditions such as acne, psoriasis, and dermatitis affect many people aged 18 to 22 and can cause lasting distress. Using the TriNetX electronic health record network, the pair matched young adults with a skin diagnosis against similar peers without one, excluding anyone with earlier anxiety.

The skin condition group developed anxiety more often at one, three, and five years, and the gap between groups widened over time. Time-to-event analysis showed a modest but steady rise in risk, with hazard ratios between 1.12 and 1.14. The authors argue that skin care for young adults should include attention to mental health.
pmc-13234010:
Duorui Wang and colleagues published a 2026 robotics study on a gecko-inspired adhesive that can grip almost any surface. Robot hands struggle with objects that are fragile, heavy, or oddly shaped when they rely on squeezing. The team's adhesive stacks three layers: tiny mushroom-tipped structures that adjust their stiffness to microscopic roughness, a rigid film, and soft pillars that bend to match large contours.

The whole structure grows in one manufacturing step under an electric field. It held ten times more strongly than conventional designs across varied surfaces. Mounted on a multi-fingered robot hand, it lifted delicate, heavy, rough, and irregular objects, even under twisting loads. The authors present the pad as a route to gentler, more versatile robotic grasping.
pmc-13234710:
Aysha Imtiaz and co-authors investigated in 2026 whether sound waves plus friendly bacteria can improve the health value of Chinese yam. Chinese yam is a tuber long used as food and traditional medicine in East Asia. It carries compounds linked to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and immune effects. Fermentation with lactic acid bacteria can free more of those compounds from the tuber matrix.

Combining multi-frequency ultrasound with mixed bacterial cultures forms the processing idea under study. Ultrasound helps break plant tissue so bacteria and enzymes can reach trapped compounds. The work sets out to measure bioactive content, antioxidant activity, and structural changes after treatment. Earlier conventional fermentation left part of the yam's chemistry underused, including many secondary compounds. The authors frame the combined method as a way to raise the functional quality of yam products.
pmc-13236610:
Shao and four co-authors pooled proof in twenty twenty-six on if lymph node state after drug care guesses life span in lung cancer that can be cut. Care that pairs chemo with defense drugs is now a key first step for such cases. Node state after that care may add news past tumor shrink.

They kept works that split life by node state after care. Poor node state went with much worse life and worse free-of-ill time in the pool. Each pool held just two past works, both read back in time. The team urges care in use till planned checks back the link.
pmc-13236810:
Sharma and colleagues build a sensor for a cancer drug from layered sheets of a material called MXene. MXene sensors suit bedside testing, but the sheets oxidise easily and often need added chemicals to work. The team trapped a dye, methylene blue, between the layers as a built-in signal source, removing the need for loose reagents.

Their screen-printed platform detects erdafitinib, a drug used against bladder and other cancers. A built-in signal trapped in the layers should stay steadier than chemicals floating free in a sample. If it holds up in real fluids, such strips could check drug levels quickly in clinics that lack full laboratories.
pmc-13237310:
Severe alopecia areata can take years to regrow hair, so patients and doctors need to know how long a fair trial of treatment lasts. Brett King and co-authors re-analyze two large trials of the drug baricitinib at its higher dose. They split patients by how severe their hair loss was at the start and how long the current episode had run.

In severe cases, most patients showed a first real improvement by week twenty-four. Three quarters of the short-episode group went on to full success by week fifty-two. In very severe cases the picture split more by episode length, and gains kept coming through the year. The authors advise giving the drug at least a full year before calling it a failure in the hardest cases.
pmc-13237410: Rice panicle research is the subject of a correction by Wu and colleagues. The study compared hybrid rice with its parent lines, profiling how gene messages are trimmed during early grain development. The correction concerns the methods wording for collecting tissue and extracting high-quality RNA, and the corrected and original versions are set out side by side. Exact extraction steps decide whether other labs can repeat the sequencing work, so the journal records the fix in full.
pmc-13239010: Jacob Salazar and co-authors solved the crystal structure of avutometinib in a 2026 structure report. Avutometinib is a cancer drug, and its solid form shapes how it can be made and stored. The team read the structure from synchrotron X-ray powder data and refined it with quantum chemistry tools. The molecule is Z-shaped, and the crystals stack in layers, with hydrogen bonds linking the layers along one axis.
pmc-13239110:
Alex W Bajcz and colleagues introduced P.I. Charter in 2026, a web application that gathers point-intercept aquatic plant survey data from across Minnesota. Dozens of agencies and groups survey lake plants for their own purposes, leaving valuable records scattered and hard to combine. The app, built in R Shiny, accepts submissions, cleans and merges them automatically, and returns recognition and visualizations as incentives to contribute.

Since launch it has drawn thousands of visitors and hundreds of submissions, with repeat contributors filing surveys in minutes. Four case studies show the pooled database planning new surveys, watching for cryptic invasions, linking plant occurrence to environment, and tracing lake plant change over time. The authors share the experience as a model, while warning that accessible design in Shiny takes real effort.
pmc-13239510:
The Nigerian Surgical Research Collaborative measures surgical site infections after abdominal operations across fifty-three Nigerian hospitals. Infection after surgery is a heavy burden in poorer countries, where it lengthens stays families can ill afford. Reliable, current numbers have been scarce in Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, which has held back efforts to cut that burden.

Their prospective study is a snapshot audit: infections counted as care happened, alongside the factors that raised or lowered risk. Hospital-by-hospital data at this scale can show whether the drivers are antibiotics, theatre practice, or patient condition. That tells surgical teams where the next naira spent on safety will do the most good.
pmc-13239710:
Satoshi Kurita and colleagues set out a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of harms from exercise programmes for frail older adults. Exercise clearly helps this group, yet falls, injuries, and other unwanted events during trials have never been gathered together in one analysis.

The review will search four databases for randomised trials involving people aged sixty or older whose frailty was measured with a validated method. Independent teams will screen studies, extract event data, and judge bias risk with a standard Cochrane tool. Pooled risk ratios will compare event rates between exercise and control groups, with extra analyses by programme length, frequency, and setting.
pmc-13239910:
Georgina V Hume and co-authors read shark bite scars on dolphins to measure predation risk along southeast Queensland in a 2026 study. Attacks by large sharks are rarely witnessed, yet healed scars on photographed animals offer a record of how often dolphins are targeted and where.

Fresh wounds pointed mainly to tiger sharks and white sharks, with bites clustered near the tail stalk. Half of the Australian humpback dolphins photographed carried scars, a higher share than either bottlenose species. Sheltered waters held more scarred animals than open coasts. Statistical models confirmed humpback dolphins, especially adults in sheltered habitat, face the greatest attack risk.
pmc-13241410:
Gajdošová's team in Olomouc built a gold cone sensor that detects a mood drug and serotonin side by side. Raman light scattering reads molecular fingerprints from the cone arrays. The cones pack gaps under twenty nanometers, creating dense, uniform hot spots. The build is large-scale, cheap, and kept simple on purpose.

Sertraline showed down to 88 nanograms per milliliter, the lowest Raman figure yet. That sits a hundredfold below levels in patient blood. Serotonin showed at 27 nanograms per milliliter, beneath levels seen even in low mood. Both were read side by side in fake spinal fluid, untreated.
pmc-13241510:
Puneet Khandelwal and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-six on aiming a light-based cancer therapy at the feeding routes of pancreatic tumors. Cancers rewire how they take in choline, glutamine, and glucose to fuel growth. Photoimmunotherapy joins an antibody to a dye that kills only when near-infrared light hits it, but it needs a target on the cell surface.

The team targeted the outer parts of three nutrient transporters, one for each fuel. In two patient-derived cell lines, the therapy killed cells in line with how much transporter each line carried. In mice, one treatment against the choline transporter wiped out four of five tumors. The authors see the best use during surgery, to clear cells invading vital structures.
pmc-13241610:
Salifu and a Ghana-UK team describe a community-led effort to build death literacy around palliative care in Ghana. Death literacy means the knowledge and confidence to face dying, death, and loss. In Ghana, open talk about death is often discouraged, and palliative care is scarce. The COMPASS-Ghana project used a participatory theory-of-change approach.

Activities included a thirty-seven-person stakeholder session, a planning workshop, and a focus group with nursing and midwifery students. Three themes emerged: shared language about death, care rooted in existing community forms, and collective agency. Participants shifted toward treating death as a shared community concern. The authors argue such locally grounded work fits public-health palliative care.
pmc-13242010:
Jingjing Wen and Hui Ye report a 2026 study of stem cell vesicles for diabetic wound healing. Fat-derived stem cells release tiny parcels called exosomes that can help wounds, but the active ingredient was unknown. The team focused on a sugar-burning enzyme named ALDOA.

In high-sugar cell cultures that mimic diabetes, the vesicles sped cell movement and raised energy output from sugar breakdown. Wounds in diabetic mice also healed faster with treatment. The enzyme was scarce in sugar-stressed cells, and vesicle treatment pushed its level above normal. Removing the enzyme from vesicles erased the benefit, while adding extra enzyme copied it. The authors identify enzyme delivery through exosomes as a route to better diabetic wound care.
pmc-13242810:
Michal Klimek and co-authors publish a 2026 comparison of online tools used to plan astigmatism-correcting lens implants in cataract surgery. Different tools can recommend different lens powers and angles from the same eye measurements. The study compared one manufacturer calculator against several society-hosted engines.

Records covered well over a hundred operated eyes, with the same measurements fed into every calculator. Relevant disagreement between the main pair appeared in about three fifths of eyes, mostly as stronger lens steps from the manufacturer tool. Disagreement clustered in eyes with one astigmatism orientation and a stronger back corneal curve. Other engines disagreed even more often. The authors advise consulting several tools for the high-risk pattern, while noting orientation groups where choice hardly matters.
pmc-13243010:
Yimin He and co-authors publish a 2026 clinical study comparing two add-on physical treatments for rosacea alongside oral doxycycline. One group used a device called the Shumin treatment instrument, while the other used red light therapy. Both groups treated twice weekly for twelve weeks, and skin microscopy tracked objective change.

The device group reached a higher overall effectiveness rate than the red light group. Life quality scores improved more in the device group, and affected hair follicle counts also did better. Mite counts fell in both groups without a clear between-group difference. Relapse after treatment was notably less common in the device group. The authors judge the device pairing safe and more effective in this preliminary comparison.
pmc-13243110:
Chao Zhang, Yunfeng Ni, and Dong Han carried out this 2026 hospital study of older patients who had both chronic bronchitis, a long-term lung condition, and a heart attack. They asked whether a simple blood-based score of immune activity and inflammation could predict who would die in hospital.

The study covered 252 patients, of whom 48 died. Those who died had higher inflammation markers at admission. The score, called SII, predicted deaths well on its own, and it did even better combined with two other blood measures. The authors suggest this cheap score could help doctors spot high-risk patients early.
pmc-13244510:
Gabriela Cejas-Añón and colleagues profiled the enzyme cocktail secreted by the fungus that feeds leaf-cutting ants. Their study appeared in Mycobiology in 2026. Leucoagaricus gongylophorus farms inside ant nests, digesting leaves the ants cannot eat themselves. The team grew it on four foods: glucose, a cellulose derivative, xylan, and pectin, then measured growth, enzyme output, and the full set of secreted proteins over time.

Glucose fed the most growth, while pectin, the food the fungus liked least, provoked its richest enzyme response. Pectin cultures topped the charts for three enzyme classes and secreted the most varied protein set. pmc-13248110:

pmc-13248510:

pmc-13249110:

pmc-13250110:

pmc-13252710:

pmc-13254210:

pmc-13254510:

pmc-13255010:

pmc-13255210:

pmc-13255910:
Gábor Lorászkó and co-authors present a 2026 case report of glaucoma in a four-year-old female Siberian tiger kept at a zoo. pmc-13256510:

pmc-13257110:

pmc-13257210:

pmc-13258010:

pmc-13258310:

pmc-13258410:

pmc-13259110:

pmc-13259210:

pmc-13264110:

pmc-13264410:

pmc-13264610:

pmc-13266610:

pmc-13267810:

pmc-13268110:

pmc-13268410:

pmc-13268710:

pmc-13268810:

pmc-13269410:

Dinara Yerlanova and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 surveying health workers on infection risks in pregnant women with inflammatory rheumatic diseases. These diseases and their treatments raise infection risk during pregnancy. An online survey with 30 questions reached specialists in many fields.

A total of 201 workers from 36 countries replied, and 72.1 percent were rheumatologists, joint and immune specialists. Lupus, vasculitis, and rheumatoid arthritis were rated the highest-risk diseases. Screening was most often advised for hepatitis B, urine infections, and hepatitis C. Uncontrolled disease and high-dose steroid use topped the risk factors. Too few specialists and missing team care were the biggest barriers named.
pmc-13269810:
Myong-Wuk Chon and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on social support among student survivors of the Sewol ferry disaster, which killed 304 of 476 passengers in 2014. Sixty-six student survivors were assessed twice a year from 2016 to 2021. Surveys measured support, traumatic stress, and complicated grief.

Support paths split into four groups, from low starting support to the highest. One group started moderate and rose over time. Compared with the highest support group, that rising group had a higher risk of strong traumatic stress symptoms. Both the low group and the rising group faced higher risk of probable complicated grief. The authors say students with low or shifting support need closest watching.
pmc-13270210:
Anna Nikula and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on children's behavior four weeks after sedation for painful procedures in emergency care. Parents of 128 children who had received nose-spray sedation or laughing gas were interviewed by phone. A standard questionnaire measured behavior changes since the procedure.

Changes were reported in only 13 children, or 10.2 percent: eight negative and five positive. Children with negative changes were younger, with a median age of 5.7 years against 9.4 years for unchanged children. They and their parents were less willing to use the same method again. Parent satisfaction was also lower in that group. Pain scores during the procedure showed no link with later negative changes.
pmc-13270710:
Anna Hörberg is lead author of a 2026 document analysis of how new staff are brought into the Swedish ambulance service. New ambulance workers must handle varied, unpredictable cases from day one, often with low confidence and strain, yet their schooling covers only part of the skills the job needs.

The authors studied induction programme materials from 23 ambulance organisations covering all 21 Swedish health regions. They grouped the training content into six areas, from driving and navigation to safe care settings and organisational knowledge, plus a seventh group on teaching methods. They conclude induction needs stronger evidence and teaching design, covering people skills, ethics, and belonging as well as clinical skills.
pmc-13270810:
Jenny Lander led a 2026 case-control study of slow, unsteady walking in older adults and its links to enlarged brain fluid spaces. Such walking problems and enlarged spaces are both common in old age, and the study asked whether standard imaging signs for a treatable condition called INPH truly match the walking problem.

From 6,467 people aged 65 to 84 who were screened, doctors identified 81 with the typical higher-level gait disorder and 192 matched controls. The disorder's prevalence was 5.8 percent. Those affected were older, scored worse on thinking tests, and showed larger fluid spaces and other imaging features more often than controls.
pmc-13270910:
Linda Åkeflo is lead author of a 2026 qualitative interview study titled Chipped but not broken. It covers life more than five years after radiotherapy for meningioma. Meningioma is the most common brain tumour in adults. These tumours are usually benign, but treatment can leave lasting headache, tiredness, and thinking problems.

Twenty people took part in online interviews, 17 treated with proton beam therapy and three with standard radiotherapy, most over six years earlier. Two themes emerged: adjusted life circumstances and reduced autonomy. Some described lasting symptoms that reshaped daily life, yet also built new routines and accepted new limits. Others felt more dependent on family.
pmc-13271510:
Xiaoyu Meng is lead author of a 2026 journal article presenting PianoGym, a simulator for two-handed piano rhythm training. Training must keep the hands in precise time while respecting limits on player fatigue. Feedback normally arrives only after an exercise ends, so the training problem is framed as decision-making with delayed, partial information.

The authors add a two-layer safety system: a slow layer tracking long-term fatigue budgets and a fast guard screening each next exercise against current fatigue estimates. Their planning controller, PianoMPC, reached mastery in about 24 to 28 steps across three learner profiles, with feasible rates of 0.90 to 0.95, beating simpler bandit and value-based agents under the same guard.
pmc-13271910:
Chenyang Li and colleagues investigate in 2026 whether a standard severity score relates to sepsis among intensive care patients with bowel disease who died. Sepsis drives much of the death toll in this group, yet early warning remains hard. The score studied sums how far body measures stray from normal on ICU arrival.

From a large critical care database, the team selected 190 adults with inflammatory bowel disease who died during their stay, 55 of them with sepsis. Higher scores tracked with sepsis even after adjustment, and the top quarter of scores carried nearly five times the odds. The authors treat the result as a lead for study, not proof.
pmc-13272210:
Martie van Tongeren is lead author of a 2026 occupational health study of heat stress among sugarcane workers in Thailand, who labour in very hot, humid conditions. The study measured environmental heat across full shifts and counted workers' heat-related symptoms, including severe symptoms linked to heat stroke.

Among 295 workers in Nakhon Sawan Province, recruited in cooler and hotter months of 2023, average adjusted full-shift heat exposure was high, with over forty percent exposed at the top range measured. Nearly everyone, 98 percent, reported at least one of 21 symptoms, and 74 percent at least one severe symptom. Each one-degree rise in exposure raised symptom counts by ten percent and severe symptom counts by nineteen percent.
pmc-13272310:
Peter Kivunike Mukasa and coauthors interview in 2026 health workers in eastern Uganda about what helps and hinders obstetric fistula surgery and care. This childbirth injury leaves women leaking urine, and many never reach repair surgery because of system weaknesses. Provider views on those weaknesses were largely undocumented.

Twenty interviews across two hospitals in the Busoga sub-region, plus national experts and policymakers, fed a thematic analysis framed on health system building blocks. Seven themes covered staffing, equipment, and other system parts, along with the workarounds staff invent when the system falls short. The findings aim to guide investment in fistula services.
pmc-13272510:
Otang Thierry Otang leads a 2026 study of deaths after road crashes in Southwest Cameroon. The team reviewed five years of records, from 2020 to 2024, at three regional referral hospitals. Weak care before hospital and weak trauma care are noted as background problems in the region.

Among 3,266 crash admissions, 153 patients died in hospital, a rate of 4.7 percent. Deaths rose by about 22 percent over the period, and rates differed by hospital. Late arrival, crashes on roads between towns, severe or critical injury, other illness, and head or spine injury were each linked to higher risk of death.
pmc-13272610:
Kevelin Barbosa-Xavier and Thiago Venancio present a 2026 study of gene activity in Cannabis sativa, focusing on flowers and the tiny glands that make its active compounds. Female flowers hold most cannabinoids and terpenoids, yet the genes that shape flowers and sex are not fully mapped. The team combined data across many samples.

They merged 117 RNA sequencing data sets and compared nine cannabis genomes, finding 31 groups of MADS-box genes, which help control flower form. Some groups were active mainly in male flowers and others mainly in female flowers. Genes for the final cannabinoid steps varied by plant type, while earlier steps stayed more alike across types.
pmc-13273510:
Jing Zhou and a large team built deep learning models to grade kidney cancer and predict its spread in a 2026 study. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma is the most common kidney cancer, and its grade strongly shapes outlook. Human grading of slides can vary between observers.

They trained a grading model on whole slide images from 305 cases, split into training, verification, and test sets. The model scored near perfect discrimination across internal, in-house, and external checks, and its agreement with senior pathologists was about equal to their agreement with each other. A second model predicted spread to lymph nodes or distant sites with strong accuracy as well. Higher model grades tracked with worse prognosis. The authors offer both tools for pathology support.
pmc-13274310:
Mitra Bagheri and a large team present a 2026 journal article on a copper framework material that turns carbon dioxide into ethylene using electricity. Ethylene is a cornerstone chemical for plastics, and making it from waste CO2 could cut emissions. Their catalyst is a metal-organic framework, a sponge-like lattice of copper and organic links, made in one green step.

The flakes have wide pores that let gases move fast and keep copper sites reachable. In a compact zero-gap cell, just over half the electric charge went into ethylene at an industrial-level current. Live X-ray tracking showed the copper reshaping into its active metallic form during use, then recovering, with almost no copper lost.
pmc-13274610:
Yaoyun Wu and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on an enzyme rebuilt from an ancient ancestor that runs two normally separate chemical reactions in one pocket. Industry often converts amines into esters, a two-step job that nature splits between two enzyme families. The team used ancestral sequence reconstruction, inferring an extinct protein's code from living relatives.

Their rebuilt enzyme, AncFO-221, chains amine oxidation straight into the oxygen-insertion step, making a continuous cycle rather than a loose cascade. Guided by that mechanism, engineering produced a variant with about eighteen-fold better efficiency and near-complete suppression of side reactions. Lactone yields reached ninety-three percent, and the enzyme could be tuned to break the classical rule for which group migrates.
pmc-13275010:
Arnulf Stenzl and a large team report a 2026 journal article on checking whether AI-written summaries of cancer research can be trusted. They tested large language model summaries, both scientific and plain-language, drawn from a prostate cancer study collection. A panel of five language models and three human experts checked faithfulness, meaning no invented facts.

The AI scientific summaries scored 88.9 percent faithful with 9.6 percent hallucinated content, far better than human-written plain-language summaries at 61.6 percent faithful and 40.6 percent hallucinated, though humans had added outside context. AI plain summaries were also easier to read. Agreement between the AI panel and humans was substantial, suggesting AI panels can police summary quality for clinical use.
pmc-13275310:
Takahisa Gono wrote a 2026 editorial on how common lung scarring is in rheumatoid arthritis, commenting on a systematic review in the same journal issue. The review pooled seventy-four studies and put overall prevalence near a fifth of patients. Gono urges readers to handle that headline number with care.

Estimates swung widely by detection method, from about a third of patients on high resolution CT down to a twentieth when billing codes were used. Study differences were extreme, and the pattern of results hinted at bias, since scans were often ordered only when disease was already suspected. Lower bias studies using several methods suggested a rate nearer a tenth. The editorial backs high resolution CT as the key test and calls for one standard screening strategy worldwide.
pmc-13275510:
Anna Lach-Gruba and colleagues wrote a 2026 narrative review of virtual reality in shoulder rehabilitation, including after shoulder replacement surgery. Shoulder rehab is long and depends on feedback and patient follow-through. The team searched the literature through May 2026 for immersive and semi-immersive tools used in shoulder and upper-limb recovery.

Consumer headsets, they found, track shoulder motion reliably within their own systems, though readings differ between devices. Virtual reality programs proved feasible and popular, with possible gains in adherence, pain, range of motion, and self-rated function across torn cuff repairs, frozen shoulder, and impingement. Evidence specific to joint replacement remains thin, so the authors advise VR as a supervised add-on, never a stand-alone replacement for clinician-led care.
pmc-13275610:
Addie Harrison and colleagues present a 2026 journal article modeling how tiny cellular capsules fire their contents, a weapon used by jellyfish relatives, dinoflagellates, and single-celled protists. These organelles, called extrusomes, hold a coiled tubule or barb inside a fluid-filled capsule that collapses to shoot it out. The team simulated the collapse numerically with a simplified elliptical shell and varied the opening size, capsule shape, and fluid conditions.

A smaller opening gap produced faster firing and quicker ejection. A wider capsule also shortened the trip to the target by moving more fluid. Faster, less viscous flow generally meant quicker target contact, though not in a simple straight-line pattern. Stiffer barbs reached targets sooner because flexible ones bent and slowed. The authors suggest lessons for designing medical microinjectors.
pmc-13276310:
Itziar Uriarte-Arrazola and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on modeling how a benign nerve tumor turns deadly. People with the inherited condition NF1 often grow plexiform neurofibromas, which can progress to malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors. The step-by-step gene losses behind that shift were only partly understood.

The team grew neural crest cells, the tumor's cell of origin, from reprogrammed stem cells and edited their genes in sequence. Losing two tumor guards produced benign-like tumors in animals. Losing a third guard reshaped the cells' DNA packaging, silenced a nerve identity gene, and drove a mesenchymal, more mobile program. Those cells formed early malignant-like tumors on nerves. A drug screen then found that a class of cancer drugs hit the triple-loss cells hardest. A two-drug combo shrank human tumors in mice.
pmc-13276610:
Chandrashekhar Jori and colleagues build an oral nanoparticle treatment for inflammatory bowel disease in a 2026 study. Swallowed drugs often pass the gut too fast or break down in the stomach. Their carrier wraps the drug rebamipide in mucin and a sticky dextran layer, over an oil-based core.

The particles held together in stomach-like conditions regardless of acidity. They clung to the colon lining and stayed in the gut for up to two days. In treated animals, colon inflammation and several inflammatory markers fell more than with free rebamipide. The particles also raised mucin 2, a protective gut protein, which supported healing of the colon surface and its mucus-producing cells.
pmc-13276810:
Jan Schjøtt and co-authors report a 2026 study of short teaching visits for family doctors in Norway. The visits covered wise use of proton pump inhibitors, drugs that cut stomach acid and are often taken too long. Surveys went out before and after visits held from August 2024 to July 2025.

Of 1,018 doctors visited, 138 filled in both surveys. Most reported gains of two to four points on a seven-point scale for drug knowledge. Doctors also said the visit answered their questions and had changed how they prescribe. No region stood out from the others. The result rests on what doctors felt they learned, not on prescribing records.
pmc-13276910:
Zi Zhang and co-authors map what it would take for wastewater plants to produce more energy than they use, in a 2026 analysis. Treatment plants consume about one percent of global electricity, and demand grows as sanitation expands. Turning plants into net energy producers would ease that load.

A national inventory of nearly three thousand plants was corrected for operating bias to set a fair baseline. Under standard practice, only plants treating strong wastewater could reach energy-positive operation. Two carbon-redirection routes, pairing enhanced primary treatment with mainstream anammox, lowered the entry bar sharply. Medium-sized plants looked like the best candidates. The framework is offered to guide pilots and future research.
pmc-13277610:
Karlen Law, Kenney Lau, Graham Shea, and Kenneth Cheung present a study dated two thousand twenty-six on early signs of a common neck spine disorder. In the disorder, wear in the neck slowly squeezes the spinal cord. Early symptoms are mild and vague, so the problem is often found late, after lasting damage.

The team tested four hundred thirty-six adults aged forty-five and older with a standard score and a full sense exam. They checked pain, temperature, fine touch, vibration, and proprioception, the sense of where body parts are. Faults in that last sense were the most common of all, found in over ninety percent of those with deficits.
pmc-13278410:
Shiming Wang leads a 2026 study of an intelligent, data-driven method for controlling costs in large commercial complex building projects. Such projects mix shopping, dining, offices, and housing, and their costs are hard to manage. The method joins value engineering, a way to raise value per cost, with a fuzzy ranking model to weigh building functions against their costs in real time.

Applied to an existing commercial complex, the optimized approach cut total cost by about two point nine percent against traditional methods across civil, building, heating, and electrical work. Continuous monitoring is meant to curb wasteful building choices as work proceeds. Post-project reviews feed lessons back into the system for later projects.
pmc-13278610:
Wendy Macias leads a 2026 social media listening study of posts about heavily advertised prescription drug brands in the United States. Drug makers spend billions on direct-to-consumer advertising, but online talk about those brands is little studied. Using a monitoring tool, the team analyzed 44,700 Twitter mentions from 26,800 authors between August 2021 and August 2023.

Four themes dominated: patient experiences and testimonials, pricing and insurance worries, pharmaceutical news, and commentary on the advertising itself. Most posts were neutral, yet the sentiment around top terms leaned negative. Information seeking was the strongest motive identified. The authors urge drug makers and policymakers to improve communication, transparency, and engagement around advertised medicines.
pmc-13278910:
Ting Wang, Wenlin Yang, Xianglun Gong, and Bing Xue report a rare womb cancer in a 2026 case study. A sixty-year-old woman, ten years past menopause, had irregular bleeding for four months. Scans showed a large uterine mass reaching deep into the muscle wall.

Surgery removed the uterus, ovaries, and pelvic lymph nodes, and tissue examination gave the answer. The tumour mixed tubular, glandular, and slit-like patterns under the microscope. Staining was positive for GATA-3 and TTF-1 and negative for hormone receptors, a signature of mesonephric-like adenocarcinoma. This recently recognised subtype behaves aggressively, and the authors document its appearance in the uterine body, where it is exceedingly rare.
pmc-13279310:
Xiaomei Jiang and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study of how often blood pressure drops during dialysis relate to anxiety, depression, and poor sleep. They enrolled 467 patients on maintenance hemodialysis at four centers in Suzhou, China, reviewing 16,812 treatment sessions for intradialytic hypotension, the sudden pressure fall that complicates dialysis. Standard questionnaires measured anxiety, depression, and sleep quality for comparison.

Pressure drops occurred in 11.7 percent of sessions, and about a quarter of patients experienced them frequently. Anxiety affected 30.4 percent of the sample, depression 44.3 percent, and poor sleep roughly 40 percent. Patients with frequent pressure drops scored significantly worse on all three symptom measures after adjustment for other factors. Because the design captures one point in time, the authors cannot say which problem causes the other. They recommend pairing blood pressure monitoring with routine psychological and sleep screening in dialysis care.
pmc-13279410:
David Pérez-Manchón and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of whether nursing shift patterns damage digestive health. Rotating and night shifts disrupt body clocks, sleep, and eating habits, all of which can unsettle the gut. Searching four databases, the team found seventeen observational studies of hospital nurses and pooled thirteen for quantitative analysis.

Rotating shifts carried a modestly higher overall risk of gastrointestinal problems, with an odds ratio of 1.15 against day shifts. The signal was strongest for irritable bowel syndrome, where odds rose by about three quarters, and for diarrhea, where odds more than doubled in their subgroup analysis. No clear links appeared for colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Most studies were judged low risk of bias, though confounding and outcome reporting were recurring weaknesses. The authors argue that schedule design belongs in occupational health planning for nurses.
pmc-13279510:
Shuai Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 study of how depression relates to adjustment disorder in first-year college students, and whether resilience and felt support carry part of that effect. Adjustment disorder is an outsized emotional reaction to clear stressors, common when students start university. The team surveyed 402 freshmen at a hospital psychology department in Zhumadian. Questionnaires measured depression, resilience, support, and symptoms, and the team modeled the pathways among them.

Depression tracked strongly with the disorder, while resilience and support moved against it. Modeling showed depression forecast more problems, and resilience and support each predicted fewer. Path analysis backed a partial mediation story: depression harms adjustment directly and by wearing down a student's resilience and sense of support. Gender and childhood trauma showed no clear differences. The authors argue that campus mental health programs should build resilience and support networks, not only treat depressive symptoms.
pmc-13279710:
Katarzyna Kwiecień-Jaguś and colleagues published a 2026 survey asking Polish hospital nurses what causes errors when nurses give medication. Fifty hospitals were randomly drawn from the national total, and 468 completed questionnaires were analyzed with a standard error scale. The survey covered intensive care and internal medicine units. It forms part of a larger patient safety project, with data collected over a year starting in 2023.

Nurses most often blamed look-alike drugs, confusing drug appearance, and illegible orders. Two further complaints scored high: pharmacists unavailable around the clock, and brand-name medicines swapped for generics. Lack of training on new drugs and heavy use of shortened forms also featured. Nurses in some wards stressed interruptions during preparation and staff shortages. The authors note many causes can be fixed through management tools and technology. Staffing shortages, though, will need action by lawmakers beyond any single hospital.
pmc-13279910:
Niloofar Sadooghi and colleagues report a 2026 study of human brucellosis patterns in North Khorasan, Iran. Brucellosis is a germ illness from livestock and raw dairy foods. The team mapped cases in space and time from 2015 to 2023 with a geographic software tool. All confirmed cases in the province were counted, two thousand eight hundred fifty five in all.

About fifty six percent were male and about seventy one percent lived in rural areas. Median age was forty one years. Most patients farmed livestock or lived in farm homes. About eighty seven percent drank unpasteurized dairy, and about eighty two percent had close livestock contact. Rural life raised the odds of both dairy use and animal contact a lot. Case clusters spread through the province, with high years in 2023 and a low in 2018. Maps can aim dairy safety work at true hot spots.
pmc-13280210:
Yarit Wiggerts and colleagues published a 2026 study testing whether planning deep brain stimulation with each Parkinson's patient's brain wiring improves motor outcomes. Stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus helps many patients, but benefit varies and electrode placement is usually guided by standard landmarks. For 102 patients, surgeons used ultra-high-field 7 Tesla MRI tractography to map how each person's target nucleus connects to motor cortex. They then aimed the leads at that individual motor subdivision. Outcomes were compared with 118 matched patients planned by classical landmarks.

On a motor rating scale, the connectivity-guided group improved by 56 percent on average against 50 percent for controls, a significant gap. The share achieving an optimal response was higher, 96 percent against 86 percent. Leads landing inside the mapped motor subdivision did best of all, averaging 60 percent improvement. The authors present patient-specific connectivity as a biomarker for implantation, usable in routine care, not only research.
pmc-13281410:
Narges Milkarizi and colleagues tested a leafy plant extract on mood in liver patients in a 2026 trial. The patients had fatty liver, a build-up of fat that harms the organ. Low mood, anxiety, and stress are common in this group. The plant, purslane, is rich in plant compounds that fight cell stress. Seventy patients were split by chance into two groups. One took the extract daily for eight weeks, and one took a dummy pill. All got a diet plan and activity advice.

At the end, depression and stress scores had improved more in the extract group. Weight and waist size also fell more in that group. The authors say the plant may ease the mind by calming swelling and cell stress in the body. They call the trial a first step and ask for larger, longer studies to test dose and safety.
pmc-13281810:
Zheng Cao and colleagues devised a homing method for protein drugs in a 2026 study. Protein drugs are potent but often miss their target and harm healthy tissue. Diseased tissue tends to burn sugar fast and turn sour with acid. The team wrapped proteins in polymer shells that sense that acid. At the body's normal balance the shells stay neutral. In sour zones they slowly gain a positive charge.

That charge shift lets the capsules drift down the acid slope toward disease. Most homing today needs a lock-and-key match that works only at close range. This method needs no key and can act over distance. In animal models of cancer, long-term swelling, and sudden injury, the capsules piled up at sick sites. Care worked better and harm elsewhere fell. The authors call it a general compass for protein drugs.
pmc-13282410:
Adekunle Adedeji and co-authors present a 2026 study developing a questionnaire on quality of life for parents of children with achondroplasia. Achondroplasia is the commonest form of dwarfism, and parents face sustained caregiving demands. No validated, condition-specific tool measured their quality of life. The team built one through interviews, item drafting, expert sorting rounds, and translation checks.

Seventeen parents shaped the domains in interviews. The resulting pilot form held sixty-three items across eight domains, from health care experiences and mental health to worries about the future. Fifty parents in Germany, Italy, and Portugal pilot-tested it, with debriefing interviews. Missing answers were rare, scores avoided floor and ceiling crowding, and consistency was acceptable to good. Parents judged the questions relevant across countries. The authors call it a strong first step, pending large-scale validation before wide research or clinic use.
pmc-13282510:
Amit Jaiswal wrote a 2026 commentary on a large multicentre study of frozen embryo transfer after caesarean delivery. Frozen embryo transfer places a thawed embryo into the womb. The study found womb lining thickness at final check was similar after caesarean and vaginal births. Yet live birth rates stayed lower after caesarean delivery, even with single genetically normal embryos and linings over ten millimetres in more than eleven thousand cycles.

Jaiswal argues the field leans too hard on thickness as a stand-in for receptivity, the womb's readiness for implantation. A lining can look adequate yet be biologically out of sync, less tolerant, or mechanically unready. Extremely thin linings do predict worse results, but within the usual range the measure resolves little. The commentary calls for judging the post-caesarean womb by function, not by a single structural number, and for recalibrating counselling accordingly.
pmc-13282710:
Michiel De Moor and co-authors wrote a 2026 letter reporting a case of inflamed aorta caused by Bartonella bacteria, urging doctors to consider this germ when cultures stay negative. Aortitis is inflammation of the aorta, the body's main artery, with infectious and non-infectious causes. Bartonella species, hard-to-grow bacteria with a taste for vessel linings, are known causes of heart valve infection that can mimic other vessel diseases.

Their patient was a healthy twenty-seven-year-old man with three weeks of fever, fatigue, and painful swollen glands near his armpit and elbow. He had regular contact with feral cats. Tests confirmed Bartonella henselae, the cat-scratch germ. The authors call this, to their knowledge, the first Bartonella henselae aortitis case without structural complications in a healthy young adult. They argue the infection belongs on the list of suspects in unexplained large-vessel inflammation.
pmc-13283210:
Hae-Ryong Yun and colleagues built a decision aid in 2026 that copies how three kidney specialists each judge whether a patient needs a kidney biopsy. Doctors often differ on the same case, so tools trained toward one answer can erase that spread. The team trained one model per expert on the same data, then joined the models by majority vote.

The work drew on 9,598 patients across three cohorts. Each single model closely matched its own expert, and the combined aid reached high accuracy in internal checks. In outside cohorts it kept strong sorting power, matching two experts and beating the third. Every case the aid flagged for biopsy in a lab-checked group did show tissue abnormality. Field testing still lies ahead.
pmc-13283710:
Paul Bergeron and a large team tested two stitch patterns in 2026 for fixing the back root of the meniscus in children's knees. Young tissue responds to repair methods differently from adult tissue, so adult results may mislead. Ten menisci from young donors were cut free to mimic a root tear and assigned at random to a double luggage-tag stitch or a Mason-Allen stitch.

Each repair was loaded five hundred times, rested, then pulled until it failed. Failure strength came out nearly the same for both patterns, around 160 newtons, and stretch after cycling matched at 2.6 millimetres. In adult tissue the Mason-Allen pattern had edged ahead, but here neither won. The authors note the luggage-tag pattern is quicker to learn and may save operating time.
pmc-13283810:
Houda Gharsallah and a large team explored in 2026 whether bacterial lipopeptides can replace synthetic additives in tomato foods. Lipopeptides from Bacillus bacteria have a water-loving and fat-loving structure that helps mix and stabilise foods. The team confirmed that structure with magnetic resonance methods, then added the compounds to tomato juice and sauce at three dose levels.

All mixes thinned as they were stirred, as tomato products do. The additions changed how texture built and held over time, improving thickness behaviour and stability at low to moderate doses. Too much lipopeptide partly broke the network and weakened stability. The authors present the compounds as natural structuring agents for functional tomato foods, if dosing stays in the sweet spot.
pmc-13284810:
Thomas Kayser and co-authors watch the heart while a dual bronchodilator opens the lungs of COPD patients. Overinflated lungs squeeze the heart, and it was unclear how fast pairing tiotropium with olodaterol relieves that squeeze. In a crossover trial, thirty-two patients took a single dose of the drug pair or saline, then two weeks of open treatment, with MRI scans and nerve recordings.

The lungs answered at once: trapped air fell by about two thirds of a liter after one dose. The heart lagged. Its filling volume rose only slightly on day one, part of the gap came from a dip under placebo, and the gain turned significant only after fourteen days. Sympathetic nerve activity barely moved. No serious side effects occurred. The authors advise staying the course: the cardiac payoff of dual therapy needs sustained use.
pmc-13285610:
Losing one ring RNA helps bowel tumors resist radiation, Wangsheng Chen and co-authors trace in a 2026 study. Radiation is a mainstay for bowel cancer, yet tumors often learn to shrug it off. A chaperone protein, BIP, balances cell self-eating against cell death to set that resistance, and ring RNAs that tune it were unknown.

The ring, circRAB5A, ran low in radiation-proof patient samples and cell lines, choked by an editor protein that blocks its birth. Low rings let BIP linger, tilting cells toward self-protection over death. Mouse tumors with the ring silenced shrugged off radiation, while cutting BIP restored weakness even at low dose. The chain hands drug hunters a fresh lever.
pmc-13285710:
Csaba Tölgyesi and co-authors reply to critics of their earlier modeling of how much carbon ecosystem restoration can store by 2100. Their 2026 response addresses a comment arguing that they overlooked emissions avoided when damaged wetlands are restored. Wetlands hold large carbon stores, so stopping their degradation prevents releases as well as adding new storage.

The authors accept the point as valid while explaining that global data on emissions from degraded wetlands were lacking. Using the critics' own figure, they estimate the size of the effect and test how their timeline changes. Their headline finding, that restoration can recapture only a limited share of past emissions, stays intact. They stress that the omission does not weaken the case for restoring wetlands.
pmc-13285910:
Ishani P Majmudar and co-authors check whether matching surgeon and patient sex affects cataract surgery results in a 2026 cohort study. Past work in other fields tied a sex mismatch to worse outcomes after big operations. Cataract care, one of the most common surgeries, had never faced the same test until this sixteen-year look back.

Records from one Chicago hospital covered 30,804 cataract operations on more than nineteen thousand patients from 2007 to 2023. Problems during or soon after surgery arose in a small share of cases, led by retinal detachment. The split of troubled cases between matched and mismatched pairs sat near even, and no firm link emerged. The authors read the result as support for alike outcomes no matter how surgeon and patient sexes combine.
pmc-13286210:
Qian Ren leads a 2026 national survey of rabies care clinics across mainland China. Rabies kills nearly every person it sickens, so fast wound care and shots after a bite carry the whole weight of prevention. Provincial officers reported clinic counts, visit totals, and how the worst exposures were handled during 2022.

More than twenty-four thousand clinics served over ten million visits that year, yet their spread across provinces stayed uneven. Fewer than half of clinics could manage the gravest bite class, and only about a third of those patients received the antibody serum that class calls for. Dogs and cats caused nearly all exposures, with cats matching dogs in the south. The authors urge fuller serum stocks, tighter pet control, and wider insurance cover for bite care.
pmc-13286910:
Meiqi Zhang, Yao Lu, and Xingxing Yuan review the tumor microenvironment, the neighborhood of cells and scaffolding around a cancer, as the center of modern oncology. Their 2026 review argues that cancer behaves like an ecosystem disease, not merely a genetic fault inside tumor cells. Fibroblasts, macrophages, abnormal blood vessels, and remodeled matrix all shape growth and treatment resistance.

New strategies aim to reprogram that neighborhood. They include precisely targeted nanoparticles, logic-gated cell therapies, viruses that attack tumors, metabolism and epigenetic drugs, vessel-normalizing methods, and microbiome treatments such as stool transplants. Lab-grown tumors, chip models, and AI-driven data analysis support personal planning. Heterogeneity and cell adaptability remain hard obstacles, the authors note.
pmc-13287010:
Han Zhou and colleagues examine whether breathing other people's tobacco smoke relates to high uric acid levels in Chinese children and teenagers. The 2026 study uses national nutrition surveillance data from 2016 to 2018 covering 13,062 young people aged six to seventeen. High uric acid, a precursor of gout and kidney trouble, affected about one in five participants.

Smoke exposure was common, reaching about two fifths of the group. Children with no exposure had lower odds of high uric acid than daily-exposed peers, a pattern clearest in boys. Kidney filtration statistically carried part of the association in boys, and nearly all of it in older boys. Stricter enforcement of public smoking bans is the authors' prescription.
pmc-13287110:
Kiana Mortezaei and colleagues survey trial evidence on treating itch in systemic sclerosis in a 2026 systematic review. Nearly half of patients with this scarring autoimmune disease report pruritus, which wrecks sleep and quality of life, yet trials usually chase skin thickening and treat itch as an afterthought. Searching two databases under PRISMA rules, the team kept ten studies spanning immune modulators, mast cell stabilizers, opioid receptor drugs, and lipid receptor blockers.

One oral agent, lenabasum, improved itch during phase II testing. Low-dose opioid modulators and the antibody rituximab showed qualitative gains in smaller reports. Measures of itch itself varied wildly between studies and were often secondary endpoints, weakening every comparison. The authors urge future trials to name itch a predefined outcome and measure it with validated instruments.
pmc-13287210:
Yunus Emre Yavuz and co-authors followed 190 patients in 2026 who had a blood clot in the main pumping chamber of a weakened heart after artery disease. Everyone received standard blood thinning and repeated ultrasound checks, and the team asked which early features predict a clot still present after six months.

A machine learning method called CatBoost separated patients best, reaching an accuracy value the authors report as 0.79 on test data. Chamber sizes, lung artery pressure, and platelet count carried the most weight. Over one year, clot size and a stroke risk score, rather than clot persistence alone, linked to major adverse events.
pmc-13287310:
Lea Rodge and co-authors reviewed peptide dressings for infected wounds in a 2026 paper. Antimicrobial peptides are short protein chains that kill germs, and makers have begun loading them into wound dressings. The test germ here is Staphylococcus aureus, a common cause of wound infection.

The team gathered animal studies where such dressings treated infected cut wounds in rodents. Their main aim was not a final verdict on how well the dressings work. They graded the proof for quality, sameness across studies, and readiness for human trials. That audit tells labs how to design the next round of tests well.
pmc-13287510:
Vincenzo Mangialardi and co-authors present 2026 real-world results for ofatumumab in relapsing multiple sclerosis. Ofatumumab is an antibody drug that lowers certain immune cells and is given by injection. The Italian multicenter study compared patients who were new to such treatment with those who switched from other drugs. Switchers came from either moderate-strength or high-strength earlier therapies. Outcomes covered relapses, MRI scans, disability, and side effects.

The cohort held 424 patients followed for about 1.3 years on average. The yearly relapse rate fell from about 0.49 to about 0.03 during treatment, a drop seen in every subgroup. At twelve months, about 79 percent of checked patients showed no sign of disease activity. Side effects were mostly mild injection reactions. Infections stood out in patients who had switched from high-strength drugs, so the authors advise closer watch on that group.
pmc-13287610:
Nilabhra Mondal and co-authors tracked cooling energy needs in 2026 across 88 Indian and 52 other world cities. Records ran from 2003 to 2023. Demand growth was linked to how each city grew in footprint, height, and density. The question was whether shape of growth matters beyond climate alone.

Cities sprawling outward in ragged patterns showed the fastest relative rises in cooling demand, from a low base. Medium cities carried the highest total demand. Compact forms rose more slowly, suggesting a heat advantage. Building volume, above all upward growth and denser packing, explained much of demand even after climate was counted. The authors urge climate-aware planning of city form.
pmc-13287710:
