Mohamed M Elkhouly and colleagues made a new dye-like ligand and its nickel, cadmium, and platinum pairings in 2026, then mapped their shapes with a battery of lab tests and computer models. The work aimed at metal compounds that might serve as future medicines.

Measurements pointed to paired metal centres with four links each, flat for platinum and pyramid-like for the other two. The plain ligand fought fungi and bacteria most strongly, clearing wide zones in dish tests. The cadmium pairing killed liver and breast cancer cells at the lowest doses. Computer checks on energy gaps and surface charge supported the measured shapes and hinted at how the compounds react.
pmc-13288310:
Liying Kang and co-authors tested ashwagandha root extract in 2026 on skin cells stressed by peroxide and in a 28-day open trial with 31 Chinese women who have sensitive skin. The target was a signal protein called CCN1 that rises with stress and drives skin ageing and soreness.

In dishes the extract restored cell survival in a dose-wise way. It lowered CCN1 and several inflammation and matrix-chewing signals, while raising collagen output. In the trial, hydration rose by 49.0% and elasticity by 27.2% over baseline. Firmness improved and wrinkle depth and sagging eased. No control group was used in the human part, the authors note by design.
pmc-13288710:
Evelina Venckute, Amanda G Jarvis, and Patricia Rodriguez-Macia guide enzyme design with electricity in 2026. Their study is a proof of concept. Designer myoglobins were fixed to carbon plates. Some had swapped metal parts. No chemical linkers were used. Voltage reads were taken for iron and manganese types.

In iron types, higher voltage reads meant stronger work. One enzyme hit a turnover count of 230. A lower-voltage type hit just 16. The test was styrene cyclopropanation. One residue swap flipped product handedness. That swap changed histidine 64 to glycine. Fast voltage reads could steer greener catalyst design.
pmc-13288910:
Weipeng Lin and colleagues study how bird flu adapts to humans. Their 2026 study looks at H5N1 virus from birds. Two bird strains looked near alike in genes. Yet one killed mice and one did not. The team swapped genes to find the cause.

Three changes in one gene made the key split. The PB2 gene carries all three changes. With them, the virus used human helper proteins well. Those helpers are called ANP32A and ANP32B. The changes also helped virus parts assemble. Bird hosts can grow this trait on their own. That raises the risk for people, the authors warn.
pmc-13289010:
Karin Alpkvist and colleagues study life after a torn heart artery in Sweden. Online focus groups supplied the voices. The tear is called SCAD for short. It is a rare cause of heart attack. It strikes mostly younger and middle-aged women.

Six groups drew 29 patients in all. Most were women, and the median age was 57. Events had struck from three months to three years back. Fear and lost trust in the body ran deep. Many shunned exercise for fear of strain. Advice from staff was patchy and mixed. Peer talk gave hope and drive. The authors want rehab that heals body and mind.
pmc-13289210:
Samantha Lorstad and colleagues rethink heart injury in sepsis in 2026. Their study reuses a Stockholm cohort. All adults had sepsis and needed pressure drugs. Heart rhythm and a heart strain marker were tracked. The marker is called troponin T.

The set held 586 patients in all. Past atrial fibrillation touched 30 percent. New fibrillation touched 19 percent. The strain marker was high in 93 percent. Rhythm status barely explained marker levels. Top heart rate did not track death. Past and new fibrillation both raised one-year death. Marker height also raised death step by step. Fast rate alone should not explain the injury.
pmc-13289310:
Ekaterina Maslova headed a 2026 review of hospital burden from viral lower respiratory tract disease in United States adults. The team used a large deidentified claims database and covered admissions from January 2015 to March 2023, spanning before, during, and after the main COVID-19 years. First viral lung admission marked the index date for each person.

Among 387 449 hospitalized patients, 38.1 percent entered intensive care within 30 days, and 30-day death was 15.1 percent in the cohort. Median stay was 7 days, with mean hospital costs above forty thousand dollars per stay as reported. Breathing support with masks or machines was common. Burden stayed high across virus types and time periods, which stresses planning for beds, staff, and winter surges.
pmc-13289410:
Robin Bouleau and colleagues report a 2026 long-term survival study on extra heartbeats called premature ventricular complexes in people with healthy heart structure. Such extra beats are common and worry patients, and they predict worse outcomes when heart disease is present. Whether they shorten life without heart disease was far less certain before this Stockholm cohort.

Patients diagnosed at three major hospitals from 2010 to 2016 totaled 803 people with normal heart scans and stress tests. Median age was 59 years, and 57 percent were women in the cohort. Survival at one, five, ten, and twelve years beat matched general population expectations at every point checked. Even frequent extra beats did not erase that favorable outlook in follow-up.
pmc-13289610:
Christian Møller Jensen and many coauthors compare a 2026 machine learning approach with a standard model for severe COVID-19 risk using trial data. Two international randomized trials from 2020 to 2021 supplied the data: one for building and internal checks, another for outside validation. Sites spanned ten and eleven countries, giving a broad patient mix for testing fairness of predictions.

The learning pipeline ran five classification models plus one survival model to find risk factors and predict death by ninety days. Factors and accuracy were set against a previously published non-learning model on the same task. External testing in the second trial checked whether gains travel to new hospitals and waves. Such head-to-head work helps teams pick tools that hold up in real care.
pmc-13289910:
Mohammad Alipour-Vaezi headed a 2026 population study on two-way links between mental health and thinking decline in people with back, neck, and spine pain. Pain plus mood and memory problems often cluster in older adults, yet which comes first was unclear. Data came from a United States network holding over 119 million patients for 2016 to 2021, with matching to balance health backgrounds.

Cohorts with pain were split by prior mental conditions or prior cognitive impairment and followed for three years. Each direction showed raised risk: mental conditions predicted later thinking decline, and thinking decline predicted later mental conditions in the data. Schizophrenia showed the largest forward risk ratio among conditions listed. Matched survival curves support screening both ways in pain clinics.
pmc-13290510:
An upgraded object-detection model spots gastrointestinal polyps in endoscopy images more accurately, Yiyan Zhang and colleagues report in 2026. Polyps hide against cluttered backgrounds, so standard detectors miss some and flag others wrongly.

Starting from YOLOv7, the team added an ECANet attention module in the network's head and neck to quiet background interference. They also swapped the box loss from CIoU to EIoU so predicted boxes hug the true outlines more closely. On the Kvasir-SEG dataset, the improved model reached 94% precision, 88.7% recall, and a mean average precision of 92.9%, each better than the original model managed on the same test. Zhang and colleagues describe the detector as robust and ready for wider evaluation as a diagnostic aid.
pmc-13290910:
A complement drug rescued a cancer patient from a triple immune attack, Yi-Xiao Li and Yan-Lei Hao report in a case report with literature review from 2026. Two weeks after his second tislelizumab infusion for lung adenocarcinoma, the 64-year-old developed drooping eyelids and weakness in all four limbs, testing positive for both anti-AChR and anti-titin antibodies.

Steroids and immunoglobulin failed and he worsened, adding chest pain, muscle pain, swallowing trouble, and breathlessness. The picture fit a probable overlap of myocarditis, myositis, and myasthenia gravis, a rare but often fatal checkpoint-inhibitor complication. Weekly eculizumab at 900 mg for four doses turned him around quickly, leaving minimal symptoms and no relapse. The authors call it the first successful rescue of this dual-antibody form and ask for prospective testing.
pmc-13291010:
Rongli Liu and colleagues follow cardiac anesthesia fellows through full-day shifts in a 2026 study at Fuwai Hospital, a large heart center in China. Eighteen anesthesiologists took part, wearing wristbands through 24-hour duties that covered emergency airway work, invasive lines, and pain pump care.

Surveys before and after each shift covered sleep quality, mood, and sleepiness, while wristbands logged sleep, activity, and energy use through the duty period. Sleep during shifts was short, and fatigue and sleepiness scores rose clearly once the shift ended, even though most other mood scales barely moved. On that basis the authors call for changes to scheduling that protect doctor health without dropping cover for urgent heart care.
pmc-13291310:
Sea fungi from the Penicillium group yield a trove of new compounds. Sarah A. Omran leads a 2026 review of finds from 2020 to 2025. These fungi live in mangroves, mud, and sea animals. Their chemistry shifts in salty, harsh homes.

The review counts 390 distinct natural compounds. Polyketides, alkaloids, and terpenoids lead the list. Lab tests show wide bioactivity across the set. Germ killing, cell toxicity, and virus blocking all appear. Some compounds protect nerves or lower blood sugar. Docking studies hint how key compounds bind targets. The sea remains a rich well for drug leads.
pmc-13291610:
Predicting gene switch activity across species is harder than it looks. Amy Z M Stephen leads a 2026 study of liver enhancers in mammals. Enhancers drive trait diversity between species. Their sequences change fast yet often keep their jobs.

Neural networks learned to predict DNA openness in liver. Data spanned five mammal species. Multi-species training helped models generalize to new species. Yet fine differences between species eluded the models. At matched DNA spots, score gaps were predicted poorly. Presence calls work better than amount calls. The gap warns against trusting cross-species scores. Better tasks are needed for trait evolution studies.
pmc-13291710:
Jonas F Ludvigsson writes a 2026 memorial for hepatologist Hannes Hagström, who died at forty-five. Hagström was a professor at Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm. Ludvigsson first heard from him twelve years earlier, when Hagström was a resident writing on fatty liver and pregnancy. The memorial traces a career that moved at record speed. Hagström defended his thesis in 2016 and soon led his own group at Karolinska University Hospital Huddinge.

He wrote almost three hundred articles, many on the fatty liver disease now called MASLD. His cohorts showed that fibrosis stage, more than inflammation labels, predicts death in that disease. Two of his papers passed one thousand citations each. He helped write European liver guidelines and served as an associate editor of a leading internal medicine journal. In 2024 he received a Rising Star award at a major European congress. Ludvigsson recalls a cheerful, skiing-loving colleague.
pmc-13292010:
This 2026 letter by van Grootel and colleagues replies to comments on their study of hospital to home transitions. Their original work involved patients in designing a shared allied health pathway for discharge. The letter writers had urged discipline specific communication, meaning each profession's input should stay visible. Van Grootel thanks them and agrees clear communication across professions is essential.

The authors add that which professions shape discharge planning depends on the ward. On neurology wards, occupational therapists and speech and language therapists are built into discharge planning more than elsewhere. They endorse practical fixes such as discipline specific checkboxes in discharge summaries and verbal handovers. Van Grootel stresses that every allied profession contributes to safe transitions, whatever the setting.
pmc-13292310:
Fengyan Zhang and co-authors build a 2026 machine learning tool to predict which dialysis patients will crash during in-session exercise. Exercise intolerance, mostly sudden blood pressure drops, interrupts rehab for people on maintenance hemodialysis. The prospective study enrolled 128 adults dialyzed three times weekly, producing 896 session records and simple functional tests.

Four algorithms competed under grouped cross-validation. Random Forest won, reaching a mean ROC area of 0.914 and accuracy of 0.845 across folds in the testing. Intolerance appeared in 29.7 percent of patients during the study period. Explanation analysis named Timed Up and Go time, pre-dialysis systolic pressure, and fluid-removal settings as the top predictors. The authors offer the clear model as support for tailoring exercise risk plans in dialysis units.
pmc-13292510:
Iryna Mogilevkina and co-authors survey a 2026 question in wartime Ukraine: do medical students still plan to have children? Ukraine's fertility rate hit 0.9 in 2022, among Europe's lowest. An online questionnaire at Odesa National Medical University in May 2024 drew 655 women and 191 men, averaging twenty years old.

Three quarters intended to become parents, mostly wanting two children. Women hoped for a first child at 26.1 years on average, men at 28.1 years in the responses. Sixty-two percent said they would carry a hypothetical pregnancy to birth, citing moral or religious grounds, while abortion choosers named money and the war. Housing and financial stability topped the preconditions, at 93 and 92 percent of respondents. Women anticipated emotional rewards more; men worried more about lost time and income.
pmc-13293410:
Linda Chan and colleagues use, in a 2026 study, Hong Kong health records to test whether statins prevent first heart disease in older adults with type 2 diabetes. Trial data for people aged 75 and older are thin, since older patients are often left out.

The team mimicked a sequence of 84 monthly trials using territory-wide records from 2009 onward, sorting each patient as a statin starter or non-starter. Follow-up ran to outcomes, death, or the end of 2018, with weights to handle changing adherence. Groups were split by age bands for fair comparison. The design aims to give real-world guidance where trial proof is scarce.
pmc-13294110:
Fabian Tomschi and Thomas Hilberg test how steady pressure pain readings are at joint landmarks in a 2026 reliability study. Healthy adults aged 18 to 40 took part in two parts of 40 people each. One examiner repeated measures three times for within-rater checks, while two examiners compared results for between-rater checks, using a digital algometer at elbow, knee, ankle, sternum, and forehead.

Within-rater reliability was excellent almost everywhere, with the elbow slightly lower but still good. Between-rater results were excellent at the sternum and good elsewhere. Error margins were smallest at the flat reference sites. Joint testing looks fit for standard pain assessments in pain-free adults.
pmc-13295310:
Zanoxolo Ntsongota and colleagues review gut-based ways to cut antibiotic use in cattle in a 2026 article. Resistance worries have pushed farms to find health support that does not rely on routine antibiotics. Shaping the gut microbe community with natural supplements is a leading candidate route.

Seventeen strong studies from the past 15 years were judged in depth. Probiotics and plant based additives improved growth, feed digestion, and disease resistance in many trials, lowering the need for antibiotic treatment. Results still varied with cattle type, farm system, and dose given. The authors argue for matching the supplement plan to each setting rather than one fixed recipe.
pmc-13295410:
Aileen Hsieh and colleagues study how a remodelled airway base layer changes epithelial behaviour in asthma in a 2026 article. In asthma, the thin sheet under airway lining cells gains extra collagen and fibronectin. Whether that change is merely structural, or actively steers cell repair and alarm signals, was the question.

Lining cells from healthy and asthmatic donors were grown on six different base proteins and tracked for 72 hours. Cells attached, spread, and sealed barriers faster on the asthma-linked proteins than on the healthy mix. Two collagens also raised release of TSLP, an alarm signal, without a broad inflammatory rise, linking scarring to lasting alarm.
pmc-13295610:
Lindsey Lemus and colleagues feed almond meal to ageing mice in a 2026 study. Anaemia in old age has many roots, including inflammation and oxidative stress that damage red blood cells. Almonds carry nutrients that might calm both processes and protect those cells.

Forty-eight older mice ate plain food or food with almond meal supplying part of their calories for 12 or 21 weeks. Almond-fed mice showed more even red cell sizes early and higher red cell counts later in the trial. Adjusted models tied almond eating to higher counts and much lower odds of anaemia, suggesting diet support for blood health in ageing.
pmc-13295710:
Mirena Chakarova and colleagues treat lab-grown arnica shoots with a plant hormone in a 2026 study. Arnica montana has served medicine for centuries, yet wild stocks are shrinking under demand. Methyl jasmonate mimics stress signals and can push cultured plants to make more valuable compounds.

Shoots received the treatment for seven days at three strengths in the trial. Growth slowed at all strengths, while antioxidant enzyme activity shifted in response. Valuable caffeoylquinic acids climbed, along with total phenols and flavonoids in the treated plantlets. The system offers a dependable way to raise useful arnica compounds without harvesting wild plants.
pmc-13295810:
Ioannis G Katsantonis studies how demanding maths teaching builds confidence in a 2026 article. Lessons that push students to argue and reason may strengthen how learners steer their own thinking. Greek results from the PISA 2022 schools survey supplied the data for a staged pathway model.

Data covered 6,403 teenagers, about half of them female. Challenging instruction tied positively to self-regulation habits, which in turn tied to stronger maths self-belief. Good results themselves fed confidence as mastery experiences, carrying part of the teaching effect. The findings support argument-rich lessons as a route to both skill and belief in mathematics.
pmc-13295910:
Anuj Kumar Pandey and colleagues review, in 2026, whether poorer countries grant mothers leave after stillbirth. Most stillbirths happen in such countries, and parents need time to recover in body and mind, yet policy often assumes a living baby.

Checking labour and United Nations sources plus national rules for 49 countries, the team find every country has maternity leave, but fewer than a fifth mention stillbirth at all. Where leave exists it averages about half the length granted after a live birth, and definitions of stillbirth vary widely. The authors press for explicit, fairer provisions.
pmc-13296410:
Yong Li and co-authors test, in 2026, whether a wearable brain scanner can tell apart rest, imagined movement and real movement from rhythms nested inside each other. The scanner uses light-based sensors needing no deep cooling, and the team extract coupling patterns between slow and fast brain waves.

Coupling features beat plain wave-power features at sorting the three states. One pairing, linking alpha rhythm phase to gamma strength, reached about eighty-six percent balanced accuracy under cross-checking. The authors offer the result as early proof that wearable scanners can support movement decoding for future brain-computer links.
pmc-13296810:
Calliope Stavrou and colleagues review treatment options when kidney cancer has spread to only a few sites, in a 2026 article. Fewer than five deposits defines this oligometastatic state, which can behave less aggressively than widespread disease. Options range from focused radiotherapy to whole-body drug therapy and heat or cold ablation.

Targeted radiotherapy carries the strongest support so far, appearing safe and effective in carefully chosen patients. Drug treatments alone show mixed results and more side effects. Combining drugs with radiotherapy may stir immune attacks at untreated sites, an effect still being studied. The authors say trials must now pin down the best combinations and which patients benefit.
pmc-13297210:
Aigerim Dyussupova and colleagues compare, in 2026, methods for detecting disease markers and germs in saliva tested outside the mouth. Spit collection is painless and simple, so the team gather detection limits from 149 lab studies and accuracy from 118 clinical ones across many techniques.

For the stress hormone cortisol, electrochemical sensors proved most sensitive, ahead of antibody tests and mass analysis. In patient studies, antibody testing and a laser-based method led on balanced accuracy, while mass and gene methods followed closely. The authors say the laser approach could shine once standardised.
pmc-13297310:
Alexandre Alberto Barros Duarte and colleagues test, in 2026, whether missing antioxidant genes raise risk of necrotising enterocolitis, a gut catastrophe of preterm babies. One hundred newborns, half with the disease, were typed for two glutathione gene deletions at one centre.

Babies missing the GSTM1 gene made up a larger share of cases and carried roughly triple the adjusted odds of disease. The second gene and combined patterns showed no clear link, and severity was not predicted. Most cases sat at middle stages. The authors label the pilot hypothesis-forming and call for larger prospective confirmation.
pmc-13297510:
Why do some liver tumors answer immunotherapy while others shrug it off? Kizuki Yuza and Timothy M Pawlik organize the possible reasons in a 2026 review of hepatocellular carcinoma, using the cancer immunity cycle as their framework.

They sort failure points along that cycle: weak immune priming, poor cell trafficking into tumors, suppression by myeloid and stromal cells, and metabolic strain from low oxygen. Checkpoint drugs alone fix only certain breaks, so combinations work best when the partner drug targets the barrier that actually dominates a given tumor. Resistance, they note, can also arise from the tumor cells, the surrounding tissue, prior treatment, or the disease's cause, arguing for biomarker-guided choices.
pmc-13298010:
Stored tumor samples can double as a genetics resource for pain research, demonstrate Christine L Watt and colleagues in a 2026 study of advanced cancer. They matched tumor bank DNA with medical records to ask whether inherited variants explain why some patients need far more opioid than others.

Several genetic differences tracked with higher or lower opioid requirements for cancer pain. Just as important to the authors, the tumor bank approach proved practical, turning archived material into usable pharmacogenomic data without new sampling. They present the work as groundwork for studies that could one day tailor opioid prescribing to a patient's genetic profile, easing the common problem of undertreated pain.
pmc-13298110:
Wrist injections risk nicking a sensory nerve, so So Hyun Park and co-authors mapped that nerve with ultrasound in a 2026 study. They scanned 58 forearms from 29 healthy volunteers, tracing the superficial radial nerve across four landmarks near the wrist extensor compartments.

Forearm length predicted the nerve's position at proximal landmarks but not at the most distal one. For intersection syndrome, the team identified a safer corridor between 24.1% and 12.7% of forearm length, approached from the thumb side downward. For De Quervain's tenosynovitis, they advise a volar-to-dorsal needle path at or beyond 0.8 cm from the radial styloid. The landmark mix aims to cut accidental nerve injury.
pmc-13298410:
Risa Tomioka-Inagawa leads a multicentre Japanese study of prostate surgery cases where no tumour remained in the removed gland, in a 2026 retrospective analysis. This pathological T0 pattern is rare and its meaning for prognosis is unclear. Records covered more than three thousand robot-assisted operations at nine centres.

Only 27 men showed the pattern, and most had received hormone therapy before surgery. Four cases occurred without such therapy, and none saw biochemical recurrence during limited follow-up. Outcomes in the hormone-treated subgroup looked numerically favourable, though very few events occurred. The authors urge caution, noting later recurrences could have been missed in short to intermediate follow-up.
pmc-13299410:
Work on the immune side of birth moves fast. Dariusz Szukiewicz marks that pace in a 2026 note that opens a fresh set of papers on the theme, the second such set in two years. The set tracks how a mom and her unborn child trade immune signs as the womb bed forms and grows.

One theme is molar growths, a rare flaw of birth that strikes near 1 in 1000 to 1200 births in the West. A slip at the egg's first join leaves the growth with too much of the dad's gene stock. Some such growths turn to cancer, so the note backs firm proof of type. A p57 stain plus gene checks now aid the scope, which on its own can mix up full moles, part moles, and lost births.
pmc-13299510:
Crina Claudia Rusu leads a team linking a blood vessel adhesion molecule to inflammation and bone-mineral problems in dialysis patients, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. E-selectin helps white cells stick to vessel walls and may mark early vessel damage. Sixty-eight haemodialysis patients gave clinical and laboratory data, plus an ultrasound test of vessel relaxation.

Four markers stayed independently tied to E-selectin after adjustment, covering a bone enzyme, parathyroid hormone, white cell count, and an immune marker. Among younger inflamed patients, higher E-selectin tracked worse vessel relaxation. Novel links with two of the markers extend earlier knowledge about cardiovascular risk in this group.
pmc-13300410:
Hyewon Jeon and co-authors validate a portable muscle sensing biofeedback system in a 2026 randomized proof-of-concept trial. Surface electromyography is cheap and portable, but whether its signals honestly reflect the deep abdominal muscles is unclear. Twenty-nine healthy adults were assigned to visual biofeedback or ordinary verbal coaching, and both groups followed the same two-week core stabilization program.

The visual group improved more on deep muscle activation and on a ratio favoring deep over surface muscles. Ultrasound imaging, the reference standard here, showed larger gains in transversus abdominis thickness and contractile activity in that same group. Changes in the sensor readings also correlated moderately with changes in muscle thickness. The authors argue the portable system can stand in for ultrasound when monitoring deep core training, widening access to this kind of rehabilitation feedback.
pmc-13301010:
Vedat Aslan and co-authors compare heart remodeling after two bypass surgery routes in a 2026 multicenter study. One route rebuilds all needed vessels through a front chest incision without splitting the breastbone, while the other is the conventional open approach. The weighted analysis covered 554 elective patients at four centers between 2020 and 2025 who had ultrasound heart scans before surgery and at least three months afterward.

After statistical weighting balanced the groups, follow-up pumping strength did not differ meaningfully between the routes. One chamber diameter ended modestly larger after the conventional approach, a difference the authors flag as clinically uncertain, while the matching systolic diameter tied. The incision route took longer in the operating room but bought shorter intensive care and hospital stays plus fewer transfusions. The authors conclude the gentler access does not cost the ventricle anything measurable.
pmc-13301510:
O Tomer and co-authors send high risk valve patients home wearing artificial intelligence monitored heart recorders in a 2026 prospective study. After transcatheter aortic valve replacement, conduction blocks can arrive days later, and about thirty percent of pacemaker needs surface after discharge. From 143 valve patients, the team enrolled thirty-four whose tracings carried warning features. Each was fitted with a fourteen day ambulatory monitor. Automated triggers flagged high degree block, severe slowing, or widening intervals.

Six patients, about eighteen percent, ultimately needed pacemakers. Five were caught during the monitoring window for progressing block or symptomatic rhythm problems. One presented at thirty days with sinus node trouble. Nobody fainted, arrested, or needed a late pacemaker across a median 160 days of follow-up. The authors call AI guided home monitoring reliable and reassuring for this nervous post discharge interval, while continuing enrollment to gain the numbers needed for predictor hunting.
pmc-13301710:
Vered Bar and co-authors evaluate a test that grows a patient's tumor tissue in the lab and tries drugs on it before the patient does, in a 2026 post market study. The platform keeps tumor fragments alive for up to a week with their microenvironment intact, exposing them to therapies and scoring the response. The analysis covered 312 patients, with reports for 278 and outcome data for forty-five.

Among patients with outcomes, the test called response: a positive predictive value of about ninety-one percent and a negative predictive value near ninety-one percent as well. Its results swayed the doctor's decision in about half the tracked cases, and the authors project utility up to about fifty-nine percent across the full cohort. They argue testing complements gene sequencing, which cannot judge most drugs, by ruling out likely failures and turning predicted non responders into patients with an option.
pmc-13303010:
A clotting starch powder modestly blunted blood loss after knee replacement, Dojoon Park and colleagues report in a 2026 matched study. Patients over fifty having a first unilateral knee replacement before and after the topical thrombin-carboxymethyl starch agent entered the routine were paired by propensity scores, giving seventy matched pairs. Hemoglobin paths and total anemia burden replaced transfusion counts as the sensitive endpoints.

The treated group's day-one hemoglobin drop was smaller by 0.30 grams per deciliter, and their two-week anemia burden ran lower as well. Estimated blood loss and transfusion rates, already rare, did not differ. The authors suggest hemoglobin kinetics as the sharper yardstick in modern low-transfusion practice.
pmc-13303410:
Maano Tshimange and co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, the mineral crusts that choke forward-osmosis membranes concentrating urine for nutrient recovery. Fresh urine and aged, hydrolysed urine behave very differently as water is pulled out. Three cycles at high recovery let scaling build, while software predicted which minerals should form.

Fresh synthetic urine caused only moderate flow decline, leaving sparse calcium-phosphate deposits. Hydrolysed urine scaled severely, with flow collapsing by the third cycle under struvite and magnesium carbonate crusts. The model correctly named the dominant mineral families for both feeds. Plain water flushing restored nearly all flow in both cases, and the membranes kept rejecting the key ions, so the damage proved mostly reversible.
pmc-13303710:
Jinguo Liu and Liangliang Yu review how aging-like cell states shape gut scarring in Crohn's disease in a 2026 synthesis. Crohn's disease is a long-term bowel inflammation, and narrowed, scarred gut segments develop in many patients within ten years.

Short bursts of cell senescence may aid repair, but lasting buildup fuels inflammation and excess scar tissue. Triggers include oxidative stress, worn chromosome ends, and cell damage signals. Senescent gut, vessel, surface, and immune cells release a mix of signals that disturb tissue balance. Drugs that clear or calm such cells are discussed as future anti-scarring options.
pmc-13303910:
Sidrit Uruci and three colleagues published a review in two thousand twenty-six on traffic jams inside the genome. Cells copy DNA and read genes at the same time on the same strands. When the copying machine meets a reading machine, the clash can stall both and damage the genome.

The review gathers new ideas on how cells schedule and route this traffic to avoid pile-ups. One reading machine, RNA polymerase II, takes a central role in both preventing and clearing clashes. Helper systems untangle RNA loops, steady stalled forks, and guard the DNA packaging. Cancers often lean hard on these rescue systems, making them tempting drug targets. The authors also flag how hard these fleeting events are to observe.
pmc-13305710:
Eva Spada tested in a 2026 Italian study whether a cat's AB blood type affects its chance of carrying Leishmania infantum. Because blood antigens can shape host responses, the team checked both antibody evidence and parasite DNA against blood group.

In all, 706 cats were typed, with 83.1% type A, 10.1% type B and 6.8% type AB in the reported breakdown. Infection appeared in 67 cats, spread across all three groups, and no link emerged with positivity, antibody level or parasite load, even after allowing for region. The authors say other factors must drive susceptibility in cats.
pmc-13306110:
Lu Wenting measured lip shape in children who breathe through the mouth in a 2026 comparison study. A total of 210 children aged 6 to 12 joined, split evenly between long-term mouth breathers and nose breathers by parent questionnaire.

Standard side-view head X-rays supplied measures of lip and chin projection, lip lengths, their ratio and two facial angles. Group comparisons adjusted for age, sex and body mass index, with correction for many simultaneous tests. Because breathing status rested on parent report without airway testing, the authors present findings as associations only and back early clinical checks.
pmc-13306410:
Ruolin Li designed a lean neural network that merges infrared and visible images in a 2026 study. Heavy fusion networks give sharp results but carry many parameters, and simple shrinking often washes out heat and texture detail.

The LWC-DenseFuse design splits standard filtering into depthwise and pointwise steps, then adds channel attention to restore strong features. Channel shuffling lets separated groups exchange information during processing. The authors aim to hold fusion quality while cutting size, serving cameras and edge devices that must blend thermal and daylight views in real time.
pmc-13306810:
Aarti Lalwani grouped back pain patients by movement patterns from skin strain tape in a 2026 exploratory study. Ten people with low back pain wore six Motion Tape sensors whose signals track skin stretch during motion and muscle effort.

Features came from body-mechanics knowledge plus causal pattern hunting across the sensor streams, revealing directed coordination between back segments. A grouping method then searched for subtypes inside the pain group rather than just splitting pain from health. The authors present tape data as a cheap, rich source for personalising back pain care.
pmc-13307410:
El-Sayed M Desoky and co-authors test in 2026 leaf sprays that might help common bean cope with salty soil in field plots over two seasons. Sprays mixed salicylic acid with silicon and chitosan particles in several blends, and growth, leaf function, stress markers, and pod yield were tracked.

Salt alone cut growth and yield and raised cell damage, while every spray softened those harms to some degree. The blend of chitosan silicon particles plus salicylic acid worked best, roughly doubling shoot dry weight and green pod yield versus the salty control. Leaf salt balance also improved, with far less sodium kept inside the leaf tissue.
pmc-13308710:
Sophia Golec and co-authors published this cancer care study in 2026. It concerns CAR T-cell therapy for multiple myeloma, a treatment that can trigger a dangerous immune overreaction called cytokine release syndrome. A drug named tocilizumab is used to calm that reaction, and the team asked whether giving it early affects heart risk and cancer outcomes. They reviewed charts for 145 patients treated at one center between 2017 and 2023.

The immune reaction occurred in 120 patients, and most received the drug within a day. Fourteen patients, about ten percent, suffered a major heart event within a year, and every one of them had had the immune reaction. At twelve months, about 58 percent of patients remained free of cancer progression. Survival and progression did not differ significantly between patients who did and did not develop the reaction. The study maps the heart risk that shadows this powerful therapy.
pmc-13309010:
Youai Song and co-authors craft in 2026 a gene score that links milk acid marks and cell self eating to outlook in liver cancer, then chase the top hit. Multi source data split tumours into two types with unlike fates, and one gene, CLEC3B, stood out in the score they built.

Single cell reads traced that gene to liver vessel lining cells, where it ran low in tumour tissue versus healthy tissue. Fluid from lining cells that made extra CLEC3B curbed tumour cell growth in dish tests run by the team. The brake worked by damping both self eating and milk acid marks at once. The gene may serve as a fate mark and drug lead.
pmc-13309610:
Evans Kwabena Abor and co-authors review computer prediction tools for designing medical nanoparticles in a 2026 article. Tiny drug carriers can target disease, yet how they act inside the body stays hard to foresee. Machine learning and structure-activity models promise faster, cheaper design before lab work begins.

Methods covered range from nano-specific descriptors and classic learning to deep learning and physics-guided hybrids, plus simulations from quantum to tissue scale. Two fields show clear promise: plant-based nano carriers with better solubility and targeting, and drugs for neglected tropical diseases that must reach hidden parasites. Data gaps and uneven reporting still limit trust. The authors propose shared data rules to firm the field.
pmc-13310010:
Maider Aguerralde-Martin and co-authors present a point-and-click app for building gene control networks from many data types in a 2026 article. Sorting which regulators drive each body state is key to grasping complex disease. An existing R package, MORE, builds such networks with sound statistics but demands coding skill.

The app, MOREshiny, wraps that package in a friendly web screen where users upload data, set model choices, and read results without code. Method picks are guided on screen, and results can be saved for later work. A pathway enrichment module is built in. The authors aim to open advanced multi-data modeling to bench scientists who do not program.
pmc-13310510:
Taichi Mori and co-authors compare yearly against every-other-year stool testing for bowel cancer screening in Japan in a 2026 study. The fecal immunochemical test spots hidden blood in stool, a cancer warning sign. Japan current program tests yearly, yet the best interval for cost and benefit was unsettled.

A simulation followed 100,000 average-risk adults from age forty across sixty years under both schedules. Yearly testing came out cheaper overall and slightly richer in quality-adjusted life years than testing every two years in the model results. Repeated uncertainty runs favored yearly testing in 92.7 percent of cases at the set value threshold. The authors back keeping the yearly schedule in national guidance.
pmc-13310710:
Xin Xin and colleagues built a 2026 prediction tool for poor ovarian response during fertility treatment. Some patients make few eggs during stimulation, which lowers the chance of success. Early warning would let doctors adjust plans in advance. The team used past cases from a hospital in Shenyang, China, to find the best warning signs.

Records covered 1,789 patients treated from 2020 to 2023, split into build and test groups by date. Four methods were compared, and a stepwise method won. Hormone levels, body weight, and follicle counts proved the strongest signs. A simple chart turns those signs into a personal risk score for clinic use.
pmc-13311010:
Xiaoyu Liu and co-authors link social media health use to confidence in managing health in a 2026 survey study. Many adults seek health facts on social feeds, where false claims spread fast. Whether reliance on such facts and trouble judging them tie to self confidence was unclear.

Data came from a 2022 national trends survey with 4,352 United States adults. About one quarter felt fully confident in managing health. People who firmly rejected using feed facts for choices, and those who found truth sorting easy, reported higher confidence. Sharing feed facts with doctors showed no link. Women and daily feed users also scored higher.
pmc-13311210:
Bo Zhao and co-authors report a 2026 study on predicting treatment response in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. The team asked whether scan features taken from inside and around a tumor could show, before treatment, which patients would have no cancer left after drug therapy and surgery.

Records from 122 patients who had CT scans before treatment were reviewed. Scores were built from tumor features, nearby tissue features, and clinical details such as tumor stage and site, then joined in one model. The combined model separated responders from non-responders well in both test groups. Features from tissue around the tumor added the most. Such a scan-based tool could help doctors plan care without extra invasive tests.
pmc-13311310:
Berhanu Kelemework Fenta and co-authors present their 2026 case of adrenal tuberculosis that arrived as an adrenal crisis. The infection had destroyed both adrenal glands, a cause of gland failure still common where resources are scarce.

The 45-year-old man came in with low blood pressure, low sodium, high potassium, low blood sugar, and darkened skin. His morning cortisol read 0.5 in the reported units, and CT scans showed both glands enlarged. No active lung tuberculosis was found. The authors warn that late spotting of this cause delays care and can prove fatal without hormone replacement.
pmc-13311810:
Chloe C. Krasnoff, Brynn A. Hathaway, and Angelo B. Lipira present a 2026 study on how common two scaphoid bone shapes are in the general population. The wrist bone's shape and blood supply pattern follow a 2019 classification.

The team reviewed four-view wrist X-rays taken in 2022 at one center, excluding fresh fractures and disease. Among 363 wrists from 345 patients, 80.2 percent held type I bones and 19.8 percent type II in this sample. Type II patients were more often left-handed, with no other clear demographic gaps. Knowing the base rates sets up studies on whether type II bones break or fail to heal more often.
pmc-13311910:
Matteo Alessandro De Rosa and co-authors detail a 2026 two-patient account of switching between under-skin levodopa infusion systems in advanced Parkinson's disease. No guidance existed for moving from ND0612 to foslevodopa/foscarbidopa.

Both patients used ND0612 plus oral levodopa before the switch. The new dose was set from total daily levodopa equivalents, then fine-tuned under close watch. Both switches finished within one day with no acute harms. At three months, off time had fallen sharply, with better movement, steadier sleep and behavior, and no infusion-site problems. The cases offer a practical template for clinics.
pmc-13312010:
Connor W Smith and co-authors in 2026 detail a case of desmoplastic small round cell tumor starting in the kidney and spreading to bone. The rare, aggressive sarcoma usually grows on the abdominal lining of teen and young adult males.

The patient was a 23-year-old man. CT and PET-CT imaging played the central role in the first workup, since this tumor copies the look of other abdominal growths. Final diagnosis required tissue study, as scans and microscopy overlap with other round cell tumors. The authors walk through the presentation, imaging signs, and the aggressive course, urging early tissue confirmation when scans suggest this tumor.
pmc-13312110:
Feng Wei and colleagues report a 2026 study of how goose astrovirus genotype 2 interacts with autophagy, the cell's recycling system, in goose kidney cells. The virus causes fatal gout in young goslings and heavy losses for Chinese goose farming, yet its disease mechanisms are poorly mapped. Working in primary kidney tubular cells from geese, the team measured whether infection switches autophagy on and whether that helps or hinders the virus.

Infection clearly raised autophagic activity. Drugs that boosted autophagy increased viral replication, while drugs that blocked it reduced replication, pointing to a pro-viral role. Blocking a signaling protein called ERK2, or silencing it with RNA interference, removed the effect, showing the virus drives autophagy through that pathway. The findings name a concrete mechanism behind this emerging pathogen and suggest autophagy control as one angle for future interventions.
pmc-13312410:
Michela Puxeddu and a large team report a 2026 medicinal chemistry study of a new compound that blocks two cancer-relevant targets at once. Dishevelled 1 proteins feed the Wnt signaling pathway and are overproduced in drug-resistant colorectal cancer cells, while the pump P-glycoprotein ejects chemotherapy drugs from those same cells.

The team synthesized a family of indole-2-carboxamides and found one member, a carefully specified stereoisomer, that inhibits Dishevelled 1 at low concentration and binds its PDZ domain specifically. The compound lowered beta-catenin levels in colon cancer cells, shrank tumors in a mouse xenograft model. It also blocked the drug pump strongly enough to restore doxorubicin sensitivity in resistant cells. It also held up in human liver preparations and showed acceptable blood levels in mice, marking it as a dual-targeting candidate.
pmc-13312610:
Taro Yoshimura and Takenori Sasaki report a 2026 study of tree snails whose camouflage switches with the weather. Two distantly related species, Hypselostyla camelopardalis and Reinia variegata, wear mottled shells when dry. Wetting erases the pattern into a uniform dark brown that returns as the shell dries, a trick suited to habitats where humidity and light swing quickly.

Microscopy showed the change lives in the shell's thin organic outer layer, which is built in two tiers. In pale patches, water fills microscopic voids and smooths the surface, matching the layer's refractive index to its surroundings so more light passes through and the mottling vanishes. The authors call the independent invention of the same mechanism in unrelated lineages convergent evolution, and note the water-responsive film could inspire humidity-sensitive coatings and adaptive optical materials.
pmc-13312910:
Víctor J. López-Madrona and colleagues publish a 2026 critique of a popular claim in speech neuroscience: that brain rhythms during listening are generated by the brain locking onto speech. A recent intracranial study read auditory activity that outlasted acoustic edges as proof of this entrainment, since a merely reactive brain should fall silent with the sound.

López-Madrona's team shows the speech stimulus itself already contains the same rhythmic spectrotemporal pattern after its edges, so a simple evoked response explains the recordings without invoking an internal oscillator. The episode, they argue, exposes a missing control across naturalistic studies: researchers model the brain's signal in fine detail while never analyzing the signal it was fed. They propose routine stimulus-signal analysis as standard practice whenever entrainment is claimed from real-world speech.
pmc-13313010:
Shudong Zhang and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, a web calculator that estimates clot risk before surgery in elderly patients with broken hips. Deep vein thrombosis stalks this group, and a quick estimate from routine admission data could guide prevention. The team pitted three machine learning approaches against each other on records from a Beijing hospital.

Data from 538 patients split into a development group and a later temporal validation group. A selection algorithm distilled eighteen candidate measures down to seven, including fracture type, injury-to-arrival time, and several blood values. The support vector machine won, reaching an area under the curve of 0.8525 in testing and 0.8360 in the later patients, with honest calibration. Prothrombin time mattered most. The authors offer the free calculator as an interpretable bedside risk tool.
pmc-13313210:
Pellegrino Cerino and colleagues report a 2026 survey of trace metals in blood across Campania in southern Italy. The SPES program asked whether levels of these metals vary in fine detail between towns grouped by how much strain their environment bears.

In 2016 and 2017 the program drew adults aged 20 to 49 years from town lists, sorting towns into high, medium, and low impact groups and into 21 town clusters. Of 4205 people enrolled, 4188 were kept for study, and 20 trace metals were measured in serum by mass spectrometry. Medium-impact areas showed higher mercury and antimony than the study-wide mean, with ratios of 1.87 and 1.95 as given in the report. Town-level maps, such as clusters near a foundry in the Irno Valley, give health teams a sharper view of where exposure runs high.
pmc-13313610:
Carlo Molfini Curci and co-authors reviewed imaging and AI in lung cancer aftercare in a 2026 paper. Tertiary prevention starts once treatment ends: watching for the cancer's return, judging how well therapy worked, and sorting each patient's outlook. Scans carry most of that watch, and AI now reads scans beside the doctor.

Their narrative review swept four databases for work from 2019 to early 2024. It weighs what AI adds to recurrence watch and response checks, and what blocks it in real clinics. The authors close with clinical outlooks for wider use. Smarter watching could catch returns while they are still beatable.
pmc-13313910:
Takumi Matsuura, Hiroshi Satoh, and Masaaki Katayama used a very strong magnetic scanner to study fine structure in cat kidneys after death. One kidney came from a cat with early chronic kidney disease, the other from a matched healthy cat. Such ultra-strong scans have barely been tried in cat medicine.

The sick kidney lost the clear border between its outer and inner zones on scans. Water-motion measures ran lower in its outer zone, matching heavier scarring seen under the microscope. Values in the deepest zone ran higher instead. The authors say these scan signs track tissue scarring well, a step toward gentler checks for kidney disease in cats.
pmc-13314110:
Akeem Moradehun Bamiro and co-authors run a 2026 pilot study on whether a routine blood ratio can predict survival in rats with chemically induced tongue cancer. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio forecasts outcomes in human cancers, but its value inside preclinical models was undefined. Female rats drank water laced with a carcinogen for twenty weeks, then had blood counts taken. Eighteen animals entered a 42-day survival watch. The team tested three inflammatory ratios for their power to separate survivors from non-survivors.

Only the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio worked. Its discrimination score reached 0.901 on the analysis curve, while the platelet and monocyte ratios performed poorly. Rats above a ratio of roughly 0.55 died at a starkly different rate, eight of nine against one of nine below the line. The authors suggest this cheap count could help researchers in resource-limited settings stratify animals and design larger confirmatory studies.
pmc-13316210:
Alberto De Lorenzo and a very large team studied in 2026 how treatment choices for chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy vary across Italian centers over time. The nerve disease is treatable and immune driven, yet real-world evidence on strategies and their change over the years was limited.

The multicentre study mixed prospective and retrospective observation to chart prescription patterns, check alignment with international guidelines, and find clinical, structural, and time factors tied to decisions and outcomes. Wide center-to-center variation in such a treatable disease flags room to standardize care and share best practice.
pmc-13316610:
Donnie Mategula heads a very large team behind a 2026 multi-country cohort study of diarrhoea outcomes in young children, centered on Shigella, a leading cause in poorer settings. The study asks what follows a clinic visit for Shigella diarrhoea: lingering illness, hospital care, or slowed growth.

Between June 2022 and August 2024, clinics in seven countries enrolled 8,756 children aged 6 to 35 months with fresh diarrhoea episodes. Stool testing by culture and gene methods sorted Shigella cases from children with no germ found. Follow-up visits at four weeks and three months track long diarrhoea, admissions, and height growth. The design gives health planners firm ground on the hidden costs of this infection.
pmc-13317410:
Monica Sciacco and a large team test a high-plex imaging tool on muscle samples in inflammatory muscle disease. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. These diseases are a mixed group of immune ills of muscle, each with its own marks. A biopsy is a key test, but old stain methods can show only a few markers at once, with low detail.

Their tool runs many rounds of stain and scan on one slice, to map many proteins in place. Signal stays strong and tissue shape holds through all rounds. Early maps show distinct patterns of immune cells, matrix change, and vessel change by disease kind. The pilot shows the route works for muscle.
pmc-13317510:
Nicolas Colmano and colleagues explain, in a 2026 study, how faults in the sodium-potassium pump's alpha1 subunit cause low magnesium with seizures that resist treatment. The pump sits in every cell membrane, and its many variants cause a family of diseases.

Every variant tied to the low-magnesium seizure picture carried a stray leak current, worked weakly, and reached the cell surface in smaller numbers. A frozen-structure image of one variant, W931R, suggests the leaks slip through the seam where protein meets membrane fat. The shared leak gives doctors a unifying mechanism and a target: plug the seam or boost surface delivery, and several pump diseases might ease at once.
pmc-13318210:
Megan Hare and Kathryn Humphreys track, in a 2026 study, how new mothers' and fathers' depressive symptoms feed each other across the first eighteen months after birth. Postpartum depression in fathers is understudied, and couples may pass low mood back and forth.

The study followed 119 couples with advanced panel modeling. Mothers' symptoms held steady across every check, while fathers' steadied only later. A relay emerged: mothers' one-month symptoms predicted fathers' at six months, which in turn predicted mothers' at twelve months. Mothers who recalled emotional or physical neglect in childhood entered pregnancy with heavier symptoms, and emotional neglect echoed again at one month. Screening, the authors argue, should treat the couple as one system.
pmc-13318610:
Lukas Retzer and Cornelia Niessen offer a 2026 qualitative interview study. They ask what workers expect from future workplace robots. The focus is social skills and independence. Twenty workers from hospitality, manufacturing, and care jobs were interviewed. The authors also built a taxonomy of robot social skills.

Workers could state clear preferences about future robot use. Basic social skills were widely wanted. Polite, readable behaviour could be built in broadly. Freedom to act alone needed careful tuning to task and setting. Too little social skill risks negative reactions. Too much independence carries the same risk. The authors turn these views into provisional design requirements. They aim them at developers of workplace robots.
pmc-13319110:
Xi Li leads a large team presenting, in 2026, an end-to-end AI system that reads surgical video and links movement patterns to patient outcomes. The system, called Frame-to-Outcome, turns dissection footage into gesture sequences. Testing used the nerve-sparing step of robot prostate surgery. Transformer models classified actions frame by frame.

The system detected short gestures of about two seconds reliably. Accuracy reached an AUC of 0.80 at frame level and 0.81 at video level in their tests. Features like gesture frequency, duration, and transitions predicted outcomes about as well as human labels. Effect directions matched across 25 shared features, with a strong correlation of 0.96 between the two. Longer tissue peeling and lower energy use tied to better erectile recovery. The authors see a base for data-driven surgical feedback.
pmc-13320110:
Juan Antonio Valera-Calero and colleagues set out, in 2026, to analyse where ChatGPT disagrees with human researchers when scoring trial quality in physiotherapy. The PEDro scale rates experimental studies on items such as randomisation, blinding and follow-up, and systematic reviews depend on those scores. Whether an artificial intelligence system can reproduce them reliably was unclear.

Rather than scoring trials fresh, the team used item-level scores already published inside systematic reviews, where dual independent appraisal and consensus had strengthened the reference standard. Eligible reviews came from indexed journals over a recent ten-year window. Blinded assessors prompted the model once per article with standard instructions and asked for brief justifications. A statistician blinded to score sources then compared item by item, so disagreement patterns could be traced to specific scale items.
pmc-13320410:
Fang-Chin Hsu and co-authors test mucus swabbed from the scope as a source for bowel growth checks in a 2026 pilot study. Bowel cancer ranks high in both new cases and deaths in the world, and early growths that may turn bad need sharp, low burden checks. Mucus that coats the bowel wall may trap loose DNA shed right at the growth site, richer than blood or stool.

A gene change tied to bowel growths was hunted in that mucus DNA in a first small group. The test caught cancer and advanced early growths with high catch rates at a low signal floor in the pilot counts, though false alarms rose as well. It beat a stool blood test and a blood marker on catch rate in this early contrast. Wider trials must set its true place.
pmc-13320510:
Rick R.A. Hendriks and colleagues adapt a climate and health survey for Dutch nurses in a 2026 study. Nurses link the public with health care and will face more heat, storm, and infection risks tied to a changing climate. No checked Dutch tool existed to gauge nurses' awareness, concern, drive, and habits on climate and health.

The team followed six stages, with forward and back translation, expert review, and field pre-testing, then checks of how well the survey held together. Nurses across the Netherlands were reached through the national nurses group and other networks from June 2025. A sound Dutch version gives leaders a baseline for training and for planning climate ready care.
pmc-13320810:
Ting Li and colleagues present, in 2026, a case where a three-dimensional printed model guided hip surgery for a nine-year-old girl. Developmental dysplasia means the hip socket forms too shallow for the ball of the thigh bone, causing subluxation and early joint damage. Her case was complicated by a cystic lesion inside the socket bone.

The girl had an abnormal gait for a year, hip pain and a shorter left leg. Imaging showed a shallow socket, a partly deformed femoral head and a cyst roughly two centimetres across. Surgeons printed a life-size model of her pelvis and rehearsed a Pemberton osteotomy, a reshaping cut, on it before operating. The authors review why printed models can shorten operating time, improve visualisation and reduce radiation in such tailored paediatric surgery.
pmc-13321010:
Suhaib Muflih and colleagues review antibiotic use before caesarean birth across Jordan in a 2026 national records study. Antibiotics given before surgery help prevent wound infection, yet compliance data from lower income settings are scarce. Records covered 60,212 women who had caesarean births from 2015 to 2022 in 20 health ministry hospitals.

Only 19.4 percent received preventive antibiotics as guidelines advise, though the monthly rate crept up over time. Planned surgery and a longer wait after admission raised the chance of proper cover. Women who got proper cover had 41 percent lower odds of returning to hospital with a wound infection. The gap points to clear room for routine improvement.
pmc-13321810:
Jun-Jie Chen and co-authors report a light driven route to fluorinated ring systems for drug design in a 2026 chemistry study. Small bicyclic scaffolds can stand in for benzene rings in medicines, but fluorinated versions are hard to build by standard methods. The team used visible light and energy transfer catalysis to fold flat ring starting materials into three dimensional shapes.

The dearomative cycloaddition joins gem-difluoro alkenes carrying varied heteroaromatic rings into bicyclo[2.1.1]hexane products. Conditions were mild, yields were good, and shape selectivity was excellent across many ring types. Mechanism checks pointed to triplet diradical steps. The route opens fluorinated stand-ins that older carbene or cycloaddition methods reach poorly.
pmc-13322910:
Zihan Zhang and colleagues describe a vasculitis case that first looked like a middle ear problem, in a 2026 case report. Their patient, a 50-year-old woman, had severe secretory otitis media with hearing loss, facial nerve palsy, ear pain and high fever, and was treated for infection for a long period.

Testing later showed granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a rare disease where inflamed small vessels and granulomas harm the airways, kidneys and other tissue. No other typical signs were present at first, which explains the delay. The authors urge ear specialists to consider body-wide disease behind stubborn ear cases, since early treatment and team care can prevent lasting damage.
pmc-13323110:
Justin C Deme and co-authors picture the bacterial Tat transport core in action, in a 2026 structural study. The twin-arginine system moves folded proteins across membranes and matters for bacterial virulence and for plant photosynthesis.

Cryo-electron microscopy gave resting structures of TatBC complexes from Escherichia coli and two other bacteria, plus substrate-bound forms at early transport stages. Cargo proteins touch the core only through their N-terminal signal peptides, whose targeting parts contact TatC while TatB clamps the peptide body. Strongly tilted helices thin the membrane sharply at the site. With lab tests alongside, the authors propose a step-by-step model for how transport begins.
pmc-13323310:
Simone Sarti and co-authors review whole network analysis of health behaviour, in a 2026 systematic review covering smoking, alcohol use, physical activity and diet. Unlike personal network studies, this method maps every tie inside a defined group, showing how habits spread and settle.

Searching six databases under PRISMA guidance, they kept 27 empirical studies with full network data. Peer influence, similarity-based bonding, cohesion and central positions recurred as structural drivers across all four behaviours. Behaviour clusters and joint change in ties and habits stood out, and long-term actor-based models best separated choosing similar friends from copying them. The authors commend the method for designing group-level health interventions.
pmc-13323810:
Mohamed Wishahi and Mohamed Badawy write a 2026 letter to the editor on the 2025 European guidelines for urinary infections. They respond to a study by Yadav and others that built a prediction nomogram from patient factors beyond the urine sample itself.

The new European Association of Urology scheme sorts infections as localised or systemic by symptoms and signs, replacing the older split between uncomplicated and complicated infection. Care follows that clinical setup rather than culture results alone, with localised cases managed as outpatients. The writers stress that symptoms, examination, labs and imaging all feed diagnosis, and that antibiotic effects on gut and urinary microbes deserve weight in treatment choice.
pmc-13324310:
Hongyue Lin and Ying Huang identify the enzyme USP48 as a brake on colorectal cancer, in a 2026 study built around its partner protein SELENBP1. Both proteins track with better clinical outcomes in this common and deadly cancer, whose aggressive behaviour resists standard care.

Raising USP48 levels suppressed malignant behaviour in colorectal cancer cells in their experiments, covering growth and stem-like traits. The enzyme works by stabilising SELENBP1, removing the ubiquitin tags that would send it for disposal. That places USP48 on the opposite side from several related enzymes that drive this cancer. The authors propose USP48 as a marker of how malignant a tumour is and as a lead for new treatment design.
pmc-13324410:
Sergey A Belokobylskij, Deokseo Ku and Hye-Rin Lee describe six new parasitoid wasp species from the Korean Peninsula, in a 2026 taxonomic paper on the braconid genus Aleiodes. These rogadine wasps parasitise caterpillars and mummify their hosts, a striking life cycle within a huge and varied genus.

The six newcomers span three subgenera and are each named, described and illustrated in full, with the authors credited inside the species names. Material came from the Korean fauna, long less documented than tropical Asian and American faunas for this group. A key to the Palaearctic subgenera of Aleiodes rounds out the paper, giving identifiers a route into a genus holding over six hundred described species.
pmc-13324510:
Åsa Carlsund and colleagues explore how specialist nurses counsel patients at risk of type 2 diabetes in a 2026 interview study from Swedish primary care. Food advice sits at the heart of prevention, but little was known about how nurses tailor it.

Semi-structured interviews ran from August to November 2025, and content analysis yielded four themes with 12 subthemes. Nurses stressed empathy, person-centered talk, and small-step goals shaped by gender, culture, and daily life. Short visits, low drive, money limits, and cultural gaps still blocked good advice. The nurses asked for training in cultural competence, fresh tools, and stronger backing from their organizations. Better support could make prevention advice fit real lives.
pmc-13325910:
Juan Aguilar-Gonzalez and team systematically tested pyrocarbon implants in shoulder arthroplasty. Their 2026 review and meta-analysis searched MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane, Scopus, and Web of Science in April 2025, comparing chrome-cobalt, pyrocarbon, and ceramic options for humeral head replacement. Pyrocarbon use is growing, including interposition arthroplasty and hemiarthroplasty, yet whether results differ by material had stayed unclear.

The review assessed implant survival, functional scores including the Constant score and Subjective Shoulder Value, pain scores, revision rates defined as reoperation involving implant removal, replacement, or conversion, complications, and radiological change. Prior reports suggested strong short-to-mid-term results, such as 93% survival at two years in one study and single-digit complication and revision rates in another, but long-term data remain limited. The authors aim to give surgeons a fuller picture of cumulative revision and complication rates across implant types.
pmc-13326810:
Clare L. Tolley and colleagues ask how best to warn vulnerable people about dirty air in a 2026 qualitative study. Those with prior illness, city poverty, or minority backgrounds carry the highest exposure risk.

Interviews and focus groups gathered 50 participants from varied at-risk groups in North East England. From their views the team built a theory-based communication framework. Messages must tailor risk facts to each group and pair them with doable protective steps. Trusted voices matter: health workers and community peers outrank distant agencies. Channels such as text messages and local networks widen reach. Behavior change trials are the next test.
pmc-13328010:
Carla Estrada-Muñoz and co-authors validate the Internet Addiction Test for wildland firefighters in a 2026 study. Digital tools now saturate emergency work, blurring needed use and harmful overuse that can erode attention and sleep. They gave the test to 205 firefighters and checked its structure and reliability.

Two factors emerged, one for broad problematic engagement and one for loss of control, and the confirmatory model fit very well, with CFI and TLI both at 0.997 on their report. The two factors overlapped heavily, limiting how cleanly they separate, yet the scale held up as a screening tool. The authors advise pairing scores with device logs and fatigue measures before judging any firefighter's use.
pmc-13330110:
Xiaoling Lin and colleagues describe building a phone-based self-care tool for bipolar disorder in a 2026 study. Bipolar illness often returns despite drug care, so support between visits matters. The tool, Mood Calm, runs as a WeChat mini program with six modules, from symptom and drug tracking to crisis spotting and thinking training.

Design drew on cognitive behaviour theory, prior literature, and an expert panel, with wearable links planned for sleep and activity. A four-week early trial then ran with five patients in remission, testing core modules only. All five finished and praised ease of use in the report. System data hinted at weaker drug routine logging. A larger randomised trial is planned next.
pmc-13330510:
Sandeep R. Reddy, Manjunatha Bangeppagari, and Prabhakar Kamarthy test potassium bromate harm in zebrafish in a 2026 study. The chemical is a food additive and pollutant known to damage genes and drive oxidation in mammals, but fish data were thin. Short tests ran for 96 hours and longer tests for 21 days.

The median lethal level at 96 hours came to 1052.6 mg per litre in the reported estimate. Short exposure slowed swimming and exploration and pushed fish toward the tank bottom. Longer exposure raised blood sugar and damaged liver tissue, with cell swelling, widened spaces, decay, and dead areas. Harm arose below lethal levels, giving baseline data for water risk work.
pmc-13330610:
Mohamed Omar Osman and colleagues pool evidence on dengue fever in Ethiopia in a 2026 review and meta-analysis. Dengue reports have risen in parts of the country, yet national pooled figures were missing. Searches followed standard review rules, and the protocol was registered in advance. Thirteen studies met the entry rules.

Eight cross-sectional studies fed the prevalence pool, which came to 25 percent in the reported estimate. Rates looked higher before 2020 than after in subgroup checks. Risk links included not wearing long sleeves, not using nets, open water storage, and no recent insecticide spraying. Spread between studies was high for risk links. Targeted community teaching and mosquito control are urged.
pmc-13330810:
Khaleel Ahmed and colleagues report the crystal structure of a long-chain aromatic ester in a 2026 article. Such phenyl benzoate systems matter for liquid crystals and drug research, where rigid cores plus flexible chains govern packing and phase shifts. Fluorine atoms in the mix can tune polarity and stability.

The central ring tilts against its two neighbours, with the first tilt measured at 74.19 degrees in the reported structure and the second at 67.86 degrees in the same analysis. The fourteen-carbon chain stretches out straight. In the crystal, weak hydrogen bonds to oxygen and fluorine link molecules into endless chains along one axis. Two chain patterns repeat through the solid.
pmc-13330910:
Dustin C. Brown and colleagues synthesise and study paired ruthenium carbonyl complexes in a 2026 article. Such phosphine-supported pairs can catalyse small-molecule changes, from alkene shifts to hydrogenation. Fluorinated acetate bridges give the metal centres a fresh electronic setting that may tune that activity.

One trifluoroacetate-bridged compound was made by two routes and its structure was solved. Measured and computed traits are set beside three kin compounds that vary the bridge and phosphine parts. Past work links the twist angle between phosphines to alkene shift activity, though one study found no such link and pointed to electron donation instead. The new data add a fluorinated case to that debate.
pmc-13331710:
Georgios Mavrogenis and colleagues present a 2026 technique report on removing a stubborn recurrent growth from the duodenum of a 70-year-old woman. The 1.5 cm adenoma had regrown after several earlier removal attempts and sat in heavy scar tissue, which makes cutting in the thin duodenal wall risky.

Their combined method filled the bowel with salt water, used clip-and-band traction to hold the tissue taut, and applied a hook-and-drag cutting motion in the scarred areas. Working under general anesthesia with surgical backup, they removed the growth in one piece, closed the site with clips, and the patient recovered without problems. The authors suggest the mix of methods can make such fibrotic duodenal cases safer to treat.
pmc-13332010:
Dandan Li and colleagues synthesize 2026 evidence on sex differences in omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acid levels. Sex hormones may shape how the body makes these fats, but it has stayed unclear how steady any male-female gaps are across blood and tissue pools. The team searched Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register through late February 2026 for cross-sectional reports giving both sexes' levels in healthy adults with mean age up to fifty. They pooled unadjusted male-female gaps with random-effects models.

Sixty-seven publications qualified, yielding 85 comparisons and 71 fatty acid markers across plasma, red cell, and adipose tissue pools. The review matters for nutrition research, since a marker read one way in men may not read the same way in women. Clearer sex-specific norms should sharpen risk estimates and keep diet studies from mixing unlike measures.
pmc-13332710:
Yu Kuei Lin and co-authors surveyed United States adults with type 1 diabetes in 2026 on how low blood sugar still affects daily life despite modern monitoring and pump technology. Nearly everyone using continuous glucose monitors or hybrid closed-loop pumps still feels the drag of hypoglycaemia.

The analysis covered 796 adults recruited through the T1D Exchange, 23 percent using monitors alone and 77 percent using closed-loop systems, who completed a 12-domain impact questionnaire. Overall, 96 percent reported at least one life domain harmed, and 31 percent reported harm in 10 or more domains, led by sleep, leisure, emotional well-being, spontaneity, and exercise. Closed-loop users surprisingly reported worse impacts than monitor-only users in leisure, fitness, spontaneity, sex life, and work. The authors urge routine clinical attention to low-sugar burden and more work on why technology alone does not lift it.
pmc-13333110:
Bader Jad Allah and colleagues report a 2026 case in which pulmonary embolism opened the door to a paradoxical thalamic stroke through a patent foramen ovale. Paradoxical clots through that heart opening are an uncommon but important cause of acute ischemic stroke, notably when lung clots are present. The patient was a 46-year-old man with bilateral grade C3-R pulmonary embolism who then developed focal nerve deficits, including word-finding difficulty.

CT lung scans confirmed the clot, and heart ultrasound with a bubble study found a patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunting. Contrast brain MRI then showed an acute left thalamic infarct consistent with paradoxical embolic stroke, after other causes were excluded. Blood-thinner and closure decisions were made through a mixed-field process with the patient. The case urges suspicion for paradoxical embolism when clot, heart opening, and new nerve symptoms coincide.
pmc-13333410:
Elena Uyy and a team profiled the blood of diabetic foot patients in a 2026 study, looking for a pattern of damage signals rather than stray markers. Diabetic foot syndrome mixes poor circulation, chronic inflammation, and wounds that will not heal, yet its molecular footprint was ill defined.

The team used high-resolution protein measurement on plasma from diabetic patients with and without the foot syndrome, including degrees of limb ischemia. They found a set of acute-phase and stress proteins shifted together. The set includes serum amyloid A1 and A2, amyloid P component, and S100A8. It also includes defensin alpha 1B, fibrinogen chains, a heat shock protein, thymosin beta 4, fibronectin, and tenascins. In diabetic mice with ischemic wounds, blocking the danger sensor TLR4 changed several of the proteins, lowering some amyloid-linked ones. The authors frame the signature as evidence that damage-associated signals drive inflammation in this complication.
pmc-13333510:
Guangbi Fu and colleagues report a counterintuitive link in a 2026 cross-sectional study: among type 2 diabetes patients, higher vitamin B12 levels went with more diabetic retinopathy, not less. B12 shortfalls are common in diabetes and earlier work tied deficiency to eye damage, so the direction of the finding cuts against habit.

The analysis reused data on 413 adults with type 2 diabetes seen in Guangdong between December 2017 and November 2018, with eye disease graded by ophthalmologists. After adjustment for confounders, each 100-unit rise in B12 carried 49 percent higher odds of retinopathy. Patients in the top third of B12 levels, at or above 398, showed higher odds than the bottom third, at an odds ratio of 11.83. Curve modelling confirmed a straight-line relationship, and no subgroup, by sex, age, or kidney function, changed the pattern. The authors stress a snapshot cannot prove B12 causes eye disease, only that the association runs the unexpected way.
pmc-13333710:
ShangJun Li, Avijit Deb Nath, and Md. Hadi Al-amin authored a 2026 computational study of how cooperation evolves in repeated games between self-interested agents. They focus on memory-two strategies, which respond to the last two rounds of play between both sides.

Their framework joins a Q-learning multi-agent engine with Moran, Wright-Fisher, and replicator selection rules, tested across eight simulation experiments. Under standard Prisoner's Dilemma payoffs, play settled at a high cooperation rate near 0.814 on average. Memory-two strategies made up 61.0 percent of the settled population and always took over when invading a fully defecting population.
