It also audits the big pooled analyses on new type 1 and type 2 diabetes after infection. Strengths and weaknesses of the underlying studies get explicit treatment. The authors separate findings that survived scrutiny from those born of the rush, giving clinicians a steadier map of the two-way link.
pmc-13424310:
Yeseul Kim leads a nineteen-author effort to find diagnoses for children with developmental delay or intellectual disability whose standard exome sequencing came back empty. Two newer technologies were applied to 87 such children: optical genome mapping, which photographs whole chromosomes for large rearrangements, and complete long-read sequencing, which reads long DNA stretches directly.

Six children gained a pathogenic or likely pathogenic answer, four large structural changes and two single-letter changes. The mapping method added diagnoses in 4.71% of cases and the long reads in 6.98%, each catching changes the other missed. Disputed cases were checked with further sequencing, and one deep intron variant was proven harmful in a lab assay. The authors propose a stepwise diagnostic route.
pmc-13424810:
Kurniawan and colleagues present a 2026 case of a baby girl with suspected Cornelia de Lange syndrome. The condition shapes growth, the face, and the limbs before birth. A twenty-eight-year-old mother was referred during pregnancy because her baby measured small. Ultrasound showed shortened forearm bones in both arms, slow growth, and excess fluid around the baby.

An elective caesarean at thirty-seven weeks delivered a girl weighing 1,446 grams. She showed the syndrome's facial signs, including thick eyebrows, a short nose with a sunken bridge, and a long, smooth groove above the lip, alongside the arm malformations. The authors review how such limb findings on prenatal ultrasound can point to the syndrome early. They stress that its severity varies widely, so prognosis depends on which organs and symptoms a given child has.
pmc-13424910:
Kawata and colleagues examined in 2026 whether a blood protein called transthyretin, measured before surgery, predicts recurrence after curative removal of stage I to III colorectal cancer. Transthyretin reflects both nutrition and inflammation and falls quickly when health declines. The team studied 536 patients treated at one hospital from 2014 to 2024, using sex-specific cutoff values for low levels.

Patients with low transthyretin had clearly worse recurrence-free survival than those with high levels. Low levels more than doubled the risk of recurrence after other factors were counted. The signal was not equal across ages, though. It was strongest in younger patients and faded steadily in older ones, and levels ran lower in women and dropped with age. The authors say the test helps most when read with the patient's age and sex in mind.
pmc-13426210:
Dianzhi Feng and colleagues evaluated planting performance of sandy soil solidified with biopolymer and plant fiber in a 2026 environmental study. Yellow River silt mixed with 1.5 percent xanthan gum and 0.6 percent jute fiber formed the growing medium, tested at three compaction levels with oat as the indicator plant. High biopolymer content can hinder growth, so the team proposed a layered structure of residual soil, solidified soil, a seed layer, and raw soil cover.

That structure produced germination above 85 percent, with moderate compaction growing best, soil temperature between 23 and 28 degrees, and moisture holding between 10 and 20 percent across depths. The design counters surface hardening while improving water and heat movement.
pmc-13426410:
Galí and colleagues showed in 2026 that winter convection in the Labrador and Irminger Seas injects fresh surface carbon deep into the ocean, a route missing from most carbon budgets. How much carbon the deep ocean receives matters for climate accounting. Drifting robot profilers in those seas caught repeated green pigment signals a kilometer down during strong mixing winters from 2014 to 2017, evidence that surface plankton were being carried down whole.

The deep particles looked like fresh plankton material, distinct from the usual sinking crumbs. Models tied the deep supply to how much water convection stirred. In strong years, mixing delivered roughly a third to nearly half of the combined carbon supply to the deep layer, rivaling sinking itself.
pmc-13427110:
Junge and co-authors describe the first nickel complexes holding tin and lead analogues of alkynes. Alkynes are the carbon triple-bond units found all through catalysis. Their heavy versions are extremely rare for the heavier elements of group 14. Direct mixing of the tin or lead dimers with a nickel starting material failed. So the team found another route.

Instead, they generated the heavy dimers inside nickel's coordination sphere. They used a reductive group elimination, with hydrogen release from tin hydride precursors bound to the metal. Structural measurements combined with computations showed the products are best described as sigma-complexes. In those, the metal binds the single bond between the two heavy atoms side-on. The authors call this a new bonding mode in organometallic chemistry. It expands how chemists can think about activating heavy-element bonds at transition metal centers for future catalysis.
pmc-13427810:
Jinbo Luo and co-authors search, in a 2026 study, for body-clock genes that matter in fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. Daily rhythm genes help run the liver, and their disruption may feed fat buildup and inflammation. The team combined two public datasets of liver samples with a list of 248 rhythm-related genes. Statistical filtering and network analysis narrowed the field to genes that shifted together with disease.

Machine learning settled on three key genes, named SOCS2, FBXO27, and HMMR. A scoring chart built from them separated patients from controls in both datasets. Immune cell checks tied two of the genes to mast cell activity, a clue about inflammation in the liver. Drug prediction pointed to compounds that might act on these genes. The work stays computational, yet it hands wet-lab teams a short, testable list.
pmc-13427910:
Jan Sönke Englbrecht and colleagues examine how a new German rule changed brain-death testing for potential organ donors on heart-lung support. Under the update, doctors skilled with ECMO must attend breath testing, and blood-flow methods no longer count as backup tests on venoarterial ECMO.

At University Hospital Münster, every potential donor on that support from 2021 to 2024 was compared before and after the rule. Eight people were found, brain death was set in seven, and four donations went ahead, equal to 15 percent of all donors in the period. Transplant teams get a plain account of what the stricter rule costs in practice.
pmc-13428210:
Mehran Mottahedi and co-authors report, in a 2026 case, emergency heart surgery during pregnancy in a teenager with Marfan syndrome. Marfan weakens the aorta, and pregnancy adds strain that can tear or balloon it. Their patient was 19, pregnant for the first time, and 15 weeks along when palpitations led to scans. Imaging showed a giant bulge of the aortic root and upper aorta, a leaking valve, and a weakened heart pump.

After counseling on risks to mother and baby, the team replaced the root and valve in a Bentall operation without ending the pregnancy. Heavy bleeding forced a delayed closing of the chest, plus transfusion support. Scans afterward showed the new valve working and the baby still alive. She went home on day 11, a rare outcome the authors credit to close teamwork.
pmc-13428310:
Lívia Maria Martins Aragão and co-authors pool, in a 2026 review, trials of light therapy for a chronic mouth condition called oral lichen planus. The disease causes sore, sometimes ulcered patches inside the mouth and has no cure. Standard steroid treatment helps but brings side effects with long use. Photobiomodulation uses low-level light to calm tissue without drugs. The team searched seven databases through March 2025 and kept 15 clinical trials.

Combined results showed light therapy eased pain slightly more than standard drug care. Disease severity and anxiety scores did not differ clearly between approaches. Light therapy did bring higher rates of complete healing of the mouth lining and fewer returns of lesions in the erosive form. No side effects were reported for the light treatment. Stronger trials are still wanted before firm guidance follows.
pmc-13428710:
Jessica L. Fernandes and co-authors explore, in a 2026 study, how anxiety disorders pair with body chemistry during the pandemic years. More than 300 million people live with an anxiety disorder, and oxidative stress may play a part. Oxidative stress means harm from reactive molecules outruns the body's defenses. The team compared 116 adults with an anxiety diagnosis against 234 adults without one, recruited in Brazil between September 2020 and July 2021.

Standard scales scored anxiety, low mood, stress, daily rhythms, thinking, and day-to-day function. The anxiety group fared worse on all of them, with more stress and more broken daily rhythms. Blood tests showed lower total antioxidant capacity in the anxiety group at first pass. Once the team corrected for the many tests run, that blood gap no longer held up. The authors keep oxidation as a thread worth more study, while the mood and rhythm findings stand on firmer ground.
pmc-13429110:
Qiu, Wu, and Liu reviewed in 2026 urinary tract infections among hospital patients with gynaecological cancers at a hospital in Meizhou, China. Such infections can halt cancer treatment, stretch stays, and raise costs. The team pulled records for 659 patients treated in 2024, covering tumor type, treatment, and infection details, and screened the data for risk factors with layered statistics.

Qiu found cervical cancer was the largest group, followed by womb lining and ovarian cancers. Just over half the patients had a ureter stent placed, and nearly three in ten kept a urine catheter for a week or more. The infection rate was about six in a hundred patients. Three factors raised risk on their own: a catheter kept a week or longer, which roughly quadrupled the odds, obesity, and having fewer than two deliveries. The authors use the findings to target prevention at catheter care and high-risk patients.
pmc-13430710:
Yang Yang and colleagues search chrysanthemum genomes for drought tolerance, a trait that limits one of the world's most popular cut flowers as climates dry. The genetic basis and causal genes for withstanding water shortage were largely unknown.

Two hundred cut-flower lines, typed at 330,710 high-quality DNA markers, were analysed with a multi-locus genome-wide method. Single-environment work found 43 stable marker-trait links, while multi-environment work added 18 stable links and 115 interactions. Eleven nearby genes matched known drought regulators in other plants, including WRKY57, MYB121, and GH3.6, giving breeders named targets.
pmc-13430810:
Weicong Fan and Xinlei Ma study how an enzyme, NAT10, drives aggression in bowel cancer by tagging a message RNA. NAT10 adds an acetyl mark called ac4C to RNA, a change seen across tumours, and the team asks how it steers bowel cancer growth.

High NAT10 in bowel cancer was first spotted in a public gene data set, then ac4C levels were checked by dot blot and NAT10 levels by a gene test. Cell growth, spread, invasion, and movement were measured, and the link between NAT10 and SERPINA1 was checked by binding tests and a reporter assay. The work traces a chemical tag from enzyme to target to tumour behaviour.
pmc-13431010:
Mukoma and colleagues reported in 2026 on the views of biokineticists, specialists in exercise therapy, about early detection of long-term diseases in rural South Africa. Diseases such as diabetes and heart disease hit rural areas hard because care is far away and diagnosis comes late. The team interviewed ten registered biokineticists, chosen on purpose, about screening, referrals, teamwork, and barriers in the health system.

Mukoma found four linked themes: weak professional recognition, screening work already under way, community-based prevention, and structural barriers. The specialists did run checks, exercise programs, and health talks, but referrals were fragmented and few people knew their role. Cost and distance also blocked rural access. Weak links to primary care and the national insurance plan broke the chain of care. The authors call these specialists an underused resource and urge policy fixes.
pmc-13432910:
Dante DeAscanis and co-authors argued in 2026 that the gate complex in the cell core does more than pass traffic. It works as a sorting hub for the most risky DNA wounds. Where a wound sits in the core shapes how safe its repair runs. Wounds in repeat-heavy, packed, or frayed-end zones carry the gravest risk of bad swaps.

Three jobs recur across life forms. Pore zones can hold risky wounds apart from poor repair ground. Pore ties can also steer which repair path a wound takes. Loose pore parts may roam to wounds and steady the local state while blocking harmful RNA-tinged scraps. The authors sort firm proof from hints based on place or gene nudges, and they flag open puzzles on pore mix and safe versus rogue repair.
pmc-13434010:
F Tessari and N Hogan tested in 2026 what caps the force a person can push, pitting wrist stiffness against arm pose in a rig built for the task. People steer touch with ease despite slow muscles and long nerve lags. Most touch work needs force, and force may hinge on how stiff the push path can hold.

Sound adults pushed at full will on a swivel rig that let the team dial wrist torque room up or down. Two arm poses faced off as well. Force fell hard as wrist room shrank. Arm pose moved force by a hair at most. The authors read stiffness, not pose, as the wall that caps human push.
pmc-13434110:
Oriol Busquets and co-authors built a stem cell bank in 2026 of sixty-five lines. The lines share one root stock, yet each carries a picked Parkinson's fault. The bank gives the field clean, matched disease models. The brain disease kills mid-brain reward cells in slow steps. Gene-cut human stem cells offer a sharp lab for its roots.

The lines span faults in eleven genes tied to the disease, from sure causes to high-risk marks. All spring from one well-read female line and faced deep quality checks. Full gene reads showed gaps between lines stay tiny, most born of drift in dish life, not cut slips. Twin clones per fault tame that drift. The bank ships free to labs, with best-practice notes for like banks.
pmc-13434210:
Xinyue Qin and colleagues model how data valorisation, turning data into value, lifts entrepreneurial quality through innovation choices. Grounded in resource-based and dynamic-capability theories, the study asks how scenario-driven data use mediates the link between data value and venture quality.

Empirical analysis of 355 entrepreneurial firms yielded three insights. First, data valorisation significantly raised entrepreneurial quality by optimising innovation pathways. Second, it showed a straight positive link with focused innovation strategies, but a curved, concave link with dispersed innovation strategies. Digital-economy firms get a nuanced guide: data pays most when innovation stays focused, while scattering it across too many fronts yields diminishing returns.
pmc-13434810:
Faryal Chaudhry's team introduced a 2026 set of shape-based scores for drug molecules, built on the idea of telling vertices apart in a molecular graph. Making good shape scores is a hard step in linking structure to properties, and older scores based only on atom connections can blur molecules that look alike. The new scores add resolvability data, which should separate near-identical graphs more cleanly.

The team computed the scores for several cancer drugs and matched them against boiling point, molar volume, heat of vaporization, flash point, and light-bending power. Both straight-line and curved fits held up well, with curved fits most exact. Chemists get a promising new descriptor set for predicting drug properties and screening candidates.
pmc-13435910:
Burton and colleagues wrote a 2026 opinion piece on antibody drugs for severe breathing diseases. New national guidance backs one antibody drug as add-on care for COPD. That stance differs from the rules for the same drug in asthma care. Many patients carry both asthma and COPD, so the split creates confusion.

The authors run a large severe asthma service and share their audit data. They ask which clinic should own patients whose diseases overlap like this. Fair access to the drug is at stake in that decision, they argue. What counts as treatment success may also need a fresh, personal definition. They question whether the drug should stay second-line in asthma care. Patients carrying both diseases often fare worse than those with either alone.
pmc-13436110:
Plank and co-authors test whether twenty minutes of talk can help tell two easily mixed-up diagnoses apart in this 2026 proof-of-concept study. Adults seeking an autism workup often wait years, and borderline personality disorder produces overlapping social difficulties, yet no tool splits them apart. The team recorded paired talks and let machine learning read the interaction itself.

From 120 conversation partners they pulled more than 800 features on speech patterns, facial expressions during speech, movement amount, and how well partners synced. Models built on each feature family alone all beat chance. They could tell autism talks from borderline ones. Stacking the models pushed balanced accuracy to nearly 82 percent using only microphones and webcams in the setup described. The authors stress clinical testing still lies ahead, but the scale is the point: no special equipment or lengthy testing.
pmc-13436810:
Fanqi Zeng comments on new standards proposed for sociology in 2026. Three standards win praise: join theory with data, practice open science, and keep a careful line between study and politics. Zeng argues the frame still centers on Europe and North America.

Two shifts demand a wider frame, the comment holds. Knowledge making clusters in the Global North, while artificial intelligence reshapes methods everywhere. Reciprocal work with Global South partners answers both shifts at once, Zeng proposes. Shared projects can absorb AI disruption and fill data gaps together. Standards grow stronger, not weaker, when the map widens.
pmc-13437210:
Dong Kyun Kim and Joon-Yong Jung warn medical researchers that a language model's hidden thinking budget can quietly shape study results. Their 2026 piece explains test-time compute: the extra processing a model spends reasoning before it answers. Newer reasoning models may sample many answers, search through paths, check their own work, or fix early drafts, and sellers now let users set how much effort the model spends.

That setting acts like an unreported lab condition, the authors argue. Two studies testing the same model at different effort levels may reach different scores and draw rival claims about skill. Reasoning models have matched or beaten doctors on some diagnostic tasks, which raises the stakes for clean methods in medicine. Its core plea is that medical studies name and fix this budget, so results can be repeated, compared fairly, and trusted when tools move toward patient care.
pmc-13438210:
Barry Brook, John Alroy, and Jessica Jones look back on four years of Cambridge Prisms: Extinction, a journal they helped launch to give extinction research a home. The field stretches from deep fossil time to today's losses crossing into policy and the humanities. Their 2026 editorial marks the journal's first impact factor and takes stock of the early years.

Review papers drew the map first, pulling conservation biology, paleontology, modeling, policy, and social science into one conversation. The journal now sits in the top rank of its fields by citation measures, which the editors cite as proof the idea was sound. A new format, Extinction Accounts, will dissect single extinctions one by one. The editors restate a boundary: broad, yes, but extinction itself must stay central, or the journal becomes a general biodiversity outlet. Their tone is that of founders handing a young venue its second, harder assignment.
pmc-13440710:
van Loon and Kaufman tested the Dutch Meaningful Roles program, which gives primary school children purposeful classroom roles to feed autonomy, competence, and relatedness and thereby build a kinder classroom climate. The cluster randomized study covered 2,337 students and 225 teachers across 42 schools, with 20 schools delivering the program and 22 serving as controls.

Across the full sample the program produced no significant effects on the student outcomes measured at mid-year or year's end. Teachers in program schools did report stronger attitudes toward stimulating prosocial behavior and autonomy in their pupils over the year. Only in the subgroup where implementation fidelity was ideal, some 202 to 253 students, did small benefits appear, mainly at mid-year in the analysis. Those students showed better need fulfillment, classroom climate, school safety and well-being, and less antisocial behavior, making fidelity the decisive factor.
pmc-13442810:
Jing-Jing Du and colleagues design one small compound that blocks two cancer shields at once in a 2026 study. The shields are PD-L1, a brake on immune cells, and CD73, an enzyme that makes a calming compound near tumors. Computer fits, binding tests, and cell assays screened and checked the lead compound, named CP-1.

The compound blocked the PD-1 and PD-L1 grip at a dose mark of 10.27 nM in lab tests. It curbed CD73 work at a dose mark of 300.2 nM in the twin assay. In a reporter cell system that reads T-cell switch-on, CP-1 restored function at a mid dose of 0.9 micromolar strength. Docking maps show the compound sits tight in both target pockets. The authors offer CP-1 as a lead for drugs that free immunity on two fronts.
pmc-13443210:
Peirong Liu presents a 2026 education study that brings brain and eye tracking into choral conducting lessons, where assessment has long relied on instructor judgment alone. The system combines EEG spectral features with eye-movement timing in a deep learning model, tested across 48 participants and 2,847 conducting trials with rubrics from three veteran instructors.

Gesture recognition reached 94.2 percent accuracy, and transfer learning from related musical tasks cut the time to reach proficiency by 34 percent, saving about 17.8 instruction hours on average. The author stresses the controlled setting and motivated learners, so the gain counts as promising rather than guaranteed elsewhere. Music schools gain an objective practice aid, not a replacement for a teacher's ear.
pmc-13444210:
Fu and colleagues chart how disability from back pain unfolds over five years in older adults who seek primary care in the Netherlands. Their 2026 study uses the BACE-Dutch cohort of 669 adults aged 55 and over, with disability scored on a standard questionnaire at set points from six weeks to five years. A grouping method sorts patients into paths, and the team checks which starting traits predict each path.

Four paths emerged. Two groups, together about two thirds of patients, improved, most of the gain coming in the first six months. One group stayed at moderate disability, and the smallest group, about one in nine, stayed highly disabled. Starting traits tied to worse paths included older age, higher body weight, stronger pain, leg pain that radiates, past back pain, depressive symptoms, and gloomy beliefs about recovery. Clinicians could use those flags early, the authors suggest.
pmc-13445210:
Markus Schwerzmann and colleagues gather expert agreement on when doctors should start serious illness talks with adults who were born with heart defects, published in 2026. These patients face earlier heart illness and death than peers, yet talks that align care with patient values often start late. Clinicians lacked shared cues for when to begin.

An international panel of thirty-nine clinicians rated sixty-seven possible cues over three rounds, with agreement set at seventy percent or more. A second panel of patients and advocates judged the agreed cues apt. Eighteen cues stood alone as major triggers, spanning patient needs, defect traits, life events, planned procedures, and disease worsening. The list gives care teams a common starting point for timely talks.
pmc-13445410:
Xuezhen Chen and colleagues survey undergraduates on how often they learn with digital tools in AI-rich settings, and whether they feel their studies move faster for it, in a 2026 study. The authors treat felt speed, named perceived academic acceleration, as an outcome apart from grades. Confidence in one's own skill forms the proposed middle step.

Replies from four hundred twenty students fed a chain of statistical checks. More frequent tool use went with stronger confidence, and stronger confidence went with a greater sense of speed. Drive to learn may set the edge of the link, though that test fell short of firm proof. The authors stress the results show links, not cause, since all measures came from one point in time.
pmc-13445910:
Duygu Tugrul Ersak and coauthors test a 2026 study of whether adding womb-bed sutures to balloon pressure helps control bleeding in placenta previa patients. Among 118 patients treated with balloon pressure for after birth bleeding, 65 got balloon pressure alone and 53 got balloon pressure plus sutures.

Blood loss ran higher in the suture group, and stitching linked on its own to severe bleeding in tuned analysis. The authors conclude balloon pressure alone may suffice for low-risk placenta previa bleeding, with added sutures giving no shown benefit and maybe marking more severe cases. Careful patient picking matters, since groups may differ in starting risk.
pmc-13447310:
Li Bai, Shuai Luo and Qiang Wang compare treatments for pneumonia with sudden kidney injury in a 2026 records review. Both organs failing at once leaves clinicians with few proven options. Continuous blood filtering, which slowly cleans the blood, formed the base treatment, while an added anti-inflammatory drug called ulinastatin was tested for extra benefit.

One hundred patients treated between 2019 and 2024 were split by the regimen their doctors had chosen. Both groups improved on inflammation, kidney, lung and urine measures after treatment. The combined group ended with lower inflammation markers and lower waste levels in blood, plus stronger breathing measures and higher response rates overall. Since doctors chose the regimens rather than chance, the authors present the added drug as promising rather than proven.
pmc-13448110:
Ayşenur Gürgen and Mustafa Sevindik test a 2026 study of tuned king oyster mushroom extracts for cell-guard, nerve-enzyme blocker, and anti-growth action. The team weighed single-goal and multi-goal extracts across cell-guard assays, enzyme blocking, lung cancer cell tests, and plant-acid mapping.

The single-goal extract led on total cell-guard status and cancer cell blocking, with richer gallic, caffeic, and plant acids, while the multi-goal extract ran higher on oxidant status. Both extracts blocked nerve enzymes strongly and by dose. The mushroom shows healing promise, though oxidant risk demands safety checks before safe use.
pmc-13448410:
Echeverria-Ortegon and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract MMDA-08, a systematic review and meta-analysis on stereotactic radiosurgery added to dual immunotherapy in melanoma brain metastases. The question was whether adding precisely targeted radiation to nivolumab and ipilimumab improves outcomes when melanoma has spread to the brain.

Pooling time-to-event results from studies found in three databases, the combined treatment was associated with better local control at treated sites. The hazard estimate pointed to roughly thirty percent lower progression risk, though the confidence interval was wide and crossed no-effect. Overall survival showed essentially no improvement, and control of new distant brain lesions was inconsistent across studies. The authors acknowledge most included studies were retrospective, with mixed treatment timing and likely selection bias. Their conclusion is measured: radiosurgery helps control treated lesions within a multidisciplinary strategy, without a demonstrated survival benefit.
pmc-13448510:
Guo and colleagues test whether nurse led, guideline driven coordination improves clot busting care for acute ischemic stroke, where a clot blocks blood to the brain. Their 2026 study enrolls 231 patients who got the nurse coordinated pathway and compares them with 231 matched patients drawn from past records. Advanced stroke nurses ran the steps from imaging to treatment, and the team scored early recovery on a standard stroke scale at 24 hours.

Early major improvement came for about 57 percent of the coordinated group against 42 percent of controls, a clear edge. Functional independence also ran higher, near 78 percent against about 69 percent in controls, and quality of life scores were better through 90 days. Each step ran faster: imaging, vessel puncture, and drug delivery all took less time. Bleeding in the brain was less common under coordination, while deaths did not differ.
pmc-13449310:
Volker Rudat and coauthors evaluate a 2026 look-back analysis of ray therapy results in 93 patients with liver-cell cancer treated between April 2019 and August 2022. Patients got pinpoint, short-course, or standard ray therapy, split into curing intent for picked surgery-unfit patients and comfort intent for late disease.

Curing-intent living reached 100, 76, and 65 percent at one, two, and three years, against 63, 31, and 11 percent for comfort intent, with no severe acute ray reactions seen. Nearly all patients had prior treatment. Ray therapy confirms its place both as curing therapy for patients unfit for surgery and as comfort care in late disease.
pmc-13449410:
Dhaliwal and colleagues pooled in 2026 trials of the Forgotten Joint Score, a patient questionnaire used after total knee replacement. Unlike older scores, it asks how far patients can forget their artificial joint in daily life, a quality tied to satisfaction. The team searched three databases for randomised trials that reported this score alongside standard measures, covering different alignment methods, implants, and robot help.

Dhaliwal included fourteen trials with 1,244 knees. Scores ranged widely, averaging about seventy-four on the hundred-point scale. The new score showed no ceiling effect, the bunching at the top that blinds older scales, while its rivals did. It also detected real post-surgery gains where two standard scores could not. No subgroup of technique or implant stood apart, though newer work hints at an edge for one alignment style. The authors back wider use of the score in knee studies.
pmc-13449510:
Ilkay Keskinel and Müzeyyen Eryılmaz surveyed obstetricians in 2026 about how they handle asthma in pregnancy. Asthma is the most common lung condition seen in pregnancy, and the authors, a lung specialist and an internist, often met pregnant patients who had never been referred by their obstetrician. The team wanted to map referral habits and delivery choices.

A twelve-item online questionnaire went to obstetricians nationwide, with full anonymity. Forty-two responded, most of them specialists and the rest senior academics. Just over half said they always consulted a lung specialist early in pregnancy, while most favored vaginal birth for asthmatic patients. The survey exposes uneven referral practice and a need for joint care pathways.
pmc-13449810:
Nesreen Shahrour and colleagues report in 2026 two teenagers with elkonyxis. This uncommon nail defect is a punched-out depression eating into the plate from its root. A review of the scattered literature accompanies the cases. The nail's growth matrix is delicate, and both chemotherapy drugs and the acne drug isotretinoin are known to disturb its keratin production. Few reports, though, describe this exact defect in adolescents on medication.

The first patient was a seventeen-year-old girl on isotretinoin at a cumulative dose of 77 milligrams per kilogram. After acrylic nails were removed she developed painful changes, including granuloma-like tissue at one thumbnail fold and elkonyxis of the other thumb. The second case arose during infliximab treatment alongside a paradoxical psoriasis-like eruption the drug itself provoked. The authors argue clinicians should recognize medication-linked matrix injury early, since stopping or adjusting the culprit drug protects nails still forming.
pmc-13449910:
Lyu and Zhou reported in 2026 a case of dedifferentiated liposarcoma, an aggressive fat-tissue cancer, growing behind the abdomen of a 66-year-old woman. Her left abdominal mass was found by chance. Contrast scans showed several neighbouring soft-tissue lumps in the retroperitoneum, the space behind the gut lining. Some held only traces of fat and showed odd ring-shaped and nodular calcium deposits.

Lyu describes the tumors' slow-in, slow-out brightening pattern on scans, a clue the authors stress for spotting this cancer type. After surgery, marker tests found both MDM2 and CDK4 proteins in the tissue, confirming the diagnosis at the molecular level. Nine months later, scans showed the cancer had returned locally, and she began further treatment. The authors urge doctors to weigh this diagnosis for fatty abdominal masses with little fat and strange calcification, and to confirm it with gene-linked testing.
pmc-13450610:
Dan Li and co-authors describe in 2026 a gel coat for tooth implants that uses sound waves to fight germs and grow bone in sore gums. Implants often fail in people with gum disease, since germ films block early bone grip and swelling weakens the hold over time. The gel joins two flat sheet materials that make an electric field when ultrasound hits them.

Early on, that field kills germs so bone can grip the implant. Later, the gel calms immune cells by way of a signal path named JAK-STAT, which shifts the tissue toward repair. New nerves and blood vessels then guide fresh bone growth, a route the authors offer for raising implant success in gum disease.
pmc-13450710:
Yogesh Dwivedi, Kevin Prall, and Richard Shelton review in 2026 the role of tiny RNA pieces in post-traumatic stress disorder. The illness lasts for years in some people after trauma, while others recover, and the reasons are still murky. The tiny pieces, microRNAs, tune how strongly many genes are used at once.

Shifts in these pieces can change stress hormone responses, fear memory, and swelling signals in the brain. The review draws on blood and tissue work in people plus animal studies of fear and stress. The authors see the pieces as a shared thread across species and a possible base for future tests and care, while proof is still young.
pmc-13451610:
Malya Hirshkowitz and Lenna Nepomnyaschy published this public health study in 2026. It asks whether playing on high school sports teams relates to depression and anxiety in the teen years and into young adulthood. The data come from a long-running birth cohort study of urban American children, with 2,766 young adults in the analysis. The authors accounted for many family and child traits, including earlier mental health.

Frequent sports participation in adolescence went with clearly lower depression and anxiety symptoms for all teens, compared with no participation. Sustained participation also predicted a lower chance of depression in young adulthood, but only among males. The link was strongest for non-Hispanic white and Latino males and for those from better-off families. The authors suggest that keeping teens on teams may be a useful piece of mental health programs, while noting the uneven reach of the benefit.
pmc-13452210:
Chen, Keeler, and Wu wrote a 2026 commentary on why some liver cancers shrug off immune therapy. Drugs that free the immune system help only a small share of liver cancer patients. Many tumors keep immune cells locked out of the tumor area. The authors focus on a study that pins part of this lockout on one protein.

The study under review found that SMYD2, a gene-tuning protein, runs high in such tumors. Blocking SMYD2 with two test drugs slowed tumor growth in lab and animal work. The blockade also reshaped the tumor surroundings so immune cells could enter. Tumors with an overactive Wnt signal, a growth pathway, benefited most clearly. Pairing SMYD2 blockers with immune drugs is the next step proposed.
pmc-13452410:
Min Ho Ju and eight co-authors study blood transfusion in adults kept alive by a heart and lung support machine called VA ECMO. Their 2026 paper asks how much red cell blood a patient gets early on, and at what blood level the first unit is given. The work draws on a shared registry from six large hospitals in South Korea.

The registry held 2,020 adults who started the support between 2018 and 2025, and the main group kept 1,708 people still on support after one day. Among those who got blood, the team tracked the blood level just before the first unit and the pattern of later units. The study links those early patterns to death in hospital, a question with no settled answer for this machine. Its design treats timing and dose as the key signals, not transfusion alone.
pmc-13453010:
Kumar and colleagues study how planarians, small flatworms with strong powers of regrowth, fight bacteria with an old family of immune proteins. These proteins, called PGRPs, sense peptidoglycan, a key part of bacterial cell walls. The team worked with the flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea. This animal has no adaptive immune system, meaning it relies only on built in defenses. That made it a clean test of whether this protein family guards worms too.

The team found seven PGRPs in the worm, three released from cells and four fixed in cell membranes, all with the same core shape seen in other animals. The proteins cluster in the gut and skin and shift after injury. When worms met Staphylococcus aureus bacteria, each protein responded by tissue and route of infection. Silencing the genes weakened bacterial clearance. Loss of one protein, PGRP-S3, let bacteria persist and invade tissue most.
pmc-13453310:
Xingyi Li and co-authors present SpatialModal, a computational framework that combines gene expression and tissue images in spatial transcriptomics, a technique mapping gene activity in place. Existing methods struggle to integrate the two data types. Their 2026 paper uses graph learning with a two-level contrastive strategy, which trains the model by matching related representations and separating unrelated ones.

The team validated the framework on diverse datasets from human and mouse tissues. It revealed brain architecture in both species, separated distinct regions of the breast cancer microenvironment, delineated Alzheimer's disease patterns, and traced developmental trajectories in the embryonic heart. Performance stayed strong even on datasets without images, which the authors say broadens its use across platforms. Code and data are publicly archived, and the authors present the tool as a robust way to decode spatial heterogeneity in complex tissues.
pmc-13453510:
Goo, Taratula, and Taratula describe a way to steer medicine-carrying nanoparticles to lung tumors in this 2026 report. Lipid nanoparticles made mRNA medicines possible, but after injection into a vein they mostly end up in the liver. Attaching targeting molecules is the usual fix, yet it complicates manufacturing. The team instead swapped one ingredient, replacing normal cholesterol with a charged version called DC-cholesterol.

That single change raised the particle's acidity measure and made blood proteins coat it differently, recruiting vitronectin, a protein that docks onto receptors common on tumor blood vessels. Imaging showed the original particles lit up spleen and liver, while the swapped version expressed its mRNA cargo only in the lungs. Its cargo produced follistatin, which neutralized a growth signal, simultaneously slowing tumor growth and reversing wasting in their models.
pmc-13453610:
Soichiro Saeki writes a letter on scientific writing in the age of AI, answering an earlier piece by Matsubara on keeping a human voice. Saeki agrees in this 2026 letter that heavy reliance on generative AI could flatten personal tone and variety in medical papers. Writing, he argues, mirrors a scientist's judgment and professional identity, not just technique.

He widens the lens to language itself, noting worry in Japan over falling submissions to Japanese language journals. Writing first in one's own language, he argues, deepens thought and builds clear logic, while AI can help later with translation. Machine translation now gives non English papers a fair shot at being found and cited abroad. He closes with a call for clear editorial rules, honest AI use, and training in sharp revision.
pmc-13454110:
Raquel Pastor-Cisneros and six co-authors ask whether exercise still protects against death when classic heart and metabolic risks are already present. Their 2026 study follows 155,156 Mexican adults from the Mexico City Prospective Study, with a mean age of 52.3 years and 67.1 percent women. Deaths were tracked over a median of 18.26 years.

In that span 27,510 deaths were recorded, including 9,192 from cardiovascular causes. Exercisers died at lower rates across the board. The gaps ran 12 to 16 percent for all causes and 16 to 20 percent for early death, with heart death 10 to 15 percent lower. The shield held even with hypertension, diabetes, obesity, or smoking in the picture. The safest corner paired no risk factor with exercise. The authors back exercise as a broadly usable lever in high burden populations.
pmc-13454610:
Xia Li and seven colleagues reveal, in a 2026 structural study, how a bacterial anti-virus system switches on. The Kongming system guards bacteria against phage attack using a two-part effector, KomBC, built from an enzyme and a SIR2 protein. A rare signal molecule, dITP, made during infection, throws the switch.

Using structural and functional tests, the team watched the effector stack into a spiral filament of paired units, four against four. When dITP docked, the filament reshaped step by step into a new form. In that form, the SIR2 partner woke with NADase activity, an enzyme action that drains a key cell molecule. The team also flagged a residue that may grant this activity across the SIR2 family. The work lays out a distinct route by which a signal molecule arms a defense complex.
pmc-13454810:
Chiara Failla leads an twelve-author review, from 2026, of immersive virtual reality headsets as tools for autistic children and adults. Worn displays can rehearse social scenes safely and record gaze and body signals. The team searched five databases for studies from 2015 to August 2025 and kept 22 that used wearable, immersive systems.

Across those studies, headset programs appeared to help social communication, shared attention, emotion control, and daily living skills. Eye tracking and smart software added objective measures of looking and response. Yet most studies were small, few used strong randomized designs, and almost none followed users long. The authors propose a starter check of sensory, thinking, and comfort profiles before any program begins. They also call for shared outcome measures so future trials can be compared fairly.
pmc-13454910:
Qian Song and five colleagues build, in a 2026 study, machine learning models that predict leg vein clots in older patients with hip fractures. Such clots are a feared complication, and diabetes, with its clot-prone blood state, may raise the danger further. The team reviewed patients aged 65 and over admitted to Tianjin Hospital in China between 2020 and 2025.

Clots struck 66 of 400 patients during their stay. Diabetes appeared in about a third of the group and more than doubled clot odds. Seven learning methods competed, and a random forest model won with strong accuracy scores. Importance analysis ranked diabetes measures, age, albumin, a clot marker, and immobility at admission among the top signals. The authors offer the model for targeting preventive blood-thinning care at admission.
pmc-13455110:
Lova Wilske and four colleagues untangle, in a 2026 optics study, why metal nanoparticles inside nanofluidic channels can look bright, dark, or invisible under a microscope. Reports in the field had clashed, with similar particles showing opposite contrast. The team built platinum and gold nanodisks inside tiny trenches that mimic fluid channels.

Whether a disk outshone its trench or faded into it hinged on the size match between disk and trench. A simple interference model explained the flip: light scattered by the disk and by the trench walls adds or cancels. In a sealed, working channel, changing the liquid's refractive index swept a disk's appearance from dark to bright to gone. The authors predict uses in sensing volumes too small for ordinary optics to resolve, where such contrast control becomes a measurement tool.
pmc-13455210:
Arantxa Pérez-Ugarte and others tracked ten years of Plasmodium malariae cases in Barcelona in 2026, at a global health hub. Plasmodium malariae is a oft-missed malaria germ, long seen as rare and mild, yet fresh proof hints its true load is under-counted from hard tests and low-density persistence.

A look-back study at Vall d'Hebron-Drassanes Global Health Unit from June 2015 to May 2025 screened over six thousand folk for malaria. Four hundred four were positive for Plasmodium kinds, and fifty-five had P. malariae. Most cases, fifty-two of fifty-five, were found in symptom-free migrants from sub-Saharan Africa at routine checks. Germ counts were very low, at eighty per microlitre or less. Thirteen patients had lived in Spain past twelve months before diagnosis, which backs long persistence. Doctors gain proof that malariae malaria hides in symptom-free migrants for years.
pmc-13455310:
Kwaku Asah-Opoku and colleagues follow women after a first caesarean birth in Ghana in a 2026 cohort study. Caesarean rates keep rising, and while the operation saves lives, it can bring wound and other troubles in the weeks after birth. The team tracked 1,013 women who had a first caesarean at Korle Bu Teaching Hospital in Accra between January 2018 and January 2020, checking them for six weeks after delivery.

About 12.3 percent had a complication, and wound infection made up about half of those cases, at 3.2 percent of women checked. Teenage mothers faced higher risk than women aged 30 to 34. Widowed women and those with repeated abnormal discharge in pregnancy also faced higher risk. Electric cutting of fatty tissue linked with lower risk. The results give clinics a short list of women to watch closely and support after discharge.
pmc-13456910:
Zhang and colleagues use genetics to test whether small chemicals in blood, called metabolites, help cause infertility rather than merely track it. Their 2026 study applies Mendelian randomization, a method that uses gene variants as natural proxies for lifelong metabolite levels. Data came from a large metabolite gene study and from the Finnish genome project, covering 486 blood metabolites and infertility outcomes for men and women.

The screen tied 19 metabolites to male infertility, split between factors that raised risk and factors that lowered it. For female infertility, 29 metabolites showed causal links, again in both directions. A smaller set held up across all three test methods used: three metabolites for men and five for women. Checks found no sign of the bias patterns that can fake such links. The authors present the lists as leads for how infertility arises and where treatment research might aim.
pmc-13457210:
Joseph G. Letner and a large engineering team demonstrate a gentler way to place 'neural dust' sensors on the brain. These tiny wireless chips, called motes, could one day power brain-machine interfaces without wires through the scalp, yet earlier batch methods pushed whole chips into brain tissue. In their 2026 method, each mote sits on the cortical surface and only hair-thin carbon fiber electrodes, 6.8 to 8.4 micrometers wide, reach about a millimeter into the rat cortex.

The team built more than 230 stand-in motes and glued batches to insertion tools with polyethylene glycol, a material that dissolves quickly and safely in the body. Of 214 motes placed in tight 4-by-4 and 5-by-5 grids, 187, or 87 percent, inserted successfully. Implanted motes tilted about 22 degrees on average and drifted less than devices buried inside the brain in earlier work. The authors conclude the geometry is mechanically sound for future wireless interface arrays.
pmc-13457310:
Tingting Hu and colleagues mine gene-expression data for markers that link mitochondrial dynamics to Kawasaki disease, a childhood vessel inflammation that can damage coronary arteries. Mitochondria help switch on the NLRP3 inflammasome, a known driver in this illness, yet their shape-shifting behavior has barely been studied here. Their 2026 bioinformatics study combines expression analysis, machine learning, and validation data to nominate candidate biomarkers.

Three genes emerged: RAP2C, DPM2, and DDX59, all tied to inflammation pathways. Immune profiling found 13 cell types differing between patients and controls, nine correlating strongly with the candidate genes; DPM2 tracked with CD8 T cells in one direction, DDX59 in the other. Network building showed the three genes share five microRNAs and three transcription factors. Drug matching suggested valproic acid and acetaminophen as targeting agents, while a third hit was dropped for being carcinogenic. The authors stress that laboratory confirmation is still missing.
pmc-13458410:
Tarun Bhatt, Dinesh Thakur, and Zuzana Münzbergová ask whether a plant stress hormone can coach a clonal grass through repeated droughts. Single drought studies dominate the literature, yet perennial grasses cycle through dry spells and recoveries. Their 2026 growth-chamber experiment put Festuca rubra through three drought-recovery cycles, half the plants sprayed with methyl jasmonate, a signaling compound plants make.

Untreated plants faded across cycles: photosynthesis sagged, shoots dwindled, and each recovery fell shorter than the last. Hormone-treated plants held chlorophyll and photosystem efficiency steadier and bounced back consistently. Allocation shifted: droughted treated plants put more into aboveground growth and lowered their root-to-shoot ratio, reversing the drought-only habit. Statistics confirmed the treated group differed from drought-only plants across biomass and several traits. The authors frame the shift as conservative trait expression, suggesting hormone priming could aid grassland resilience as droughts repeat.
pmc-13458510:
Kamran Ahmad Awan and colleagues propose a quantum-enhanced spiking network for industrial anomaly detection in a 2026 paper. Industrial sensor networks stream varied, shifting data under tight latency limits, and spiking networks handle timing well while quantum circuits promise richer joint features. The proposed QESNN links five modules: quantum neurons for sensor fusion, entanglement-based device synchronisation, probabilistic quantum spiking for anomaly scoring, adaptive quantum learning, and decoherence management.

On the MVTec anomaly dataset, the model reached 98.7 percent accuracy with 512 logical quantum-spiking units and 3.29 seconds inference time. Removing sensor fusion dropped accuracy to 92.5 percent, while removing decoherence management dropped it to 88.9 percent, showing both modules matter. The work is a simulated architecture, so hardware quantum implementation and factory trials must still prove its speed and robustness.
pmc-13458610:
Shigeru Obayashi and colleagues pilot magnetic stimulation plus physiotherapy for stroke arm recovery in a 2026 study. Sensory ataxic hemiparesis, weakness plus lost proprioception, recovers worse than pure motor weakness, and early acute treatment options are scarce. Eighteen early acute stroke survivors were randomised to 20 minutes of repetitive peripheral magnetic stimulation plus 20 minutes of physiotherapy, or 40 minutes of physiotherapy alone.

The stimulation group received far fewer sessions, 6.5 versus 12.8 on average, yet showed greater gains in Wolf Motor Function and Fugl-Meyer arm scores after dose correction, with a robust treatment effect on Fugl-Meyer post-scores in covariance analysis. Thumb localisation showed a moderate effect size. The pilot supports feasibility and faster motor gain per session, pending larger trials with balanced dosing.
pmc-13459010:
Patrick K. Mukadi leads a large Congo-based team that measured prior mpox exposure in 2026 among people at higher risk in Kinshasa and Goma. Their blood survey enrolled 1,823 participants between April and June 2024, including sex workers, men who have sex with men, and other at-risk residents. A four-part antibody test searched for signs of earlier monkeypox virus infection.

Overall, just under three percent of participants reacted to the test, with the highest share among the broader at-risk group rather than sex workers. Age was the strongest predictor in their model, with older participants more often reactive. The findings suggest quiet exposure in Congolese cities before sustained city outbreaks, a pattern that matters for watching mpox return.
pmc-13459210:
Rui-Bin Cao and co-authors followed gene activity inside developing acorns of the oak Quercus glauca to learn how the fruit builds its two main stored compounds. Starch provides energy, while proanthocyanidins, bitter defensive chemicals, protect the seed. Their 2026 study sampled fruit at five developmental stages, measured both compounds, and sequenced active genes to find the programs controlling each substance and the candidate master switches coordinating them.

Starch climbed steadily across development, from 5.0 to 9.5 milligrams per milligram of protein in the reported measurements. The defensive compounds instead rose and fell, peaking at the middle and final stages sampled. Sequencing found 2,637 genes changing activity, mostly during the rapid growth phase, and network analysis flagged fifty hub genes. Defense genes switched on early then faded as the fruit matured, while starch genes kept rising. One regulator, QgMYB33, was linked to both programs at specific stages.
pmc-13459410:
Matsui and colleagues work out how Chaetomium fungi build chaetophenols, a varied family of aromatic compounds with possible drug value. These molecules carry a prenyl group, a small carbon chain, attached either through oxygen or directly to carbon, and that placement steers how they pair into dimers. Their 2026 study rebuilds the pathway in a host fungus and tests single steps in glassware to separate enzyme work from plain chemistry.

Enzymes make the oxygen linked forms first. The carbon linked forms then arise without any enzyme, by spontaneous reshaping of the oxygen linked starting material. The team also found a no enzyme route that builds the chaetoline skeleton, a distinct frame in this family. Fungal diversity, they show, grows from a handoff: enzymes craft a reactive starter, and ordinary chemistry multiplies it into many final shapes.
pmc-13460510:
David Kayekjian and co-authors check whether hormone therapy affects the voice after menopause in a 2026 study. Hormone replacement therapy eases menopause symptoms, and hormones can also change the voice box. Past reports disagree on whether users face more voice disorders. The team used a large shared health record network to compare users with non-users.

More than sixteen thousand users were set against a far larger group of non-users, all women aged forty to sixty. Many other hormone and throat factors were excluded. Users showed higher odds of hoarseness in the first nine months, but not of broader voice and resonance disorders. By one year, rates of both problems were low in each group and mostly alike. The authors conclude the therapy likely has no large clinical effect on the voice, and they call for more research.
pmc-13461310:
Cai and colleagues profiled in 2026 stress and burnout among schoolteachers in urbanising China, where both problems run high. Past work often treated teachers as one group, missing hidden subgroups. The team surveyed 2,769 primary and secondary teachers with standard stress and burnout inventories, then applied latent profile analysis to find subgroups and network analysis to map how symptoms connect.

Cai found two clear profiles: a low stress-burnout group and a high stress-burnout group. The symptom networks differed in shape. In the low group, physical symptoms sat at the centre of the web. In the high group, emotional exhaustion was the hub instead. The webs were tightly linked overall, which suggests stress and burnout feed each other dynamically. The authors say support should be targeted by profile, attacking the central symptom of each group rather than using one plan for all.
pmc-13461410:
Asiedu, Adjoh-Baliki, and Opoku studied in 2026 how household mental distress relates to children's thinking skills in Ghana. Evidence from poorer countries is scarce, though home wellbeing should shape learning. The team used a national panel survey spanning 2009 to 2018, covering 8,755 children aged 5 to 17 years. Thinking skills were scored from memory and pattern tests, and distress was averaged from adult household members' answers on a standard scale.

Asiedu found children in distressed households scored clearly lower on thinking tests than peers in calm homes. The gap ran from about four-tenths to half a standard unit, a large effect in education terms. It appeared in both younger children and teenagers, and grew steadily with the level of distress. Extra methods, including matching and placebo checks, backed the pattern. The authors argue child development policy should treat adult mental health at home as part of the job.
pmc-13461610:
Xu Yuan, Xiaoli Wei, and Yong Xie use a 2026 survey analysis to study how migrants from ethnic minority groups settle in psychologically within China. Many such migrants face money and social disadvantages, yet keep moving to cities, which raises a puzzle. Feeling psychologically settled means feeling at home and accepted in the new place. The team test whether close social ties, such as family and community bonds, help explain group differences.

Data came from a national 2017 survey of migrants in China. Minority migrants reported stronger psychological settling than Han migrants, and the gap held across several subgroups and under a second outcome measure. Moving with family, larger households, and active social networks each carried part of that advantage. The authors urge policy to treat ethnic communities as resources, not burdens. They suggest making family and community the main units for support, with plans fitted to each group's situation.
pmc-13461710:
Gautam and co-authors decoded a 2026 comparison of drought responses in two horsegram types, a hardy legume grown in dry regions. Circular RNAs, ring shaped RNA molecules, may help plants manage water stress, but their role in horsegram was unexplored. Plants were grown in pots under shelter and drought was imposed by withholding water.

One type, IC-94637, kept more leaf water, leaked fewer cell contents, and held more chlorophyll under drought, Gautam reports. It also rushed into seed production early, a drought escape strategy that yielded well despite later wilting. The other type closed its pores more and resisted longer stress but wilted faster under acute shortage. Transcriptome scans found circular RNA related genes switching on only in the first type, including two transporter genes that rose under drought.
pmc-13461810:
Wang and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica, a rare childhood bone disorder, in the knee of a nine-year-old boy. In this condition, cartilage at one side of a joint's growth end overgrows, forming a mass that causes pain and can deform the limb. A community hospital first read the lesion as osteochondritis dissecans, a loose cartilage problem, and prescribed two months of rest and immobilisation.

Wang describes how the pain did not ease, and referral led to the corrected diagnosis, confirmed after surgery by tissue examination. Surgeons removed the growth through an open operation. Three months later the boy walked normally, and by six months his pain had gone and knee movement was full again. At two years there was no sign of return. The authors urge doctors to weigh this rare diagnosis when a child's knee lesion mimics the commoner cartilage problem.
pmc-13461910:
Matsuda tested a 2026 rat study of gentle early exercise after a focal stroke, asking whether it protects the calf muscle that holds the body against gravity. Muscle wasting after stroke slows motor recovery, and the soleus muscle is especially vulnerable. Stroke was induced by blocking a brain artery for ninety minutes.

Forty-six male rats were split into exercise and control groups after the induced stroke for this experiment. From the next day, exercising rats ran twenty minutes daily on a treadmill at low intensity for up to twenty-eight days. Matsuda found better beam walking and neurological scores by day twenty-eight in the exercise group. Brain lesion size also shrank from day five onward, while soleus weight, fibre mix, and fibre size showed no harmful change.
pmc-13462210:
Yurong Wu and Rui Xu review, in a 2026 article, how gut microbe chemicals from a family of amino acids may drive heart and blood vessel disease. Standard risk factors predict heart disease only partly. The chemicals come from three related amino acids in protein foods: phenylalanine, tryptophan, and tyrosine. Microbes convert them into products that can help or harm vessels. Tags on tyrosine also play a part.

One product makes platelets overactive and injures heart muscle, raising the risk of heart events. The tryptophan route splits: one branch promotes artery clogging and kidney-linked vessel harm; a sister product protects vessels. Tyrosine tags draw immune cells to vessel walls and disable protective enzymes. High levels of one tag predict bad heart events. Combining several markers may sharpen prediction beyond standard models, though proof across populations is still needed. Blocking the gut routes shows promise.
pmc-13462810:
Min-Jae Kim and co-authors wrapped antiviral RNA in shell derived nanoparticles to make a sprayable crop vaccine that survives on leaves. Sprayed double stranded RNA can silence a plant virus through RNA interference, but naked RNA degrades and enters leaves poorly. In their 2026 study, RNA matching the coat protein of turnip crinkle virus was made in bacteria and complexed with chitosan tripolyphosphate particles. They were sprayed on Arabidopsis plants, with imaging and sequencing tracking delivery and protection.

Full complexing occurred at a one to one particle to RNA ratio, and the particles shielded the RNA from degrading enzymes and heat in the stability tests. Treated leaves showed stronger RNA uptake signals and more virus targeting small RNAs than naked RNA controls, evidence the cargo was processed inside plant cells. Most importantly, sprayed plants carried significantly less viral RNA systemically at seven and fourteen days.
pmc-13463010:
Min Young Kim and colleagues examined emergency nurses in 2026 to see how job stress, sleep, movement, professional identity, and colleague support shape job satisfaction. Emergency nurses face crowding, violence, and shift work, and their stress runs higher than on other wards. The study frames these links through Roy's adaptation model, which treats people as systems adjusting to stimuli.

Sleep and movement were measured with wrist sensors rather than recall alone, while identity, support, stress, and satisfaction came from surveys. The design lets the team test which factors lift or lower satisfaction once stress is in play, and whether sleep and movement carry part of that effect. Findings of this kind can guide ward leaders toward supports that keep emergency nurses steadier and less likely to quit.
pmc-13463510:
Ma and colleagues described in 2026 a new species of crocodile newt from the Xuefeng Mountains of southwestern Hunan, China. Specimens from the Huangyan area had long been filed under a known species, Tylototriton wenxianensis. Gene trees and body measurements together showed the mountain population is distinct, adding to a genus that has grown fast this century.

The authors name the animal Tylototriton sheni and give a full account of its looks, measurements, and the traits that set it apart from close kin. The genus now counts more than 50 species across Asia, with about half in China. These salamanders favor cool, moist highlands and are sensitive to habitat change, so each newly separated species matters for protection plans.
pmc-13463710:
Song and colleagues pooled in 2026 the evidence linking a simple blood index to atrial fibrillation, the common irregular heartbeat. The triglyceride-glucose index combines two routine blood values and stands in for insulin resistance, a state where the body responds poorly to insulin, which is thought to drive this heart rhythm problem. The team searched five databases to September 2025 and pooled observational studies with a random-effects model.

Song included 19 studies with over twenty-five thousand people in total. Patients with the fibrillation had clearly higher index values than those without, including in new-onset and post-surgery subgroups. Each one-unit rise in the index came with more than double the overall risk of the condition. Results varied a lot between studies, though sensitivity checks held up. The authors present the cheap index as a useful risk flag, not a diagnosis on its own.
pmc-13464010:
Djeneba Dabitao leads a large team in Mali that links sex hormones to tuberculosis outcomes. Men fall ill with active lung tuberculosis more often than women, and biology may drive part of that gap. The team followed patients with active disease, people with latent infection, and healthy peers of like ages.

Before treatment, men with active disease carried lower testosterone than the other male groups. Levels climbed back to healthy ranges by month two of treatment. Testosterone strongly foretold cure, while estradiol, the main female hormone, shifted little with disease. Hormone levels also tracked with immune signal levels in blood. The shifts hint that the disease itself bends hormone balance in men.
pmc-13464310:
Erika Zonari and colleagues built a clinical-grade method in 2026 to grow blood stem cells outside the body for gene therapy. Mobilised peripheral blood offers a rich stem source, yet standard cultures let stem function slip as cells mature too fast. Single-cell gene reading mapped how cultured cells drifted while keeping lineage fidelity in committed offspring.

Tuned cytokines, media, timing of viral gene delivery, and small molecules that block maturation programs let the team expand gene-carrying stem cells from children and adult donors. The process beat validated cord-blood methods on the same blood source, and barcode tracking proved true self-renewal divisions in culture. A trial for recessive osteopetrosis is now planned to test the process in patients.
pmc-13465010: Fuguang Zhao and eleven co-authors publish a correction to their 2025 study of artesunate in drug-resistant bladder cancer cells. The notice is a correction only. It reorders the first two authors to reflect their contributions and rewrites the statement of who did each task. It also adds a data note saying the raw data come from the first author's doctoral thesis, held at the university library in Mainz. The authors state the fix is administrative and leaves the science untouched.
pmc-13465610:
Yuanjie Cao and colleagues describe a real-world program, published in 2026, using templates printed in three dimensions for each patient to guide brachytherapy in advanced cervical cancer. Shaped from scans taken before treatment, each template steers catheters along planned paths into hard-to-reach tumor areas. The program treated 120 patients in a row at their center.

Curved channels with flexible plastic catheters handled spots that straight needles could not reach well. Target coverage met guideline aims while doses to bladder, rectum, and bowel stayed acceptable, and placement proved quick with few severe side effects during follow-up. The authors offer the workflow as a workable route for bulky or uneven tumors that standard applicators fit poorly.
pmc-13466310:
Furong Wang and colleagues model how steel fibers change the way cemented mining backfill breaks, in a 2026 simulation and testing study. Backfill made from coal waste fills mined voids, and its failure behavior matters for safety underground. Their computer model used the real size spread of waste rock and sand particles rather than uniform grains, with fibers scattered at random.

Compression tests and microscope images backed the model, which captured stress bunching inside coarse lumps and fibers bridging across cracks. A fiber share just under one percent worked best, lifting peak strength by about a quarter and leftover strength by about two fifths. Failure shifted from brittle snapping toward a slower, squeezing mode.
pmc-13466410:
Giovanni Ventura and Mariachiara Bianco introduce a special issue on two lab methods used in medicine, writing in 2026. Paired together, mass spectrometry and chromatography can reveal a molecule's makeup and measure its exact amount inside messy body material. Eight papers make up the set.

The editors read the papers along two lines. The methods serve as tools for measuring things that answer real clinic questions, and as engines for grasping disease itself. Topics include marker hunting, how the body handles drugs, and care fitted to the person. Sharpness and reach are the selling points, since body fluids mix thousands of compounds that weaker methods cannot pull apart.
pmc-13466510:
Shihao Wang and colleagues tested in 2026 whether cancer patients face extra heart-rhythm danger from extreme temperatures in China. Cold and heat already trigger heart events, and cancer raises fibrillation risk through disease and treatment, yet added vulnerability was unproven. The registry analysis covered 1,665,014 fibrillation admissions from 2014 to 2023, comparing 243,482 cancer patients with matched controls.

Extreme cold raised fibrillation admissions far more in cancer patients, at a risk ratio of 1.80 against 1.27 in matched controls. Cold accounted for most of the temperature-linked burden, at 19.7% of admissions against 10.2%, with stronger effects in men and northern China. Cancer care should thus add cold-weather warnings and monitoring, especially for northern men in winter.
pmc-13466710:
Michele Golino and a large team review two look-alike heart emergencies that strike mainly women: a torn inner wall in a heart artery and a stress-stunned heart chamber, in a 2026 article. Both can follow emotional or physical stress and share roots in adrenaline surges, fragile vessels, and hormone effects. Because their signs overlap, one is often mistaken for the other.

Newer evidence suggests the two conditions appear together more often than once thought. The authors propose a stepwise diagnostic path combining risk sorting, artery imaging, inside-the-artery pictures, and heart MRI. Care advice then branches by which condition, or which mix, the work-up finds.
pmc-13466810:
Dingpei Han and colleagues report the first use of a 5G-linked remote robotic scope to mark lung nodules before surgery, in a 2026 case report. A fifty-three-year-old man with no symptoms carried two hazy nodules in his right lung, one in the upper lobe and a smaller one below. Both needed removal, and precise marking beforehand guides the surgeon to tissue that fingers cannot feel.

Working from a remote console, the surgeon steered the robot to each spot and injected a glowing dye, with network delay holding steady at roughly twenty-odd milliseconds. Keyhole surgery then removed wedges of lung around the marked sites, guided by the glow. The case targets the gap between expert centers and distant hospitals.
pmc-13467510:
Lei Tian, Kaixin Shi, and Siyi Pan report a 2026 rat study on whether breathing bergamot essential oil can ease long-lasting fatigue from heavy exercise. The citrus oil is known for calming inflammation and oxidative stress, a form of cell damage from reactive molecules. Rats were put through a progressive exercise program and exposed daily to the oil or its main components, then tested for endurance and muscle condition.

Oil inhalation improved swimming endurance and steadied fatigue-related body measures. In the muscle itself, two inflammatory signals fell, a damage marker dropped, and a protective enzyme grew more active. The treatment also shifted markers tied to muscle repair. pmc-13490410:

pmc-13490610:

pmc-13491710:

pmc-13491810:

pmc-13491910:

pmc-13492010:
Parinaz Sedighi and others compare two gene-based drugs for spinal muscle atrophy in western Iran. pmc-13493910:

pmc-13494110:

pmc-13494410:

pmc-13495010:

pmc-13495310:

pmc-13495410:
Fredrik Folke leads a large team reporting the design of the HeartRunner trial, a 2026 randomized study in Denmark's capital region on app-summoned help for cardiac arrest outside hospital. pmc-13495510:

pmc-13498910:

pmc-13500710:

pmc-13500810:

pmc-13501810:

pmc-13504210:

pmc-13504810:

pmc-13505110:

pmc-13506110:

pmc-13507110:

pmc-13507210:

pmc-13508410:

pmc-13509410:

pmc-13509910:

pmc-13510510:

pmc-13510610:

pmc-13511210:

pmc-13513110:

pmc-13513610:

pmc-13515810:

pmc-13516210:

pmc-13516810:

pmc-13518810:

pmc-13518910:

pmc-13519010:

pmc-13519610:

pmc-13520210:

pmc-13520310:

pmc-13520410:

pmc-13520510:

pmc-13520710:

pmc-13522310:
Jie Xue and colleagues review in 2026 the anticancer potential of dipyridamole, a long-used anti-clotting and vessel-widening drug, focusing on how platelets shield travelling cancer cells and help them seed new tumours.

Mechanistic evidence remains incomplete and scattered, which the review organises by pathway. Repurposing a cheap, familiar drug appeals strongly, yet patient-level proof of anticancer benefit is still lacking.
pmc-13522410:
Klein and co-authors examine how anxiety and stigma intertwine when Australians with borderline personality disorder try to use mental health services. Their 2026 analysis draws on a 2017 national consumer survey covering 423 adults with the diagnosis, over nine tenths of them women. pmc-13522510:
Chen and a large team watch quantum effects speed up a chemical reaction inside frozen helium droplets. Nuclear quantum effects, the fuzziness of light atoms, are suspected of reshaping such ultracold chemistry, but their timing had never been resolved directly.

pmc-13523210:
Mehdi Dehghani, Farzam Sariri, and Mehrdad Zeinalian report a possible new link between an inherited enzyme disorder and recurrent anal infection in a 2026 case report. pmc-13523310:
Kelechi Ichie, Azuoma Asomugha, and Izuchukwu Okafor test whether age changes vulnerability to a Parkinson-linked weed killer in rats in a 2026 study. Tissue partly recovered after exposure stopped, yet residual changes persisted, especially in adults. Alpha-synuclein levels in brain and blood mostly did not track the damage, leading the authors to question blood levels as a stand-alone marker.
pmc-13524610:

pmc-13526110:

pmc-13526710:
Jianting Ke leads a large team in mapping how human antibodies disarm Shiga toxin. The paper is from two thousand twenty-six. pmc-13527910:
Remziye Semerci Şahin leads a seventeen-author team reporting in 2026 on ChemoNurse, a mobile guide built to help oncology nurses handle chemotherapy drugs safely at the bedside. pmc-13528010:
Alime Aksel, Yasemin Çelik, and Pakize Özyürek survey nursing students in western Türkiye about attitudes toward diabetic foot care in a 2026 study. pmc-13528710:
Aykut Kankoç and colleagues asked whether the share of lung removed in cancer surgery predicts recurrence. No pooled link survived adjustment. The authors conclude that the ratio's meaning depends on stage, cautioning against one-size volume rules.
pmc-13529610:
Mahshid Mandani, Mohammad Javanbakht, and Abolfazl Mirani harden tool steel surfaces with a welding arc in a 2026 study. The steel, H13, serves in hot, wearing jobs. pmc-13529810:
Sara Crance and four colleagues describe Arizona's rollout of a state-mandated dementia training program for memory care staff. Between August and December twenty twenty-five, 3,409 staff in varied roles completed it.

pmc-13530110:
Jianan Yang and colleagues build a 2026 risk model for lung adenocarcinoma based on genes tied to basement membranes. These thin sheets support cells and guide their growth, so changes there may shape how a tumor behaves. Single-cell and bulk gene data together mapped the tumor surroundings.

Trajectory analysis traced five cell groups at different stages of change, each with its own clinical pattern. One signaling route, called MIF, stood out as highly active in the tumor setting. Six membrane-linked genes formed a score that predicted survival on its own and may help guide choices about immune therapy.
pmc-13530710:
Nault and colleagues present in 2026, as conference paper 23, a motion analysis study of walking after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in children. pmc-13531810:
Dominik Sons and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 on a semi-automated system that finds wound infections after surgery from routine hospital data. Re-review of its false alarms uncovered ten real cases the bedside study had missed, lifting its sensitivity near ninety-five percent. The authors present it as a cheaper, deeper way for hospitals to track a costly complication.
pmc-13532910:
Ju Hyun Lee and colleagues pooled evidence on a thyroid antibody test for predicting hives treatment response. The authors present antibody status as a practical triage aid for targeted therapy.
pmc-13534410:
Elisabetta Lambertini and colleagues study in 2026 the P2X7 receptor inside the nucleus of human cartilage cells. The receptor is best known at the cell surface as a sensor of damage signals. Finding it in the nucleus hints at roles in gene control and force sensing.

pmc-13534710:
Ranjit R Desai and colleagues build in 2026 an AI-driven framework to judge local permitting processes for energy projects across the United States. Varied local rules delay projects and raise soft costs for builders. A language model tuned for energy gathered rules from nearly 300 state, county, and city documents.

pmc-13538510:

pmc-13538710:
Sunyong Park, Kwang Cheol Oh, and DaeHyun Kim compare heating fuels for Korean greenhouses across climates in a 2026 cost assessment. pmc-13539210:

pmc-13539710:
Daniel W Nebert, Zijuan Liu, and Vasilis Vasiliou argue in a 2026 invited review that self-copying lipid droplets preceded genomes at life's origin. Acting as protective capsules, they would shelter early nucleic acids and proteins while evolution proceeded inside. pmc-13539810:

pmc-13539910:

pmc-13540110:

pmc-13540510:
