pmc-13540810:

pmc-13540910:

pmc-13541610:

pmc-13542110:

pmc-13542210:

pmc-13543010:

pmc-13543610:

pmc-13543910:

pmc-13545010:

pmc-13545610:

pmc-13546710:

pmc-13547210:

pmc-13547410:

pmc-13548210:

pmc-13548710:

pmc-13548810:

pmc-13549010:

pmc-13549610:

pmc-13550110:
Arzu Dinç Yavaş and Sümeyye Akçay compare three low doses of injected ozone gas for knee osteoarthritis in forty-five patients treated weekly for three weeks. Ozone therapy is used for joint pain, but the best concentration is unsettled. Groups received the lowest, middle, or highest of three low doses.

Pain and function scores improved significantly in every group by week four, with no significant differences between doses on the main scales. The lowest-dose group did gain more walking distance than the highest-dose group, an exploratory finding the authors treat cautiously. No adverse events appeared. Given the retrospective design, they call for larger prospective trials before dose recommendations harden.
pmc-13550610:
Sara Milijanovic, leading nine colleagues, published a 2026 comparison of extracts from Gentiana dinarica, an endangered Balkan plant, grown wild and in laboratory culture. Chemical makeup can shift with growing conditions, so the team tested extracts from leaves and roots of both sources. They measured antioxidant, antibacterial, tumor-cell, and immune effects.

Cultured shoots carried more of two compound families and killed bacteria and tumor cells differently from wild leaves, while also flipping an immune response from calming to stimulating in spleen cells. Cultured roots lacked compounds found in wild roots yet scavenged free radicals most strongly. Effects could rise, fall, or vanish by source, so the authors urge detailed checks before cultured plants substitute for wild ones.
pmc-13551410:
Mathias Krogh Pedersen, leading nine colleagues, published a 2026 study checking whether two preservative allergens still appear in Danish cosmetics ten years after European regulation. Methylchloroisothiazolinone and methylisothiazolinone, known as MCI and MI, prevent spoilage in water-based products but cause contact allergy. Using a Danish product database, the team found 257 products listing them, then chemically analyzed thirty shampoos and liquid soaps.

Most identified products were shampoos and conditioners. Two of twenty-five labeled products exceeded the 15 parts per million limit for rinse-off goods, and four missed the required ratio between the two preservatives. Since allergy remains common despite rare use, the authors suggest the legal limit may still be too high to protect users.
pmc-13551510:
Rong Guo, Boyang Ni, and Megan L. Fritz published a 2026 genome-wide study of smell genes in the moth Chloridea virescens, part of the Heliothinae group. Two gene families, odorant receptors and odorant-binding proteins, let insects detect scents for feeding and mating. The team catalogued both families across the moth genome and compared them with relatives.

They found 81 receptor genes and 49 binding protein genes, the latter sorted into three types by a structural pattern. Family trees suggested gene gains and losses that may track differing scent behavior among species. A shared region in pheromone receptors looked central to detection, and the authors propose testing its function experimentally as a route to understanding ecological adaptation.
pmc-13551710:
Lihong Yang, Jing Li, Jiawei Han, and Yinan Qin published a 2026 review of nanobiosensors for detecting the vessel and brain damage behind cerebral infarction, the commonest disabling stroke. Standard tests often miss early injury or cannot monitor it in real time. Nanobiosensors use tiny materials such as nanoparticles, nanowires, and quantum dots to amplify signals from damage markers present at very low levels.

The review surveys recent platforms and their contribution to spotting neurovascular injury early. Obstacles remain: materials must prove safe in the body, production must scale reproducibly, and clinical validation is thin, with protocols and regulation lagging. The authors still see point-of-care testing and personalized stroke management as plausible futures if those gaps close.
pmc-13551810:
Jiawei Wang and eight colleagues examined, in a 2026 study, umbilical cord blood from overweight and obese pregnant women with and without gestational diabetes. Chemical marks on DNA, called methylation, may record the womb's metabolic environment and shape the baby's immune system. Samples from thirty women were scanned on a large methylation array, with immune cell shares estimated computationally and checked in a separate single-cell data set.

Tens of thousands of methylation sites differed between groups, with loss of marks predominating in the reported counts. Affected pathways covered brain development, metabolism, and immune regulation, and the diabetes group showed fewer helper T cells with more killer T cells and neutrophils. Seven sites built a classification model that separated the groups strongly within this small cohort.
pmc-13552110:
Roberto De Pascalis and co-authors published this vaccine study in 2026. It deals with Francisella tularensis, the germ that causes tularemia and was once eyed as a war weapon. No shot against it is licensed in the United States. An older live strain helps some, but it guards poorly against the most deadly type breathed in as spray.

The team gave rats one of two live shots and read blood cells soon after. Both shots raised like levels of germ-fighting proteins in the blood. Yet gene activity in the blood split the two shots apart, switching whole sets of pathways on or off. The authors argue that these early blood signs could sort strong shots from weak ones, and could help judge new shots for people without large field trials.
pmc-13552510:
Kevin Pflaum, Julia Albright, Sherry Cox, and Joe Smith published a 2026 study of a calming drug in dogs. The drug, clonidine, is used for fear-based problems in dogs. Vets see it as short-acting, yet dog data were lacking. Six lab beagles got one oral dose of the standard form. Blood levels were tracked over the hours after dosing. Sedation scores and heart rate were watched too.

Blood levels peaked at about one and a half to two hours. They fell below lab detection within four to eight hours. The half-life was short, at well under an hour in the reported figures. All dogs showed slight drops in heart rate. Sedation scores rose a bit in all dogs. No other side effects appeared at this dose, and the team calls the dose well tolerated.
pmc-13554110:
Yujin Suzuki leads an eleven-author team tracing a missing gene block that weakens a dangerous germ against two natural antibiotics in a 2026 study. The germ, Staphylococcus aureus, normally resists nisin A and bacitracin through genes called vraDEH. Some clinic strains from one family line lacked those genes and proved far easier to kill. The missing stretch also held genes for slime growth and for making a key nutrient.

Public genome banks showed every strain with this gap sat inside one branch of that family line. Matching repeat elements flanked the block, suggesting the gap arose when the repeats crossed and cut the segment out. Repeat counts and spots tracked family ties across the whole species. The authors link repeat placement to how this deletion formed.
pmc-13554610:
Zhiyuan Bai leads a six-author team charting kidney cancer in China across three decades in a 2026 study. Figures came from the Global Burden of Disease project for 1990 to 2023. In 2023 China saw more than sixty-one thousand new cases and close to twenty-two thousand deaths. New and living case counts had more than tripled since 1990.

Rates adjusted for age rose for new cases, deaths, and people living with the disease. The burden of years lost to illness, though, eased over the same span. Men carried a heavier burden than women at every step. Cases clustered in ages fifty to seventy-four, with the oldest group growing fastest. Smoking, high body mass, and a solvent exposure drove much of the blameworthy share.
pmc-13554910:
Satoshi Watanabe leads a nine-author team rescuing a side branch trapped behind a sealed stent in an eighty-seven-year-old woman in a 2026 case report. Her artery procedure had torn the vessel, causing delayed bleeding that squeezed the heart. Emergency drainage plus a covered stent sealed the leak, yet the stent blocked the neighbouring branch artery. Restoring that branch without reopening the leak was the challenge.

A high-penetration wire was threaded back through the covered stent's wall. Two balloons were then inflated together in a kissing pattern, one in each branch. Flow returned to the side branch while the seal held, with no further leakage seen. The authors offer this recrossing manoeuvre as a workable bailout for similar emergencies.
pmc-13555910:
Hande Seyithanoğlu Doğruer and Ayşe Pınar Sumer examine stuck upper canine teeth with three-dimensional scans in a 2026 study. Records held 209 impacted canines from 175 patients, mostly women, with a mean age of thirty-five. Scans mapped each tooth's position and its ties to the sinus, nasal floor, a nerve canal, and neighbouring teeth. Any linked damage was also recorded.

Most canines sat on the palate side and leaned toward the midline. About two thirds of patients had a stuck tooth on one side only. Roots reached into the sinus in a small share, and ties to the nasal floor were slightly more common in men. Linked problems appeared in about a fifth of teeth, led by inner tooth wear and root damage to side incisors.
pmc-13556010:
Sha Yu and four colleagues reported in 2026 a gene change that may explain early ovarian failure in one Han Chinese family. Premature ovarian insufficiency ends fertility early and often runs in families, with faulty DNA repair among the suspected causes. Whole-exome sequencing across three generations pointed to a frameshift change in LIG4, a gene that helps mend broken DNA strands.

The change travelled with the condition through the family and is predicted to cut off the part of the protein that partners with another repair factor. In cell tests, the altered protein was less stable and ended up in the wrong compartment, while removing LIG4 aged ovarian cells faster and weakened repair. Extra copies of the faulty gene harmed repair in a dose-dependent way. The authors propose that carrying even one damaged copy can be enough to affect the ovaries.
pmc-13557710:
Caitlin Dudzik, Andrew Chin, and Eva C. McClure counted tiger shark attacks on young albatrosses at Kure Atoll in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Each year, tiger sharks gather as albatross chicks take their first flights from the colony. The team watched through a full fledging season, logging sharks, chicks, and strikes day by day.

Shark sightings peaked about four weeks before chick numbers peaked. Risk was thus highest early in the season, when the first young birds hit the water at their most exposed. Single strikes often missed, but sharks that kept trying often won in the end. Weather and sea conditions mattered less than the calendar. The study shows how a short, set pulse of prey can shape when predators strike.
pmc-13558610:
Paolo Zamboni and co-authors chart how the neck vein pulse adapts during long spaceflight, in work from twenty twenty-six. The jugular pulse mirrors pressure in the heart's right atrium without any invasive gear. No one had mapped its full wave shape across a long mission.

Ultrasound tied to heart tracings measured the vein's width through each beat in four astronauts, with in flight data for one. After flight, the vein's average width shrank a lot in three astronauts, a change that grew over months in orbit. The pulse swing grew sharply, hinting that pressure waves travel more freely toward the brain without gravity. One astronaut showed the reverse pattern, likely a vein clot.
pmc-13558710:
Akmal Zubair and three colleagues designed in 2026, entirely by computer, an mRNA vaccine against the Merkel cell polyomavirus that causes a rare and aggressive skin cancer. The virus infects most children silently, yet in a few people it drives Merkel cell carcinoma decades later. Candidate targets were the virus's two capsid proteins and its large and small T antigens, from which the team fished out immune-triggering fragments for both helper and killer T cells.

Nineteen chosen fragments were screened for safety traits, then assembled into one construct and tested in simulation. Structure checks put most of its building blocks in allowed conformations. Docking against an immune sensor scored strongly. A hundred-nanosecond dynamics run in a virtual water box held the design stable, and codon tuning promised good production in bacterial factories. The authors state plainly that laboratory and animal experiments must come next.
pmc-13560310:
Stephanie Salia's team untangled how sex chromosomes and gonads separately shape immune replies to maternal infection during pregnancy, in a 2026 mouse study. Boys receive neurodevelopmental diagnoses up to four times as often as girls, and maternal immune activation hits male offspring harder, but the roles of chromosomes versus hormones were unclear. Using the Four Core Genotypes model, the team exposed mice early or late in gestation to a viral mimic.

Placental replies split by sex. XX females mounted balanced pro- and anti-inflammatory replies, while XY offspring and gonadal males showed relative suppression, especially late in gestation near the testosterone surge. Early exposure erased the usual social advantage of gonadal females in juveniles. The placenta emerges as a key site where timing, chromosomes, and gonadal signals jointly shape later brain and behaviour.
pmc-13560410:
Beril Nisa Yaşar and Gülhan Erkuş Küçükkelepçe measure xenophobia and intercultural sensitivity among nursing and midwifery students in Mardin, Türkiye. Their 2026 cross-sectional study surveys 472 students with proven scales for both traits, plus social-life questions. Care that fits patients' cultures is a stated goal of health training, yet how the two traits relate is unclear.

Students scored mid-range on xenophobia and fairly high on cross-culture sensitivity. The two totals, surprisingly, did not correlate. Two parts of sensitivity, a sense of duty in contact and carefulness, tracked weakly upward with xenophobia scores. Xenophobia varied a bit by age, study year, home region, and how often students mixed across cultures. Wanting to live abroad stood out as a marker of higher xenophobia. The authors conclude that sensitivity training alone will not dissolve xenophobic attitudes, so training should tackle both head-on.
pmc-13560710:
Alexander Webber and co-authors published this study in 2026. It rechecks a striking claim: that metal-rich nodules on the deep Pacific floor make oxygen in darkness. The claim rested on a link between nodule surface area and oxygen rises inside seafloor chambers.

The team redid the area measurements from chamber photos and added more chambers, plus nodule weights. With the fuller data, the link between nodule size or weight and oxygen rise vanished. Chambers with no nodules at all had also shown rising oxygen, which the nodule story cannot explain. The authors conclude the original correlation was a fluke of a small sample. They say no causal tie between nodules and the oxygen rises has been shown. The paper joins a wider debate over mining the Clarion Clipperton Zone.
pmc-13562410:
Puth and colleagues argued in 2026 that Cambodia needs coordinated One Health research to prepare for H5N1 bird flu. One Health means treating human, animal, and environmental health as one system. H5N1 keeps spreading in Cambodia, with most human cases tied to sick or dead poultry contact.

They propose a multi-sector H5N1 research working group for the country. Such a group would bring together outbreak, clinical, gene, and behaviour data into shared tracking. Ongoing spread, they argue, reflects unresolved gaps between veterinary, medical, and environment agencies. Cambodia's case fatality share has been high, and mild infections likely go undetected under current event-based tracking. The authors frame coordination as the missing step between data collection and real readiness for animal-borne disease threats.
pmc-13562710:
Huifang Xian leads a large team linking shaky DNA copying to the gut inflammation of inflammatory bowel disease. Patients show extra genome instability, but whether that damage drives the disease was unknown. Their 2026 work homes in on RADX, a protein that guards stalled copying forks and restrains a partner called RAD51. Mice missing RADX developed far worse induced colitis, and transplant experiments pinned the effect on macrophages, the immune cells that patrol the gut wall.

The mechanism is a contest for loose single-stranded DNA. Without RADX, that DNA piles up and a sensor named IFI16 grabs it, switching on inflammatory signalling and an inflammasome that pumps out IL-1β. Two variants found in bowel disease patients lowered RADX levels and showed the same signature. A drug blocking RAD51 eased colitis in normal and deficient mice alike. The authors nominate calming replication stress as a fresh treatment strategy.
pmc-13563310:
Hatem Mousa Taha and three co-authors tell, in a 2026 case report, of liver injury in a young man who dosed himself with muscle-building drugs. He took oral oxymetholone daily and a second drug, testosterone, by injection each week. Such steroids are known to block bile flow and raise bilirubin, the yellow pigment in blood. He presented about a month after starting.

His bilirubin peaked at 24.6 mg/dL, while core liver measures such as clotting and albumin stayed preserved. Scans showed no blocked bile ducts, and tests ruled out viral and autoimmune causes. Both drugs were stopped, and bile aids plus itch care were given. The bilirubin fell by about seven tenths in four weeks and by over nine tenths in eight. His itch cleared and daily life returned. The authors name oxymetholone as chief suspect but note that two drugs at once blur the attribution.
pmc-13563710:
Shuyu Li and six colleagues review antibody-drug conjugates, guided missiles that pair a targeting antibody with a poison payload, and their reshaping of breast cancer care. These drugs reach from late rescue therapy into curative-intent treatment. The 2026 review sorts their targets in a new way, by biology. Some antigens drive the cancer, others mark its tissue lineage or fetal past, and still others sit in the tissue around the tumour. Successive drug generations are traced alongside.

Toxicity management and the ways tumours resist these agents get treatment, since payloads harm healthy tissue and cancers learn to shrug off the warhead. Looking ahead, the authors call for bispecific versions that grip two targets, pairings with immune therapy, and biomarker-guided ordering of drugs across a patient's course. The review aims to give clinicians a map of the field, from mechanism to the sequencing choices that decide outcomes.
pmc-13563810:
Qingyuan Xu and ten colleagues build a rheumatoid arthritis model from patterns of programmed cell death, then single out one gene as a lever. Cell death routines shape diseases, and their joint role in this autoimmune joint disease was unmapped. Their 2026 team fed eighteen death patterns into a model built from 113 combinations of twelve learning algorithms, checking it across eight gene datasets, single-cell and bulk. Two patient clusters emerged, differing in macrophage numbers, which flagged those immune cells as central.

One gene, S100A9, stood out in the model. In arthritic mice it ran high in joint lining tissue alongside aggressive M1-type macrophages. Silencing it with a gene snippet cooled joint inflammation, spared cartilage, cut the M1 shift, and raised a survival protein in cartilage cells. Dish experiments agreed. The authors propose blocking S100A9 as a treatment aimed at the macrophage engine of the disease.
pmc-13563910:
Wen Deng and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective study of people with chronic hepatitis B who had cleared the surface antigen after pegylated interferon treatment at Beijing Ditan Hospital. The group followed 390 non-cirrhotic patients treated between 2008 and 2023 and tracked how their surface antibody levels rose, stayed steady, or fell over time.

Only four liver-related adverse events occurred during follow-up, and all four were in patients whose antibody levels were declining. Falling levels also showed a modest link with higher event risk in the analysis. Readers get a clear cohort design, grouped antibody levels, and a cautious suggestion that a downward trend after clearance deserves closer monitoring.
pmc-13565310:
Costanza Franchini and six co-authors track anxiety and depression in students after brief counseling, in a paper dated 2026. University students are prone to both conditions, yet proof for short psychodynamic counseling is thin. Their program ran just four weekly sessions, with one follow-up meeting three months later.

The study followed 108 students, most in their early twenties, and measured symptoms at four points: first visit, treatment start, treatment end, and three months on. Standard Beck scales tracked both depression and anxiety. Symptoms held steady during the wait before treatment, setting a baseline for judging change. The design tests whether gains arrive during the brief course and whether they last. The title's hint is that change takes time.
pmc-13566410:
Cristina Marrocchio, Michele Ligorio, and Nicola Sverzellati review, in a 2026 article, precision imaging for interstitial lung diseases, a family of more than two hundred disorders that scar lung tissue. Standard high-resolution scans and breathing tests can miss mild change and depend heavily on patient effort. The authors survey computer-measured scan features and AI tools instead.

Newer programs now beat older ones at diagnosis, measuring disease extent, and predicting outlook, with better agreement between readers. Routine clinical use still lags behind the published results. Radiologists get a balanced view of tools that could standardize lung assessment once proof and workflow hurdles are cleared.
pmc-13567310:
Shinichi Nakagawa and Akira Yamamoto present a 2026 study on how a persona prompt skews AI estimates of food nutrition. Vision-language models judge nutrients from meal photos, and portion size is their biggest error source. The team tested six models from three vendors on Japanese cafeteria dishes and American meal photos. Each model judged photos with no persona, with a Japanese-dietitian persona, or with an American-dietitian persona.

The Japanese-dietitian prompt lowered energy estimates in every model and both data sets. It left the balance of nutrients roughly intact. The American persona shifted estimates only slightly and inconsistently. A direct order to assume smaller portions behaved differently and less steadily. The persona's effect cut error on the small-portion Japanese set but was neutral on the larger-portion American one. The authors warn the trick needs testing on each target domain before use.
pmc-13570010:
Noemie Gross, Anna Molto, and Renaud Felten review spondyloarthritis in the span near birth. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-six. This joint ill oft hits women of child age, yet facts on birth odds, course, and post-birth flare stay split. The team searched a large base with no date cap for English and French work.

Of more than three hundred finds, near half fit. Some women show low egg store and long wait to conceive, in part from pain drugs. Course in birth is most oft firm for one form and mixed for the spine form. Birth fates are most oft sound, with small lifts in early birth risk. Post-birth flares are common.
pmc-13571410:
Anna Jones and co-authors report real-world results for a targeted ovarian cancer drug in a 2026 study. Mirvetuximab soravtansine is an antibody-drug conjugate that homes to folate receptor alpha, found on most ovarian cancers, and delivers its payload there. Trials showed good results under strict entry rules. This review covered sixty-six patients treated for recurrent disease at one university cancer center and its partner hospital between late 2022 and spring 2025.

Survival with and without progression was charted, and side effects catalogued from the records. Adjusted models hunted for traits tied to longer survival. Real-world cohorts include the frailer patients trials skip, so these numbers tell oncologists what to expect in the clinic.
pmc-13571610:
Tamer Othman and Ibrahim Aldoss present a 2026 literature review of immune therapies for adult B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Returned or resistant disease once left adults with poor odds, and transplant in a second remission was the only path to cure. Three immune treatments changed that picture in the last decade.

The review sums the key trials of blinatumomab, inotuzumab ozogamicin, and CAR T-cell therapy, weighing benefit and side effects for each. All three improved outcomes in returned disease while cutting reliance on harsh chemotherapy, and all are moving into first-line care. The authors add their own guidance on fitting the drugs into practice.
pmc-13571710:
Almeida Souto and co-authors tracked a 2026 cohort of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension patients diagnosed before and after a pulmonary embolism response team was set up. This form of high lung pressure can often be cured, yet diagnosis often drags for years after the first clot. The single centre study took place in a general hospital in Argentina.

Among twenty-nine patients, those diagnosed after the team launched reached diagnosis far sooner after their pulmonary embolism. Median time fell from 256 weeks to forty-three weeks, a sharp drop Almeida Souto reports. The later group also trended toward lower risk levels at diagnosis, though that gap was not significant. The authors credit team follow-up after embolism for catching the condition beyond specialist centres.
pmc-13572210:
Haruna Iriyama and thirteen colleagues published a case report in two thousand twenty-six on treating two diseases at once. A forty-two-year-old woman had triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive type. She was also taking an immune-suppressing antibody for multiple sclerosis, which raised doubts about adding a second immune drug.

After consulting a nerve specialist, the team gave standard chemotherapy plus the immune drug pembrolizumab before surgery. Scans then showed a complete response. Surgery removed part of the breast, and lab checks confirmed no cancer remained. Her multiple sclerosis has not flared so far. The authors present the case as evidence the combination can be given safely in such patients.
pmc-13572310:
Joshua Reitz and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, whether diabetes and weight-loss drugs that mimic the gut hormone GLP-1, including newer dual-action versions, could also treat alcohol use disorder. Heavy drinking and metabolic dysfunction overlap heavily and together drive liver disease, making a shared treatment attractive.

The drugs are already approved for diabetes and obesity and are under study for fatty liver disease. Evidence so far suggests they may cut alcohol intake while steadying metabolism, with the dual approach possibly filling a gap for people carrying both problems. The authors map ongoing trials and open questions, framing addiction care around metabolic circuits rather than willpower alone.
pmc-13572510:
Minjae Cho and Chuangchuang Sun present a 2026 method that helps robot learning agents pick up new tasks fast. Agents that learn by trial and error often forget old skills when a new task clashes with them. The method stacks three levels: one reads the task, one finds broad moves that fit many tasks, and one picks fine actions.

The broad moves, called macro-actions, are found on their own and stripped of task-specific detail, so they can be reused across jobs. They point the fine policy toward goal states and ease the load on each level. Each level trains on its own tailored scheme, which keeps the stack stable. On the MetaWorld test suite, the method learned with fewer trials and won more often than past leaders. Code is posted online for others to check.
pmc-13575210:
Avinash Singh and Mohammad Soyeb Alam model ground sinking above an underground copper mine in India in a 2026 study. Mining out ore can let the surface sag, harming buildings, land, and safety. The mine uses blast-hole stoping, a method that removes ore in large blocks.

Their three-dimensional computer model built in faults, rock joints, and the planned mining sequence. It simulated the untouched state, current workings, and forecasts five and ten years ahead. Rock properties were tuned by matching the model back against observed behaviour, which sharpened the predictions. Output maps show strain and movement in all directions for each phase. The authors present the approach as a practical route to site-specific subsidence forecasts for working mines.
pmc-13575310:
Jing Zhou and ten co-authors published a plant pathology study in twenty twenty-six on how the late blight pathogen rewires potato defenses from inside the nucleus. A Phytophthora effector protein was already known to target the potato transcription factor StKNOX3. The new work shows what that factor normally partners with.

StKNOX3 binds two enzymes that tag histone proteins, stabilizing them in the nucleus, and the trio together helps the pathogen infect. The effector strengthens the trio's assembly, raising the histone tag and switching defense genes off. Genome-wide binding and expression maps showed the factor repressing genes for cell walls, hormones, and stress responses. The study exposes an epigenetic lever the pathogen pulls to disarm its host.
pmc-13576210:
Lorena Maestre and colleagues assembled an antibody panel that identifies blood-cell types across many animal species, a long-standing gap in veterinary medicine. Immunohistochemistry is essential for diagnosing animal cancers, but few antibodies cross-react reliably beyond humans. Their 2026 study tested 69 antibodies on lymph node, spleen, and bursa tissue from 13 domestic and 28 exotic or wild species, plus human lymph node.

Sixteen antibodies survived the screen, covering T cells, B cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells through markers including CD3, CD4, CD8, CD20, and CD163. The panel enables precise detection of the main haematopoietic populations in diverse species. The authors present it as a versatile tool for veterinary diagnosis and research, and a step toward diagnostic accuracy in animals matching human standards.
pmc-13576310:
Linlin Wang leads a 2026 study building a prediction score for a common snag in heart stent work: loss of blood flow in a side branch after the main vessel is stented. Forked artery narrowings are frequent and tricky to treat. Records covered 830 patients treated at one Chinese hospital between 2022 and 2023.

Four factors made the final score: age, plaque position on the same side as the branch, flow grade before stenting, and a heart stress blood marker. The chart-style model scored 0.651 on the accuracy curve, easing to 0.641 after internal correction, a modest level of discrimination. Calibration checks showed predictions matched observed rates well. The authors offer the score for sorting risk before the procedure and choosing a strategy, while noting its limits.
pmc-13577110:
Se Kye Kim and co-authors present a 2025 journal article comparing the genomes of a reference Escherichia coli strain and its plasmid-cured offspring. The parent strain, ATCC 43894, is a standard for studying enterohemorrhagic disease, and the offspring lost its large virulence plasmid. Researchers had assumed the pair share one genetic background apart from that plasmid.

Whole genome reads showed the expected plasmid difference, plus surprises. The parent carried extra mutations, including a 2.5-thousand-letter deletion that removed two acid resistance genes and a third gene. The authors warn that the cured strain is not a clean match, which matters for past and future experiments.
pmc-13577510:
Mengyao Li, Yongchun Guo, and Su Wang study walls printed from titanium alloy with a mixed laser and arc heat source, in a paper from 2026. The method lays molten wire layer by layer to build metal parts. Settings like laser power shape the wall's grain and strength. The team varied the settings and then pulled, struck, and probed the printed walls.

More laser power widened each layer and shrank its height. At a middle power, strength ran near even in both test directions. That balance matters for parts loaded from many sides. The top of each wall proved harder than its middle. Break stretch also stayed close across directions at the sweet setting. The authors give builders a tested base for printing flight-grade titanium parts.
pmc-13578110:
Marta Skowron Volponi and co-authors test whether a moth that looks like a hornet also copies the hornet's scent. The hornet clearwing moth resembles the European hornet in shape and sound, which may keep predators away. The team asks whether the match extends to the waxy chemicals, called cuticular hydrocarbons, that coat both insects. These chemicals often serve as recognition cues between insects.

Comparing the chemical profiles, the authors find no sign of copying. The moth carries about six times less of the coating than the hornet, and it lacks alkenes entirely, a class of these compounds that predators use to spot prey. Related moth families show very different profiles as well. The authors suggest the moth's thin, simple coating may instead make it harder to detect at all. They note that trials with real predators are still needed to test that idea.
pmc-13578710:
Miao Xie and colleagues present a two unit tracked machine that bolts mine tunnel roofs in tight spaces, in a 2026 study. Most coal tunnels in China are too narrow for big automated rigs, so roof supports still go in by hand after cutting, a slow and risky order. Their machine links two tracked units in a line, with four crawler sets in total, so it fits slim tunnels.

The hard part is keeping the front and rear units moving as one. A physics model of track and ground contact feeds a motion simulator, run under matched, squeezed, and pulling modes. A full size prototype matched the simulator within a few percent on average. The authors offer the design as a safer path for the bulk of tunnels that big rigs cannot enter.
pmc-13579410:
Yayu Wang and Lily Yeh Jan lay out a lab protocol for testing chloride channels inside cell compartments called endolysosomes, published in two thousand twenty-six. These channels sit in the walls of tiny sacs deep in the cell, so they are hard to reach with standard tools. The patch-clamp method reads the small electric currents that pass through a channel.

The steps start with swelling the sacs so they grow large enough to work on. Next the team makes fine glass pipettes, polishes their tips with heat, and frees the swollen sacs by cutting them out. They then form a tight seal on a sac and open it into a whole-sac recording mode. The protocol points readers to the pair's earlier work for full detail on use.
pmc-13579610: Jacq, Picherit, and Bas reported in twenty twenty-six how a printed jaw model helped a girl aged nine and her folks grasp her jaw cyst care. She has a rare inborn ill that oft brings such cysts, and two large ones showed on scans. Talk and scan pics left the folks unsure, with a tongue gap in the way. A life-size print with cysts in color made the plan plain at last. The folks then gave clear consent and kept the checks.
pmc-13580310:
Danielle Naegeli and co-authors present a 2026 study of how culture shapes the silent gestures people invent to say who did what to whom. Two groups played a gesture game in pairs, passing their signs down a chain: Dutch players and Balinese players. pmc-13586910:

pmc-13587910:

pmc-13588910:

pmc-13589710:

pmc-13593310:

pmc-13594010:

pmc-13595010:

pmc-13595610:

pmc-13596010:

pmc-13596110:

pmc-13598110:

pmc-13598410:

pmc-13599710:

pmc-13600810:

pmc-13601310:

pmc-13601510:

pmc-13601910:

pmc-13609610:

pmc-13612710:

pmc-13614810:

pmc-13616610:

pmc-13616710:

pmc-13617210:

pmc-13617610:
Ellen Oudkerk-Sodia and eight colleagues introduce nanolipogels, hybrid lipid and polymer nanoparticles designed to deliver messenger RNA into cells more cheaply and gently than current carriers. Existing carriers can need costly multi-step synthesis, vary between batches, or provoke immune reactions. The particles start from a synthetic phospholipid made in a single enzyme-catalyzed step, then polymerize in water in one pot.

Two partner chemicals give either a permanently charged or an acidity-responsive shell for loading the negatively charged RNA. The finished particles measure under two hundred nanometers, capture more than three quarters of their RNA cargo, and release it steadily over seven days in cell-like conditions. In human and mouse cell tests they kept cells alive as well as optimized liposome controls and far better than a common commercial reagent. One version produced about eleven times more reporter protein than the commercial reagent.
pmc-13618910:
Michelle Heck and five colleagues test whether human sign-trackers, people whose eyes lock onto reward-predicting cues rather than the reward's location, also show stronger bias toward alcohol. Animal work links sign-tracking to addiction vulnerability, and this Pavlovian framework is being translated to human eye-movement tasks. One hundred fifty-nine volunteers completed the cue task, an alcohol attention test, and questionnaires on drinking and personality.

Sign-trackers showed a tendency toward greater alcohol bias than intermediate responders, though not compared with goal-trackers. No differences in alcohol consumption appeared across the behavioral profiles, failing to replicate earlier reports. The authors blame a weak setup: fictitious token rewards and a passive task likely muted the effects. They call the support for the theory preliminary and small. They urge better paradigms with more engaging stimuli and real rewards before the framework's boundary conditions can be judged.
pmc-13619010:
Longfang Chen and co-authors published a 2026 study of a rare gene variant that fires up a cell-death pathway and drives a Still-like inflammatory illness in one family line. Still disease is a whole-body inflammatory illness of the immune system, with no clear root. Family clusters of it had not been reported. This family broke that pattern: three people in three generations bore the illness.

Gene sequencing of the family found one variant, in RIPK3, a gene that runs a bursting form of cell death called necroptosis. Laboratory tests showed the variant is a gain of function: the gene product works too hard and clumps, firing the death pathway. Blood readings from one patient showed two inflammatory pathways lit high and two inflammatory markers raised. A drug blocking it damped the inflammation. The team presents the case as an inherited form of the illness.
pmc-13620210:
Julieta Benítez-Malvido and seven colleagues studied how gut worms affect male and female spur-thighed tortoises differently across southern Spain. The team sampled tortoises in five land types, from Mediterranean shrubland to farm fields and pine plantations, and measured body traits, growth, and the roundworm communities living in each animal's hindgut.

Worm burden and spread looked similar in both sexes, yet the costs split sharply. Heavier infestation tracked with smaller size and slower growth only in males, while females kept growing steadily. Females also carried more diverse and evenly spread worm communities, arranged in networks that suggest easier transmission among them. Infestation fell in both sexes where unproductive land made up more of the landscape. The authors argue tortoise conservation should plan for the sexes separately, since females seem harder for worms to drag down.
pmc-13623010:
Tadahiko Ohtsuru leads a study comparing one injection against three injections of a freeze-dried platelet concentrate for knee osteoarthritis, the wear-and-tear joint disease that limits walking in older adults. The concentrate, made from the patient's own blood platelets, aims to ease pain without surgery. Earlier work tested single shots only, so the benefit of repeat dosing was unknown.

Patients chose their schedule with their doctors: 1,054 took one injection and 317 took three. Both groups reported pain and function on a standard knee survey over twelve months. The three-injection group edged ahead in the first month, and the edge lasted longer for early-stage disease but not for advanced disease. After adjusting for patient differences, the repeat group more often met the bar for a real clinical response at one year. Side effects per injection were similar, which the authors read as acceptable safety.
pmc-13623110:
Lele Chang and co-authors test a drug pairing for recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer that carries a PIK3CA mutation, a common gene change. The pairing combines immune checkpoint inhibitors, which release the immune system to attack tumours, with tyrosine kinase inhibitors, which block growth signals. No standard approach targets this mutation group.

Data came from two prospective trials plus hospital records, covering fifty-five patients. Twenty-seven received the pairing and twenty-eight received doctor-chosen conventional treatment. Tumours shrank in most patients on the pairing, more often than on conventional care, and the time before cancer grew again more than doubled. Survival leaned the same way without reaching statistical ground. Side effects such as high blood pressure, rash, and thyroid problems were more common with the pairing but were managed, with no treatment-related deaths. The authors call the results a strong case for larger trials.
pmc-13623810:
Samir J Sheth and colleagues published a 2026 follow-up survey of long-term results after a sixty-day nerve stimulation treatment for chronic low back pain. Thin wires placed through the skin deliver stimulation to nerves in the lower back for two months, then come out. Earlier studies hinted the relief could outlast the treatment, and this survey tests that idea in everyday practice.

The survey reached 602 patients who had responded to the treatment, at times ranging from six months to over five years later. Four in five had needed no follow-up procedure such as nerve burning, a permanent implant, or surgery. Among those who avoided further procedures, most reported pain relief or clear gains in quality of life, movement, mood, or sleep. People hoping to dodge surgery or a permanent implant succeeded. The authors present the short treatment as a possible long-lasting, low-risk option.
pmc-13623910:
Fan Zhu and three colleagues published a cohort study in two thousand twenty-six on uric acid swings in kidney disease. Average uric acid is a known risk marker, but how much it bounces between visits may signal instability. Its link to near-term death in chronic kidney disease was unclear.

Over ten thousand five hundred adults with at least three uric acid readings were followed. Higher swing levels tracked with clearly higher short-term mortality, even after full adjustment. No such link appeared for kidney events or heart events. Most deaths came within ninety days, and the signal vanished beyond that window. A large intensive care database reproduced the short-term pattern. The authors read variability as a warning sign of fragile health.
pmc-13624310:
Jiaxin Li leads a study of how colorectal tumours recruit neutrophils and turn their web-like DNA traps into a spreading weapon. The white cells cast these traps, called NETs, to catch microbes, yet inside tumours the same webs help cancer cells spread. The team focused on a tumour protein, MIIP, known to restrain cancer growth.

In patient tissue, tumours low in MIIP carried neutrophil loads and traps, and patients showed more distant spread and fared worse. In dish experiments, fluid from low-MIIP cancer cells drew neutrophils and triggered trap release, and the traps made the cancer cells more mobile. Tracing the wiring, MIIP binds a signalling protein and damps a pathway that produces a neutrophil-summoning chemical. In a mouse model of liver spread, a trap-dissolving enzyme slowed metastasis, and restoring MIIP strengthened that effect. The authors propose the traps as a treatment target.
pmc-13625210:
Lucas Berger Munaro, Daniel J Tolhurst, and Jessica E Rutkoski show how a profit-based scorecard can steer wheat breeding in Illinois. Breeders often pick lines by yield alone, yet farmers earn from test weight and maturity too. The team priced each trait from the region's cropping system and grain price rules. They then fed a genomic model data on 2,995 wheat lines, five traits, and twelve test settings from 2022 to 2024.

The combined multi-trait model explained most inherited variation and predicted breeding values with high accuracy. Picking by the profit index returned about 120 dollars per hectare, beating both a single-trait model and yield-only picking, which returned under 100 dollars. Trait links also shifted with setting, a warning that one fixed recipe fits poorly.
pmc-13628910:
Guo Guo and two colleagues reviewed the evidence linking childhood adversity to disturbances of oxytocin, the hormone system tied to bonding and stress control, in people with severe mental illness. Their 2026 systematic review gathered fourteen studies with 5,624 participants, covering schizophrenia, major depression, and bipolar disorder.

Nearly every study found that patients carried heavier childhood adversity scores than healthy controls. In most studies that measured it, oxytocin levels ran lower in the patient groups. Variants of the oxytocin receptor gene also nudged risk in both directions, some raising susceptibility and others appearing protective. The authors read the pattern as support for oxytocin signalling as one biological bridge between early trauma and later severe illness.
pmc-13629410:
Azhar Hussain, Jack Moniot, Mohsena Sumaya, and David Hughes wrote this review, published in 2026. It explains how multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow, damages the kidneys. Kidney failure is one of the disease's most serious complications, and it worsens the outlook when missed.

The review walks through the ways the cancer hurts kidneys. Rogue proteins made by the cancer can clog the kidney's filters or settle along its membranes. High blood calcium, common when tumors eat into bone, adds a third route. Diagnosis rests on blood and urine tests, protein measures, scans, and marrow checks. Treatment must control the cancer while sparing the kidneys, with adjusted drug doses and careful hydration. The authors give pharmacists a central role in guarding kidney safety.
pmc-13629510:
Morgan Walker and Chris Baugh walk through a case of hemolytic anemia in an emergency department, where the urgent work up led to a hidden cause. This anemia, from red cell breakdown inside or outside vessels, is rare but can kill. The report came out in twenty twenty-six.

A man in his sixties came in with two weeks of breathlessness on effort and fatigue, with steady vital signs. Lab work showed low hemoglobin and red cell share, plus marks of cell breakdown. Careful lab checks, early specialist input, and a wide list of possible causes were key. The root cause proved to be diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, a blood cancer.
pmc-13629810:
Kah Shuen Thong and ten colleagues audited the use of antibacterial drugs among COVID-19 patients in northern Malaysia. The audit covered ten government hospitals. Their study sampled 476 patients from over nineteen thousand hospital stays. The span ran from February 2020 to December 2021.

Just over a third of patients got these drugs. Most were ordered on suspicion, not on proven infection. Drugs against fungi were rare. Resistant germs appeared in under a tenth of cultured patients. Drug use rose and fell with surges in admissions. Severe disease drove the ordering. So did conditions like diabetes and chronic lung or kidney disease. The authors argue that pandemic ordering followed severity more than proof. They recommend stewardship ready for outbreaks, plus steady tracking of use.
pmc-13630810:
Rex Fernando and two colleagues present a protocol that lets a network of computers reach agreement. It works even when up to a third of the members are malicious. Each member sends remarkably little data. Such Byzantine agreement underpins blockchains and secure joint computation. The challenge is scaling it without exotic assumptions.

Earlier efficient designs leaned on strong, non-standard proof systems. The new protocol rests only on the Learning With Errors assumption. That is a standard, well-studied hardness base for post-quantum cryptography. It still needs a public key setup and a shared reference string. Its route runs through a generic use of batched argument systems. The authors frame the result as scalable agreement on conservative foundations.
pmc-13631310:
Ricardo Gutiérrez and colleagues traced a decade of drug-proof gene spread in Costa Rica. NDM enzymes destroy nearly all beta-lactam drugs, even last-resort ones, yet national foothold routes were poorly mapped. Their study merged ten years of country-wide survey work with genome reads from first sighting in 2014 through a COVID-era hospital outbreak.

Hundreds of NDM samples spread across wards, with leading hosts shifting from 2020 onward. A single hospital outbreak hit 247 patients with a 51 percent death rate. Genome analysis showed both plasmid and chromosome homes, with a world-shared plasmid backbone splitting into multi-drug-proof giant plasmids. Gutiérrez and colleagues urge steady genomic watch.
pmc-13632510:
Emily Gracey, Sylvie Kandel, and Jed Lampe build a lab model for newborn drug safety in a 2026 paper. Testing drugs in newborns is ethically hard, and no good human cell model existed for how a newborn liver handles drugs. Babies in intensive care often get many drugs off-label, raising the risk of harm. The team grew liver-like cells from adult stem cells that keep a fetal enzyme active.

The cells showed a mix of fetal markers and newborn drug-handling genes, distinct from mature liver cells. They processed a key hormone and a common sedative in the same pattern as newborn liver cells. The model also responded to drug interaction tests, offering a platform for this fragile group.
pmc-13632810:
Anja I. Frei and seven colleagues published this 2026 study of aggression and violence against intensive care nurses in Basel. They reviewed nurses' reports from 2023 and 2024 at a large university hospital unit. Aggression meant hostile behavior or resistance without intent to harm. Violence covered verbal, physical, or sexual acts meant to threaten or harm. The team counted incidents and searched for signs that an incident would repeat.

Across more than two thousand shifts, three hundred eight incidents were reported, touching about one shift in seven. Three quarters involved violence, and patients caused nearly all of them. Repeat incidents happened in about one quarter of cases. Longer stays and a first incident built on aggression or verbal violence predicted repeats. Nurses were rarely hurt themselves, yet patients often suffered complications from sedation or restraints used in response. The study names early warning signs units can act on.
pmc-13642110:
Shuang Xu and three colleagues present a neural network method, IPGRU, for filling in missing values in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Dropout events hide many true gene readings, which biases later analysis and weakens conclusions about cell identity.

The method recasts the filling task as many single-gene predictions handled by parallel gated recurrent units, a network type that learns patterns across genes. Tests showed accurate recovery of missing values and cleaner data for cell clustering and for tracing how cells change type over time. The authors offer the approach as a sturdy preprocessing step for single-cell studies and precision medicine.
pmc-13643810:
Maria-Eleni Parakatselaki and four colleagues present a 2026 study showing that fathers' mitochondrial DNA leaking into offspring is genetically controlled in fruit flies. Mitochondrial DNA is normally inherited only from the mother, and leakage has been treated as random error.

Crossing several Drosophila simulans lines with a sister species, the team measured mixed mitochondrial types in hybrids. Leakage levels ran consistently within families, repeated across experiments, and ran higher in males than females. Estimated heritability was high, and wild-derived lines varied more than inbred stocks. The authors argue leakage is a governed trait with possible long-term effects on mitochondrial genome stability.
pmc-13645610:
Wei Yang and three colleagues build a risk model for thyroid nodules whose needle test results land in an uncertain middle class, Bethesda category III. Their records cover ninety-three patients treated at a Jiangsu hospital between July 2020 and June 2025, all of whom later had surgery. The model combines two antibody blood tests, an ultrasound grading system, and a gene mutation test. A chart called a nomogram turns the model into individual risk estimates.

Most nodules in this surgical group proved cancerous, which reflects the high-risk setting. The gene test alone was the strongest single predictor, yet the combined model scored clearly better than any one part. The authors say the combined approach can help doctors sort patients before surgery and choose who needs an operation most. They also note the model was checked only within the same patient group, so wider testing is still needed.
pmc-13645810:
Yalong Deng and twelve colleagues examine a membrane protein called CYBRD1 in the deadliest form of ovarian cancer, in a 2026 study. Spread of the disease and resistance to the drug cisplatin drive most deaths in high-grade serous ovarian cancer. Earlier work by the group had flagged this protein as a marker of poor outlook. Here they test what the protein actually does in cancer cells and mice.

Resistant cancer cells carried more of the protein than sensitive ones. Blocking it restored drug sensitivity and slowed growth, movement, and invasion. The protein switched on a growth pathway through a partner called JAK2, and one precise chemical tag on the protein proved essential for that link. In mice, pairing the blockade with cisplatin cut spread. The authors propose drug pairs aimed at this protein for patients whose cancers resist standard treatment.
pmc-13646110:
Li Wang and three colleagues report the survival of a woman poisoned by the weed killer paraquat while thirty-two weeks pregnant, a situation that usually ends in death. Paraquat has no specific antidote, and dose decides most outcomes. Her blood carried very high levels of estrogen-related hormone, which the team links with protection of her lungs, the organ paraquat harms worst. An emergency cesarean delivery was performed, and the baby also survived.

Lab testing found a trace of paraquat in the newborn's blood, firm proof that the poison crossed the placenta. That finding explains the baby's short-lived liver and kidney problems. Care also covered mouth ulcers and psychological support for the mother. The authors present the case as a call for paired mother-and-baby poison testing in future cases, and as a hint that pregnancy hormones may blunt this poison's worst effects.
pmc-13647310:
Mikhail V. Polynski and four colleagues shine visible light on a family of ring compounds to see how side groups steer their shape-shifting. These styryl pyrimidinones can flip between two forms under light, and the flipped forms of some members already show antifungal promise. The team watched the flips live with a light-equipped magnetic resonance setup. Computer calculations then explained why members behaved so differently.

Compounds carrying electron-donating side groups flipped most eagerly, reaching up to ninety-five percent conversion within a few hours under modest light. The flipped forms lasted from hours to days before relaxing back. A competing reaction that welds two molecules together also varied with the side groups. One computed measure of light absorption predicted performance best. The authors offer the scaffold as a tunable light switch for chemistry and drug design, with a cheap screening workflow attached.
pmc-13648310:
David Reissig and a large group for the IVDK network analyze in 2026 how often workers become allergic to parts of epoxy resin systems. These are the strong glues and coatings used in construction and manufacturing. They drew on patch test records from German dermatology departments spanning 2008 to 2022.

Allergy to the main resin ingredient fell over the period, from about four percent to under three percent of tested workers with job-related skin disease. Risk ran highest in plastics processors, bricklayers, and painters. Many resin-allergic patients also reacted to thinners and hardeners in the same products. Testing the main resin alone would have missed hundreds of sensitized workers. The authors urge fuller test panels and tighter workplace exposure control.
pmc-13649410:
Yaqian Li and three colleagues introduce a set of 11 studies on helpful microbes and the chemicals they make for plant health. Farms need to keep yields high while using less chemical fertiliser and spray. Helpful microbes can feed plants, fight germs, and ease stress, but their effects hinge on the crop, the local microbes, and the weather.

The studies span new microbe finds, how they attack plant germs, and how products are made and tested in fields. One predatory bacterium harmed a wilt fungus and shielded cotton seedlings. A newfound species stopped a sugarcane smut fungus from mating by making its surroundings acidic. The editors stress that names alone do not predict what a microbe will do.
pmc-13650010:
Guixiang He and six colleagues look for what travels with anxiety in people who have just been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease and have not yet started medication. Anxiety is common early in the illness, yet its companions among the non-motor symptoms, the problems beyond movement, are poorly mapped in untreated patients.

The study compared 284 newly diagnosed patients with 147 healthy controls of similar age and sex. Anxiety was far more common in the patient group, and the mental-worry form dominated. After accounting for movement severity and background factors, stronger depressive symptoms went with more anxiety, while better sleep and a sharper sense of smell went with less. Movement problems themselves showed no clear link once other factors were counted. The authors suggest routine checks of mood, sleep, and smell at diagnosis to flag patients who may need support.
pmc-13650710:
Misa Iizawa and two colleagues, publishing in 2026, investigate a curious pattern in plasma medicine, where ionized gas is used on living cells. Treated cells first lose viability, then recover beyond expectations with longer waiting, and the team asked whether undamaged neighbors share in the effect through signals released into their shared liquid.

Liquid that had bathed plasma-treated mouse tumor cells was transferred onto untreated cells of the same types. The borrowed liquid significantly raised viability in the fresh cells, in a pattern resembling hormesis, where a mild stress provokes a strengthening response. Two different plasma sources produced the same behavior, which argues against a quirk of one device. The authors conclude that soluble factors shed by damaged cells drive a bystander effect that helps explain the rise-and-fall shape of plasma responses, a finding that matters for dosing plasma therapies.
pmc-13650810:
Anubhav Dhull and co-authors build a targeted drug carrier that delivers an old drug to the immune cells that drive endometriosis, in a 2026 study. In this disease, tissue like the womb lining grows where it should not, causing pain and swelling. A class of macrophages marked by a receptor called FRβ helps the growths spread, and the drug niclosamide can blunt those cells, but it dissolves poorly in water.

The team attached niclosamide to a branched carrier decorated with a sugar-like tag that the receptor grabs. In mice with the disease, the carrier piled up in the growths and entered the target cells, with little lodging in other organs. One dose cut the number and size of growths and sharply eased the animals' pain sensitivity two weeks later. The authors offer the design as a hormone-free, cell-targeted route for treatment.
pmc-13651610:
Yu-Cheng Liu and eight colleagues review tandem catalysts that turn carbon dioxide into multi-carbon products with renewable electricity. Copper is uniquely able to stitch carbon atoms together into fuels and chemicals, yet it wastes effort on hydrogen and spreads its output across many products. It fades at industrial current levels, largely because carbon monoxide coverage on its surface runs short.

A tandem layout stations a carbon monoxide factory next door: silver-copper interfaces, single-atom alloys, or isolated-atom sites on copper generate the monoxide and hand it to copper coupling sites. The review organizes recent work in flow cells and near-industrial conditions around four design levers. The levers are how much monoxide is made, how it travels, how the interface is structured, and which coupling paths it feeds. Done well, the division of labor sharpens selectivity toward the valuable two-carbon-and-beyond products.
pmc-13651910:
Laura Taylor and four co-authors present a 2026 study on which light level suits eye-function testing in inherited retinal disease. Microperimetry maps sensitivity point by point across the retina and now serves as a trial outcome measure. It can run in dim light or in near darkness after adaptation. The team compared both modes in twenty-nine patients and forty healthy controls, with repeat dark-mode tests in a subset.

Dim-light testing proved reliable and sensitive in both groups. Dark-mode testing in patients failed often: many tests were thrown out as unreliable, and results hit the floor of the scale. It also showed no edge in accuracy over dim-light testing. The authors recommend dim-light microperimetry as the stable choice for trials. Whether dark-mode testing helps in very early disease, where dim-light vision is still near normal, remains an open question.
pmc-13659210:
Mariam Sherif and Panayoti Bachkangi argue in a 2026 review that midlife female sexual health care suffers a systemic failure, where market and digital pressures shortcut careful diagnosis. Menopause affects physical, mental, and sexual well-being, and wider access to information has reduced stigma. Yet it has also let marketing and social media set expectations before the consultation begins. The authors trace how time pressure and mental shortcuts then push clinicians toward quick fixes, notably premature testosterone therapy for low sexual desire.

Drawing on evidence about clinical inertia, market forces in health, and diagnostic bias, they show how many-sided symptoms get reduced to simple hormonal stories. That bypasses full mind-and-body assessment. They warn, via the mid-urethral tape controversy, that unchecked diagnostic expansion could trigger blunt regulatory overcorrection that restricts even proven therapies.
pmc-13682410:
Yolanda Lau and co-authors study how often people with multiple sclerosis in England develop diabetes, and what that pairing does to their outcomes, in a cohort study from 2026. The data came from linked primary care, hospital, and death records. Each person with the nerve disease was matched with up to ten people without it.

Over an average of fifteen years of follow-up, diabetes arose more often in the sclerosis group. Once diabetes appeared, hospital visits rose sharply and stays grew much longer, a median of twelve days against two. Death risk also climbed by a strong margin. Similar patterns held in the comparison group. The authors argue that preventing diabetes matters greatly in this population.
pmc-13685610:
Younis and co-authors test whether the actin shell of white blood cells is needed for them to stick to vessel walls. Sticking is the first key step when these cells leave the blood to fight inflammation. Prior work in cystic fibrosis cells hinted the shell helps integrins cluster.

The team used a drug that blocks actin growth in human and mouse monocytes. The drug cut shell formation after chemokine signals, yet left total actin levels in place. Early results split two jobs: the shell seems needed for integrin clustering, not for switching integrins on. That split may explain sticking defects in some diseases.
pmc-13689010:
Francesca Cristetti and co-authors track the microbes at work in wine made from Nebbiolo grapes grown in several vineyards, in work published in 2026. The fungi and bacteria on grapes at harvest help drive the ferment and shape the wine. They also carry marks of the place the grapes grew. Whether those marks last once a commercial starter yeast is added was not clear.

The team charted fungi and bacteria through the ferments and paired those charts with measures of the wine's chemistry and aroma. The mix of microbes shifted over time in clear patterns of succession, and marks tied to region held up from start to finish. The wines' chemical and aroma profiles differed in step with the microbes. The findings show that a sense of place stays readable in the wine even when a starter is used.
pmc-13689210:
Harrison and a team including Pandher hunt Ontario soils for bacteria that feed common bean plants in twenty twenty-six. Beans partner with root bacteria that pull nitrogen from the air, but the pairing often underperforms. The team trapped over two hundred strains from farm soils using four bean types. Full genomes sorted the catch into eleven species, two of them new.

Soil source shaped which species turned up far more than bean type did. One new species fixed nitrogen best on average in greenhouse tests. Strong strains appeared across several species, though. The genome library now stands ready for picking starter strains tuned to Ontario fields, the authors say.
pmc-1852410:
Gupta, Stamatoyannopoulos, Bailey, and co-authors explain Tomtom, a method for comparing DNA motifs. Motifs are short patterns in DNA that proteins recognise when switching genes on or off. New patterns are found often, but judging whether one matches a known pattern needs sound statistics.

Tomtom measures how similar two motifs are and tests whether that likeness could arise by chance. Users can search a database of known motifs with a newly found one as the query. Reliable matching helps researchers name the proteins likely to bind a site and plan follow-up tests.
pmc-2707010:
Liberati, Altman, Tetzlaff, and co-authors explain the PRISMA Statement for reporting systematic reviews. Systematic reviews and pooled analyses judge whether health care treatments work. Readers can only trust such reviews if the methods are reported fully and clearly.

This long companion paper explains each item of the updated PRISMA guidance and gives examples. It shows authors what to report about searching, selecting, and combining studies. Journals worldwide adopted PRISMA, so the explanation shaped how evidence summaries in medicine are written and checked to this day.  Checklists in the paper show authors exactly which details reviewers will seek.
pmc-2816710:
Larsen, Vogensen, van den Berg, and co-authors compare gut microbes in adults with type 2 diabetes and adults without it. Recent evidence had suggested a link between metabolic disease and the bacterial populations living in the gut. Whether diabetic gut communities truly differ was still an open question.

The team assessed the make-up of intestinal microbes in both groups as controls against each other. Finding real differences would support the idea that gut bacteria play a role in diabetes, not merely reflect diet or drugs. The study helped launch wide interest in microbe-based diabetes care.
pmc-2946910:
Huynh-Thu, Irrthum, Wehenkel, and co-authors test tree-based methods for inferring gene regulatory networks from expression data. Rebuilding the wiring diagram of which genes control which others is a pressing open problem in systems biology. Gene expression measurements from microarrays offer clues, but the network itself stays hidden.

The authors assess their approach within a community benchmarking effort for reverse engineering networks. Tree-based methods treat each gene's activity as something to predict from other genes. Knowing which methods recover real networks best guides the search for drug targets and disease mechanisms.
pmc-3965110:
Finn, Bateman, Clements, and their co-authors described Pfam in 2014, a database of protein families. A protein family is a set of proteins that share a common part and often a common job. Pfam is served from sites in the United Kingdom and the United States and is used worldwide.

Release twenty-seven held close to fifteen thousand entries, each checked by hand by an expert. Users can search a new protein sequence and learn which known families it belongs to. That match gives a strong first clue to what the protein does, which guides lab work on genes, disease, and drug targets.
pmc-4402510:
Ritchie, Phipson, Wu, and their co-authors described limma for RNA sequencing in 2015. Limma is an R and Bioconductor package that gives an integrated way to analyze gene expression data. It handles complex study designs and borrows information across genes to cope with small sample sizes.

The paper shows how limma's methods, first built for microarrays, were extended to RNA-seq counts. Borrowing strength across genes steadies results when only a few samples exist. That is the common case in costly patient studies. Limma became a core tool for finding genes that differ between healthy and diseased tissue or before and after treatment.
pmc-4614810:
Eren, Esen, Quince, and their team presented Anvi'o in 2015, a platform for omics data. High-throughput sequencing and related technologies were transforming studies of natural microbial communities. Full study of microbial lifestyles needs ways to organize and view genetic information interactively.

Anvi'o lets users explore genomes and metagenomes together with their own added data layers. Researchers can inspect, compare, and share analyses through a visual interface. That interactivity helps teams form and test ideas while looking at the data, not after. The platform supports work on how microbes live, interact, and drive processes in oceans, soils, and hosts.
pmc-5715110:
Peter Bankhead and colleagues introduced QuPath, open source software for digital pathology, in 2017. Pathologists now scan whole slides into large digital images, but viewing and measuring them by hand is slow. A free, flexible tool was missing for research use.

QuPath lets users view whole slides, mark regions, and train the software to find tumor areas. It can measure large numbers of cells in a batch and export the results for statistics. Because the code is open, labs can adapt it and share methods. The tool helped make digital slide analysis routine in cancer research.
pmc-6004510:
Godfred Boateng, Torsten Neilands, Edward Frongillo, and colleagues wrote best practices for building survey scales in 2018. Health and social research depends on scales that measure attitudes, symptoms, and behaviors. Building a sound scale takes many steps that are easy to do badly.

The primer walks through item writing, expert review, pilot testing, and checks for structure and reliability. It explains common traps, such as too few items or samples that are too narrow. Each stage has clear advice a small team can follow. New researchers can use it to produce measures that others can trust and reuse.
pmc-8012210:
Jeffrey Granja and co-authors introduced ArchR in 2021, a software package for studying how accessible the DNA is inside single cells. Methods that profile chromatin accessibility one cell at a time can map the regulatory landscape of a tissue in fine detail. The data grew faster than the tools, leaving researchers with huge datasets and slow ways to read them.

ArchR was built to handle that scale, pulling biological meaning out of accessibility data quickly and in an integrated workflow. The authors describe how the package aligns cells, finds marker regions, and links them to genes. For labs working with single-cell regulatory data, it turned an unwieldy analysis into a manageable routine.
podcast-joerogan-ZkJjqGLoK10:
Director Neill Blomkamp talks about eternal recurrence in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Blomkamp, who made District 9, is known for gritty science fiction with real-world teeth. Here the subject is an old idea: that time loops, and all things return exactly as they were.

He and Rogan test the notion against his films, his life, and the strange pull of patterns that repeat. Rogan asks whether living as if life recurs would change how a person acts. The segment is the filmmaker's most philosophical hour on the show, a break from craft talk into the deep structure of time itself.
podmore-newer-spiritualism-1910:
Frank Podmore took his keen tools to fresh marvels in The Newer Spiritualism, his book of 1910. New stars of the dark room then drew crowds with forms that took shape and things that moved at no touch. Podmore sat, watched, and checked each claim as he had for years. His finds are grave for the faith's fans.

Trick ropes, hid hands, and stage craft fill his case. He grants the odd scrap, yet finds the new wave weak. The book is the best bust of its age. It ends his long watch with a sigh.
pound-provenca-1910:
Provença, published in Boston in 1910, is Pound's early collection of translations and originals drawn from the troubadours of medieval Provence. Before Pound was a modernist leader, he was a scholar of these twelfth-century love poets, and this book shows why.

He renders Arnaut Daniel, Bertran de Born, and others into English verse that strains to keep their music and difficulty. Original poems in the same manner stand beside the translations. Pound believed modern poetry had to pass through this medieval discipline. The book is the record of that apprenticeship, and of a young poet finding his masters.
price-cost-indexes-from-1875-to-1989-est:
Michael S. Hart, the founder of Project Gutenberg, wrote this essay on price and cost indexes running from 1875 toward 2010. First published as a column called the Rate of Change of the Rate of Change in the Electronic Journal of Virtual Culture and expanded for release in November 1993. His opening paradox sets the argument: computers look like an incredible bargain. They are twice the bargain they seem, because the dollars themselves keep shrinking.

Hart works the arithmetic of his own drives, where each year's gear is cheaper and faster than the last. His tables of indexes turn anecdote into series, an early attempt to measure deflation in information goods. The essay is also a Gutenberg manifesto in disguise: if computing power halves in price while doubling in worth, free digital libraries become inevitable.
prize-money-sailor-s-knots-part-10:
W. W. Jacobs placed a comic tale from his Sailors' Knots of 1909 in the tap-room of the Cauliflower inn at Claybury, where an old man holds court by the fire. Snow lies on the fields, horses steam outside, and talk turns to how Claybury men amuse themselves.

The old man rails against Bob Pretty, whom he calls the biggest rascal and poacher in the village, and hints at a story about a prize hamper. Jacobs builds the tale from pub talk, sly tricks, and village rivalry. Readers get his well-known blend of dry humour and seaside character.
promptuarium-alchemiae-das-ist-vornehmer: A German title page, worn and hard to read in the scan, announces a storehouse of writings on the stone of the wise. The book gathers choice pieces by learned philosophers, with skilled alchemist hand-work and tested ways of making medicines. Its sources come from animals, plants, minerals, and metals, offered as needful to alchemists and doctors alike. The page carries a grant of privilege and names its publisher, the front door of an old German work on hidden arts.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-158-19:
Charivaria fronts Punch for March 10, 1920, in volume 158, gathering short comic notes on Ireland, Poland, boxing, and dentistry. The London weekly kept its peacetime readers supplied with a joke for nearly every headline.

London is said to hold one hundred thousand more people than New York, though they are only just living. A warning that the Home Rule Bill would cause friction in Ireland is met with sorrow at the very thought. Poland's finance minister asks for a loan of three thousand million francs, Dempsey faces a draft-dodging charge, and gold in the mouth is declared out of date.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: A publisher's header alone introduces the tenth volume of The Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte in the pages shown. Title, author, and language are its whole news: the work is Constant's, and the text is English. No preface explains this part, no contents page maps it, and no opening line of narrative is printed. What Constant recounts in volume ten, and at what point of Napoleon's life it begins, are facts that these opening pages do not supply.
ricardo-high-price-bullion-1810:
David Ricardo made his name with The High Price of Bullion, a pamphlet of 1810. Britain's Bank Restriction had freed the Bank of England from paying gold for notes. Bullion prices rose, and Ricardo blamed paper money issued in excess. His tract applies the quantity theory of money to the case.

Too many notes, he argues, cheapen each one against gold and goods. The cure was a return to cash payments under strict rule. The pamphlet's clarity won him a hearing among statesmen and thinkers. It set the terms of the great bullion debate. Economists still cite it as a model pamphlet. Ricardo the theorist enters history here.
rilke-malte-laurids-brigge-1910:
Die Aufzeichnungen des Malte Laurids Brigge, Rilke's only novel, appeared in German in 1910. The text here is the German original; the first English translation came in 1930 and is not in the public domain. Malte, a young Danish nobleman without money, lives in a cheap Paris room and writes what he sees.

Fear walks with him through hospitals, crowds, and streets full of the poor. Memories of his childhood home in Denmark break into the Paris notes without warning. Rilke breaks the tale into fragments, more diary than plot. The book became the first great German novel of modern city consciousness. Its dread and pity still feel new.
robinson-town-down-the-river-1910:
Edwin Arlington Robinson published The Town Down the River in 1910, returning to the Tilbury Town portraits that had made his reputation. By then Robinson had won powerful admirers, including President Theodore Roosevelt, who found him a government job. This volume is the essential middle collection of his career.
